stories.Headline: Experts attribute bank and Microsoft 365 outages to concentrated technology dependencies as Mullin suggests AI role
stories.Summary:
Major technology outages struck several large United States institutions in mid November 2026, and experts say heavy reliance on a small number of technology providers is the common thread behind them. On November 16, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a software bug in its own systems caused disruptions at major United States banks, and the bug affected Chase as well as other banks that make transactions with it. Microsoft's 365 suite of apps, including Outlook, went down for millions of users around the world for nearly 36 hours after a server update. Separately, the United States Federal Aviation Administration cancelled more than 10,000 flights following a router update, although a United States Transport Secretary confirmed there was no link to artificial intelligence in that case.

The Microsoft 365 outage reached users in 74 countries, including the Indian airlines IndiGo and SpiceJet, which shows how far a single provider's failure can spread. Mayank Morya, chief technology officer at Mitigata, told India Today Tech that the underlying vulnerability across these incidents is a concentration of technology dependencies. Saakar S Yadav, founder of Lexlegis.ai, added that reliance on a few cloud, identity and payment providers raises the risk of disruption. Mandar Patil, executive vice president at Cyble, warned that artificial intelligence may let hackers carry out autonomous attacks by interacting with APIs and enterprise applications, and Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported that hackers built an AI framework to scan security patches for flaws in older software versions and then execute attacks.

Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin suggested that artificial intelligence may have played a role in the high profile disruptions of the past week, saying a technology expert had raised the idea that superintelligence could be responsible for the outages. The technology coverage, however, reported that the Transport Secretary ruled out an AI link to the flight cancellations, and it described the bank and Microsoft failures as stemming from a software bug and a server update. Experts quoted in that coverage pointed instead to concentration of dependencies, and they warned that AI is speeding up the discovery of flaws, producing what one called a vulnpocalypse in which rushed fixes break systems. Patil said companies need gradual rollouts, innovative deployments, operational tests and versioning of changes so that threats can be fixed without breaking systems.

Sunil Peter, vice president at Maveric Systems, recommended that companies develop and test independent fallback mechanisms so that operations can continue even if primary systems fail. Peter also stressed the need for crisis management communication, saying IT, incident response and executive leadership teams should coordinate through independent encrypted messaging tools. Professor Himanshu Joshi from IMI Delhi noted that technical failures are not new, but their impact is greater now because systems are interconnected. The articles do not say what the companies or agencies plan to do next beyond these expert recommendations.

stories.Headline: Saskatchewan introduces bill letting courts remove deceptive AI content and award victims compensation
stories.Summary:
Saskatchewan's provincial government introduced The Prevention of Deceptive Artificial Intelligence Act on Nov. 17, 2026, according to a Digital Journal report by Jennifer Kervin published Nov. 18, 2026. The bill targets deceptive content made or altered using AI or similar technology, including fake images, videos and audio recordings. It covers AI-generated impersonations that make someone appear to say or do something they did not. The government says Saskatchewan is the first Canadian jurisdiction to establish a legislative framework specifically addressing deceptive AI-generated and manipulated content. The Canadian Press report by Jeremy Simes, first published Nov. 17, 2026, says the province introduced the bill Tuesday.

The bill would let courts order the removal of manipulative AI content and allow victims to seek compensation. Those who fall prey to deepfakes could seek legal action against creators of deceptive content in audio or visual formats. If creators are found guilty, they would provide compensation to the victim at a cost determined by the court. The court could also force creators to destroy the content and remove it from platforms. The bill would require disclosure of AI use in certain circumstances, and it says if content could reasonably be believed as authentic, creators would need to put clear markings that it is AI.

The legislation would amend existing provincial laws covering elections, consumer protection and privacy, and Saskatchewan says the changes would help those laws keep up with the technology. Minister of Justice and Attorney General Tim McLeod, K.C., said when used responsibly artificial intelligence can create great opportunity. McLeod said when used for deceptive purposes it can damage reputations, undermine public trust and create economic hardship. He told reporters the province wants a framework to hold accountable individuals who use AI inappropriately to deceive or target vulnerable individuals. McLeod said it would be up to policing agencies to enforce the law, and the legislation would also apply to AI-generated intimate images.

Prabha Ramaswamy, CEO of the Saskatchewan Chamber of Commerce, said Saskatchewan businesses depend on trust and the legislation protects that trust by giving employers, entrepreneurs and customers real tools to fight AI-enabled fraud and impersonation. Ramaswamy said the Chamber looks forward to working with the government on making sure the legislation is practical and clear for all businesses. Rod McKendrick, social prescribing coordinator with Saskatchewan Seniors Mechanism, said the legislation should provide a stop gap for older adults to make a more informed decision and give authorities tools to hold accountable those who generate and use deceptive AI. McKendrick told reporters there have been cases of grandparents receiving calls from scammers pretending to be grandchildren and asking for money. He said this is happening but authorities are unable to do anything because there is no legislation.

McLeod said Saskatchewan is the first Canadian jurisdiction to provide a legislative framework on deceptive AI, and the government's press release says the province is the first Canadian jurisdiction to establish a legislative framework specifically addressing deceptive AI-generated and manipulated content. Alberta has passed legislation that prohibits the creation of fake AI content of politicians and targets the use of AI for spreading intimate images. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe previously raised concerns about online deepfakes using his likeness to promote cryptocurrency schemes. Asked if the province is working to find out who is responsible for those deepfakes, McLeod said he can't speak to any details. The bill does not limit the use of AI for other content, including parody or satire, as long as it is not manipulative.

McLeod said if the bill passes, people would still be able to express themselves freely using the technology, and if it is all meant in good fun and not rising to the level of defamation or deception, those purposes will continue to be used safely. For now, the bill has only had its first reading, and the announcement does not indicate when the law could take effect. The province has not explained when the disclosure requirements would apply or who would have to comply. The government also has not explained who would have to make those disclosures or what information they would have to provide. The Canadian Press report was first published Nov. 17, 2026.

stories.Headline: Apple develops autonomous AI agent to rival OpenAI and Anthropic
stories.Summary:
Apple is reportedly developing an advanced AI agent to rival OpenAI, Anthropic and Grok, according to reports from November 20, 2026. This new system would autonomously control devices, use various apps, browse the web and write code for the user. Bloomberg first reported the news on Thursday after spotting fresh job postings on the official website of the tech giant. The company aims to create a tool that can navigate computers just like a capable person would do. This development follows a record breaking Wall Street debut by the AI firm Anthropic on that same Thursday.

The agent will run on Apple operating systems and compete with Meta's Muse, ChatGPT's Dots and Claude Code. It requires a senior engineering manager to build a proactive assistant that can use terminals, services and APIs. The system must plan multi step tasks and coordinate specialized sub agents to complete complex goals for the user. In macOS 27.3, Apple will increase authorization steps from four to 14 for third party AI agents. These changes to Full Disk Access were introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta to provide more granular control.

Mark Gurman, the executive editor of Bloomberg, stated that this project is far beyond the capabilities of today's Siri. He noted that the job listing describes an ambition for an agent that can write and debug code privately. Gurman also mentioned that Apple cites security as the reason for the new, stricter macOS authorization requirements. The job posting emphasizes that the final product should have the polish that people expect from the Apple brand. Apple has not yet confirmed the development of this agent despite the details found in the job listings.

Some users view the new macOS restrictions as anti competitive, while others are affected by the tighter privacy controls. Meta's Muse agent has seen massive success, surpassing 10 million downloads in 40 days according to data from Sensor Tower. Muse currently sits at number two among free apps in the US, trailing only the popular app TikTok. Third party AI agents are now facing more warnings and hurdles when attempting to gain total control over Mac computers. TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information regarding these reports but did not receive a response.

Autonomous AI agents have become very popular since the breakout success of OpenClaw, putting pressure on Apple to catch up. Other major tech brands like SpaceXSI, OpenAI and Anthropic are already offering their own autonomous solutions to the public. Apple is currently trying to expand its AI offerings during the new era led by executive John Ternus. The company previously allowed users to enable agents from ChatGPT and other apps to carry out functions on devices. These systems usually coordinate tasks across different apps and devices to accomplish goals that are increasingly complex.

Mark Gurman suggests that Apple could introduce these new autonomous capabilities as soon as next year for its users. The company may also make Siri more like an autonomous agent that proactively carries out tasks without user initiation. However, the language in the job listings suggests that the development of this agent is still in early stages. The articles leave open whether the technology landscape will change before Apple is ready to launch its own solution. It remains unclear if Apple will officially announce the project or change its strategy before the next year.

stories.Headline: US bishops approve updated pro-life plan and racial justice prayer day and weigh AI guardrails
stories.Summary:
The U.S. bishops held a fall plenary assembly in Baltimore from November 16 to 19, 2026. On November 18, the prelates held their second day of public sessions to address several major issues. They focused on artificial intelligence, young adults, immigration, racial justice, and pro-life priorities. The bishops also approved a new Mass lectionary and Book of the Gospels without any amendments. These changes will harmonize Mass readings with the forthcoming Catholic American Bible for the faithful.

The bishops approved a resolution on diocesan financial reporting through 2031 and updated socially responsible investment guidelines. Auxiliary Bishop Richard Umbers discussed the 2028 International Eucharistic Congress in Sydney themed This is my body given for you. Bishop Daniel E. Thomas sought to update the 2001 pro-life pastoral plan with a 205 to 0 vote. Bishop Daniel E. Garcia proposed a day of prayer for racial justice on the last Sunday in October. The bishops approved this racial justice day of prayer with a vote of 180 to 15.

Bishop Oscar Cantú said the Church must ensure that progress in artificial intelligence remains ordered to the human person. He stated that the Church should not fear the future but instead help shape it with humanity at the center. Bishop Daniel E. Garcia said that ending racism begins with prayer to heal hearts of wounds from the past. Bishop Brendan J. Cahill warned that a culture of indifference informs the treatment of migrants globally and in America. He criticized the U.S. government for manipulating the truth and dismissing God given human dignity.

Young adults under 30 are affected by the research conducted by experts from The Catholic University of America. These experts noted that young men gravitate toward identity while young women focus more on the interior life. Hispanic Catholics make up 58 percent of those aged 18 to 29 but attend Mass weekly at lower rates. Migrants are affected by mass detention, mass deportation, and the sudden revocation of legal status and work authorization. The bishops also addressed the needs of Catholics in immigrant detention who require pastoral and sacramental ministry.

The 2026 Beauty and Belief Gallup survey from March and April showed 64 percent of young Catholics value religion more. This is higher than the 41 percent of Catholic adults over 30 who feel religion is more important now. Bishop Cantú referenced Pope Leo XIII's 1891 encyclical Rerum Novarum and Pope Leo XIV's 2026 encyclical Magnifica Humanitas regarding technology. Bishop Thomas noted the overturning of the 1973 Roe v. Wade decision and the rise of in vitro fertilization. A CARA report from October 26 found 60 percent of adult Catholics believe racism exists in their community.

The task force on AI will provide formation for leaders and help Catholic education with AI literacy and best practices. They will work with the government relations team to advocate for clear guardrails on the development of artificial intelligence. The pro-life plan will be revised to include advocacy for banning human surrogacy, which is described as worldwide trafficking. The bishops will continue the Justice for Immigrants campaign, the Cabrini Pledge, and the You Are Not Alone initiative. stories.Headline: Anthropic completes largest IPO in history with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the largest initial public offering in history on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. The artificial intelligence research company launched its stock market debut during a challenging period for AI stocks. This record breaking event occurred just a few months after the record setting IPO of SpaceX. The company saw its market value surge immediately following the debut of its shares. This massive financial event took place despite general fears that artificial intelligence is running amok.

The offering raised 81.31 billion US dollars and priced shares at 83 dollars apiece. This price was above the initial target range of 70 to 78 dollars per share. The company upsized the offering by 19 percent to 980 million shares from 825 million shares. Anthropic is also raising 26 billion dollars through a private placement at the IPO price. These figures value the company at approximately 1.5 trillion dollars on a fully diluted basis.

Anthropic is the entity responsible for this offering and the resulting record breaking valuation. The company stated that the final IPO price was set above its previously targeted range. Filings show the company decided to increase the number of shares available for the public. The lab chose to enter the public market despite the difficult backdrop for AI stocks. They managed to eclipse the previous record held by the offering from SpaceX.

Investors in the public market were affected by the surge in the company's market debut. Some observers expressed fears that artificial intelligence technology is currently running amok in the world. The broader financial market is struggling, with the Dow dropping 1,100 points recently. Wall Street is currently experiencing its longest losing streak since the year 2024. These market conditions created a challenging environment for the launch of new AI stocks.

Anthropic is a US company focused on artificial intelligence safety and research. The company had an initial plan to sell 825 million shares to the public. A photograph of the company logo was taken in Brussels on June 10, 2026. The company's valuation includes securities such as restricted stock and various stock options. This IPO follows the recent record setting public market entry of the company SpaceX.

The company will now operate as a public entity with a 1.5 trillion dollar valuation. It will integrate the 26 billion dollars raised through its separate private placement. The articles do not state how the company will spend this massive capital. They leave open whether the market surge will continue despite the Dow's recent losses. The text does not explain how the company will address fears about AI.

stories.Headline: Trump administration approves exports of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
stories.Summary:
The administration of President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. These approvals occurred from December 2025 through May 2026, according to the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The chips were manufactured by Nvidia and AMD for use by various firms in China. This data was released publicly by the committee on a Thursday in November 2026. The release follows scrutiny over former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy.

The Department of Commerce approved 879,000 chips, while companies sought permission to ship 3.4 million units. Approvals included 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD. These shipments included Nvidia H200 and AMD MI325X chips, which are prized for their advanced artificial intelligence capabilities. All four Chinese companies are on the Pentagon list of alleged military-backed firms. Brian Mast used the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to reveal this licensing information.

Committee Chair Brian Mast stated this is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of the Export Control Reform Act. Nvidia claimed the approvals were subject to limited volumes and strict conditions, but they stopped shipping H200s. AMD stated that it maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all applicable United States export control laws. Jeffrey Kessler of the Commerce Department testified in July that shipments had begun but were very few. The Chinese Embassy, Baidu, Alibaba, BYD, and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to comments.

Former official Chris McGuire said it is astonishing that over 30 percent of chips went to military companies. He questioned if the Commerce Department conducted any serious national security review before approving these specific export licenses. China hawks across the political spectrum criticized the rollback of restrictions that were previously established by Joe Biden. Tencent is affected by these trends, reporting third-quarter revenue of 207.34 billion yuan and operating profit of 59.15 billion. Tencent also faced a free cash flow drop to minus 69.1 billion yuan due to AI spending.

Joe Biden previously restricted Chinese access to these chips to prevent the supercharging of the Chinese military. He feared such access would erode the lead the United States holds in the field of artificial intelligence. President Trump rolled back these restrictions in December by giving Nvidia the green light to ship H200 chips. Tencent previously stated that a shortage of AI chips under export curbs was holding back its cloud growth. Tencent recently leased 100,000 Nvidia-class chips from Oracle for roughly 7 billion dollars over five years.

Nvidia stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent following the committee report. The Nasdaq and S&P 500 also fell by 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively, during the same period. Tencent is now moving to raise 5 billion dollars in bonds to fund its ongoing AI buildout. It remains unclear how many of the approved licenses actually resulted in physical shipments to Chinese shores. The articles leave open when Tencent's heavy AI spending will ease or turn into significant cloud revenue.

stories.Headline: VodafoneThree tests Nokia AI-RAN technology using Nvidia GPUs in the UK
stories.Summary:
VodafoneThree announced plans on November 18, 2026, to test Nokia's AI-RAN technology. The company will use Nvidia GPU-based hardware for these upcoming trials. These tests will occur in both lab and field environments in the UK. The trials are scheduled to take place during the next calendar year. This initiative aims to improve mobile network performance and overall efficiency.

The project uses Nokia AI-native anyRAN software running on the Nvidia Aerial RAN computer. The architecture includes a Red Hat OpenShift cloud management layer and Nvidia compute. Vodafone Group also opened an AI-RAN test center in Malaga, Spain, for broader studies. This Spanish facility evaluates Nokia, Nvidia GPUs, purpose-built ASICs, and Intel Granite Rapids x86 processors. Nokia aims to double spectral efficiency by the year 2028.

Valeria Baiamonte is the director of network strategy and transformation at VodafoneThree. She stated that AI-RAN is extremely important for differentiated services like SuperMobile 5G slicing. Baiamonte said AI is needed to predict and reconfigure resources for customers moving unpredictably. She believes AI for RAN is the first monetization case for varied connectivity services. This framework will eventually support physical AI as another type of customer.

Gabriel Brown is a senior principal analyst for mobile networks at the firm Omdia. He said operators will get revenue uplifts by enabling new AI-enabled devices and services. Affected devices include XR glasses, smartphones, cars, and Meta Charms connected to Muse AI agents. These new AI endpoints will have different connectivity profiles than current mobile devices. The industry must prepare for vast numbers of these agents and endpoints.

Vodafone mainly uses Ericsson and Huawei for RAN equipment across its European footprint. Nokia has been deployed in Albania and for 7,000 sites in the UK. Only ten of those UK sites were activated as of April this year. VodafoneThree is also working with Ericsson on AI-RAN using custom silicon and neural accelerators. A new massive MIMO radio from Ericsson was recently rolled out in London.

BT plans to trial the Nvidia platform next year in the EE mobile network. First AI-RAN sites from Nokia and Nvidia are expected to deploy in Birmingham. Deutsche Telekom, Elisa, and Orange also plan AI-RAN field trials with Nokia and Nvidia. T-Mobile recently completed the first voice call using Nokia software and Nvidia Aerial hardware. Ronnie Vasishta expects commercial deployments of the Nokia and Nvidia platform to start next year.

stories.Headline: Senator Warner links AI-driven patching to US tech outages and cosponsors a transparency bill
stories.Summary:
Senator Mark Warner, the Vice Chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, linked recent tech outages to artificial intelligence. These digital systems failures occurred across the United States over the course of one week in November 2026. Warner stated that companies are using AI to prevent AI hacks but struggle with the speed of programs. He believes the entire AI field needs more federal oversight because the government has been too hands off. The senator is now cosponsoring a bipartisan bill to increase transparency regarding investments made by AI companies.

The bill requires companies with significant AI exposure to provide more information on potential risks to the public. Outages affected banks, Microsoft Outlook, and ground stoppages, though the Federal Aviation Administration issues involved replacing a router. Anthropic released Claude Mythos Preview in April, which helped identify thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities in various systems. Mozilla developers shipped over 400 fixes in April, compared to fewer than 30 bugs patched monthly in 2025. Microsoft Patch Tuesday grew from under 100 fixes before April to over 1,000 vulnerabilities in two months.

Senator Warner said the U.S. economy has made a large bet on technology without enough regulatory agency oversight. He claimed that trillions of dollars of investment are flying blindly without the necessary guidance from the investment community. Dan Schiappa of Arctic Wolf said organizations face a balancing act between rapid remediation and avoiding IT disruptions. He explained that rushed patching in complex environments with legacy infrastructure can overload systems and trigger critical business outages. Shane Fry of RunSafe Security stated that the goal should be reducing risk without creating new failures.

Pieter Arntz of Malwarebytes said it is wrong to patch everything blindly and teams must prioritize based on risk. Jason Healey of Columbia University said people pushing AI out when we are not ready are responsible for outages. Some Americans grew suspicious of a cyber attack, but few of the AI discovered bugs were actually exploited. Patrick Garrity of VulnCheck found only 0.45 percent of 442 newly assigned CVEs were being exploited in wild. These exploited vulnerabilities were identified specifically as CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980 during the seven months since Glasswing launched.

Anthropic expanded Mythos access through its Cyber Verification Program six months after the initial Project Glasswing sample testing period. OpenAI launched its Daybreak program in May for select enterprises and broadened it into two tiers in August. Open-weight models advanced rapidly, allowing inexperienced bug hunters to find serious vulnerabilities without the usual frontier model guardrails. Many open source projects paused their bug bounty programs because vendors could not keep up with AI discoveries. Google's Project Zero team recently changed its vulnerability disclosure policy due to fears of hackers using the flaws.

Project Zero is shortening its disclosure timeline from 120 days to 90 days to prevent researchers from leaking flaws. The team will further reduce this disclosure window to 30 days by the year 2028 to increase security. The articles leave open how the bipartisan bill will be implemented or if regulatory agencies will actually increase oversight. It remains unclear if companies will change their patching processes to avoid the risks of an AI driven rush. The text does not state if the current surge of tech outages has fully ended for all Americans.

stories.Headline: TSMC restricts Chinese chip designers following new US export control rules
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's TSMC tightened restrictions on Chinese chip designers on Thursday, November 19, 2026, following new US Commerce Department export control rules. The company suspended some advanced manufacturing orders and limited affected customers to older technology to block powerful AI processor production. These measures complicate efforts by Beijing to develop domestic alternatives to chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by TSMC. The world's largest contract chipmaker now requires US export licenses for orders using processes of 16 nanometres and below. This move closes a manufacturing loophole that previously allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced services without individual licenses.

Chinese designers are generally limited to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided they avoid advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory. Data centers providing large-scale computing to China must obtain export licenses within 90 days or face US chip procurement restrictions. Additional licensing restrictions apply to companies in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to higher risks of chip diversion. TSMC must now scrutinize shipping routes, parent companies, major shareholders, packaging providers, and operating locations for all affected customers. These checks include orders placed through intermediaries or subsidiaries in Europe, Japan, Southeast Asia, Taiwan, and the United States.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Nvidia for resisting regulations and ignoring alleged chip smuggling. Lutnick reportedly slow-walked the rules, arguing that China's reliance on American hardware is in the strategic interest of the US. Bessent, Jamieson Greer, and Marco Rubio pushed to close the data center loophole and sanction the Singaporean company Megaspeed. The new rules were written by the National Security Council and Treasury Department, despite the Commerce Department having ultimate authority. President Donald Trump framed the rift as a policy disagreement between those wanting to be friendly or have a blowup.

Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed. Chinese companies developing alternatives to Nvidia processors, including technology giants and independent designers, are particularly affected by these new restrictions. Senator Richard Blumenthal called for Lutnick to resign, claiming he had a conflict of interest in scaling back export controls. Senator Pete Ricketts and Senator John Kennedy expressed bipartisan support for tightening regulations and investigating how China circumvented previous controls. Emily Kilcrease stated the rules are a good step, but the conversation regarding export controls is far from over.

The US government list of approved designers includes Apple, AMD, Nvidia, MediaTek, and Realtek, but contains no mainland Chinese firms. In May 2025, President Trump reversed Biden-era restrictions on chips Nvidia could export, a move that Jensen Huang welcomed. Trump also announced plans last December to allow approved Chinese companies to buy a newer, more powerful chip model. Nvidia donated 25 million dollars to the White House ballroom renovation project and contributed to the president's inauguration fund. Taiwan previously indicted a TSMC employee and a Nvidia employee for selling secrets or smuggling AI servers to China.

Howard Lutnick and his deputy Jeffrey Kessler are scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on December 10, 2026. Congress is considering legislation to govern advanced AI technology exports and may attach bills to a defense appropriations bill. Democrats are expected to increase congressional investigations into Nvidia and Trump administration conflicts of interest after taking control in January. The Senate Banking Committee and other bodies have requested briefings from Nvidia's general counsel and former CEO Jensen Huang. The articles leave open whether the new rules will effectively stop China from training AI models on advanced chips.

stories.Headline: Anthropic says Claude writes and reviews about 90% of code on its Claude Code team
stories.Summary:
On the Claude Code team at Anthropic, about 90% of code is written and reviewed by Claude, Addy Osmani wrote in a claude.dev blog post published Nov 16, 2026. The post, titled “How the Claude Code team thinks about verification,” appeared in the Engineering category with a reading time of 10 minutes. MarkTechPost reported on Nov 18, 2026 that Anthropic added Code Mode to Claude Code, letting Claude chain tool calls in JavaScript. The claude.dev post said verification loops let the team run dozens or hundreds of Claudes in parallel instead of one or two. The post said that without verification loops, you have to check everything yourself.

In internal testing around structured file generation, a separate grader checking Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. The team keeps a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger readable from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matches, usually 3 to 10. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human. The team’s commit gate can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify, and it has off, observe, and enforce modes.

The post said the people who own the code write the checks for it and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. It said a check that pulls in a reviewer should say why, so the reviewer does not have to work it out from the diff. The team does not stack on more reviewers, because adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often worse than tuning the primary. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request’s changes. The team reserves reviews for commits, because a passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing.

The post said E2E tests are difficult to fool, because either the whole feature works or it doesn’t, and they have definitive done criteria. A unit test may show “Error: Timeout after 30 seconds,” but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of what’s broken. Property test libraries named in the post include fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, and proptest for Rust. Differential tests run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs, using randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. The post said Claude can test the whole app using the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or by running the service locally for backend work.

The post said the team stamps each commit with how it was verified, and the stamp even includes “none” so the team can query for commits that weren’t verified. Observe mode logs what would have been blocked, so the team can review false positives and ensure no one is impacted. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn’t get stuck. The team tracks how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean. Code Review tags things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing, and the “pre-existing” tag means the reviewer shouldn’t hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug.

The post said the team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs. In the Claude Code repo, the team has two methods of turning missed cases into rules, and the first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. The post said three agents will try to di, and the article text ends there. The post said the team has previously written about how code review works at Anthropic, and this article aims to go deeper on how the team verifies its work.

stories.Headline: DataMeds AI agrees to acquire TBIA cancer blood test platform for Helomics
stories.Summary:
DataMeds AI announced on November 19, 2026, that it agreed to acquire specific assets from the estate of Todos Medical Ltd. This acquisition was made for the benefit of Helomics, Inc., which is a wholly owned subsidiary of the healthcare technology company. The deal involves the purchase of the TBIA Cancer AI blood testing platform and several other related business assets. This announcement was released through ACCESS Newswire on November 20, 2026, from the company headquarters located in Tampa, Florida. The company is listed on the NASDAQ exchange under the ticker symbol MEDS and focuses on integrating pharmaceutical and laboratory infrastructures.

The deal includes TBIA blood tests for colorectal cancer TM-C1 and breast cancer TM-B1 and TM-B2, which were developed at Ben Gurion University. DataMeds AI also acquires a license for the LymPro Alzheimer's diagnostic blood test and 100 percent of Todos Medical Singapore PTE Ltd. This Singaporean subsidiary previously held equity in Pathnova Labs PTE Ltd., which merged with Angsana Molecular and Diagnostics Laboratory to become Archerfish Precision Diagnostics. The TBIA platform uses Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy to analyze blood plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cell components to identify cancer. Issued European and United States patents provide the company with market exclusivity for this specific technology into at least the year 2034.

Interim Co-CEO Gerald Commissiong stated that the TBIA platform was ahead of its time and can now flourish during the current AI era. He explained that using one vial of blood to detect multiple cancers is transformative and could be less expensive than liquid biopsies. Commissiong noted that digitizing the immune system might identify cancer at the earliest carcinoma in situ stage, allowing for much earlier treatment. He expressed excitement about implementing this technology at the Helomics Cancer AI laboratory located in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to validate the tests. The company intends to use an oncologist network to source blood samples under IRB-approved protocols and with the consent of patients.

Patients whose physicians send tumor biopsies for the ChemoFx Assay evaluation will be the primary source for the necessary validation blood samples. This process will help the company generate revenue while gathering data to support a commercial launch as a Laboratory Developed Test. The global cancer diagnostics market was valued at 189.19 billion dollars in 2024 and is projected to reach 386.19 billion by 2035. The ChemoFx Assay already helps oncologists make chemotherapy decisions for gynecologic cancers and is billed under CPT codes 81535 and 81536. This existing assay has been granted two unique CPT codes and has already begun to receive various insurance coverage decisions.

DataMeds AI, formerly known as Wellgistics Health, Inc., integrates its EinsteinRx AI platform and PharmacyChain blockchain contracts into the Health Lives Here app. Its subsidiary Corexa Health provides pharmacy dispensing and distribution services for products developed by Tollo Health, LLC, to improve consumer experiences. Helomics Corporation operates a CLIA-certified clinical laboratory in Pittsburgh and uses its Predictive Oncology division to help partners speed up drug discovery. This division combines a large annotated biobank of over 130 tumor types with multi-omic data and artificial intelligence to predict responses. The TBIA technology was also previously utilized to distinguish between bacterial and viral infections before being applied to the detection of cancer.

The acquisition of these assets from the estate of Todos Medical Ltd. remains subject to the final approval of the court. The TBIA tests have not been cleared or approved by the FDA and are not currently available for commercial use. DataMeds AI must still advance the technology through the FDA regulatory process after the initial launch as a laboratory developed test. The articles leave open whether the company can successfully revalidate historical data correlations with biopsy results and imaging results for patients. It remains uncertain if the company can obtain the necessary licensor consent for the assignment of the LymPro Alzheimer's diagnostic license.

stories.Headline: Analysts urge investors to buy semiconductor stocks during a market sell-off
stories.Summary:
Investors booked profits in semiconductor stocks recently, causing the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index to slide 25 percent since the start of October. Harsh Chauhan and Prosper Junior Bakiny wrote about these market trends on November 19, 2026, for The Motley Fool. This sell-off happened as investor sentiment became fragile due to high inflation and a hawkish Federal Reserve. Recent developments at Nvidia also dented confidence in the sector, contributing to the downward pressure on chip stocks. These writers suggest that the current dip presents a bargain opportunity for investors to buy top AI stocks.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing shares dropped 22 percent since October, while Applied Materials shares fell 34 percent during that same period. Alphabet shares are down 11 percent this year, and the Nasdaq-100 index has an earnings multiple of 30. TSMC trades at 25 times earnings, and Applied Materials trades at 20 times forward earnings, while Alphabet has a PEG ratio of 0.5. Amazon has a PEG ratio of 0.6, and Micron Technology has a PEG ratio of 0.2, making these stocks look cheap. Alphabet reported third quarter revenue of 127.6 billion dollars, while Amazon reported net sales of 201.9 billion dollars.

The Motley Fool analysts state that the AI industry is only finishing Act 1, which was the research and development phase. They believe Act 2 will be the global rollout and could be 16 times bigger than the first phase. Harsh Chauhan says TSMC is the kingpin of the AI chip revolution and is a prudent move for investors. Prosper Junior Bakiny believes that several AI stocks are great bargain buys if the market maintains its recent momentum. He suggests that long-term investors bullish on AI prospects can hardly go wrong by buying the stock of Amazon.

Some investors and analysts are not convinced that the artificial intelligence industry will continue to expand rapidly over the medium term. These skeptical investors are worried about high capital expenditures and declining free cash flow, which affected companies like Alphabet this year. Alphabet's free cash flow was a negative 9.1 billion dollars, and its earnings per share declined to 2.12 dollars. Amazon faces stiff competition in the cloud computing market from Microsoft and Alphabet, though it remains the current market leader. Micron Technology faces potential regulatory problems and the risk of slowing growth in its top and bottom line figures.

The Semiconductor Industry Association noted that global semiconductor revenue increased 144 percent in August 2026 to reach 159.7 billion dollars. Worldwide revenue crossed 1 trillion dollars in the first eight months of 2026, and the SIA expects 1.6 trillion by year-end. McKinsey expects the semiconductor market revenue to cross 2.3 trillion dollars by 2030, showing the industry's continued secular growth. TSMC controls 73 percent of the global pure-play foundry market and manufactures chips for Nvidia, Broadcom, and Advanced Micro Devices. Micron Technology designs critical memory chips and has gained significant pricing power due to a shortage in the industry.

TSMC plans to increase chip manufacturing prices by 10 percent in 2027, and its EPS is expected to reach 17.50 dollars. Morgan Stanley expects the wafer and fab equipment market to reach 191 billion dollars in 2027 and 215 billion in 2028. Alphabet expects to recognize 308.55 billion dollars of its cloud backlog over the next 24 months, which is 55 percent of total. Some projections suggest the memory chip shortage that benefits Micron Technology could last until 2028 or potentially until the year 2029. The articles leave open whether Wall Street is wrong about AI momentum and if these stocks will actually go parabolic.

stories.Headline: South Korea inspects exam candidates glasses and blocks Wi-Fi to stop AI cheating
stories.Summary:
South Korea will inspect all glasses worn by students taking this week's national college entrance exam to prevent AI-assisted cheating. This action follows a confession on Sunday by a person who placed first in the 2026 tax accountant exam. The individual admitted to photographing questions with a microcamera and using an AI tool and smartphone to find answers. These events shook public confidence in the country's high-stakes testing system and caused panic before the college test. The government is now implementing strict security measures to protect the integrity of the upcoming national examinations.

The Education Ministry will inspect all glasses in every session of the College Scholastic Ability Test in Seoul and other centers. Smart devices were added to the banned items list in July, and public Wi-Fi will be blocked during the exams. Every exam room will have warning notices about criminal penalties, and each center will have one staff member monitoring devices. A hotline will link centers to local education offices and the ministry's control room to judge difficult cases on the spot. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced that emergency alerts will be sent before the exam to detect any hidden mobile phones.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin told a parliamentary hearing on November 16 that the ministry would inspect all eyewear worn by candidates. He stated that the ministry would work with parliament to lengthen the current one-year exam ban to three or ten years. Choi also noted that offenders may be reported to the police for obstructing official duties during the national testing process. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook said the government would form an emergency team to prepare measures to safeguard the college entrance exam. She urged officials to develop AI-based detection technology and called for strengthened penalties for those who cheat using technology.

Some people called for the university entrance exam to be postponed to ensure fairness, but the Education Ministry ruled out delays. The Suneung exam is seen as a ticket to well-paid jobs and better marriage prospects in a hyper-competitive society. Students are affected by these changes, as anyone caught using smart devices will have their results invalidated for the current year. They will also be barred from sitting the exam the following year under the current rules and potential new penalties. The national exam is so intense that much of South Korea will stand still on Thursday to minimize student distractions.

The scandal began when the top tax accountant candidate confessed on November 15 to using a microcamera and AI for cheating. Smart glasses are a global concern because they can record confidential material or people without their knowledge or any consent. Grepp, a company with a 90 percent market share in online proctoring, uses a service called Monito for recruitment exams. This technology is already used by major corporations like Samsung Electronics, LG Electronics, and SK hynix for their own hiring processes. Grepp recorded 13.5 billion won in revenue last year and is now expanding into physical test center AI solutions.

The ministry will consult specialists on radio-signal detectors and may introduce this technology for the 2027 test to stop AI cheating. Grepp CEO Lim Sung-soo is discussing a pilot deployment of Monito at Prometric test centers in the United States next year. The company plans to seek accreditation as a private operator of nationally recognized qualification assessments and pursue an IPO in 2028. Articles leave open whether thermal imaging cameras or radio-frequency detectors will be used, as they face legal and technical challenges. It remains unclear if the government will successfully implement these high-tech tools due to interference with nearby wireless communications.

stories.Headline: HHS secretary Kennedy announces final HIPAA rule cutting patient record response time to 15 days
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights finalized a 363-page HIPAA Privacy Rule overhaul late Monday, November 16, 2026, according to BankInfoSecurity. The rule is titled HIPAA Privacy Rule: Changes to Support Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement and Reduce Regulatory Burdens. It is slated for publication Thursday, November 19, 2026, in the Federal Register. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the finalization. The changes aim to give patients faster and easier access to health records, including through third-party applications.

The rule cuts the deadline for responding to patient requests for protected health information from 30 calendar days to 15 days, with a one-time extension of up to 30 additional days under specific circumstances. It becomes effective 60 days after publication, on January 18, 2027. HIPAA-regulated organizations must comply with applicable provisions 180 days after the effective date, or July 17, 2027. Business associate agreements must be updated by January 18, 2028, at the latest. The rule also clarifies patients' rights to obtain electronic health information through personal health apps, including consumer apps not subject to HIPAA.

HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. said Americans should never have to fight for access to their own health records. He said the rule modernizes HIPAA to serve patients and helps providers spend more time delivering care and less time navigating bureaucracy. Privacy attorney Adam Greene of Davis Wright Tremaine said he appreciated the deletion of the requirement to obtain acknowledgments of receipt of the notice of privacy practices. Greene said the requirement was founded on good intentions but led to administrative burden and confusion with minimal corresponding benefit. Privacy attorney Kirk Nahra of WilmerHale said HHS chose coordination over individual privacy.

Nahra said the rule essentially allows disclosure over the objection or lack of permission from the consumer. Greene said the proposal would have led to a substantial unfunded mandate taxing covered entities' already limited resources. Privacy attorney Iliana Peters of Polsinelli said her biggest concerns involve administrative burdens, including the new 15-day access deadline, which she called a very short amount of time. Healthcare organizations participating in the federal Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement generally should not refuse access requests through personal health apps when digital identity verification conditions are satisfied. Those conditions include a cryptographically signed token issued by a credential service provider certified consistent with NIST Identity Assurance Level 2 and Authentication Assurance Level 2.

HHS OCR issued the proposed HIPAA Privacy Rule modifications in January 2021, during the final days of President Donald Trump's first term. The proposal remained on the back burner during the Biden administration. The final rule retains several key patient-access and care-coordination provisions proposed in 2021 but abandons or scales back others. HHS OCR dropped a proposal that would have relaxed HIPAA's minimum necessary standard for certain disclosures of sensitive health information. Several healthcare industry groups signed a letter to HHS last week expressing concerns that loosening identity verification requirements involving third-party apps could expose providers to security threats and regulatory scrutiny.

The final rule clarifies that health plans may use and disclose PHI for individual-level care coordination and case management. It expressly permits covered entities to disclose PHI to social services agencies, community-based organizations and similar third parties for care coordination and case management. The rule eliminates the requirement for covered healthcare providers to make a good-faith effort to obtain patients' written acknowledgment of receiving a Notice of Privacy Practices. Regulated entities must update, redistribute and post their notices, update websites with required information about fees for accessing health records, and revise applicable business associate agreements. The signatories of the letter, including the College of Healthcare Information Management Executives, did not immediately respond to ISMG's request for comment on the final rule.

stories.Headline: Kansas State proposes a master's degree in AI systems as the board of regents weighs it
stories.Summary:
The Kansas Board of Regents considered a new master's degree in artificial intelligence systems and their applications during the week of November 18, 2026. The University of Missouri Board of Curators unanimously approved a new bachelor's degree program in artificial intelligence on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This undergraduate program will be offered at Missouri University of Science and Technology, which is located in the city of Rolla, Missouri. The K-State degree will be part of the Department of Computer Science in the College of Engineering at Kansas State University. The Missouri S&T program is set to launch in fall 2027, pending approval from the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education.

The Missouri S&T degree requires 120 credit hours and will be housed in the College of Engineering and Computing computer science department. Six new courses include Introduction to Modern AI Tools, Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Introduction to Machine Learning, Intelligent Robots, Responsible AI and Computing, and AI Capstone. Students will study programming, algorithms, machine learning, data science, computer organization, databases, cybersecurity, calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and neuroscience. The program aligns with Missouri Executive Order 26-02, which directs higher education and workforce agencies to support the development of AI-focused degrees. This will be the first standalone undergraduate AI degree offered in Missouri, following a similar program at Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

Dr. David Borrok, the vice provost and dean of the College of Engineering and Computing at S&T, said demand for AI education grew. He stated that graduates will be prepared to understand and innovate within modern engineered systems that are increasingly using artificial intelligence technologies. Dr. Seung-Jong Jay Park, the Kummer Endowed Chair of Computer Science, said that experiential learning will be a key program component. He explained that students will complete project-based coursework and a senior capstone experience sponsored by government laboratories, university researchers, or industry. The K-State proposal stated that the new degree will help students compete in a changing job market as AI job demand grows.

Graduates will prepare for careers as AI application developers, machine learning engineers, data scientists, intelligent systems developers, AI solutions analysts, and AI-enabled cybersecurity analysts. The program will affect students by providing comprehensive preparation in both the theory and practice of artificial intelligence beyond traditional computer science. Educators noted that the curriculum will teach students about responsible AI practices and the societal effects of emerging technologies in the world. Missouri S&T projects that the new program will enroll approximately 110 students within five years of the official program launch date. The K-State degree targets students who need to compete in a market where AI engineer jobs have grown nearly 150 percent.

A market analysis by the AI company Veritone showed a 25.2 percent increase in AI jobs in early 2025 versus early 2024. AI technologies are becoming increasingly integrated into various industries, including financial services, healthcare, transportation, and manufacturing, according to the dean at Missouri S&T. The Missouri S&T proposal supports strategic goals related to academic innovation, workforce preparation, and enrollment growth for the university in Rolla. The K-State proposal was based on the fact that demand for AI-related jobs is growing rapidly across the current professional job market. These educational initiatives respond to a broader trend of increasing standalone undergraduate AI degrees appearing in recent years across the United States.

The next step for Missouri S&T is for the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education to review the university's bachelor's degree proposal. Pending that specific approval, the university aims to admit its first group of students into the new major starting in fall 2027. The articles do not state if the Kansas Board of Regents has officially approved the master's degree for the Kansas State University students. There is no information regarding the specific start date or the total credit hours required for the proposed K-State master's degree program. The texts leave open whether other universities in Kansas or Missouri will launch similar standalone artificial intelligence degrees in the future.

stories.Headline: Azerbaijan security official Davud Rustamov warns AI agents speed up attacks on critical infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Davud Rustamov warned of cyber threats to critical infrastructure on November 19, 2026, during a panel discussion in Baku, Azerbaijan. He spoke at the 2nd International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy regarding risks posed by artificial intelligence and outdated software libraries. Rustamov is the Head of the Cybersecurity Operations Center of the State Security Service of Azerbaijan and addressed the event. He explained that AI applications often contain vulnerabilities that allow for cyberattacks using other AI driven solutions and tools. State affiliated actors specifically target critical information infrastructure, which makes the continuous monitoring of the threat landscape a national priority.

Azerbaijan began establishing a legislative framework for critical infrastructure in 2020, drawing from the experience of Italy, Türkiye, Israel, and the US. The State Security Service is now the primary authority for security in this domain and exercises state oversight over the infrastructure. Rustamov noted that the legislative process concerning the security of critical information infrastructure has been completed to protect the national systems. Azerbaijan uses a platform called MISP for the exchange of information regarding malicious software and threats with the private sector. The country also joined international MISP Threat Sharing platforms to share malicious indicators with local partners and other global stakeholders.

Rustamov stated that AI enables existing attack tactics, such as reconnaissance and impersonation, to be executed more rapidly and on a larger scale. He said that national cyber centers, intelligence services, and infrastructure operators must collaborate and exchange information regarding all observed cyber threats. The official emphasized that reliable, 24/7 communication channels among national incident response teams are needed for the rapid exchange of threat intelligence. He argued that a unified national cybersecurity landscape rooted in collective defense would integrate data from regulators, law enforcement, and intelligence services. Rustamov mentioned that timely sharing of malicious IP addresses, domains, and hashes strengthens capabilities and plays a crucial role in combating threats.

Esmeralda Kazia said AI can speed up the analysis of cyber threats and the processing of large data sets and evidence. She warned that AI results are not always reliable because the system can produce erroneous conclusions with a high degree of confidence. Kazia noted that governments must distinguish between facts, analytical assessments, and the decisions made based on those specific AI generated results. She stated that a machine cannot exercise constitutional powers or bear diplomatic and moral responsibility for the decisions a state makes. Small states are affected and should participate in shaping international rules for AI rather than merely adapting to other countries' decisions.

The articles mention a July 2022 cyberattack on Albania that affected the country's digital infrastructure and various government services during that time. Albania attributed responsibility for that specific attack to Iran and decided to sever diplomatic relations with Tehran with support from NATO. The 2nd International Conference on Cyberdiplomacy was jointly organized by the State Service for Special Communications and Information Security of Azerbaijan. Romania's National Institute for Research and Development in Informatics also helped organize the event, which focused on digital sovereignty and international relations. Other participants included the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport, and the Office of the President of Azerbaijan.

Next, national security agencies must assess how quickly threats are identified and how rapidly action is taken in coordination with international partners. Azerbaijan will continue monitoring current trends in cyberattacks, including those targeting government institutions and utilizing various forms of artificial intelligence. The State Security Service will continue conducting digital forensic investigations, security audits, and penetration testing to protect the critical information infrastructure. Rustamov highlighted the serious risk posed by uncensored artificial intelligence models circulating on darknet resources to automate complex and sophisticated attack scenarios. The articles leave open whether law enforcement agencies are fully prepared to counter these sophisticated attacks using traditional digital investigation methods.

stories.Headline: Allianz Commercial says reported AI losses hide the true scale of risk
stories.Summary:
Allianz Commercial published a report on November 19, 2026, saying reported AI losses understate the true risk and are only the tip of the iceberg. The report found that AI-related incidents and litigation have rapidly increased in recent years. Allianz Commercial is already tracking AI-related insurance claims with substantial values in the millions of euros. Examples include accidents caused by alleged defective AI safety systems in vehicles. They also include shareholder-filed securities litigation alleging misleading AI-related disclosures and omissions by company executives.

The report says these cases could easily result in total insurance industry losses in the region of $100-million. Many current confirmed losses show only part of the exposure because AI involvement can be difficult to identify, quantify or attribute. Some losses may be recorded under established categories such as cyber, directors' and officers' liability, product liability, or crime insurance. When AI is embedded into everyday business processes, even a small error rate can translate into a significant number of critical issues very quickly. AI soared from #10 to #2 in the Allianz Risk Barometer 2026, the largest year-on-year rise of any risk category.

Thomas Lillelund, CEO of Allianz Commercial, said AI is transforming how companies operate, make decisions and compete. He said AI is becoming embedded into business models and operations of businesses and supply chains. He said AI offers huge value and benefits but also represents a risk management challenge like never before. He said today's apparently modest number of confirmed AI claims hides the true extent of exposures for businesses. He said business leaders should prioritise AI within governance and resilience planning, supported by clear accountability, appropriate controls, human oversight, and workable fallback arrangements.

Michael Daum, head of the AI Risk and Claims Centre of Excellence at Allianz Commercial, said what is observed today with confirmed AI losses is almost certainly just the tip of the iceberg. He said many incidents go under the radar, creating a significant gray area of hidden exposure. He said we are at an early stage of a broader transformation in which the true scale of AI-related risk will become more visible over time. He said losses likely lag the emergence of risk and a future wave of AI claims is starting to build. He said insurers are in a unique position to use emerging claims data to show the real business impact of AI risks and to help companies calibrate their risk management.

The report introduces a framework organised into four main categories. Direct AI loss is when the AI system is the primary cause of harm through an incorrect action, decision, recommendation, or output. AI-related loss is when AI is a material factor but the loss arises from wider business, governance, legal, reputational, or third-party issues. AI-accelerated loss is when AI enables, scales or accelerates malicious activity, including cyberattacks, deepfakes or fraud. AI-dependency loss is when the initial event is not caused by AI but reliance on AI-driven processes and insufficient fallback capabilities increases the duration or cost of the loss.

The MIT AI Risk Initiative recorded 179 incidents in 2023, 307 in 2024, and 453 in 2025, an increase of more than 150% in just two years. There were well over 100 IP lawsuits filed against AI developers by artists, entertainment, and media companies through the middle of 2026. As of August 2026, there have been 22 AI-related securities class action lawsuits filed in the US this year compared to just 16 during the whole of 2025, and seven in 2023. Organisations using AI-driven prevention and detection tools have materially lower breach and business interruption costs, and the cost of an AI-enhanced ransomware attack that progresses to data theft and encryption can be 1,000 times higher than an incident detected and contained early. Current claims data would not rank AI among the top 20 loss drivers for commercial insurers, but AI is very much on the radar of senior business leaders.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share and reaches a $1.5 Tn valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic held its record-breaking initial public offering on 19 November 2026, and the listing triggered a debate among Indian business leaders about India's ability to build globally competitive AI companies. The Claude parent priced its shares at $83, above its price range of $70-78. The IPO valued the company at around $1.5 Tn and was oversubscribed by over 10X. The listing gave public market investors an opportunity to back one of the companies at the centre of the AI race. The conversation in India gained momentum after veteran banker and Kotak Mahindra Bank founder Uday Kotak compared Anthropic's valuation with the combined market capitalisation of India's top 10 companies.

Anthropic's $1.5 Tn IPO valuation is equivalent to nearly 37% of India's projected nominal GDP of $4.06 Tn for FY27, as per the IMF's October estimates. Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, over 4X the year-ago period. AI emerged as the defining theme in Q3 2026, with Indian startups in the segment raising a record $438 Mn across 35 deals, up 265% YoY. This took the sector's total funding in the first nine months of 2026 to more than $1.1 Bn. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, while the deal count fell 13%.

In a post on X, Uday Kotak questioned whether Indian businesses were undervalued or whether the country needed to catch up with the new tech economy. Adani Group CFO Jugeshinder Robbie Singh labelled the Anthropic IPO a "textbook category error in asset pricing" in a post on X titled "Cross-Regime Category Error: Why Legacy Bankers Can't Price Synthetic GDP". Singh wrote that India's blue chips are neither undervalued nor behind, and argued they are yield vehicles monetising the physical human economy. He argued that frontier AI companies are being valued for their potential to create "synthetic GDP" through autonomous AI agents and digital workforces. Ex-Infosys CFO Mohandas Pai wrote that every disruption creates new companies with huge valuations and that comparing is silly.

Pai argued that the more pertinent question the IPO raises for India is what exactly is needed for an Indian company to recreate an Anthropic-like scale. Inc42's Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half expect a correction within the next 18 months. Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said rising AI valuations are part of a global trend, particularly in the US, and that distribution becomes the moat especially in India. Vertical AI applications across BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in the survey, with 39% of investors expecting them to capture the most value over the next five years.

AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%. An analysis by General Catalyst's Utkarsh Bajpai of companies valued at over $5 Bn highlighted the role of technical talent in value creation. Researchers lead 16% of these companies but account for 31% of their combined $170 Bn valuation. Nearly 80% of the founders have technical backgrounds. Mehta said the days are gone when you could just build wrappers on top of foundational models, and that you have to build vertically focused products that solve real problems with an AI-first approach.

Whether the funding momentum continues will depend on sustainable revenue, defensible businesses and valuations that can withstand a potential correction. The findings suggested that investors were increasingly prioritising commercially viable AI applications over capital-intensive foundational technology. Building globally competitive businesses in these areas requires patient capital and sustained investment in research, talent and infrastructure, often years before commercial returns materialise. India's challenge, therefore, is to move from participating in the AI market to building technology that competes globally. The articles leave open whether the funding momentum continues and whether India can translate rising funding into durable businesses.

stories.Headline: OpenAI says its models cut AMD chip design time to under five months and lift GPU performance by up to 14%
stories.Summary:
OpenAI engineers used the company's frontier models to accelerate development of OpenAI's first custom inference chip, Jalapeño, and OpenAI shared that work in August before publishing a closer look on November 18, 2026. OpenAI started using GPT-4o to help design Jalapeño in early 2025, and even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements. In Jalapeño's vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. In the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. The optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño's silicon bring-up.

One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one, and a separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. The team estimates that model-proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. OpenAI partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and saw up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP, with the model identifying further improvements by rewriting SystemVerilog RTL. OpenAI says this represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months, and AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing and added others to its production design files for future versions. AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by OpenAI's model.

OpenAI says it has observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect, and that the model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. According to OpenAI, the model used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block's behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area. OpenAI says it expects further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline. OpenAI says its models can explore new processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD's next generation flagship GPU and CPU. OpenAI says it is partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys, a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation tools the way expert chip designers do.

To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, OpenAI tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores, PicoRV32, a compact core designed for FPGAs, and OpenTitan's Ibex, the embedded processor in its security chip. OpenAI gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput, scoring designs zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core's area. For each core, OpenAI assigned the best throughput observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0, and with a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT-6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores, while GPT-6.1 Sol also outscored GPT-5.6 Sol on both. On PicoRV32 at around 112,000 tokens, GPT-6.2 Astra's score is about twice GPT-6 Astra's, and on Ibex GPT-6.2 Astra's mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches while GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol are closer together. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

For the second task, OpenAI gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system, and the model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, OpenAI kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task. At about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design, for both PicoRV32 and Ibex, and GPT-6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT-6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets. On Ibex, GPT-6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification, and its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets.

OpenAI says starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions, and that those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. OpenAI says requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design. OpenAI says it is working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips. OpenAI says it is partnering with Synopsys to train GPT-Synopsys to ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed. The articles leave open what further PPA improvements OpenAI expects on top of GPU and CPU and what results GPT-Synopsys will produce.
