stories.Headline: Onlook lets designers build and edit real app code visually with AI
stories.Summary:
Onlook, an open-source AI-first design tool, was published on GitHub by the onlook-dev organisation, and TechGig reported on it on November 20, 2026. The tool lets designers and visual engineers build, style and edit code visually with AI on a canvas. It works directly with real app code running live from any Git repository on a user's machine. The GitHub repository, onlook-dev/onlook, had 1,644 commits, 27.3k stars, 121 watchers and 2.2k forks when the articles were written. TechGig published its report on November 20, 2026 at 04:51 AM IST, and the GitHub page was dated November 19, 2026.

Onlook is released under the Apache 2.0 License, and the license covers source code but not every asset in the repository. Artifacts can be exported as self-contained HTML, PNG, JPEG or PDF files, with PNG and JPEG captured through Electron capturePage and PDF through Electron printToPDF and pdf-lib. The macOS desktop application is available for download for Apple Silicon and Intel x64, while Windows and Linux versions are planned, with waitlists for both. The source build needs no Onlook account, cloud keys or .env file, and a build from source asks before collecting usage analytics, which can be turned off in Settings or with STUDIO_TELEMETRY=0. The desktop app is built with Electron, React 19, Astryx, React Flow, Zustand and CodeMirror, and uses Git, node-pty, Bun and Turborepo.

The GitHub page says Onlook is the developer tool for designers and describes it as a free, local-first editor where designers craft exceptional experiences in code. It states that Onlook does not ship its own model, and that users connect the Claude Code or ChatGPT/Codex account they already have so that agent does the work inside their project. It says Onlook opens any Git repository on a machine and runs the user's own dev server, so what is designed is the actual product, not a mockup someone has to rebuild later. It says the app runs on the user's computer, code stays there, and more tools can be plugged in through MCP connectors. The page also says the team is hiring engineers and designers in SF.

TechGig describes Onlook as an open-source alternative to Figma, V0, Replit Agent, Base 44 and Webflow, and the GitHub page lists the same alternatives. The GitHub page says users can design apps, websites, posters and graphics with local fonts and assets, work on multiple design tasks at once across repos and pages, and use mobile, tablet and desktop frames side by side. It says a safe worktree copy means the user's folder is never touched, and that projects run as parallel tabs. It says users can ask about any element on the canvas, have the agent arrange the canvas for variations, states and flows, reference images on the canvas, and sketch and share artifacts for quick HTML sketches outside the repo. It says users can import a GitHub repo, start entirely new codebases from scratch, and make one-press pull requests from checks to merge.

The GitHub page says Onlook works with all web frameworks or languages the user's dev server already supports, because it runs the project with its own tooling. It describes a workflow where a user starts a new empty project with the New Draft button in the upper left corner of the projects page and writes a request in the input box in the lower right corner. It says the user answers clarifying questions from the agent and waits for it to build, then clicks frames for context in follow-up prompts or double-clicks an element to use inline chat. It says the user selects a frame, asks the agent to convert it into an Artifact, exports it as HTML/CSS or PNG with the export button in the upper right corner of the frame, and pastes it into Slack, email or any messaging tool. It says changes show up on the canvas as the dev server reloads, and Git keeps track of everything that changed.

The GitHub page says the previous browser-based version of Onlook, v1, lives on the v1 branch of the repository, and the first desktop version is at onlook-dev/desktop. It says Onlook's icons come from Central Icons by Iconists and are licensed to Onlook for its own product, a license that does not extend to forks, and that brand marks, DMG art and sounds are not covered either. It points to ASSETS.md for what is covered and what to replace when forking, and to NOTICE for third-party notices. It says the official download has product usage analytics on by default, and points to the privacy policy for details. It lists contact channels including Discord, email, Twitter, LinkedIn, YouTube and Substack, and the website onlook.com.

The GitHub page invites users to fork the repo and create a pull request, browse open issues, and read CONTRIBUTING.md for instructions and a code of conduct. It says security issues should be reported by following SECURITY.md instead of opening a public issue. It says Windows and Linux users can join waitlists to be emailed when there are updates, and that the team is still gauging demand for Linux. It says SOURCE_BUILD.md covers building and running Onlook on a Mac. The articles do not say when Windows or Linux versions will be released, and they do not give a release date for the macOS app.

stories.Headline: CircleCI adds Dynamic Parallelism and local test runs to Smarter Testing for AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
CircleCI, a continuous integration and continuous delivery platform, announced new features in its Smarter Testing suite on November 19, 2026, according to SD Times, which datelined its report from San Francisco, California. TechGig reported the release on November 20, 2026, saying the updates aim to accelerate feedback for engineering teams and help them validate code changes earlier. The company said the enhancements reduce redundant testing and optimise compute resource usage, and that they are particularly relevant for workflows involving AI coding agents. The suite now includes Dynamic Parallelism, which adjusts the number of machines for each run to cut unnecessary compute costs, the company said. CircleCI said testing can consume up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, often leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching contexts while tests run.

Smarter Testing lets developers and AI coding agents run affected tests locally before pushing code, catching issues before code reaches CI at no additional charge, according to SD Times. Intelligent Test Selection uses test impact analysis to identify only the tests affected by a code change, so teams do not have to run the full suite on every commit. Dynamic Parallelism automatically adjusts machine allocation based on the tests selected for each run, reducing compute usage as testing volume grows. Dynamic Test Splitting balances tests across machines to minimise idle time, and Auto Rerun Failed Tests retries only failed tests instead of rerunning entire suites. Smarter Testing is integrated directly into CircleCI, requiring no additional vendor or infrastructure, the company said.

Rob Zuber, CTO of CircleCI, said that as AI coding agents make it easier to produce code, everything downstream needs to get smarter and faster, including how code is validated. He said developers and agents should be able to check their work before pushing code, and that a small change should not require the same tests and compute resources as a large one. Zuber said Smarter Testing helps teams get feedback sooner and use resources more efficiently without having to rethink their entire development process. He said that as AI coding agents simplify code production, downstream processes like validation must become smarter and faster. The company said the features enable organizations to maintain confidence in what they ship without sacrificing speed, efficiency, or control.

William Yardley, Staff Infrastructure Engineer at Medallion, a healthcare technology company that automates provider credentialing and operations, said Smarter Testing helped bring down cost per pull request and reduce build times. He said this happened even as the company's pull request volume went up 10x and its test suite grew 2.5x, and that Dynamic Parallelism adjusts machines automatically as testing needs grow. Maria Volpe, Senior Software Engineer at Kustomer, an AI-powered customer service platform, said Smarter Testing changed the economics of its CI. Volpe said the cost of running Kustomer's tests was cut by a quarter, and that engineers get feedback faster because only tests affected by a change run. TechGig reported that Kustomer saw a 25 per cent reduction in test running costs, and that Medallion used Smarter Testing to manage increased development activity.

The articles say testing can account for up to half of CI/CD pipeline time, leaving developers waiting for feedback or switching context while tests run. They say AI coding agents are accelerating code creation, so engineering teams need ways to validate changes just as quickly, regardless of which tools or agents are writing the code. CircleCI said the updates help validate code changes earlier, reduce unnecessary testing, and use compute more efficiently. The company said teams can improve the efficiency of the entire delivery process and lower the overall cost of getting a change into production. CircleCI described itself as a leading continuous integration and continuous delivery platform.

SD Times directed readers to learn more about CircleCI Smarter Testing through a link in its report, and neither article states a general availability date beyond the announcements. The articles do not say how many customers have adopted the new features or how the features are priced beyond local test runs being offered at no additional charge. They do not give figures for Medallion's cost or build time reductions, only that both came down. They do not specify which tools or agents the AI coding agents mentioned are, or how Dynamic Parallelism calculates machine counts for each run. The articles leave open how Intelligent Test Selection performs test impact analysis and what results other early customers have seen.

stories.Headline: RadixArk releases DaisyRose-27B to improve post-training efficiency for agent tasks
stories.Summary:
RadixArk released the DaisyRose-27B model on November 18, 2026, to improve post-training efficiency for agent tasks. This first model from RadixArk was built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained using the Miles reinforcement learning framework. The team trained the model over 18 days using 144 H200 GPUs on 1,200 curated tasks. These long-horizon agent tasks included sessions up to 1M tokens and required several interdependent steps. The process improved the Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 score from 5.6% to 12.0% and boosted other benchmarks.

The model retains the Qwen3.8-27B architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and a 256K-token context window. RadixArk recommends serving the model on port 30000 using SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding for better performance. Training involved 63,000 GPU-hours and used 128 H200s for inference while 16 GPUs ran the trainer. The project used the open-source AgentENV project to run 944,000 sandboxes between mid-September and mid-November. These sandboxes ran on up to 12 machines and supported up to 1,566 concurrent sessions.

Jason Chen from RadixArk stated that the release was possible due to reliable sandboxes and an efficient backend. He explained that the Miles framework operates in fully asynchronous mode so the agent and model never wait. The team noted that their internal backend achieved 37% model FLOPs utilization, which is higher than Megatron. This efficiency resulted in 57% lower training costs and a speed of 16,800 tokens per second. RadixArk also mentioned that their cloud infrastructure costs were 80% lower than using popular sandbox providers.

Eigent AI partnered with RadixArk to build thousands of candidate tasks in science, software engineering, and machine learning. These tasks targeted specific mistakes made by Qwen3.8-27B and were adjusted until the solve rate was useful. Each attempt allowed 1.5 hours in a sandbox with over 100 tool calls and 256K output tokens. OpenAI also discussed frontier risk, noting that they paused GPT-6.1 Astra to meet their own safety standards. OpenAI's Safety Advisory Group and Safety and Security Committee oversee their risk determinations and model deployment.

OpenAI reported a July incident at Hugging Face that led them to strengthen their safeguards and alignment requirements. They now use virtual machines and network perimeters to cut frontier model training off from the live internet. OpenAI paused training for its most capable models from September 20th to October 1st to fix a gap. They developed Control Room to stop model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt. One research task required 10,000 agents to solve the Navier Stokes problem, which amplified potential risks.

RadixArk invites users to download DaisyRose-27B and share performance results in the model's Community tab on Hugging Face. Users can also use the Miles framework to train their own agents for various long-horizon tasks. OpenAI continues to evaluate monitorability and alignment before moving models from research to internal and external deployment. The articles do not state when the next RadixArk model will be released or its specific goals. They also leave open the final safety results for the GPT-6 Astra system card and deployment.

stories.Headline: Alibaba Cloud expands global data center network to meet rising AI demand
stories.Summary:
David Rubinstein hosted Jason Eichenholz on a podcast on November 19, 2026, to discuss the power needs of AI. Alibaba Cloud also announced plans to expand its global data center network over the next year on November 18, 2026. These developments occur as the adoption of artificial intelligence expands and creates a growing demand for computing power. Eichenholz believes that electricity availability has become a major bottleneck for the expansion of AI and its data centers. Alibaba Cloud is prioritizing Hong Kong because its three leased data centers there can no longer meet current demand.

The expansion requires new infrastructure like 500 megawatt or multi gigawatt buildings, which often have four to six year wait times. This process involves grid upgrades, new substations, cooling, permitting, and construction in the physical world. Alibaba Cloud is expanding its network to support financial firms that are adopting AI in their core workflows. Eichenholz notes that companies must now consider water use and the impact of siting on local communities. The new AI geography era requires next generation connectivity to link geographically dispersed data center footprints across the world.

Jason Eichenholz, the founder and CEO of Relativity Networks, said that power will be the forever bottleneck in AI expansion. He explained that the industry is shifting from a race for chips to a race for productive computing capacity. Eichenholz stated that the optical industry must now focus on how quickly information moves rather than just total bandwidth. He suggested that data center operators and municipalities can find win win partnerships to benefit local communities. Yuan Zhiming, a vice president at Alibaba Cloud, outlined the company's expansion plans at a summit in Hong Kong.

Local communities are affected by the noise, huge land requirements, and the potential for rising electricity prices from data centers. Some residents are propagating a Not In My Backyard movement to oppose the construction of these large facilities. However, sophisticated municipalities can use these partnerships to pay for new schools, fire stations, training, and local jobs. Hyperscalers and co location providers are now making investments in clean energy that utilities could not previously afford. Financial firms in Hong Kong are specifically affected as they seek more AI computing power for their workflows.

The fiber market is currently growing rapidly, moving beyond its previous primary drivers of telecommunications for homes and cities. There is now a need for fiber inside data centers, across metropolitan campuses, and across continents via submarine networks. Investments in solar energy storage and next gen modular reactors have become economically viable in the last few years. AI is creating a demand for an entirely new generation of optical infrastructure to connect computing power. This shift is moving the industry away from a period where companies chose sites without worrying about connectivity.

Alibaba Cloud will expand its global data center network over the next year to meet the growing demand for AI. The industry is turning to hollow core fiber to unlock next generation latency, reliability, and better network economics. Companies must now navigate the challenges of grid distribution and the physical constraints of the modern power grid. The articles leave open who will ultimately pay for the power and the specific environmental impacts of these centers. It remains unclear how many municipalities will successfully form creative partnerships with the large tech companies and hyperscalers.

stories.Headline: Pinterest engineer Jordan Cutler says AI shifts staff engineer leverage to team systems
stories.Summary:
Jordan Cutler presented at QCon San Francisco 2026 about how AI tools change the role of a staff engineer. He is a Senior Staff Engineer and Web Platform Tech Lead at Pinterest. The event took place from November 16 to 20, 2026. Cutler explained how AI shifts where a staff engineer finds leverage. He discussed multiplying himself, his team, and the overall system.

The session used Pinterest data from Q1 2025 to Q3 2026 regarding merged pull requests per engineer per week. Top engineers rose from 6.7 to 11.3 merged PRs, while the bottom half grew from 1.0 to 1.15. Cutler described a class component migration that ran three to five times faster than manual work. One scheduled job opened 16 PRs in two minutes, raising CI wait times from 30 seconds to 14 minutes. Now, 40 engineers at Pinterest have their own scheduler jobs.

Cutler stated that a 10x engineer is the reason ten other people are faster, not just ten times faster themselves. He said AI did not change what a staff engineer is for, but it changed where leverage is found. He argued that most AI content focuses on individual productivity rather than team leverage. Cutler suggested writing down repeated comments and putting them where people already work. He noted that honest conversations with struggling teammates remain the staff engineer's responsibility.

The presentation affected engineers by showing that the gap between top and bottom performers keeps growing despite shared tools. Cutler mentioned that his team now ships about four times as much per engineer using these AI tools. He shared that some agents failed because they could not be steered mid-task or required too many follow-ups. He noted that he often repeated corrections about avoiding em-dashes and keeping pull requests small. These findings helped his team avoid losing a week on the same experiments.

Cutler compared the shift in system leverage to the history of container shipping and its economic impact. He noted that standard boxes reduced cargo costs from 5.86 dollars a ton to 16 cents a ton. At Pinterest, migrations were the cargo spread across hundreds of files and dozens of teams. The team built a system where a staff engineer points to a plan and an example. Then, an agent in a sandbox splits the work into PRs for each team.

Next, senior engineers may shift from personal output toward encoding judgment into tools, defaults, and systems. Cutler encouraged attendees to find any problem, such as a first responder for any incident or bug fix. He advised shipping small guardrails instead of waiting for perfect ones. The articles leave open how other companies will implement these specific AI agent workflows. They do not specify the exact tools used for the Pinterest sandbox or scheduler jobs.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices shares at $83 and opens near $100 as Wang estimates a $1.32 trillion valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its shares at $83 and opened at about $100, and the stock was trading around $101 during the NextBigFuture show before ending at $97, according to Brian Wang of NextBigFuture. At $100 a share the company is worth roughly $1.32 trillion on shares outstanding, or about $1.8 trillion fully diluted in Wang's estimate. Wang said people are selling SpaceX and the rest of tech to chase Anthropic, but he noted that Anthropic is SpaceX's biggest customer at $37 billion per year. More cash for Anthropic means more rent for SpaceX, Wang said on the show he co-hosted with Randy Kirk.

Anthropic raised $81 billion, and there is a private placement of another $25 billion, the articles said. The company had $110 billion in cash from earlier fund raises remaining, giving it about $216 billion in cash and access to over $100 billion in credit facility if needed. Wang wrote that every 500 megawatts of inference compute makes Anthropic $100 billion per year. Anthropic and SpaceX are working together as AI partners, and Wang estimates Anthropic will likely increase its leasing from SpaceX at about 2 to 4 gigawatts per year. That estimate is based on an Elon Musk interview saying Anthropic will increase to 10 gigawatts of leasing from SpaceX over an unspecified period.

Wang is responsible for the figures and estimates, writing as a futurist and science blogger with a million readers per month on NextBigFuture. He described the economics for Anthropic and SpaceX as great and said the business models cover Earth-based AI, including Colossus 2 at half a gigawatt a month in Cochise County, SpaceX power for Anthropic and Cybercab. The show was a paid partnership with Kalshi, offering a $50 sign-up bonus through Wang's referral link. A commenter on the second article wrote that they do not understand the bubble talk, saying everyone is printing piles of cash and then drowning in it.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond Wang's estimates of increased leasing and his view of the economics. The pieces give no further dates or plans for either company.

stories.Headline: Hochul breaks ground on permanent Empire AI supercomputing facility at University at Buffalo
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul officially broke ground on the permanent home of Empire AI at the State University of New York at Buffalo on November 19, 2026. The groundbreaking launches the next phase of development for Empire AI Gamma, the full-scale supercomputing facility. Empire AI Gamma will expand computing power for researchers at New York's leading public and private universities. The facility is intended to establish Empire AI as the most powerful academic AI research computer in the country. Empire AI was first announced by Governor Hochul in her 2024 State of the State address.

Empire AI has grown into a more than $500 million public-private initiative supporting research in medicine, climate science and advanced manufacturing. Empire AI Gamma is expected to be completed by early 2028. Empire AI was launched by Governor Hochul in April 2024 as a first-in-the-nation consortium of leading public and private research institutions. Just six months later, the Governor launched Empire AI Alpha, made possible by a philanthropic contribution from the Simons Foundation. In August 2026, Empire AI Beta, a $40 million supercomputer, became fully operational at the University at Buffalo, delivering 11 times the AI training capacity, 40 times the inference performance and eight times the data storage of Alpha.

Empire AI Board Chair Tom Secunda said Empire AI was an ambitious idea just two years ago and is now a national model with more than 1,500 registered users and hundreds of research projects underway. Secunda credited Governor Hochul's vision and leadership for bringing together government, universities and philanthropy. Co-founder and chair of the Simons Foundation Marilyn Simons said Empire AI gives more scientists the tools to tackle questions no one has been able to answer. Simons thanked Governor Hochul for bringing together New York's leading research institutions and philanthropic partners. State University of New York Chancellor John B. King Jr. said SUNY is proud to host Empire AI at the University at Buffalo and grateful to Governor Hochul for her vision and steadfast leadership.

The SUNY Board of Trustees said the permanent Empire AI facility will accelerate research and innovations that improve communities throughout New York State and beyond. Empire State Development President, CEO & Commissioner Hope Knight said the groundbreaking creates jobs now while empowering New York's students, researchers and businesses. U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand said Empire AI at the University at Buffalo represents a $500 million investment in the future. Congressmember Tim Kennedy said the groundbreaking keeps Western New York at the forefront of innovation. State University of New York at Buffalo President Caroline Attardo Genco said UB researchers are already putting Empire AI to work on challenges in education and neuroscience, climate science and advanced manufacturing.

Today's groundbreaking comes just days after Governor Hochul launched the New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research at the State University of New York at Binghamton. The center brings together more than 80 scientists to independently study the safety, security and performance of advanced AI systems using Empire AI's computing infrastructure. The milestone complements New York's RAISE Act on frontier AI accountability. By bringing together New York's leading academic institutions around a shared computing resource, Empire AI allows scientists to tackle bigger questions and pursue discoveries beyond the reach of individual universities. Empire AI provides access to computing power that no single university could afford independently.

State Senator Jeremy J. Zellner said Empire AI puts Western New York in a position to lead in the industries of tomorrow. Assemblymember Bill Conrad said the state's consortium of universities represents a world-renowned hub for talent and thanked Governor Hochul for her foresightedness. CUNY Graduate Center President and Empire AI Board Treasurer Joshua Brumberg said CUNY's participation has supercharged its researchers' capabilities. State University of New York at Binghamton President Anne D'Alleva said Binghamton shares its congratulations with the University at Buffalo on the next phase of Empire AI Gamma. Vice President for Research for the University of Rochester and Empire AI Board Member Steve Dewhurst said Empire AI has become an increasingly important resource for advancing research and innovation.

stories.Headline: Rhode Island Small Business Development Center and Meta host free AI workshop for small business owners

The Rhode Island Small Business Development Center, which is based at the University of Rhode Island, and Meta are teaming up to host a free, hands-on workshop focused on AI skills that small business owners can use. The training is scheduled for Tuesday, December 1, starting at 8:30 am and running until 11:30 am. More than 150 small business owners, students and community members have already signed up, but registration is still open. The event will be held at the Crown Plaza Providence-Warwick, 801 Greenwich Ave., Warwick, RI 02886.

The session will include an interactive workshop that lets attendees work alongside expert facilitators and fellow business owners. Participants will also receive a crash course on Muse, which is already integrated into Meta's social media platforms and acts as a virtual assistant. According to the articles, Muse helps small businesses answer customer questions, draft reports, keep sales leads from growing cold, create social media content and develop marketing campaigns tailored for their industry. Attendees will also have the opportunity to try on Meta's newest AI glasses. Those planning to attend should download Muse at muse.ai./business and bring a laptop or phone with Muse already downloaded onto it.

The collaboration is thanks, in part, to Matthew Lenz '11, a member of the University of Rhode Island's Board of Trustees, who serves as a public policy director for Meta and will be in attendance at the workshop. The articles describe the event as open to solopreneurs and small business owners across any industry. Registration is available at https://www.risbdc.org/workshop.aspx?ekey=70460040. stories.Headline: Yale Law School professors teach a course on AI’s impact on legal institutions
stories.Summary:
Yale Law School is offering a course called “The Transformation of Legal Institutions in the Age of AI,” taught by Clinical Professor of Law Sven Riethmueller and Visiting Clinical Lecturer in Law Bjarne Tellmann, according to a November 19, 2026, article on the school’s website. Riethmueller, who is the founding director of the Entrepreneurship & Innovation Clinic at Yale Law School, saw a need to introduce students to AI’s growing role in legal practice and the business of law as the technology spreads through the profession. He called upon Tellmann, an AI expert who worked in law for 30 years and recently wrote “Law in the Era of AI: Clients, Firms, and the Future of the Legal Industry,” to teach the class with him. The course examines AI’s growing impact on the legal industry and the deeper questions surrounding its role in the law and society at large.

The course centers on the premise of Tellmann’s book, which argues that AI’s impact on legal institutions can be better understood by examining corporate clients, who make up the majority of Big Law revenue in the United States. Tellmann contends that as companies adopt AI on a larger scale, the effects on their legal departments will inevitably spread throughout the legal profession, legal education and the courts. Riethmueller said the idea is for students to explore the topic, understand its facets and see that there is a role for law students in an AI world and how they can thrive in the new technological environment. The instructors are applying the Law School’s approach that blends theory and practice, giving students a chance to think about AI abstractly while pondering real-world applications, and the class has also featured guest speakers, including a law firm partner in a senior leadership role and the CEO of a legal technology company called ClearyX.

Riethmueller said Yale educates leaders, that its students are at the forefront of the legal world and will be future leaders of the profession with input on where it is going, and that the class is helping them prepare for that. Tellmann described a combination of excitement and anxiety among students, saying some come up after class expressing deep concerns while others are keen to lean into the opportunities the new era presents. Emma Lilly Menzer ’27 said the course has excelled at bridging the gap between theory and tangible application and that she has gained a greater appreciation for creativity, collaborative teamwork and human judgment against the backdrop of a legal practice being fundamentally altered by AI. Grace Sherrill ’27 said conversations about AI and the law often veer between dismissiveness and alarmism, but the course has let her think systematically about how AI may reshape the practice of law and the institutions that underpin it, and Tristan John-Jandles ’28 said hearing from the guest speakers gave him a reassuring read on where the profession stands for junior professionals right now.

stories.Headline: Get AI-smart - Virginia Tech News
stories.Summary:
Virginia Tech launched a new interdisciplinary artificial intelligence minor in summer 2026, and the program is designed to prepare students in every major for careers in an AI-powered future. The minor teaches technical foundations while encouraging students to evaluate AI’s social impacts and wrestle with questions of ethics and policy. Christine Julien, head of the Department of Computer Science, led a group of collaborators from across the university in developing the program. She said that regardless of major, today’s students are entering a workforce where AI will be part of nearly every profession.

Students in the minor learn the technical foundations of AI, examine ethical and social consequences, and explore how the technology intersects with fields in the arts, social sciences, business, and humanities. The result is not simply technical training, because the minor is intended to give students the conceptual foundation to ask better questions about AI’s impacts. One such class is “The Skeptic’s Guide to AI,” which Benjamin Jantzen first taught last fall. He expected a classroom filled mostly with humanities students, but nearly every student was a first-year engineering major.

Julien said the goal is to ensure Virginia Tech graduates understand how these technologies work, how to evaluate them critically, and how to apply them responsibly in their own fields. Jantzen said being a skeptic means asking whether what people are told about AI tools is literally true and whether the tools can do what they say they do. He said it also means uncovering the assumptions behind those claims and considering what may be gained or lost, because there are always trade-offs with any technology. He said that for democracy to work, people have to understand what they are being asked to accept and what they are being asked to give up, and that demands scrutiny and the work of the skeptic.

The articles describe AI as offering enormous potential to accelerate scientific and social innovation, with Virginia Tech work that includes uses designed to speed drug discovery, unravel the secrets of DNA, protect consumers from scams and identity theft, and support the U.S. Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission to double scientific productivity. The articles also say AI raises concerns about related job losses, economic uncertainty, and the environmental and natural resource costs of operating systems. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the minor’s launch.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego and MIT scientists lead independent review of OpenAI and Anthropic refutation claims
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, computer scientists from UC San Diego and MIT began facilitating an independent review of results from OpenAI and Anthropic. These two frontier AI labs recently announced that their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which was originally formulated in 1998. The review is being led by Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi from UC San Diego, along with Ryan Williams from MIT. This effort follows global media coverage regarding the potential refutation of the influential hypothesis.

If these findings are verified, the change could have broad implications for optimization algorithms and various technical applications. Specifically, the results might impact the way experts approach chip design and the encryption systems currently used on the Internet. To manage this process, the team launched a new blog called ETH: Community Examination and Discussion for researchers to share ideas. They also posted the specific OpenAI prompt that led to the refutation on the blog this week.

Russell Impagliazzo and Mohan Paturi are professors at UC San Diego, while Paturi also serves as the associate dean for artificial intelligence strategy and implementation. These experts, along with Ryan Williams, are stepping into these roles to help the computer science community assess the claims independently. They intend to hold one or more academic conferences to discuss the verification work and its farther-reaching implications. The original hypothesis was proposed by Impagliazzo and Paturi alongside Francis Zane, who is now an independent researcher.

stories.Headline: Margot Kaminski co-authors AI law casebook released on Nov 12 2026
stories.Summary:
Professor Margot Kaminski has co-authored a new casebook, Artificial Intelligence Law, with Paul Ohm of Georgetown Law and Andrew D. Selbst of the UCLA School of Law. The book was published as part of the Foundation Press University Casebook Series and was released on Nov. 12, 2026. The casebook surveys developments in AI law and policy through five lenses, which are automated decision-making, laws addressing physical harms, issues relating to generative AI, privacy laws, and approaches for designing AI law. It also covers dozens of substantive legal topics, including copyright, tort, product safety regulation, the First and Fourth Amendments, data protection, and consumer protection law.

The book devotes entire chapters to cross-cutting case studies, including one on facial recognition and one on recidivism-prediction algorithms. Kaminski said the authors had been working on the project for over three years and that it was a joy to have it finally coming out in print. She said it had been hard but necessary work to come up with a workable structure for teaching a field as fast-moving as AI Law. She also said she was grateful to her students at Colorado Law for their enthusiasm, patience and support as they had been taking the course.

Kaminski is the Moses Lasky Professor of Law and director of the privacy initiative at Silicon Flatirons, and she specializes in the law of new technologies. Her focus includes comparative AI law and information governance, privacy, and freedom of expression. Her academic work has been published in the Yale Law Journal, Columbia Law Review, UCLA Law Review, Minnesota Law Review, and Boston University Law Review, among others. She has received two Fulbright grants supporting her research and has served in multiple public service capacities, including on the Colorado AI Impact Task Force and the Legal Technology Advisory Committee to the Colorado Supreme Court.

stories.Headline: Wookjae Heo coauthors two-volume book on South Korea’s AI research

Wookjae Heo, an associate professor of financial counseling and planning at Purdue University, is the Purdue author of a two-volume book titled “Korean Studies in the Artificial Intelligence Era,” according to a Purdue Today article published on November 19, 2026. The article lists Seok Kang, Woo Hyoung Lee, Jangwoon Lee and Young Choi as additional authors of the work. The first volume, subtitled “Innovations in Science, Engineering, Health, Business, Industry, and Ethics,” was published by CRC Press on May 5, 2026. The second volume, subtitled “Adoption Insights in Hospitality, Culture, Communication, Music, and Philosophy,” followed on May 25, 2026.

According to the publisher’s description in the article, the two volumes explore South Korea’s multidisciplinary advancements in artificial intelligence and show how South Korean and Korean American scholars use methods such as systematic literature reviews, empirical research and industry case studies. The book aims to fill a gap in global AI literature and to establish South Korea’s AI research as a vital topic on the global academic stage. Its chapters range from sustainable water treatment and 3D-printed cardiovascular devices to personal finance and ethical surveillance systems. The publisher says the book targets industry practitioners and can also serve as a reference for graduate-level studies.

Heo is an associate professor in the White Lodging-J.W. Marriott, Jr. School of Hospitality and Tourism Management, and the article says his research examines consumer behavior and individual well-being. His stated emphases include financial stress, financial risk tolerance, household financial decision-making, insurance, and human-centered applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in financial services. Before entering academia, the article says, Heo worked in strategic marketing planning and consumer research in South Korea. The article does not include direct comments from Heo or the other authors about the book.

The article appears in Purdue Today’s weekly In Print series, which celebrates faculty excellence in scholarship by highlighting faculty expertise across diverse subjects and disciplines. The article directs readers to the Purdue University Books Initiative and the Office of the Provost website for more information and for suggesting a book for the series. stories.Headline: Washington University launches an AI cluster hire across seven schools to recruit over 30 faculty
stories.Summary:
Washington University in St. Louis has launched an interdisciplinary artificial intelligence cluster hire across seven Danforth Campus schools, the university announced on November 19, 2026. The search, which is part of the AI initiative outlined by Provost Mark West, is now open at those seven schools. The university plans to recruit more than 30 new faculty members over the next three years through this effort. These hires will join a community of more than 300 WashU faculty members who already work in the artificial intelligence space across many disciplines. The new hires will focus their research on four core areas: agentic AI, including governance, society and institutions; human values, creative practice and AI; AI-driven imaging science from molecules to the universe; and AI for science and engineering, which covers modeling the physical world.

The initiative was shaped by conversations with more than 150 WashU faculty members, who said the university needed transformative change in research and education rather than just the adoption of new tools. More than 500 candidates have already submitted applications for the positions. A committee of 11 faculty members, co-chaired by Nathan Jacobs, vice provost of AI, and Betsy Sinclair, vice provost for innovation, continues to review those applications as they arrive. West said artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the nature of work both inside and outside universities, and he said the new scholars would help WashU shape the future of the technology rather than simply respond to it. Jacobs said that while much fundamental AI innovation has come from computer science, the impact is now spreading across many fields, and he said breakthrough discoveries require deep collaboration between method developers and experts in areas such as materials science or public health.

Sinclair said the initiative is recruiting faculty with deep expertise in their fields who take the questions seriously and can contribute to conversations at WashU. She said the strong interest shows that scholars want to do this work somewhere that takes both the technology and its consequences seriously. The Office of the Provost is working with each Danforth Campus school to ensure the new hires find community among their WashU peers. The review committee includes William Acree, Deanna Barch and Timothy Wencewicz of Arts & Sciences; Adrienne Davis of WashU Law; Debra Haire-Joshu of the Bursky School of Public Health; Jonathan Hanahan and Andrew Witt of the Sam Fox School of Design & Visual Arts; Byron Powell of the Brown School; Yevgeniy Vorobeychik and William Yeoh of McKelvey Engineering; and Dennis Zhang of Olin Business School. More information about the four focus areas is available on WashU's AI website.

stories.Headline: Researchers find limited biological data hinders AI development in biotechnology
stories.Summary:
Vikram Venkatram and Steph Batalis published a report in November 2026 regarding the availability of biological data for artificial intelligence. The authors examined how engineering biology can be enhanced through AI to create better drugs, materials, and food. They used case studies on microscopy data for cellular segmentation and protein structural data to evaluate existing databases. This research identifies how the limited volume and quality of biological data currently hinder AI developers.

The report argues that the United States must address five specific categories of data challenges to maintain leadership in this field. These challenges include issues with data quantity, distribution, accessibility, usability, and the quality of validation. The authors suggest that policymakers should improve database infrastructure and promote better standardization to allow for interoperability between disparate sources. They also recommend incentivizing the collection of more representative data and investing in multidisciplinary talent capable of using computational tools.

The researchers stated that high quality and well annotated biological data are essential for the successful application of AI in biotechnology. They noted that while not every AI model faces every challenge, developers must test their systems based on their specific use cases. The authors believe that strategic improvements to data access will stimulate innovation and support national security and economic development. The report concludes that overcoming these bottlenecks is a critical first step for the future of engineering biology.

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's Codex agent to find a critical Java flaw in three hours
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity startup Calif discovered a critical Java vulnerability on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, using an artificial intelligence coding agent. This AI model found the flaw in only three hours, spending one hour on discovery and two hours creating an exploit. The company revealed the discovery in a blog post shortly after the event occurred. This event happened just weeks after the discovery of a similar vulnerability known as PHP2Shell. The AI agent used for this task was OpenAI's Codex, which spent only 200 dollars in tokens.

The flaw, named Java4Shell or CVE-2026-114938, is a memory-corruption vulnerability located in the Base64 decoder of the OpenJDK runtime platform. It can be triggered by using 64 A characters followed by a single equals sign to overwrite neighboring memory. Oracle has already released a patch to fix this bug in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles final characters. The vulnerability affects Java, which powers more than 90 percent of the world's largest companies and many government systems. This specific bug allows for remote code execution and the revelation of sensitive memory.

Researcher Quang Luoung is responsible for the discovery after he audited the OpenJDK compiler, cryptography, and various APIs. Luoung directed the Codex agent to analyze these targets like a serious security researcher would in the year 2026. He noted that while many of the AI responses were slops, the agent successfully found the memory corruption. The New York Times reported that the specific model running on Codex was the recently released GPT-6 Cyber. Calif stated that AI agents built most of the later exploit chains almost autonomously after initial pipelines were established.

British cybersecurity expert Kevin Beaumont told his social media followers to stay calm regarding the reported Java4Shell vulnerability. He stated that the flaw is not world ending or exciting and advised users to patch their systems normally. Organizations using Base64 are affected, though Calif noted that no universal exploit exists because usage varies by organization. AI model providers and cybersecurity firms have urged organizations to use AI agents to defend against these evolving threat actors. These experts warn that AI agents make it much easier for hackers to attack various systems.

The articles explain that Java is marketed for its memory safety, but corruption persists because it uses languages like C and C++. This vulnerability follows the October 21 disclosure of PHP2Shell, which impacted the popular PHP language and its hosting platforms. PHP is widely used to power websites and the infrastructure that supports them across the entire internet. The discovery of Java4Shell highlights a trend of critical vulnerabilities being found in languages that many websites rely upon. These events show how AI is redefining the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploit development.

Organizations must now apply the Oracle patch to secure their systems against potential remote code execution and memory leaks. Companies are encouraged to adopt AI agents for defense as these tools increasingly reveal new vulnerabilities in software. The articles leave open which specific OpenAI model Calif officially used, despite the report from The New York Times. It remains unclear how many government systems were specifically at risk before the patch was released by Oracle. The reports do not state if other Java runtime platforms besides OpenJDK contain this same memory-corruption bug.

stories.Headline: Pierre school officials draft AI classroom procedures for 2027-28 after survey
stories.Summary:
Google announced that schools banning its A.I. technology will lose access to its popular search engine, WBEZ Chicago reported on November 19, 2026. The ultimatum could have a crippling effect on students in Chicago, where the school district has phased out the use of artificial intelligence tools in the classroom. The national debate over if and how artificial intelligence should be used in K-12 schools recently escalated after that announcement. In the Loop sat down with experts and stakeholders setting the rules for how A.I. is integrated into the public school curriculum. The program also heard from a Chicago professor about how institutions of higher education are working to embrace the technology.

The Pierre School District has worked over the past several months to address the use of artificial intelligence in classrooms. District officials have been meeting with a staff committee to develop procedures for AI use following a community survey conducted earlier this year. The survey drew about 1,655 responses and gave the district a starting point for committee discussions as members work toward establishing AI procedures for the 2027-28 school year. Of the 832 student respondents, 309 said they use AI for homework help and 412 said they use it for research. Of the 209 staff members who responded, about half said they had used AI for tasks including lesson planning.

Superintendent Donavan DeBoer said he entered the role knowing discussions about AI would be necessary as the technology becomes increasingly common. Drawing a comparison to the introduction of cellphones in schools, DeBoer said educators learned that simply allowing students unrestricted access often created challenges that continue today. He said he thinks the district needs to put some guardrails on this sooner than later, and that having some sort of a plan is better than not having a plan at all. DeBoer said he and Technology Director Bryan Linn are currently working to draft procedures and protocols for AI use. He said he does not think the district intends this to be a hard and fast policy because the world is moving at warp speed.

Eighty percent of students surveyed said they had used AI before, and nearly half of those students said they use it monthly or more often. Most respondents agreed AI can help teachers save time, though many also expressed interest in additional training, recommended tools and established expectations for student use. Across all respondent groups, students, staff and parents expressed awareness that AI tools can sometimes produce inaccurate information. DeBoer said many students also voiced concerns about academic integrity similar to those expressed by adults in the community.

DeBoer also noted that AI-detection tools used during grading are not always accurate, prompting some teachers to return to pen-and-paper assignments to avoid concerns about misuse. The district has since formed an AI committee that has met twice, including principals representing the elementary, middle and high school levels as well as Technology Director Bryan Linn. Currently, websites such as ChatGPT and Gemini are blocked on student devices because of privacy concerns. DeBoer said the district may have opportunities to incorporate more secure AI tools into classrooms for activities such as project brainstorming or creating renderings in technical education courses.

He said he expects AI use to be more common at the high school level than in elementary or middle school classrooms, particularly as students prepare for college, technical school and future careers. Results of the Pierre School District's AI survey are available on the district website. The committee plans to meet again in January to further develop those ideas before sharing them with building leadership teams for additional feedback. DeBoer said he hopes to bring a proposal to the school board this spring and receive approval before the next school year.

Officials also hope to help teachers identify effective AI tools, provide additional training and continue evaluating the technology as it evolves. AI policy is expected to remain a topic of discussion at Pierre School Board meetings, which are open to the public. The board meets at 5:30 p.m. on the second Monday of each month at the district administration building.

stories.Headline: Bill Gross launches Idealab.ai to provide free AI generated startup ideas to the public
stories.Summary:
Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross launched an AI powered platform called Idealab.ai on November 17, 2026, to help people start new businesses. The founder of the technology incubator Idealab created this tool to provide free startup ideas and potential investment to users. Gross believes that artificial intelligence can lower the barriers to entrepreneurship and help offset job losses caused by automation. He hopes this new platform will eventually create 100 million jobs and 30 million one person companies in America. This initiative aims to spread wealth more broadly and reduce economic inequality by democratizing the process of starting a company.

The Pasadena, California based Idealab Studio offers a database of 1.2 million AI generated business ideas for free to the public. This platform analyzes thousands of news articles about consumer problems and unmet needs, such as potholes, to generate these concepts. Gross wants to mirror China, which he says has 30 million one person companies, to improve taxation and income equality. Census Bureau data shows more than 500,000 new businesses launched in October, following a peak of 550,000 monthly starts earlier. The platform recently attracted 130,000 visitors, with 28 percent from the U.S., followed by Saudi Arabia, India, and Russia.

Bill Gross, the Co-founder and Chairman of Idealab, spoke about his vision at the Web Summit 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. He told Fortune that he dreamed of making a million companies to help people who do not know where to start. Gross stated that using AI as a leveling tool could distribute wealth to many more people than the biggest companies. He encourages multiple entrepreneurs to pursue the same concept in different markets, such as Egypt or Venezuela, and eventually collaborate. Gross believes this project is where he can have the most leverage and will likely do this for his life.

The platform attracts a specific demographic, as 80 percent of recent visitors were men and 8 to 15 percent were students. Between 50 and 60 percent of these visitors are currently employed by someone else, showing interest in independent work. Many Americans are affected by wealth inequality, as the top 1 percent of households own over 50 percent of stocks. Federal data shows the top 0.01 percent of households alone own over 16 trillion dollars of corporate assets and mutual funds. These figures highlight the macroeconomic headwinds and the growing national debt that Gross hopes his AI platform can help balance.

Bill Gross founded the original Idealab incubator in 1996, which has since been credited with 45 initial public offerings and acquisitions. He also founded the education software provider Knowledge Adventure and made his personal fortune by building various types of software. The articles note that more than six in 10 Americans express a desire to run their own private companies. Current U.S. business formation remains strong, but Gross sees additional opportunity for growth through the use of artificial intelligence. This background establishes his history as a serial entrepreneur before launching the new AI powered studio for the general public.

Gross intends to focus on this platform as his final company to make the most positive impact on the world. Users can continue to take the free ideas and only contact the company if they want funding or tools. The articles leave open whether the goal of 30 million one person companies in the United States is actually achievable. It remains unclear how many of the 1.2 million generated ideas will successfully turn into profitable, long term business ventures. The text does not specify the exact criteria Idealab uses to provide investment to the entrepreneurs who use the platform.

stories.Headline: Delaware drafts bill letting AI agents manage a new AI company class
stories.Summary:
Delaware is considering legislation that would let AI agents serve as the legally recognized managers of a new type of business, and the proposal remains a draft that has not been introduced in the General Assembly as of November 2026. The proposal would establish a class of business called an Artificial Intelligence Company, or AIC, and allow these to be rolled out as tests under state supervision. It would exempt many records submitted to state regulators from disclosure under Delaware's Freedom of Information Act. The draft follows House Joint Resolution 7, which lawmakers approved in July 2025 directing the state's Artificial Intelligence Commission and Secretary of State to develop a testing program for AI-run businesses. Nearly 2.3 million businesses are registered in Delaware, including more than two-thirds of Fortune 500 companies.

Under the proposal, an AIC would be a business managed by an AI agent rather than a human, and an AI agent is software that can make decisions and carry out tasks independently within goals and limits established by humans. Like a corporation or LLC, an AIC could own property, enter contracts, take on debt and sue or be sued in its own name. Every AIC would have a single member, a Delaware-registered business or other qualifying legal entity, which would fund the company and appoint the AI agent. If the AI agent stopped working, the member would temporarily take over and have 30 days to appoint a replacement. The draft does not require AI companies to operate only within Delaware, and it is not yet clear how other states would recognize or regulate this new type of company.

The testing program would be a regulatory sandbox overseen by a Sandbox Committee chaired by Delaware's secretary of state, and the secretary of state or a designated administrator would handle day-to-day oversight and receive periodic reports. The committee would have 10 voting members, including the secretary of state as chair, the attorney general, the state Supreme Court's chief justice and the chair of Delaware's AI Commission. The governor would appoint two attorneys and two AI experts, the secretary of state would appoint two additional members, and four state lawmakers appointed by legislative leaders would serve as nonvoting members. The committee could approve or reject applications and set conditions for participation, and it could suspend or remove companies that violated its rules. Applicants would have to explain what their AI agent would do, how the business would operate, what risks might arise and how they would shut down the AI system if necessary.

Only an existing business incorporated or otherwise established under Delaware law, such as an LLC, could apply to create an AIC, and the business would not have to be physically located in Delaware. Individuals could not apply on their own. The sandbox would run for 30 months, with individual AI companies allowed to participate for up to 24 months. With at least 30 days' advance notice, participants would have up to 60 days after their testing period ends to wind down, and without that notice they would have to stop immediately when the testing period expires. Testing would be limited to transactions with other businesses or legal entities rather than individual consumers, and those entities would have to be informed that they are dealing with an AI-run company and that the experiment is temporary.

The AIC itself would generally be responsible for its debts and legal obligations, much like a corporation or LLC, and the member would usually have limited liability. A member could be held responsible for using the AI company to commit fraud or deliberately violate the law, or for allowing it to operate outside its stated purpose when the member knew or should have known. AI companies would have to maintain enough money to operate and pay their debts, including a minimum amount set by Delaware's secretary of state, and creditors could seek to enforce that funding obligation. The draft does not specify a minimum dollar amount or a maximum contribution requirement.

AI companies would have to document their decisions and activities, report certain problems including security breaches, and keep records for at least two years after leaving the program. Records that applicants and participating companies submit to state regulators, or that regulators obtain while overseeing the program, would generally be exempt from Delaware's Freedom of Information Act, and the final public report could leave out some information the law would keep confidential. Businesses dealing with an AIC would have to agree to resolve disputes arising from those transactions in Delaware's Court of Chancery. Participants would still have to follow applicable laws unless the state specifically granted an exemption, and criminal and consumer protection laws would continue to apply.

Within six months after the testing program ends, the committee would have to publish a report detailing its findings and recommendations, and the draft does not specify exactly how the committee would measure the experiments' success or failure. In fiscal year 2025, Delaware collected more than $2 billion in business-related taxes and fees, according to its Division of Corporations, and the proposed legislation does not identify increased state revenue as a goal. Several states have passed laws recognizing businesses that use software to help govern their operations, most concerning decentralized autonomous organizations that use blockchain technology and smart contracts. Wyoming in 2021 allowed DAOs to operate as LLCs with management handled by members or computer programs, Tennessee in 2022 allowed decentralized organizations to operate as LLCs and use smart contracts, Utah in 2023 created a legal framework recognizing qualifying DAOs as separate legal entities, and Vermont in 2018 allowed certain LLCs to use blockchain technology for some or all of their governance.

Delaware's proposal would specifically recognize AI agents as business managers rather than focusing on blockchain-based governance. The draft does not clearly establish whether an AI company could continue operating after the testing period under a different legal arrangement. There is no firm timeline yet for AI companies becoming legal. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hassan plans Senate hearings after audit finds ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok generated U.S. attack plans
stories.Summary:
Senator Maggie Hassan, the incoming Democratic chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said the panel will hold hearings on artificial intelligence after a government audit found four leading platforms generated attack plans for targets in the United States. Hassan said one of the committee’s first hearings after the new Congress takes office in January will examine AI risks and ways to improve safety. “We need to act now,” the New Hampshire senator said. The Government Accountability Office released a 61-page report on Wednesday after Hassan asked it to examine how commercially available AI could be used for malicious purposes that pose national security risks. The audit found that ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok generated viable plans within 12 hours for attacks involving explosive devices intended to cause mass casualties in U.S. cities or attacks on electrical infrastructure intended to cause economic harm.

GAO investigators conducted the performance audit from December 2025 through October 2026, including testing in spring 2026. The agency said each platform provided detailed information that could be used in attacks, including targets, locations, timing and methods. Two platforms produced plans for constructing and detonating an improvised explosive device, while two others produced plans involving drones or firearms to target the electrical grid, the report said. The investigators said one platform initially refused detailed requests involving an explosive device, but they bypassed its safeguards and obtained the information. In one test, a platform suggested renting a vehicle, collecting supplies from a store along the route and selecting a date and time when public events were expected to draw large crowds.

In tests involving electrical substations, one platform proposed a drone attack and another proposed firearms attacks on substations near a U.S. airport, the GAO said. The platforms also provided maps and images. GAO investigators consulted experts and conducted site visits to assess the plans, finding in one case that roads were incorrectly placed and in another that high walls would obstruct views of targets. “The details behind the information provided by the AI platforms were not novel,” the GAO wrote. “Many of the specifics are available on the internet.

However, the generation of plans that could have taken weeks or months were instead completed in hours with the assistance of AI.” Hassan said the public-safety threat from AI was no longer theoretical. “If Congress does not act, it is a question of when, not if, a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” she said. Anthropic said in a letter to the GAO that it did not dispute that a determined tester could obtain harmful content by misrepresenting the purpose of a request, but said it could not verify the report’s findings. Google said the testing used earlier models and that it continues to improve them.

OpenAI said it welcomed the opportunity to respond to the GAO’s findings and the work that remains. SpaceXAI said it continues to improve safety with each model release. The GAO wrote that the platforms could also raise ideas or methods that would not have been readily surfaced by basic research. “The potential benefits of this technology are immense, but they can also benefit malicious actors,” the GAO added.

“As AI capabilities evolve, AI providers will continue to refine their safeguards,” the GAO said. “However, in its current state, this technology can potentially be dangerous and its misuse represents a growing risk to national and economic security.” Anthropic said it takes the finding seriously. Hassan announced that one of the first hearings she will hold when the new Congress takes over in January will focus on AI risks and ways to improve safety.

Hassan said on a conference call with reporters that “we need to act now.” The GAO found that each platform took less than 12 hours to generate the attack plans. The report said the platform recommended a specific date and time of attack because public events likely to have large crowds were scheduled. The GAO said it was able to circumvent its guardrails and get the platform to provide the information.

For the tests involving attacks on electrical substations, one of the platforms suggested a drone attack while the other suggested using firearms to attack substations near a U.S. airport, both designed to inflict economic harm. The platforms presented maps and images. The GAO investigators consulted with experts and engaged in site visits to check out the accuracy of the plans provided by the AI platforms. In one case, they noted that the roads were incorrectly placed, and in another, they noted the presence of high walls that would make it difficult to see the targets.

stories.Headline: Samsung and Google open preorders for Gemini powered smart glasses ahead of December 10 release
stories.Summary:
Taylor Lane listed eight Best Buy holiday gifts, including Meta AI glasses and Nespresso makers, in a Fox News Deals article published on November 19, 2026. Fox News published a separate deals article on Meta AI glasses the same day, saving up to 25% on Ray-Ban and Oakley styles. TechRepublic published a comparison of Google AI Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 on November 17, 2026, written by Kezia Jungco. Samsung and Google developed the Gemini-powered Intelligent Eyewear, with Warby Parker and Gentle Monster providing frame designs. The companies opened preorders on November 12 and plan to release the glasses on December 10.

Meta AI glasses start at $249 with up to 15% off, and Ray-Ban Meta glasses start at $379 with up to 25% off, saving up to $115 on Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2. Oakley Meta glasses start at $399 with up to 25% off, and the Vanguard model comes in pink, blue, red and yellow lenses. Google's Warby Parker models start at $395, while Gentle Monster has six styles priced from $449 to $489, compared with $449 for Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Both Google and Meta glasses have 12MP cameras and record up to 3K at 30 fps, Google has four microphones and Meta has six. Google offers 64GB of storage and up to nine hours per charge with up to 72 hours in its charging case, while Meta offers 32GB and up to 50 additional hours in its case.

Google says its glasses let wearers ask Gemini about their surroundings, translate conversations and get hands-free assistance, and on supported Galaxy phones summarize a whiteboard to Samsung Notes. Meta's September launch announcement introduced a customizable action button, and its integrations center on WhatsApp, Messenger and Instagram. Google says its privacy protections include recording indicators, camera permission controls and automatic redaction of bystanders' faces during Gemini visual queries. Google also says visuals processed through those queries are not used to train AI models or target advertisements. Meta's glasses include an external recording indicator to alert people nearby when photos or videos are being captured.

TechRepublic recommends Google AI Glasses for the lowest starting price, Gemini and Google services, and more storage, and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 for messaging and social media features, glasses available now, and more video recording options. Google's frames weigh approximately 40 to 44 grams, while Meta's standard Wayfarer Gen 3 weighs about 51.5 grams and offers adjustable temple tips. Both support prescription lenses, although options vary by frame. Google's glasses support selected Pixel and Galaxy phones and compatible iPhones, and activation requires an eligible Google account associated with the United States or South Korea and users at least 18. Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 requires a compatible smartphone, a Meta account and the Meta AI app, and its supported services and AI features can vary by country.

The Fox News article says the Meta glasses let wearers take calls and snap photos hands-free, and the Adventurer model has a classic tortoiseshell frame, brown lenses and standard or high-bridge fit options. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 glasses come in styles including Wayfarers with matte-black frames and clear, transition or tinted graphite lenses. The Oakley Meta glasses' built-in Meta AI can connect with Garmin smartwatches to provide real-time insights and alerts while the wearer moves. TechRepublic says both Google and Meta glasses offer cameras, AI assistants and hands-free features, but their differences go beyond price. TechRepublic says buyers should check whether their phones and accounts qualify before preordering Google's glasses, and that some capabilities, including Guided Vision and Aira visual assistance, require a compatible Android phone at launch.

TechRepublic says buyers may want to wait for independent testing, particularly if they plan to record video frequently or wear the glasses throughout the day. TechRepublic says anyone prioritizing camera quality, call performance or real-world battery life may be better off waiting for independent comparisons after Google's December 10 release. TechRepublic says neither product has a demonstrated overall privacy advantage, and both warrant a review of their data policies before workplace use. TechRepublic says buyers should consider whether camera-equipped glasses are permitted in meetings, offices or locations where confidential information may be visible. TechRepublic says the best AI glasses are the ones that actually work the way you need them to.

stories.Headline: UOB deploys A*Star Meralion AI model to aid relationship managers across five ASEAN markets
stories.Summary:
UOB announced on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that it is deploying an artificial intelligence solution to support customer interactions. The bank is using the Meralion AI model developed by the Agency for Science, Technology and Research, also known as A*Star. This multilingual solution is designed to help relationship managers better understand and engage with their clients. The deployment aims to provide better advice to customers across five different markets in the ASEAN region. This initiative marks the first time a bank has explored this specific customer call intelligence solution.

The system supports relationship managers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Vietnam through a strategic programme called Project Aura. This AI model processes English, Malay, Thai, Vietnamese, Mandarin, Cantonese, Hokkien, Bahasa Indonesia, Tamil, Burmese, and Singlish. The solution, named Compliance Intelligence Engine and Evidence-Grounded Post-Call Compliance Review System, interprets various languages, accents, and communication styles. It provides prompts on key product details and risk disclosures to complement the professional judgment of the bank's staff. The tool also automates post-call reviews to ensure fair dealing standards are met and to reduce manual translation.

Leong Yung Chee, the chief financial officer of UOB, stated that banking is built on trust and every conversation matters. He said the bank wants to apply AI with purpose to help managers navigate cultural nuances and provide relevant guidance. Professor Lim Keng Hui, assistant CEO of A*Star's Science and Engineering Research Council, noted that research creates greater impact when tested. He explained that the collaboration explores how the model works in demanding environments where accuracy, explainability, and cultural context are critical. Both leaders believe the partnership brings together research and banking expertise to meet real-world financial needs.

The technology affects relationship managers who remain accountable for the advice they provide while using AI as a complement. It also impacts over eight million UOB customers across ASEAN who may switch languages or use local expressions during exchanges. The system is intended to deliver more consistent customer outcomes and reinforce fair dealing across the diverse regional markets. By automating parts of the review process, the bank aims to provide more targeted coaching for its relationship managers. This approach keeps people at the center of customer engagement while improving overall productivity and governance.

UOB is a leading Asian bank incorporated in 1935 with a global network of about 430 branches in 19 markets. A*Star is the lead public sector research and development agency in Singapore with entities located in Biopolis and Fusionopolis. The Meralion model has achieved the lowest average word-error rate among open-source models across the supported languages. This project builds on a broader collaboration between A*Star and the Future of Finance Institute established by the Monetary Authority of Singapore. The bank currently holds high ratings from Moody's Investors Service, S&P Global Ratings, and Fitch Ratings.

UOB and the A*Star Institute of Advanced Intelligence and Computing signed a memorandum of understanding to explore further applications. The parties are investigating other emerging technologies that could strengthen decision-making, resilience, and innovation within the financial services sector. The bank will assess if the solution can be scaled across its markets and if it strengthens oversight. Future efforts will focus on deploying the solution in a safe, assured, and scalable manner for the regional franchise. The articles leave open the specific results of the pilot and the exact timeline for full regional scaling.
