stories.Headline: Scholars Keller and Kilg argue personifying AI undermines human agency and urge human rights assessments for AI
stories.Summary:
Brazilian legal scholar Clara Iglesias Keller and German AI expert Marie Kilg spoke at an online session of the Bonn Symposium, organised by the Germany-based Development and Peace Foundation in September 2026, where they argued that personifying artificial intelligence undermines human agency and that the conversation should focus instead on the real people responsible for the technology. They stressed the need to discuss the concentration of power in the hands of a few private companies, and they described AI as a multidimensional tool embedded in society, politics, economics and science that is increasingly shaping decision-making and social interaction. The article says AI regulation is currently composed mainly of voluntary frameworks rather than binding mandates, with legislation falling behind and allowing Big Tech to fill the governance vacuum. Private corporations are dictating the rules of the AI conversation and granting themselves the responsibility of abiding by them.

Keller and Kilg called for the public sector to join in and steer the private sector towards democratic values of transparency and accountability, and they argued that the widespread approach to digital governance based on risk assessment is limited and obscures the political construction of the technology. They are therefore calling for AI technologies to be subject to a human rights assessment obligation. Keller stressed that people need to know what could happen and what their rights are where technology and inequalities overlap, while Kilg said the history of product regulation could be useful in building an AI framework based on the idea of rights. Kilg described repositories in charge of monitoring and creating best practice baselines, such as the African Observatory on Responsible Artificial Intelligence, as a positive first step, although an institution for reinforcing compliance with existing policies is still lacking in many places.

Keller sees little space for global governance on the matter, while Kilg contends that this is a positive thing, arguing that meaningful AI governance cannot be globally imposed and must be attentive to each country's public-sector capabilities and socioeconomic asymmetries. Kilg favours regional and multilateral agreements that foster a broader diversity of approaches, and she points to gaps in digital and AI readiness across nations that may lead to economic, social and political shifts disproportionately affecting vulnerable communities and lower-income countries. The article says Big Tech is strengthening its political lobby while states fear regulation would impede innovation and market competition. It concludes that AI is a tool built by humans for human purposes, that every aspect of it is man-made, and that human rules and obligations therefore apply.

Articles.Title: AI is man-made and should be subject to human regulation | D+C - Development + Cooperation

stories.headline_source: AI is man-made and should be subject to human regulation | D+C - Development + Cooperation

stories.Headline: Lloyds Banking Group publishes a practical guide on responsible AI
stories.Summary:
Lloyds Banking Group published a practical guide on responsible artificial intelligence on 19 November 2026, drawing on its own experience of using the technology at scale across a business with 28 million customers. The guide, titled Responsible AI: A practical guide for organisations, shares what the bank calls real-world experiences and real-life examples of responsible AI in practice, including AI that assists customers and the guardrails built around it. Suzanne Brink, the bank's head of responsible AI, said the technology should not be the goal in itself for organisations. She said the bank always starts by asking not only whether it can use AI but whether it should, and how it can do so responsibly. The guide sets out three key lessons for organisations: embedding responsible AI expertise from the start, testing controls and guardrails rigorously and monitoring AI after deployment, and making evidence-based decisions that balance the value of AI against its risks.

It draws on the bank's work introducing an AI-powered investing assistant on the Scottish Widows app, where responsible AI specialists and the product team identified potential risks and embedded responsible AI into the design. In January the bank announced plans to train all 67,000 employees in AI use during the year through its AI Academy, and in a June update it said around 65,000 staff had taken 400,000 courses. The bank is also training 200 senior leaders with training provider Cambridge Spark to embed AI skills in the leadership ranks. Brink said the bank decided to share its learnings because many organisations are grappling with the same questions, and she described responsible AI as a way to give organisations confidence to pursue opportunities where AI can genuinely add value while keeping the trust of the people it serves. She said responsible AI is not about holding back innovation.

In July the bank said all customer interactions will be supported by AI by 2030 as part of its Accelerate 2030 Strategy, which targets £100m in value generation and aims to cut another £2bn in costs over four years, on top of the same amount over the previous four years. That earlier saving contributed to a 23% increase in profits, which reached £4.2bn in the first half of 2026. The bank's own Financial institutions sentiment survey for 2025 found that 59% of surveyed firms reported AI-driven productivity gains in the past 12 months, compared with 32% in the 2024 survey. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the bank's stated targets of all staff being AI-literate by the end of 2026 and AI supporting every customer interaction by 2030.

Articles.Title: Lloyds Bank shares learnings from doing artificial intelligence at scale

stories.headline_source: Lloyds Bank shares learnings from doing artificial intelligence at scale

stories.Headline: Mayor Mamdani and Chancellor Samuels launch a 70-member schools technology coalition
stories.Summary:
Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani and New York City Public Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels announced on November 17, 2026 the launch of the Technology in Schools Coalition. The coalition is a group of 70 educators, parent leaders, students, elected officials, advocates, union partners and experts. It marks a continued pivot away from reliance on technology-based instruction in the nation's largest public school system. The announcement follows a September moratorium on generative AI for students in grades 2-K through eighth grade. The group will provide recommendations by the end of June on how New York City Public Schools should or should not engage in technology-based instruction.

Those recommendations will inform policy decisions for next school year. The coalition's first meeting will be in December. The group will explore whether research supports some targeted use of AI, such as learning a second language. The September moratorium was implemented under the 2026-2027 AI and screen time policy. The coalition is a response to concerns from parents, educators and elected officials, as well as a growing body of research on the dangers of excessive screen use and the cognitive offloading allowed by AI.

Mamdani said a strong education is about human connection, curiosity and the ability to work through difficult problems independently. He said there is no substitute for a great teacher or the friendships that help young people learn and grow. He said the coalition will help guide the approach to these questions and ensure decisions are shaped by the people who know schools best. Samuels said the September policy set a new standard for protecting students' data, learning and critical thinking skills. Samuels said the coalition will let families, educators and partners directly shape AI and screen time policy for next school year and beyond.

Councilman Eric Dinowitz, Education Chair, said any technology in classrooms must be backed by peer-reviewed research and called the coalition a good step. Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, Chair of the Committee on Technology, said technology cannot be blindly implemented and called the coalition the community-centered approach they had called for. NYS Senator Kristen Gonzalez, Chair of the Committee on Internet & Technology, said tools not properly stewarded can replicate bias, exacerbate inequality and lead to unknown risks for data privacy and learning outcomes. Council Member Rita Joseph, Chair of the Higher Education Committee, said she spent more than two decades in the classroom and that a screen cannot replace productive struggle. Assemblyman Bobby Carroll, Chair of the Committee on Libraries and Education Technology, said AI must not undermine teachers, evidence-based curriculum and human connection.

Alan Ong, Chair of the Panel for Educational Policy, said appropriate technology use has been a main area of concern and feedback raised by parents and school communities to the Panel. The announcement builds on previous work by Mamdani and Samuels, including developing and instituting the nation's most aggressive policy on Artificial Intelligence. That work includes launching free, high-quality 2-K for more than 2,000 families, expanding to 10,000 additional families next year. It includes continued investments in high-quality 3-K and pre-K, saving families thousands of dollars per year, and continued progress on reducing class size through focused planning and a $1.5B billion investment. It also includes raising teacher pay, dramatically improving procurement practices, investing nearly $70 million into preschool education for students with disabilities, and expanding New York City Reads and New York City Solves.

The coalition will provide its recommendations by the end of June, and those recommendations will inform policy decisions for next school year. The group's first meeting will be in December. The coalition will explore whether research supports some targeted use of AI, such as learning a second language. The articles do not name the 70 members of the coalition. The articles do not say what the recommendations will cover beyond technology-based instruction and AI and screen time policy.

stories.Headline: California researchers find little evidence of widespread AI job displacement but warn effects may be hidden
stories.Summary:
A Public Policy Institute of California blog post published on November 19, 2026, by Sarah Bohn, Julien Lafortune and Daniel Payares-Montoya examined what the state's next governor should understand about artificial intelligence and jobs, reporting that nearly half of employed Californians expect AI to reduce available jobs while about one in three worry it could cost them their job or cut their hours or pay. The authors wrote that current evidence does not support widespread AI-driven job displacement in California, since employment has not changed much for workers whose tasks overlap most with AI capabilities and unemployment claims have not surged among them since public AI tools were released in 2022. They cautioned that aggregate trends may hide effects on specific occupations, regions or demographic groups, noting that unemployment claims for college-educated and Bay Area workers in the most affected jobs rose shortly after ChatGPT was released. They added that 55 percent of California workers in the most AI-exposed jobs hold a bachelor's degree or higher while 45 percent do not, and that the least exposed occupations are mostly low-wage and employ workers with a high school diploma or less at 68 percent.

The post reported that California is home to 33 of the top 50 AI companies according to Forbes, and that these companies added almost 30,000 jobs between 2022 and 2026 according to PitchBook data, some of which may be located in other states. It said growth in AI-related jobs in California has been 8.3 percent since 2022 compared with 0.5 percent statewide, and that AI adoption varies by firm size and industry, at 37 percent of large US firms versus less than 20 percent of small businesses and 40 percent in information and professional services versus less than 20 percent in manufacturing or retail. It also said evidence suggests the buildout of data centers, computing equipment and software may support over 300,000 manufacturing jobs nationally, though there is little indication so far of an uptick in California construction and manufacturing jobs. The authors wrote that how businesses adopt AI will shape the labor market, that AI will likely transform jobs or create new roles whether or not it replaces them, and that access to AI tools and opportunities to learn will matter for workers.

The authors said the range of possible effects calls for broad workforce policy focus, with thoughtful planning around scenarios that consider new jobs and businesses that may emerge along with how others may decline. They wrote that California's education and training systems may need to help young people prepare for modernized careers and give working adults chances to update their skills, and that state systems supporting workers may need to serve a broader range of Californians than in the past. Beyond retraining, they said, ensuring a robust unemployment insurance system and considering alternatives such as wage insurance may help ease labor market disruption. For the next governor, they wrote, a central question will be whether California's institutions can respond to changing employer needs and worker opportunities, and tracking hiring, earnings, career entry and layoffs can help identify pain points, though aggregate economic data may be slow to detect emerging trends. They said incorporating real-time insights from business leaders, workers, and education and training providers will be important to design timely policy, and that PPIC will continue to monitor AI's impact across business and the workforce.

Articles.Title: What California’s Next Governor Needs to Know About AI and Jobs - Public Policy Institute of California

stories.Headline: Indian AI startups raise $1.6 billion as US AI firms raise $329.2 billion
stories.Summary:
US AI-native companies raised $329.2 billion across 981 equity funding rounds between January 1 and November 3, 2026, according to Tracxn data. Indian AI-native companies raised $1.6 billion across 90 rounds during the same period. The artificial intelligence boom has put India's startup ecosystem in a strange fix, the article states. India is pitching itself as an attractive technology investment destination while global venture capital concentrates around American AI companies. For Indian AI startups, the challenge is convincing investors their businesses can deliver growth, commercial returns and technological differentiation.

India's startup equity funding was $11.7 billion across 1,362 equity rounds between January 1 and November 3, 2026. That compares with $11.2 billion across 2,180 rounds during the corresponding period in 2025. Early-stage funding covering Series A and B rounds increased from $3.7 billion to $5.1 billion. Seed funding declined from $1.3 billion to $873 million, while late-stage funding remained broadly stable at $5.7 billion against $5.8 billion. Tracxn data shows Indian startup funding touched $39 billion in 2021 across over 2,000 rounds.

Siddharth Pai, Founding Partner at 3one4 Capital, says caution around AI has been in the market for a while because the business case for AI has lagged the industry's growth. He says three AI companies, SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, will raise more capital in their IPOs than the US markets have in the past 15 years. He says Anthropic cut its valuation expectations from $2 trillion to $1.4 trillion. Pai traces the difficult funding environment to 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and says India is yet to reach the high watermark of 2021's fundraising. He says India has the capital for its AI ambitions but lacks the policies to channel this capital.

Supratik Shankar, Co-founder of AI-native data intelligence platform Dview, says confidence in the technology and confidence in a particular valuation are two different things. He cites US Federal Reserve figures showing productivity grew about 1.5% a year from 1973 to 1995 and about 3.3% a year from 1995 to 2003. Bhaskar Majumdar, Founder and Managing Partner of Unicorn India Ventures, says US AI startups reach $10 million ARR within six months of launching. He says the rush for capital in US AI is having a knock-on effect on follow-on investments in India. Pai says early-stage AI businesses need strong customer traction and repeat business, and cautions they risk having their offerings absorbed into larger platforms.

Pai points to pension funds, provident funds, insurance companies and banks facing unfavourable regulations when investing in alternative investment funds that finance startups. He calls for reforms to pricing for foreign investors, tax-free share swaps, a shift to residence-based taxation and better taxation of employee stock ownership plans. Shankar says a company can build valuable intellectual property in its data architecture, domain logic, evaluations, integrations and workflow execution. He says investors will examine compute costs, implementation time and effort, dependencies, renewals and margins after deployment. Pai expects it to take another two to four quarters for this to register with investors and for more capital to flow back into the system.

The article was published on November 19, 2026, and updated the same day. It was written by Ridhika Basnet, a journalist covering the real-world impact of artificial intelligence. The article carries the headline that America is flooding AI with billions while Indian startups fight for survival. It states the disparity in funding amounts between US and Indian AI companies raises concerns for emerging markets. It states market caution persists due to the lagging business case for AI compared to its rapid growth.

Articles.Title: America is Flooding AI With Billions. Indian Startups are Fighting for Survival - Analytics India Magazine

stories.Headline: South Korean authorities tighten exam security after student uses AI and miniature cameras to cheat
stories.Summary:
A student surnamed Han cheated on a national tax accountant certification exam this year. He confessed on Sunday to using generative AI and electronic devices for the fraud. Han used a miniature camera to photograph questions and send them to AI. He then checked the answers on a smartphone to secure the top score. Police say he previously tested this setup during a CPA exam for refinement.

The government will inspect glasses for hidden cameras during Thursday's College Scholastic Ability Test. Officials will check clothing and personal belongings for concealed devices and deploy more supervisors. These measures affect 551,864 students sitting for the 2027 exam nationwide. The government aims to prevent the use of AI powered smart glasses and phones. Miniature cameras are currently sold on Chinese online shopping websites as of November 15.

The government vowed to crack down on cheating during the upcoming college entrance exam. Park Ji-hyun criticized the government for delaying regulations under the pretext of technological advancement. She stated that this neglect now undermines fairness in society and haunts the government. Professor Lim So-yeon said laws and regulations should be used to protect the society. She warned that people should not assume that technology is inherently neutral.

Women's rights advocates say the cheating crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras. Heo Min-sook said the situation exposes an ugly truth about how society views women. Online commenters called the controversy a disaster of the lawmakers' own making. They claimed lawmakers worked hard to make the country a paradise for illegal filming. These advocates argue that the devices could have faced tighter controls years ago.

Legislative efforts to regulate disguised cameras began in 2015 during the 19th National Assembly. Rep. Chang Byoung-wan introduced bills in 2015 and 2017 that expired without any passage. Rep. Jin Sun-mee proposed registration for the sale and possession of cameras in 2017. Similar bills were introduced in 2018, 2021, and 2022, but none of them passed. These proposals aimed to stop illegal filming, known as molka, which targets women.

Public petitions in 2018 and 2021 gathered over 200,000 and 230,000 signatures for camera bans. The Blue House pledged to participate in legislative discussions in August 2021, but failed. A legislative specialist in 2021 argued for a balance between regulation and industrial growth. The articles leave open whether new laws will finally pass after this scandal. They do not state if the government will now ban miniature camera sales.

Articles.Title: Oh, now you care: Women's rights activists say AI cheating crisis reflects years of ignored warnings about hidden cameras

stories.Headline: IRS advisory council urges IRS to expand AI guidance for tax practitioners
stories.Summary:
The IRS Advisory Council recommended in its annual report, released Wednesday, November 19, 2026, that the IRS revisit and expand recent guidance on tax practitioners' use of artificial intelligence, saying existing standards for preparer conduct and taxpayer information were not developed with modern AI-assisted tools and workflows in mind. The 37-member council said in the report that AI is increasingly used in ways affecting how practitioners receive, process, analyze, transmit, and store taxpayer information, yet there appears to be little or no direct guidance addressing these uses. The council recommended that the IRS seek comments on guidance issued this year by the Office of Professional Responsibility, reissue that guidance after reviewing the comments, and expand AI guidance to all preparer tax identification number holders rather than limiting it to practitioners subject to Treasury Circular 230. The recommendation arrives as tax practitioners and regulators debate how existing professional standards apply to rapidly evolving AI technology, and the AI proposals were among 33 in the annual report. IRSAC also pointed to uncertainty about how AI vendors handle taxpayer information, saying the taxpayer and preparer may not fully understand how an AI provider receives, stores, uses, or retains information submitted to the system.

The council said increasing AI use creates a gap in the IRS's model security guidance concerning vendor selection, data handling, access controls, retention, and other risks specific to AI-enabled systems. The report repeatedly emphasized the need for technology-based solutions as the agency operates with a substantially smaller workforce, saying digital tools, analytics, and automation can improve productivity and direct scarce personnel to higher-value work but do not eliminate the need for experienced employees to resolve complex cases, protect taxpayer rights, and administer a changing tax code. IRSAC also recommended that the IRS create a business version of its Identity Protection PIN program to help combat employer identification number theft, urging the agency to pilot an EIN Protection PIN or similar filing authorization tool and expand alerts in Business Tax Account. The council said businesses lack a protection comparable to the IP PIN available to individual taxpayers, calling business identity theft a persistent tax-administration risk in which a stolen or misused EIN can support an unauthorized return, refund or credit claim, information return, or account change. IRSAC urged the IRS to create a public-facing tracker for tax-related identity theft cases, since victims now can obtain updates only by phone or correspondence, and it proposed a tool modeled on the IRS's Where's My Application for Tax-Exempt Status system.

Average resolution times for identity theft cases exceed 15 months, IRSAC said, noting an inventory of roughly 387,000 unresolved cases. The council also urged the IRS to increase efforts to combat ghost preparers, improve processing of penalty and interest abatement requests, simplify Form W-4, enhance worker-classification determinations, expand small business tax literacy efforts, and study elective withholding by partnerships on behalf of domestic partners. The AICPA has raised concerns about portions of the OPR guidance regarding practitioner fees, and OPR director Thomas Curtin said at last week's AICPA National Tax Conference that additional guidance is forthcoming. The article does not say when the IRS will respond to the council's recommendations or whether it will adopt them.

Articles.Title: Tax practitioners need updated AI guidance, council tells IRS - Journal of Accountancy

stories.Headline: Scott Carr urges accounting firms to adopt AI tools for HR operations
stories.Summary:
Scott Carr, owner of Farmhouse Networking in Grants Pass, Oregon, published an article on CPA Practice Advisor on November 19, 2026, arguing that accounting firms should adopt practical AI tools in their human resources operations. He wrote that AI tools built for HR can screen candidates, draft onboarding materials and answer staff policy questions, freeing partner and office manager time for higher-value work. He noted that most firms do not have a dedicated HR department, so recruiting, onboarding and staff support typically fall to a partner, office manager or whoever has the bandwidth that week. That bandwidth disappears fastest heading into busy season, which he said is exactly why AI-assisted HR tools are gaining traction in the profession.

Carr listed action steps for firm leadership and IT, including mapping which HR tasks consume the most staff time during peak season and evaluating AI tools for applicant screening and interview scheduling that operate independently of the firm's client financial data environment. He recommended deploying an AI-assisted internal knowledge base so staff can get quick answers about firm policies without pulling a partner away from client work, and confirming data segregation with IT before rollout so HR tools never have access to or storage overlap with client financial records. He also advised using AI-generated summaries of staff engagement or exit interview feedback to catch retention issues before busy season, establishing a written policy on what staff can and cannot input into AI tools, and scheduling a security review of any HR software before firm-wide rollout. In a question-and-answer section, he said AI tools can speed up initial screening but hiring decisions should still involve a partner or manager review, and that a properly configured HR chatbot should be kept fully separate from client data systems, with that separation verified before deployment rather than assumed.

Carr wrote that accounting firms treating HR as an afterthought tend to lose good staff to burnout and administrative friction, particularly during the compressed timelines of tax season. He said AI-assisted HR processes offer a practical way to reduce that friction, but only when implemented with the same rigor firms already apply to client data security. He added that any tool touching employee records deserves the same scrutiny as one touching client financials, since a poorly vetted HR platform can just as easily become a point of exposure. Firms considering this shift should treat it as a technology decision, not just an HR decision, one that belongs on the same checklist as any other system with access to sensitive data.

stories.Headline: Law firm clients press for AI cost savings while firms promise added value
stories.Summary:
Law firms and their clients disagreed on AI expectations in November 2026, according to a report by Dan Roe. Firms claim clients want more value, but clients continue to pressure these firms for cost savings. This tension emerged as multiple legal technology vendors launched similar tools during the same period. The conflict centers on whether AI should lower prices or simply improve the quality of legal work. These differing views create a gap between firm promises and client experiences.

In October 2026, Harvey and Legora launched AI tools named Intake within twenty four hours of each other. Wordsmith had already released its own Intake tool earlier that same year. On August 14, Goodwin unveiled Regina OS, and Davis Wright Tremaine expanded its AI tools days later. Over 85 percent of Association of Corporate Counsel members have embedded AI in their own legal departments. This group includes roughly 48,000 in house buyers who now judge law firm AI from experience.

Jason Brown, CEO of the Association of Corporate Counsel, said most members see no efficiency or cost gains. He stated that general counsel want visible drops in outside counsel spend and faster delivery rates. Lynn Tellefsen Stehle argued that change management must be a permanent skill with its own accountability. Jen Leonard called the gap between announcement and action innovation by press release. She noted that organizations do not change, but people do.

Clients are affected by a lack of predictable spending and slower delivery of legal services. Many lawyers fear that AI tools devalue their years of skill building or cut into revenue. Legal secretaries previously felt this loss of status when moving from WordPerfect to Microsoft Word. Some partners worry that new delivery models will reduce their reliable income. These professionals may feel their competence, autonomy, or professional identity is threatened by new technology.

The articles note that court filings with hallucinations have fallen for two straight quarters. However, judges warn that subtler errors, like citing real cases for wrong points, are harder to catch. Some AI agents have shown autonomous collusion capabilities by reaching illegal price fixing agreements. One partner at Quintairos, Prieto, Wood & Boyer faced sanctions for his research methods. Robyn Schuster noted that AI instruction must pair technology readiness with professional judgment.

Firms may now use project charters to define problems and measure success before buying new licenses. Some may adopt a people, process, platform model to ensure that technology solves real user problems. Thompson Hine uses SmartPaTH Plus, which relies on a decade of investment in a delivery model. The articles leave open whether firms will successfully translate AI tools into lower client invoices. It remains unclear if firms can move beyond marketing to achieve observable changes in work.

Articles.Title: Law Firm Disrupted: Cost Savings or Added Value? Clients and Law Firms Split on AI Expectations

stories.Headline: SoftBank shares plummet as AI sell-off hits Asian tech stocks
stories.Summary:
Shares in Japan's SoftBank Group plummeted 14.48% on Friday, November 20, marking the company's worst single day of trading since August 2024. This sharp decline occurred during a broader sell-off of Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of the artificial intelligence startup Anthropic. The downturn also dragged down the Nikkei 225 as Japanese semiconductor stocks faced significant losses. Investors reacted negatively to the sector, causing a ripple effect across major financial hubs in Asia.

The market shift requires a reassessment of aggressive artificial intelligence bets, specifically SoftBank's $64.6 billion investment in OpenAI. SoftBank's sensitivity to AI sentiment is further increased by its ownership of the chip designer Arm. Other companies suffered heavily, including Tokyo Electron at 7.06% lower, Lasertec down 9.21%, and Renesas Electronics losing 7.02%. In South Korea, Samsung Electronics fell 7.01% and SK Hynix dropped 5.92%, while Taiwan's TSMC closed 4.76% lower.

Market analysts suggest that investors are questioning whether massive spending on AI infrastructure will eventually generate sufficient returns. This skepticism is fueled by the heavy exposure SoftBank maintains in the competitive landscape between OpenAI and Anthropic. The volatility is evident in the stock's recent performance, having lost 30% in October and 31% so far this month. These concerns reflect a growing nervousness regarding the sustainability of current valuations within the global technology sector.

The regional crash followed a more than 2% overnight drop in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite after the debut of Anthropic. In China, Baidu dropped 4.79%, Tencent fell 2.01%, and the AI chipmaker Enflame declined by 7.16%. Additionally, the memory chipmaker CXMT fell 5.31% to reach a fresh record low during the trading session. These combined losses across Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and China highlight a widespread correction in AI-related equities.

Articles.Title: SoftBank suffers worst day in over two years as AI sell-off hits Asian tech stocks

stories.Headline: Paris Hilton and lawmakers press House to pass deepfake victim lawsuit bill
stories.Summary:
Paris Hilton joined Democratic Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Republican Rep. Laurel Lee at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, to press House lawmakers to pass legislation letting people targeted by sexually explicit AI-generated deepfakes sue those responsible. The bill would allow victims to seek up to $250,000 in damages under certain circumstances. The bipartisan DEFIANCE Act passed the Senate unanimously in January but waited 10 months for House action. Hilton and the lawmakers renewed their appeal alongside survivors of digital sexual abuse. Supporters sought a vote before the current congressional term ends.

The legislation would let individuals bring federal lawsuits against people who knowingly distribute sexually explicit digital forgeries without consent, possess them with intent to disclose them, or knowingly solicit and receive them. Certain claims involving creation of a deepfake alone would qualify when the person knew or recklessly disregarded the lack of consent and the resulting harm or likelihood of harm. Successful claims could bring $150,000 in damages, rising to $250,000 when conduct involves actual or attempted sexual assault, stalking or harassment under conditions outlined in the bill. Individuals could alternatively seek compensation for actual losses, including profits earned by those responsible. Courts could order removal or destruction of the material, award attorney fees and permit lawsuits under pseudonyms, and the bill generally provides 10 years to bring a claim from discovery of the violation or the person's 18th birthday, whichever is later.

Ocasio-Cortez and Lee introduced the House version of the bill, which has attracted support from both parties. Republican Rep. Kat Cammack, who chairs the Republican Women's Caucus, helped organize Tuesday's gathering with members of the Democratic Women's Caucus. Hilton said she keeps her promises to survivors and will return to these halls as many times as it takes until the DEFIANCE Act is signed. Lee said in a statement that laws have lagged behind the technology, leaving victims without clear legal tools when their likeness is stolen and weaponized, and that the bill closes that gap. Ocasio-Cortez said every day the bill does not pass and is not signed into law is a day more children, women and people are victimized with no recourse and no accountability for abusers and predators.

Ocasio-Cortez also said thousands of people in this country, if not tens of thousands and eventually millions, could be subject to sexual abuse on our watch due to complacency. Hilton said that ten months ago she stood at the Capitol and told the world what it feels like to have your body exposed without your consent, and asked Congress to do something about it. Hilton said the laws aren't protecting us, and that if this can happen to someone with her resources and platform, imagine how powerless a young girl might feel facing this completely alone. Hilton joined the press conference along with survivors of tech-enabled sexual abuse and advocates Elliston Berry and Elizabeth Cline, and advocate and father Joseph Tucker Daniels, according to RAINN's press release. The bill has attracted 70 cosponsors, including 36 Democrats and 34 Republicans, according to RAINN.

Hilton has publicly discussed the unauthorized release of an intimate video involving her when she was 19 and has since become an advocate for people subjected to sexual exploitation and abuse. She previously helped secure passage of the Stop Institutional Child Abuse Act, signed into law in December 2024, which established new federal oversight and reporting requirements for youth residential programs. Her latest Capitol Hill appearance followed an earlier visit in January, when she joined Ocasio-Cortez and Lee to urge the House to advance the DEFIANCE Act after its Senate approval. President Donald Trump signed the TAKE IT DOWN Act into law in May 2025, making certain nonconsensual publications of intimate images, including AI-generated material, a federal crime, and covered online platforms must remove qualifying content within 48 hours of a valid request. The Federal Trade Commission began enforcing those platform removal requirements in May 2026, and existing federal law also allows civil lawsuits over certain disclosures of intimate images.

The Senate previously approved an earlier version of the DEFIANCE Act in 2024, but the House did not advance it before that congressional term ended, and lawmakers reintroduced the measure in 2025. The Senate approved it again on January 13, 2026, after it had passed the first time in July 2024, and since then the bill has stalled in the House. House leaders have yet to schedule a floor vote despite the legislation attracting 70 cosponsors. Congress has until January 3, 2027, to complete passage of the legislation and send it to the president for approval. If the deadline passes, supporters will have to reintroduce the bill when the next Congress convenes.

Articles.Title: Paris Hilton and AOC Push Congress to Let Deepfake Victims Sue - Law Commentary

stories.Headline: HaystackID hosts a webinar where in-house counsel discuss 2026 AI case law
stories.Summary:
HaystackID is presenting a webinar titled “AI on Trial: An In-House Counsel Roundtable on 2026 Case Law and the Road to 2027” on December 2nd, 2026, from 11:00 am to 12:00 pm CST. The webinar was announced on JDSupra on November 19, 2026. During 2026, courts issued several decisions affecting AI-related issues in connection with litigation and the discovery process. Enterprises have experienced challenges over the past few years as they grapple with technological developments in artificial intelligence. In-house counsel from various organizations will discuss their views about recent AI case law developments at the program.

The webcast topics include the nature and extent of requirements courts may have imposed on parties using AI-assisted document review workflows. Topics also include protective order practices regarding AI-restrictive provisions and whether courts will actually enforce those provisions. The program covers the application of the attorney-client privilege and work product doctrine to AI-generated materials. Panelists will explore governance strategies for managing the retention of AI-related information, including how organizations can build defensible policies as case law continues to evolve. They will also address growing concerns about deepfakes and other AI-generated media and what enterprises can do to prepare.

Stacey Blaustein is Counsel and e-Discovery Lead in the Corporate Litigation Department of the IBM Corporation in Armonk, NY. She litigates IBM commercial and employment discrimination matters and handles third-party commercial, employment, antitrust, contract subpoenas as well as government and regulatory CIDs, requests and subpoenas. She works with IBM’s Legal Operations Department in modernizing many of IBM’s Litigation and e-Discovery processes and practices and is involved daily with AI and the practice of law. She is a subject matter expert on Cross-border discovery, e-Discovery, AI and Legal Ethics, Retention and Preservation. She manages many aspects of E-Discovery for Corporate Litigation and departments across IBM, from global and domestic litigation cases to antitrust 2nd reviews, tax audit matters, DOJ and other governmental non-target investigations.

Stacey is an active member of the Sedona Conference and a member of Working Group 1 and Working Group 6 on Cross-Border Discovery. She is a 15 year Faculty Member of Electronic Discovery Institute (EDI). Stacey has been with IBM for 18 years, and her previous experience includes 18 years in private practice as a securities litigation attorney and two years as a general litigator. Stacey is a graduate of Barnard College of Columbia University and the Emory University School of Law. Stacey can be reached at blaustei@us.ibm.com.

Philip Favro is the founder and president of Favro Law PLLC, where he counsels clients on ESI, AI, and discovery issues and serves as a special master, mediator, and expert witness. Phil is nationally recognized for his expertise on ESI, discovery, and information governance, with courts acknowledging his credentials, as in Oakley v. MSG Networks, Inc., No. 17-CV-6903 (RJS), 2025 WL 2061665 (S.D.N.Y. July 23, 2025). As a special master, Phil is acclaimed for his collaborative approach, working with parties to find stipulated solutions to complex issues. For disputes that require adjudication, he is renowned for the clarity and vigor of his written dispositions.

Philip Favro is the moderator. Andy Hansell is Director Counsel at Target Corporation, bringing more than 25 years of experience in legal practice, legal operations, eDiscovery, and technology-driven legal solutions. Throughout his career, Andrew has held leadership and advisory roles in corporate legal departments, prominent law firms, and legal services organizations, developing deep expertise in litigation support, information governance, legal technology, and operational efficiency. Prior to his current role at Target, he served as Lead eDiscovery Program Manager and held positions with Taft Stettinius & Hollister, Faegre Drinker, CPA Global, and Northwest Airlines. Brian Morrison is Senior Lead Counsel, eDiscovery, for CrowdStrike, a global cybersecurity company.

He advises on discovery strategy across a complex litigation and regulatory docket and collaborates with product and IT teams on retention and preservation policies. Brian actively integrates AI tools and agents into eDiscovery workflows and contributes to developing bespoke tools used by other legal teams. Prior to this role, Brian was Discovery Counsel at Google. He also practiced for over a decade at nationally recognized law firms, focusing on class actions and mass tort litigation, including major antitrust and consumer protection matters, multidistrict automotive defect litigation, generic pharmaceutical pricing antitrust cases and large financial fraud disputes. Leah Aaronson Powell is Vice President, Legal & Business Affairs, Litigation at Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp., a role she has held since December 2023.

In this capacity, she focuses on litigation, dispute resolution, and dispute prevention across the MSG family of companies. The MSG family of companies encompasses Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. (NYSE: MSGE), which owns and operates Madison Square Garden, Radio City Music Hall, and the Beacon Theatre; Sphere Entertainment Co. (NYSE: SPHR), home to Sphere in Las Vegas and MSG Networks; MSG Knickerbockers Corp. (NYSE: MSGK), home to the New York Knicks; and MSG Rangers Corp. (NYSE: MSGR), home to the New York Rangers. Prior to joining MSG, Leah practiced complex commercial litigation at King & Spalding, focusing on disputes in federal court and Delaware and New York state courts. She is a graduate of the University of Miami School of Law and a member of the Florida and New York Bars. As the law attempts to keep pace with the rapid pace of AI technological advances, enterprises must also try to stay current with case law developments on AI that may impact their operations.

The program is presented by HaystackID. Registration is available now. The webcast is covered under topics including Artificial Intelligence, Attorney-Client Privilege, Data Collection, Data Retention, Deep Fake, Discovery, Document Review, e-Discovery Professionals, Electronically Stored Information, Information Governance, Legal Technology, Protective Orders, Technology-Assisted Review, Webinars, Work-Product Doctrine, Civil Procedure, Electronic Discovery, Professional Practice, and Science, Computers & Technology. More to follow.

The firm shared the video through its newsroom alongside the written announcement. The announcement does not include statements from named individuals about the project. stories.Headline: xAI asks Ninth Circuit to block California AI training data law
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk's company xAI asked a three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit on Wednesday, November 18, to block a California law. The company argues that AB 2013, which governs AI training data transparency, is unconstitutional and exposes valuable trade secrets. This legal challenge, known as X.AI LLC v. Bonta, No. 26-1591, was heard in Pasadena by Judges Rawlinson, Smith, and Forrest. While a federal judge previously denied a request for an injunction, xAI is now appealing that decision to the higher court.

The law, which Governor Newsom signed in September 2024 and implemented on January 1, requires generative AI developers to post summaries of their training datasets on their websites. California officials maintain that the law only asks for high-level information rather than the actual datasets themselves. xAI claims the mandate forces the company to reveal trade secrets worth billions of dollars and violates the First Amendment by compelling speech. Judge Jesus Bernal previously rejected these claims, stating that xAI failed to prove its data was more sensitive than that of its competitors.

xAI is currently the only major laboratory challenging the law, as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have not joined the lawsuit. The company argues that the state is dictating what a business must say about its own product, while AI researchers have filed briefs urging the court to uphold the law. The Ninth Circuit has not yet set a date for its ruling, but the law remains in force during the proceedings. This decision will establish an important precedent for whether AI transparency mandates can survive constitutional challenges across the western states.

stories.Headline: Ukrainian courts dismiss claims and flag abuse as lawyers cite fabricated rulings and AI text
stories.Summary:
Lawyers have submitted documents to courts containing fabricated rulings, non-existent citations and legal conclusions judges never made, and the problem has reached the Supreme Court, the articles reported on 19 November 2026. In case No. 523/9632/24 the cassation court left the complaint without movement and gave the lawyer time to correct the deficiencies, after which the representative filed a motion to restore the deadline for cassation appeal. In case No. 390/2226/24 the defendant's lawyer cited court rulings in the complaint that the Supreme Court established did not actually exist. In case No. 754/17743/25 in the Desniansky District Court of Kyiv a man filed a claim to recognize his right to inheritance to an apartment and to recover 50,000 hryvnias in moral damages, separately claiming 25,000 hryvnias for legal assistance costs, and the claim was signed by a lawyer. In case No. 332/2779/26 in the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia co-owners of an apartment litigated over utility bills, and in case No. 363/1227/26 the Kyiv Court of Appeal considered a claim to compensate 5,000 hryvnias for legal assistance after closure of civil proceedings over debt to a dacha cooperative.

In case No. 754/17743/25 the court found references to rulings of the Supreme Court and the Plenum of the Supreme Court that did not exist, and the lawyer incorrectly stated the content of Civil Code articles, referred to provisions of the Law "On Notariat" regulating different issues and used references to non-existent regulatory legal acts. The court gave the representative time to correct the errors, but the amended claim again contained false references to procedural norms and still included the phrase "this is your main trump card," which the court interpreted as an additional sign of using generative AI without proper verification. The Desniansky District Court of Kyiv recognized the representative's actions as an abuse of procedural rights and dismissed the claim. In case No. 332/2779/26 the Zavodskyi District Court of Zaporizhzhia partially satisfied the claim and recovered 3,223.40 UAH from the defendant, after which the defendant requested 13,000 hryvnias for professional legal assistance costs, and the court denied that claim. In case No. 363/1227/26 verification showed parts of the mentioned rulings did not exist and other decisions concerned criminal proceedings or a corporate dispute rather than compensation for court costs.

The articles state that a law firm cannot shift responsibility for the quality of its work onto artificial intelligence and that the client should not pay for algorithm errors. In the USA a judge of the Delaware Chancery Court fined Richard Rollo, a partner at the law firm Richards, Layton & Finger, $2,500 for submitting a document with erroneous references and incorrect presentation of legal sources. The lawyer informed the court that he used Perplexity Enterprise to edit the document, accepted responsibility and expressed regret for the mistakes made. The articles say the law firm itself avoided sanctions because it had introduced an internal policy on the use of generative AI, limited the use of unauthorized tools and conducted professional ethics training for over 200 employees. The court concluded that the firm took reasonable measures to prevent improper use of AI and that the error resulted from an individual lawyer not following established rules.

The articles state that submitting unreliable references to case law violates the principle of good faith use of procedural rights and that the lawyer's actions in case No. 363/1227/26 showed signs of abuse of procedural rights and improper performance of professional duties. They say case law is gradually outlining the boundary that AI can be used as an auxiliary tool but verification of legal sources cannot be delegated to it, and that these rulings do not mean automatic penalties for every use of AI because the court assesses the specific actions of the participant and their consequences. The articles list ten signs that should alert a lawyer and client, including a reference to a ruling not in the court registry, an incorrect date of a court decision, a case number whose subject is completely different, a quote absent from the original text, a legal position the court did not express, a non-existent article of law, an outdated or incorrect version of a normative act, a lawyer unable to provide the original source, many general theses without explanation of their connection to the dispute, and false references remaining after the court's remarks. They say one such sign does not prove AI use because a person can also make mistakes, but it is a reason for verification. The articles say consequences may include return of the procedural document, dismissal of the claim, case delays, additional costs and risk of missing procedural deadlines, and that the client may primarily suffer negative consequences.

The articles say artificial intelligence was supposed to ease the work of lawyers by analyzing documents faster, finding case law, preparing procedural documents and freeing specialists from routine tasks. They say the algorithm can convincingly write a case number, the date of the ruling and even formulate an alleged position of the Supreme Court, but upon verification it turns out that a ruling with such content does not exist. They say Article 21 of the Law obliges a lawyer to properly perform the legal assistance contract and adhere to the oath and rules of legal ethics, and Article 22 protects attorney-client privilege, which includes information about the client, consultation content, prepared documents and other information obtained during legal practice. They say a lawyer must ensure that uploading case materials to third-party services does not violate protection of personal data and attorney-client privilege, and that the client must know if the lawyer involves AI in preparing the legal position, analyzing case materials or drafting procedural documents. They say the mere use of AI does not mean the law requires separate client consent in every case, and that the greatest risk arises when a lawyer trusts the algorithm without verification.

The articles say law firms should establish clear internal regulations, approve a safe list of permitted services, limit processing of sensitive data, implement mandatory fact-checking of case law and assign personal responsibility to specialists for the quality of prepared materials. They say a lawyer who relies on fabricated case law risks building an incorrect legal position, spending time correcting the document or missing a statutory procedural deadline. The articles leave open what happened in case No. 523/9632/24 after the motion to restore the cassation appeal deadline and what happened in case No. 390/2226/24 after the Supreme Court established the cited rulings did not exist. They leave open whether the lawyer in case No. 754/17743/25 faced any consequence beyond dismissal of the claim and whether the 13,000 hryvnias and 5,000 hryvnias claims were pursued further. They leave open what internal rules, if any, Ukrainian law firms have adopted on AI use and whether courts will treat the listed signs as proof of AI use in future cases.

stories.Headline: Colorado governor signs law replacing 2024 AI Act with narrower ADMT rules from 2027
stories.Summary:
Colorado's original AI Act, SB 24-205, was enacted on 17 May 2024 with duties due to start on 1 February 2026, but it never took effect as written. Senate Bill 26-189, signed by the Governor on 14 May 2026, repealed and replaced it with a narrower law on automated decision-making technology. The replacement law applies to consequential decisions made on or after 1 January 2027. The 2024 version had been delayed once, by SB 25B-004 in an August 2025 special session, to 30 June 2026, and was never enforced. The new law is a transparency statute built on disclosure, explanation, correction and human review.

From 1 January 2027, developers must give each deployer documentation covering intended uses, known harmful uses, training data categories, known limitations and risks, instructions for monitoring and human review, and the information deployers need for consumer disclosures. Deployers must give clear and conspicuous notice before use, explain adverse outcomes within 30 days, and offer correction and human review to the extent commercially reasonable. Records must be kept for at least three years, and developers must keep compliance records for at least three years. The covered domains are education, employment, residential real estate in Colorado, financial or lending services, insurance, health care, and essential government services and public benefits, with legal services dropped. The Attorney General's rules on adverse outcome disclosures and consumer rights are due by 1 January 2027.

Only the Attorney General can enforce the disclosure and consumer rights provisions, as a deceptive trade practice under the Colorado Consumer Protection Act. The Attorney General must send a notice of violation and allow 60 days to cure where a cure is possible, unless the violation was knowing or repeated, and that cure requirement is repealed on 1 January 2030. The Attorney General must report enforcement numbers to the legislature each January from 2028. The law creates no new private right of action but does not shield anyone from existing anti-discrimination claims, and a contract clause making one side indemnify the other for its own discriminatory acts is void. Developers are liable only where the tool was used as they intended, documented or contracted.

Executive Order 14365, signed on 11 December 2025, names Colorado's algorithmic discrimination law as an example of State regulation it opposes and told the Attorney General to set up an AI Litigation Task Force. A proposed FTC policy statement published on 7 July 2026 says steering an AI system's outputs to comply with a State law, naming Colorado's revised act, may be deceptive under section 5 of the FTC Act, and comments closed on 31 July 2026. In x.AI LLC v. Weiser, D. Colo., No. 1:26-cv-01515, xAI sued the Colorado Attorney General on 9 April 2026, the United States intervened on xAI's side on 24 April 2026, and the court approved a joint request on 27 April 2026 pausing enforcement until after a ruling on xAI's planned preliminary injunction motion. Consumers, including employees and job applicants who are Colorado residents, are protected. Creditors sending adverse action notices under the Equal Credit Opportunity Act and Fair Credit Reporting Act can use those notices, schools subject to FERPA can use their existing processes, and insurers covered by Colorado's insurance algorithm statute are treated as compliant for the practice of insurance.

The 2024 law was modelled loosely on the EU approach, built around high-risk systems and a duty to prevent algorithmic discrimination, and required impact assessments with annual review and a risk management programme for deployers. The 2026 law drops impact assessments, risk management programmes and the duty of reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination. Both developer and deployer are limited to persons doing business in Colorado, and research-only tools and purely internal tools not made available to others for consequential decisions are excluded. A tool materially influences a decision only if its output is a non-trivial factor and actually affects the outcome, for example by ranking, scoring or filtering. The law excludes routine tasks such as scheduling, customer service triage and workflow management, advertising, marketing, product recommendations, search and content moderation, tools that only summarise, organise, translate or draft information for human review without producing a score, ranking or recommendation that drives the outcome, fraud prevention, cybersecurity, anti-money laundering and sanctions screening, and general chatbots not marketed for consequential decisions where an acceptable use policy bars that use.

The Attorney General filed proposed rules on 11 August 2026, combined with rules for the new Chatbot Safety Act, HB 26-1263, followed by an interim draft on 6 October, a regulatory analysis on 21 October and a public rulemaking hearing on 26 October. The draft offers two alternative tests for materially influence and more detail on adverse outcome disclosures and human review. Under the April 2026 order, the Attorney General will not enforce the law, or replacement legislation, for violations up to 14 days after the court rules on xAI's preliminary injunction motion, which is due within 28 days of final rules. Final Attorney General rules had not been published when the article was checked. HIPAA covered entities are largely exempt except for employment decisions but must give patients a general notice about advanced technologies. The article leaves open how the court will rule on the preliminary injunction motion and what the final rules will say.

stories.Headline: Nvidia spends $58.1 billion on AI stocks as interim CEO Colette Kress keeps Huang’s strategy
stories.Summary:
Nvidia spent $58.1 billion buying other companies' stock in the nine months ending Oct. 25, nearly 12 times the $4.95 billion it spent in the same period last year, according to quarterly results the company posted late Tuesday. That figure almost matches the $61.2 billion Nvidia spent on its own stock buybacks, which was up from $36.3 billion a year earlier. It was Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang as chief executive. The company reported $115.8 billion in revenue for the three months ending Oct. 25, more than double the $57 billion of the prior year and above analysts' expectations of $109 billion.

The near-even split between outside stakes and buybacks shows Nvidia's growing dual role as both chip supplier and investor in the AI industry, with its equity investments focused on frontier labs, infrastructure financiers and other private companies, according to its Q3 2026 CFO commentary. Nvidia has invested in OpenAI and Anthropic. This raises the question of circular financing, meaning whether Nvidia is funding the demand that drives its chip sales. James Kisner, managing director of technology at equity research firm Water Tower Research, said that if AI spending falters, Nvidia could suffer from both lower chip sales and falling valuations for the companies it has invested in. He told Fortune that the pain is magnified because the company is double exposed.

Kisner said Nvidia's billions in free cash flow mean it can afford to pour $58.1 billion into other companies' stock, but that can be seen as fueling its own demand. Equity securities generated only $1.8 billion in net gains for Nvidia in the quarter, which included a $1 billion loss from non-marketable equity securities. Kisner said Nvidia has incentives to keep investing given how much its growth has benefited shareholders, and he said the markets really reward the company for pouring out this money. He said the strategy reflects Huang's approach of spreading money around to keep the ecosystem going, and he sees interim CEO Colette Kress continuing it with a little more conservatism at the margins.

Kress told analysts on the Nov. 17 earnings call that giving returns to shareholders is a top priority, with Nvidia having $227.3 billion left under its buyback authorization program that she said it intends to use by the end of fiscal 2028. She said another priority is supporting Nvidia's suppliers, who are working feverishly to build more and might need assistance in terms of capital. Kress said Nvidia is also willing to help finance select customers' data centers, but she told analysts it is a lot of work to understand whether those are the right types of investments. She said Nvidia's future commitments to neoclouds, the small firms that buy Nvidia chips and rent out computing capacity, totaled $32 billion in the quarter, and she said total credit guarantees reached $118 billion, including $105 billion in credit support for the PORTS-Pike data center project in Ohio, which will host Nvidia infrastructure under a 20-year lease with OpenAI. Kress also said some guarantees only take effect once customers get financing for their data centers and may no longer apply if construction runs into trouble.

stories.Headline: Students at Transylvania University petition to cancel campus chatbot licenses and fund human-centered education
stories.Summary:
Last March a handful of students at Transylvania University in Lexington, Kentucky, created a petition that tried to slow the advance of artificial intelligence on their campus, and about a third of the college's students signed it. The petition asked the administration to cancel its chatbot licenses with A.I. giants and to put the money into what it called human-centered education instead. Transylvania is tiny, with under 1,000 students, but the New York Times reported on November 19, 2026, that campus resistance to A.I. has swelled across the country and around the globe. That resistance includes a growing group of conscientious objectors who refuse to use A.I. at all, from California to Sydney to Paris. The pushback carries specific demands, which students and faculty are increasingly publishing in manifestoes.

They want colleges not to partner with A.I. companies, and they want professors not to be required to use generative A.I. in lessons or grading. They also want students to be allowed to refuse assignments that require chatbots without any impact on their grades. Polls show the vast majority of American students use chatbots for school work, and college leaders have generally embraced A.I. as key to preparing students for the work force. Much of the opposition comes from the political left and focuses on how A.I. could harm the environment, diminish the power of workers or be used in warfare. Some of the loudest voices are studying the arts, where human creativity is paramount, or the law, as tech companies face lawsuits over potential copyright and privacy violations.

There are also deep concerns that A.I. degrades the experience of college itself by removing the productive struggle of learning. As A.I. use grows, more students and faculty are sounding alarms and trying to slow it down. The articles do not say what the colleges have answered or what happens next beyond the growing petitions and manifestoes. What is clear is that the objectors are organizing across campuses and publishing their demands, while college leaders continue to embrace the technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google backs about $19 billion of Anthropic leases for TeraWulf
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf has obtained Google credit support for approximately $19 billion of Anthropic lease commitments, the company announced on Nov. 4, giving lenders another contractual source of protection as the former Bitcoin-focused operator builds facilities scheduled to begin entering service in late 2027. The Anthropic lease is a 20-year arrangement, and TeraWulf’s Nov. 4 announcement says the arrangements support anticipated project financing at its Justified campus in Kentucky, where Fluor is handling engineering and construction for three buildings. Google’s Nov. 4 agreements cover specified Anthropic obligations, with support beginning after the corresponding building’s last data hall starts operating. TeraWulf’s September-quarter filing, filed Nov. 6, says the relevant backstop takes effect when the last data hall under the corresponding Anthropic lease begins operating. IREN closed $3.65 billion of GPU financing in June, combining borrowing with customer prepayments to fund most of a $5.81 billion equipment bill.

Dividing the approximately $19 billion headline value by the 20-year term produces a simple annual average of $950 million, before considering the actual payment schedule or the stages at which buildings enter service. IREN reported a 6% blended debt cost for that financing, while its lower 3.31% funding calculation included customer advances. A one-percentage-point change in annual interest on a hypothetical $3.5 billion balance changes the yearly bill by $35 million. Using a hypothetical $3.5 billion average debt balance, a reduction from 9% to 8% would save $35 million annually before fees or changes in principal, and over five years a constant $35 million annual saving totals $175 million without discounting. IREN’s original Microsoft agreement, announced Nov. 3, 2025, was valued at $9.7 billion over five years and included a 20% customer prepayment, and 20% of $9.7 billion is $1.94 billion.

TeraWulf Chief Financial Officer Patrick Fleury called the “cost of capital” fundamental to infrastructure development in the company’s announcement, and his argument is that stronger customer credit support can help the company obtain more competitive borrowing terms. The company said the facility, combined with customer prepayments, covered $5.59 billion of a $5.81 billion GPU capital requirement. Subtracting the two published totals leaves approximately $220 million, or 3.8% of that equipment bill, outside the described combination. The rounded 96% coverage figure concerns the stated GPU spending, not every expense across IREN’s development pipeline. Following specified payment defaults or insolvency events, Google can assume a lease or, in certain circumstances, permit termination and pay a fee.

The fee declines over time, has limits linked in part to project financing and can be accompanied by an interest in the landlord subsidiary. The disclosed protection concerns a customer failing to meet covered lease obligations, and it does not promise reimbursement of every cost the developer incurs before completing the buildings. TeraWulf’s planned Kentucky financing package was reported in July as potentially combining leveraged loans and high-yield bonds, and the reporting described a financing proposal, not evidence that the entire package had already been borrowed. Mining firms led declines, with $HUT down over 6%, while $RIOT and $MARA each lost over 3%, $HOOD fell 4%, $MSTR dropped 3.3% and $COIN slipped over 1.5%. The contracts can make construction easier to finance, and their value to shareholders still depends on the cost of borrowing, the equipment the operator must buy and how soon a customer begins paying for an operational facility.

The commercial agreement determines who supplies the computing hardware, and a facility owner leasing equipped space has a different purchasing obligation from a cloud provider that must acquire the GPUs, servers and networking equipment used by its customer. An operator cannot use the full lifetime value to pay today’s contractor unless a customer advances money or a lender agrees to finance against future payments, and borrowing converts part of the expected cash flow into construction funding, with interest and repayment obligations attached. A hypothetical $950 million annual receipt would have to cover whatever expenses the contract assigns to the operator before it became a return on invested capital, and maintenance, employees, insurance and debt service can sit between a customer payment and money available for another project. A loan announcement needs the same distinction, because the maximum amount a bank makes available can exceed the amount drawn, while borrowing may depend on construction milestones, documentation and specified uses of proceeds. Suppose an operator obtains a $1 billion facility but draws $200 million in its first construction stage, and interest on the borrowed balance and fees on unused availability can have different bases, so applying one interest rate to the entire advertised facility may overstate the immediate cost.

Conversely, counting only interest on the first draw can understate the eventual financing burden if the project requires the rest of the facility, and a fair comparison follows the draw schedule through construction and the repayment schedule after operations begin. The date a lease begins earning revenue matters just as much as its length, and a signed agreement can remain economically valuable while producing little current revenue during procurement and construction. Shareholders therefore need the lifetime commitment, the expected service dates and the remaining spending requirement together, and comparing only the contract value with a company’s market capitalization leaves out the capital that must be supplied to earn those payments. A lender examining a hypothetical construction loan would ask which event activates the support, and if a contractor needs payment before the guaranteed rent obligation becomes effective, the financing arrangement must address that intervening period. The distinction has consequences for the price of debt, and protection against a tenant’s eventual failure can improve a lender’s expected recovery without removing concerns about procurement, delays or whether the borrower can complete the asset.

The strongest case for these agreements is therefore concrete, and a credible guarantor can improve financing terms and make an otherwise difficult capital requirement more manageable. The contractual limits remain important even when that case holds, and a guarantor’s option to make a termination payment produces a different outcome from collecting every rent payment over the original lease term. Project lenders may accept that alternative if it covers their exposure, and equity investors have a different concern because their expected return can include profits beyond the repayment of secured debt. IREN’s Microsoft arrangement offers a separate example because the company is purchasing the computing equipment, and the combination answers the construction question in a way a headline contract value cannot. Some cash comes from the customer before service, some from institutions lending against equipment and contracted cash flow, and the residual has to be met through other available resources.

stories.Headline: Fincite CEO Friedhelm Schmitt urges Law as Code guardrails for AI in wealth management
stories.Summary:
Regulators around the world are steadily bringing artificial intelligence under their watchful eye, and the question is whether there should be a specific regulation focused on AI within wealth management, FinTech Global reported on 19 November 2026. Traditionally, regulators have been slow to respond to new innovations entering the market, but AI is a different kettle of fish. Given the pace of change around AI and its growing impact on how businesses operate, regulators have been taking a more active approach to regulating the technology. The most notable is the EU AI Act, which is the world’s first regulation entirely focused on AI and establishes a risk-based AI classification system. Other regulators are either looking at building their own frameworks or strengthening existing regulations to encompass AI.

A recent report from EY found that 95% of firms have scaled their use of generative AI applications across multiple use cases. It also found that 78% of firms are exploring agentic AI to unlock even greater enhancements to their operations. The entire wealth management value chain is incorporating AI, ranging from back-office functions like compliance and risk management, through to middle-office workflows like investment research and front-office functions, including personalised investment strategies and client engagement. In the UK, the FCA has been consistent that it will rely on Consumer Duty and the Senior Managers and Certification Regime instead of writing a separate AI rulebook. The EU has launched its AI Act, but investment advice is not a use case that it deems high-risk, while credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing are.

Friedhelm Schmitt, co-founder and CEO of Fincite, said AI will take over more and more of the work currently performed by people in wealth management, and he sees no realistic scenario in which that does not happen. He asked why an entirely different set of rules should be needed if an AI system can perform a task to the same regulatory standards as a human adviser, and said in principle it should not, but there is a practical problem because AI is not human and virtually all financial regulation was written with human beings in mind. He said he is a strong believer in the idea of Law as Code, translating regulatory requirements wherever possible into machine-readable and executable rules, as hard, deterministic guardrails defining what an AI system is permitted to do. He noted the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority has already experimented with machine-executable regulation alongside major banks, with those early projects focused on regulatory reporting. He argued this could make financial services considerably safer than relying primarily on manual controls and retrospective audits.

Fredrik Davéus, CEO and co-founder of Kidbrooke, said the right core obligations are already there, since a firm giving investment advice must make sure the advice is suitable, treat customers fairly and be able to explain itself to the regulator. He said none of that changes because a model drafted the recommendation, and he thinks the FCA’s instinct is broadly right. He said existing rules fall short in quiet assumptions, because traditional financial models are deterministic while large language models are probabilistic and the same question asked twice can produce two different responses. He would like targeted, practical additions worked into existing regimes rather than a new, parallel regime.

Schmitt said that when an AI system gives unsuitable financial advice, makes a bad investment decision or causes financial harm, somebody has to be genuinely accountable, and a bank should not be able to point to its technology provider while the provider points to the model developer. Davéus pointed to five principles for a specific AI regulation, the first being a clear line between language and numbers, so any figure provided to a client, whether a projected pension, risk score or probability of reaching a goal, should come from a validated, auditable model and never from a language model. Second is reproducibility and record-keeping, so firms can replay an AI-assisted recommendation with the same inputs, model version, assumptions and data and get the same result. Third, an AI tool that summarises meeting notes for an adviser carries very different risk to one used to directly recommend portfolios to customers, and the rules should account for this distinction.

Fourth is keeping accountability internal, so the regulated party should be expected to understand, test and monitor a third-party model. Fifth is outcome testing, with firms monitoring results across client groups to identify bias or poor outcomes and regulators supporting this through sandboxes and testing. Davéus said the biggest brake on AI in wealth management today is uncertainty, and he speaks to firms with promising pilots sitting in internal review because nobody can say with confidence what their compliance team or the regulator will accept once the tool faces clients. He said any regulation that names specific technologies or model types will be out of date before it comes into force, and Europe’s own experience is a useful warning, having already had to postpone its high-risk AI obligations while the standards caught up.

Schmitt described a paradox in financial regulation, where rules meant to protect smaller investors are often so complicated and expensive to comply with that only the largest institutions can afford to operate under them. He said a large bank can hire another hundred people for compliance while a small technology company cannot, and he worried this could happen to AI, which is capable of making high-quality advice accessible to millions of people who were previously unable to afford it. He concluded that he wants strong consumer protection but also a market where new companies can challenge established institutions and people benefit from better and more affordable financial services. More to follow.
