stories.Headline: AI tools drive school book removals as states expand restrictions
stories.Summary:
As a growing number of states pass or propose restrictions on what books children can access in school libraries, authors and advocates are concerned about the role artificial intelligence is increasingly playing in books being removed from shelves. The free speech advocacy group PEN America said in a report published during Banned Books Week in early October that the phenomenon of using AI to guide removals will worsen the snowball effect of book bans that has already gone much too far. Some districts have had AI review their collections to flag certain types of content and make recommendations on what to remove. The first known example of AI being used for such purposes was in 2023, when an Iowa school district used it in response to legislation prohibiting books depicting sex acts in school libraries. Several Texas districts followed in 2025, according to the Houston Chronicle.

The Florida Freedom to Read Project reported in October that a local school district's use of AI to scan library collections led to more than 1,800 titles being removed from shelves to undergo further review. A Utah law requires that if three public school districts, or two school districts and five charter schools, take a title off library shelves, all public and charter schools must follow suit. There are 44 books currently banned statewide under the law, according to PEN America. The organization's October report found that Texas and Florida's bans made up more than 11,400 of the nearly 12,000 total book bans recorded during the 2025-2026 school year. Texas enacted a law in 2025 that prohibits schools from having library materials with indecent or profane content, and Florida has sought to impose similar restrictions for several years.

The Florida Department of Education sent a memo in September to the state's 67 public school districts, as well as charter schools, that directed them to review their library collections and compare them to the department's list of books that have been removed from schools around the state. Florida Education Commissioner Henry Mack wrote that the Department will hold districts, and the superintendents who lead them, accountable for failing to protect students from inappropriate content and material. Maggie Tokuda-Hall, an author and co-creator of Authors Against Book Bans, told USA TODAY that we've crossed the Rubicon and are in a really different place. A spokesperson for Moms for Liberty told USA TODAY the group believes AI recommendations should always be followed by human review. The spokesperson said anyone who blindly trusts AI to make decisions for them is using it in an irresponsible manner.

A Knight Foundation report in 2024 found that more than three-fourths of all adults felt very or somewhat confident that local public schools select appropriate books, including nearly 90% of public school parents, more than 60% of conservatives and 69% of Republicans. Stephana Ferrell, a public school parent who is also the director of research and insight at the Florida Freedom to Read Project, said these are not things public school parents want prioritized right now, and yet it's being amplified at the state level. Moms for Liberty, which describes itself as the nation's largest grassroots organization fighting for parental rights, has chapters that have called for scores of titles to be removed from school library shelves, including Colleen Hoover's "It Ends With Us," "The Kite Runner" by Khaled Hosseini and John Steinbeck's "Of Mice and Men." In October, the group announced a new AI tool to scan school board meeting agendas and identify topics related to parental rights, free speech, the curriculum and diversity, equity and inclusion efforts. A spokesperson for the organization told USA TODAY it may also be used on school library collections.

James Joyce's 1922 work "Ulysses" was deemed legally obscene and faced a nationwide ban until a court reversed it in 1933. J.D. Salinger's 1951 classic, "The Catcher in the Rye," has stirred controversy for decades and was the 10th-most challenged book of the 1990s, according to the American Library Association. A book that was even more widely challenged in that decade was "Heather Has Two Mommies," a 1989 children's book about a young girl raised by lesbian parents. The book's author, Lesléa Newman, told USA TODAY that while there have been longtime battles over her work, as well as other books with LGBTQ+ themes or written by non-White authors, she's noticed a change in recent years.

Newman said things have really escalated in a way that's very disturbing and frightening, and noted that statewide bans now affect dozens of titles. According to the American Library Association, pressure groups, government officials and other decision-makers were behind more than 90% of all book challenges in 2025. Author Lee Wind, whose 2021 book, "No Way, They Were Gay? Hidden Lives and Secret Loves," has faced several bans, criticized what he called very calculated attacks on books and said book bans further marginalize certain groups, such as the LGBTQ+ community.

Wind said he thinks all it's doing is empowering people that want there to be fewer books about diverse people in public spaces to do it more thoroughly. Sarah Lamdan, executive director of the American Library Association's Office for Intellectual Freedom, told USA TODAY she has some optimism that the trend will taper off. Lamdan said one thing that gives her hope is people are becoming fatigued by AI, and the overuse of AI, and the use of AI in contexts where maybe it shouldn't be used. Kris Austin, CEO of Draft2Digital, a self-publishing and distribution platform for independent authors, pointed to the negative feedback loop created by having more state restrictions alongside more advanced AI.

Austin said the next time we see this data, it's going to be worse, and it's going to be shockingly worse. The article carried an editor's note stating the story was updated to add additional information. BrieAnna Frank's role covering First Amendment issues at USA TODAY is made possible by a collaboration among Freedom Forum, Journalism Funding Partners and the USA TODAY Network, and Freedom Forum does not provide editorial input. The article originally appeared on USA TODAY and was reported by BrieAnna J. Frank, USA TODAY, via USA TODAY Network and Reuters Connect.

stories.Headline: South Korean universities issue gowns and ban correction tape to stop AI cheating in admissions tests
stories.Summary:
South Korean universities implemented strict security measures in November 2026 to prevent cheating with artificial intelligence devices during admissions tests. These actions followed the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test and were prompted by reports of a top scorer in a tax accountant exam using a miniature camera. Sogang University issued an urgent notice on November 18 regarding smart glasses and cameras before its science exams on November 21 and humanities exams on November 22. Korea University also released guidelines on November 17 for its own essay exams held on November 21 and 22.

The new rules require specific clothing and writing tools to block hidden electronic devices. Seoul National University provides interview gowns to prevent cameras from being hidden in buttonholes, while Sogang University asks applicants to avoid garments with buttons on the sleeves. Korea University banned correction tape and requires answer sheets to be written in a single pen color. Sungkyunkwan University only allows the use of specific pens previously given as souvenirs to prevent cameras from being attached to writing instruments.

Inha University and other schools may use metal detectors on suspicious applicants or those using the restroom. University officials and education bodies are taking responsibility for these heightened security protocols. A Sungkyunkwan official stated that the school increased the number of proctors and sent text messages with guidelines to all applicants. Sogang University warned that violations of these rules could lead to legal action and criminal complaints.

The Korean Council for University Education stated it would respond sternly to AI cheating and urged the Ministry of Education and the National Assembly to revise the Higher Education Act. These measures aim to align university exam security with the rigorous standards of the national CSAT. The Korean Council for University Education is seeking budget funding to expand equipment and proctoring staff for future tests. Efforts to build a comprehensive anti-cheating system for university-administered exams are expected to accelerate.

stories.Headline: Delaware judge fines lawyer Richard Rollo $2,500 for AI-generated errors in a legal brief
stories.Summary:
Vice Chancellor Lori Will fined a Delaware lawyer 2,500 dollars for errors in a legal brief. Richard Rollo of the firm Richards, Layton & Finger caused the issue using an artificial intelligence tool. The errors appeared in a January brief regarding legal expenses for a broader investment fund matter. This brief contained fabricated quotations, inaccurate citations, and misleading legal arguments that the AI tool generated. The court decision highlights the challenges law firms face as AI tools become common in legal research.

The fine applies to Richard Rollo, but the court did not sanction the Wilmington based firm Richards, Layton & Finger. The brief used an AI tool called Perplexity, which the firm was testing but had not approved. Rollo was the head of the AI subcommittee at the firm that was studying the use of Perplexity. The errors included hallucinated legal propositions, which are false or unverified pieces of information that sound plausible. The revised filing removed quotation marks from fabricated passages but kept inaccurate descriptions of the court decisions.

Vice Chancellor Lori Will stated that the firm acted reasonably to prevent the misuse of generative AI tools. She noted that the firm established clear verification policies and trained its personnel through a multi layered approach. Will wrote that the firm should not be sanctioned because an individual lawyer bypassed those internal firm controls. She also mentioned that the court does not oppose using AI in filings to improve case handling efficiency. The judge concluded that the firm did the right thing by warning of the risks of AI.

Opposing attorneys identified the problems in the brief, which prompted the firm to submit a corrected version. The lawyer Richard Rollo is the person affected by the fine for bypassing the firm's internal AI controls. Perplexity told Reuters that it is focused on achieving 100% accurate AI through the use of verifiable citations. The firm Richards, Layton & Finger was sent a message seeking comment on the ruling and the fine. These parties are the primary actors involved in the dispute over the AI generated legal errors.

The articles explain that hallucination occurs when AI tools generate false information in a way that sounds plausible. The firm had a subcommittee studying Perplexity to determine if the tool should be approved for official use. This specific case arose from a dispute over legal expenses connected to a larger investment fund matter. The court recognized that AI can improve efficiency, but it requires strict verification to avoid fabricated legal citations. The firm had already implemented a substantial training approach to warn staff about the risks of generative AI.

The court has now issued the fine, but the articles do not state if Rollo has paid it. It remains open whether the firm will change its AI subcommittee leadership or its testing protocols for Perplexity. The articles do not say if other lawyers at the firm used the unapproved tool in other cases. There is no information on whether the opposing attorneys will seek further remedies due to the fabricated quotations. The final response from Richards, Layton & Finger regarding the ruling was not included in the text.

It impacts Tribal sovereignty, Native American rights, and various public lands.

Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York voted in favor of the legislation. Ruffalo said Schumer and other Democrats are handing a major win to the fossil fuel industry. Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon told the New York Times he does not support the bill. Wyden said he cannot trust a handshake promise from the current administration. Twenty one Democrats voted for the bill, including Martin Heinrich, John Fetterman, Jon Ossoff, and Raphael Warnock. Republicans Shelley Moore Capito and Mike Lee also supported the measure.

The Bipartisan Policy Center stated that federal reviews of business applications now take years or decades. stories.Headline: California analyst Gabe Petek warns governor-elect Xavier Becerra of a $2 billion deficit driven by an AI stock slowdown
stories.Summary:
California is collecting billions in unexpected tax revenue from a stock market driven by enthusiasm over artificial intelligence, but the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office warned in its annual economic forecast on Wednesday that the state should not count on that money to solve its deeper budget problems. If the market slows next year, the state would face a small deficit of $2 billion by the end of fiscal year 2027-28, the office estimated. That gap could grow to $15 billion a year by fiscal year 2028-29, according to Legislative Analyst Gabe Petek. An abrupt crash could produce an annual $35 billion shortfall by fiscal year 2028-29, and the state would not have enough money in reserve to cover it. The forecast marks the fifth consecutive year the state has projected a deficit despite revenue growth.

Closing a hole that large would require state leaders to essentially scrap all service expansions since fiscal year 2019-20, including the extension of Medi-Cal to undocumented immigrant adults, Petek said. Alternatively, he said, it would take a new tax larger than the current 10% to 12% income tax on top earners, which voters just made permanent through Proposition 3. The report offers a first look at the financial challenges facing Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, who will unveil his first budget in January along with an updated outlook from the state finance department that could differ sharply from the analyst’s analysis. In June, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a budget he said would balance the state’s finances for two consecutive years and cut future deficits in half, but that plan largely depended on AI boom revenue to delay major cuts to healthcare services, especially for undocumented immigrants. Those cuts will take effect next year unless Becerra finds new funding to sustain the services.

Becerra has said little about his budget priorities, though he signaled openness to new taxes such as a “fair share” tax on the wealthy and a charge on drivers by the miles they drive to fund road repairs. He also said he would seek to reverse cuts to healthcare access for undocumented immigrants but has not shared specifics. In a Wednesday statement, Becerra’s spokesperson Jonathan Underland said the governor-elect is “hard at work” preparing his January budget proposal and “remains committed to delivering a responsible, balanced budget that protects the services Californians depend on and focuses on bringing down costs.” The analyst’s office said the risk of a downturn requires the incoming administration to “rebuild budget resilience” by saving aggressively, repaying outstanding debts and implementing long-term cuts or revenue increases. Assembly Democratic leaders responded to the forecast by praising voters’ passage of Proposition 2 earlier this month as a directive for the Legislature to be prudent with tax dollars.

The funds come from both new and existing investors, though the company did not name the specific contributors behind the raise. Founded in 2015, Imagen currently provides radiology services across 28 states and handles more than 2 million imaging studies every year. Imagen estimated that its physician head count has grown 100% year over year, with the company now employing a team of more than 230 radiologists and cardiologists. Leaders said they will use the funds to further build out what they believe is the best place for radiologists to practice their craft.

As part of the capital raise, Imagen also secured the rights to up to 150 million additional imaging studies, which it will use to train its AI models. Those scans include X-rays, CTs, MRIs and ultrasounds, and the company plans to build and validate models against the diverse, real-world caseloads that its radiologists handle every day. Imagen's AI strategy centers on improving the experience of practicing radiologists while boosting clinical quality and efficiency, and as its technologies advance it plans to reinvest the resulting benefits into its radiologists and the resources that support them. Laurence Eckel, an associate chief medical officer who joined the company in April after spending 26 years with the Mayo Clinic, said in a November 18 statement that Imagen is building the entire practice around the radiologist, from the technology they use to the clinical teams supporting them. He said the goal is to create a place where physicians can do the best work of their careers and feel proud of the practice they are helping build.

Serge Sicular, the chief medical information officer who also leads emergency imaging at the Mount Sinai Health System, said the greatest opportunity for AI in radiology is not simply to make physicians faster but to give them better tools to deliver exceptional patient care. Imagen said the growth capital will also help further accelerate radiologist recruitment and retention, and it plans to invest in other clinical resources, operational infrastructure and technology to support physicians. Previous contributors have included venture capitalists, hospitals and health systems, and technology entrepreneurs, with institutional investors including Google Ventures and DFJ. The company also previously touted new leadership appointments in August amid rapid growth and recently published new research in Population Health Management.

stories.Headline: AI code generation erodes developer comprehension of software systems, researchers warn
stories.Summary:
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence for code generation is quietly weakening a crucial architectural characteristic, which is human comprehension of software systems, according to a TechGig report updated on August 11, 2026. The article says this erosion of understanding is termed cognitive debt and intent debt, and it poses significant risks to a system's ability to evolve safely. It cites Margaret-Anne Storey's expansion of Peter Naur's idea of programming as theory building, which holds that a system includes not just the code but also the mental model held by its developers. A system that is not understood cannot evolve safely, the article states.

The article names three forces that accelerate this decay. Decentralised architectural decision-making can fragment global understanding of a system's why, and team churn compounds this as departing engineers take their mental models with them. The most recent and rapid force is generative AI, which commoditises code generation and removes the comprehension naturally formed during design, implementation and verification. Architects can watch for large pull request sizes, reliance on agentic code reviewers as sole approvers, superficial human review feedback and missing design reviews for critical changes. Further signals include knowledge concentration around a few individuals, shown by a high Degree of Authorship or a low truck factor, and growing onboarding friction measured by the time new hires take to contribute to design and architecture.

The article says a lack of documentation for design decisions, particularly the why behind them, contributes to intent debt, and monitoring pull requests that touch core modules without adding Architecture Decision Records can help. Domain leakage, where changes degrade architectural boundaries and cause unintended side effects, signals a breakdown in local reasoning and shared understanding. In an AI-assisted workflow, human code reviews must shift from mere quality gates to comprehension checkpoints that validate and spread the understanding reached before code generation. The article adds that shared mental models across teams are vital, especially at bounded context seams, and this requires deliberate team topologies and rotating engineers across modules to prevent knowledge silos.

Treating comprehension as an inherent architectural characteristic demands leading indicators, fitness functions and continuous practices, the article states. If comprehension gaps are discovered only after AI-generated code is in production, the opportunity for cheap intervention is lost. The article says deliberate and continuous engineering of comprehension, particularly at core domains and system seams, is essential for building truly evolvable software systems. It does not say what specific actions organisations have taken or what happens next beyond these recommendations.

stories.Headline: Trump tells APEC leaders the US will not let regulation stifle the AI industry
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump spoke to leaders at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on Thursday, November 19, 2026, regarding the future of artificial intelligence. He stated that the United States government will not allow regulation to stifle the growth of the AI industry. This announcement occurred just three days after Washington tightened its export controls on advanced chips. The president framed his argument around the concept of superintelligence and expressed opposition to rules that would control it.

The new administration rules announced on Monday, November 16, restrict the shipment of advanced AI chips to data centers in Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. Operators that supply significant volumes of computing power to firms based in China must obtain US export licenses within 90 days. This deadline for securing licenses will fall in early 2027, or these facilities will face further restrictions. These measures target the way Chinese companies rent computing power to train their models through overseas facilities.

President Trump described the technology as being almost entirely good, though he noted that countries must carefully manage its bad elements. He emphasized that the United States will not accept rules that slow down AI while the government writes its own rules for chip buyers. The administration views rules regarding who can buy a chip as a matter of national security rather than industry regulation. These remarks were delivered during a leaders' plenary in China amidst discussions involving Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping.

The current situation involves a divide between national security export controls and the international frameworks used for governing advanced AI. While the president spoke against regulation, the cost of compute is changing for cloud providers in Bangkok or Kuala Lumpur. Some restricted Nvidia chips are already selling for two to three times their US prices on the Chinese gray market. Frontier labs and startups that rent capacity in the affected countries must now verify the licensing status of their providers.

stories.Headline: Calif uses OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model to uncover Java4Shell flaw in Java
stories.Summary:
Security researchers have identified a critical vulnerability in Java, the widely used open-source programming language, which is listed as CVE-2026-114938 and known as Java4Shell. The flaw allows hackers to gain remote access to sensitive internal systems and affects Java 17.0.6 on systems running x86-64 Intel and AMD chips with AVX-512 VBMI support. The cybersecurity startup Calif brought Java4Shell to light using OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber AI model. Oracle, the owner of the Java trademark, and the OpenJDK project have released software patches, while Amazon has issued fixes for its Corretto Java builds and Red Hat is rolling out patches for its Java distributions. Other at-risk Java distributions include Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, and SAP SapMachine.

The flaw resides in a performance shortcut Java uses to decode Base64 data faster, and when this shortcut receives a specially crafted Base64 string, it writes data beyond its allocated memory and corrupts other information. Attackers could exploit this to access application memory containing credentials or to run malicious code on the server. Calif researchers demonstrated this by exploiting Java4Shell to breach Keycloak, an authentication system. Other applications potentially compromised include Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has urged organisations to immediately patch the Oracle Java vulnerability, and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory warning that Java4Shell could allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code.

CERT-In advised users of affected Oracle Java SE and Oracle GraalVM products to implement available patches immediately. Google has rolled out mitigations and patches across its services and developed detection to ensure no exploitation, according to The New York Times. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security also issued an alert advising organisations to identify affected systems and apply vendor updates as they become available, and it stated that no active exploitation of Java4Shell has been observed yet. The use of AI tools to uncover critical security vulnerabilities, as seen with Java4Shell, highlights underlying infrastructure flaws. Fouad Matin, who leads cyber preparedness and safety at OpenAI, noted that this research shows how AI can assist expert security researchers in finding serious software flaws.

He noted that Kazakhstan is integrating artificial intelligence into various sectors, with particular emphasis on science and education, and that the development of universities in the coming years would be closely linked to the adoption of new technologies.

The initiative concerns an approach to international coordination in the field of AI safety, and it builds on an earlier proposal by the President. The Head of State also highlighted domestic research achievements, saying that Kazakhstani scientists have developed the core components of the KazLLM and AlemLLM language models. To develop a skilled workforce, Kazakhstan is implementing the AI-Sana programme, which aims to strengthen students' competencies in artificial intelligence, foster technology entrepreneurship and support the development of DeepTech startups. stories.Headline: AI finds software flaws and firms rush patches, raising outage risk, experts say
stories.Summary:
Recent tech outages at Microsoft, JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab disrupted businesses and consumers, and a temporary ground stop at US airports also caused chaos, though Department of Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited aging air traffic control infrastructure for that one. Politicians and tech executives, including Armadin CEO Kevin Mandia, suggest organisations are using AI to discover software vulnerabilities in their systems. That has led to a mad rush to apply patches quickly, according to Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Mandia stated that updating at speed may prevent testing all potential outcomes of an update. Nicole Perlroth, a former cybersecurity reporter, noted that pressure to patch faster increases the likelihood of breaking things in unexpected, cascading ways, in a post on X. The article, published by TechGig on November 19, 2026, says organisations are rolling out a higher volume of fixes, potentially overwhelming systems.

Fast updates may hinder full testing, leading to system disruptions, experts say, and more tech outages are expected as firms accelerate patching in the AI era. Last month, AI discovered significant flaws in a programming language used by up to 70 per cent of websites, contributing to the increased patching activity. The report ties the recent outages at the banks, Microsoft and the FAA to the rush to fix cybersecurity flaws discovered by AI. Mandia added that while nobody wants an outage, organisations will become operationally better at updating in the AI age, and he anticipates near-term cybersecurity pain will lead to long-term gains. Warner, the senator who described the mad rush to patch, and Mandia are among those pointing to AI vulnerability discovery as the driver of the faster patching.

Perlroth's warning focused on the risk that speed creates, with pressure to patch faster raising the chance of unexpected, cascading breakage. The article does not say what the organisations themselves said about the outages. The context given is that organisations use AI to find software vulnerabilities, which prompts quick fixes, and that the fast updates may skip full testing. stories.Headline: Commonwealth Bank releases CodeCheck, an open-source AI tool for finding software vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Bank of Australia released CodeCheck, an open-source AI cybersecurity tool, on November 19, 2026, according to TechGig. The tool is designed to help businesses identify potential software vulnerabilities earlier in their development processes. Security engineers at the bank developed CodeCheck based on an internal AI capability already used in the bank's own software development. The public version lets other businesses apply a similar approach when reviewing their code. The tool works with OpenAI's Codex and Anthropic's Claude Code to analyse software, investigate potential security weaknesses, and provide evidence for engineers to review.

CodeCheck uses an AI harness that guides coding agents through a structured security review of individual code changes, files, or entire codebases. Businesses can supply extra context about what their applications are meant to do, which helps the AI judge vulnerabilities based on the software's design. According to the bank's GitHub documentation, the tool reviews security in four stages, examining entry points, data flows, and potential weaknesses before assigning agents to investigate using the Common Weakness Enumeration framework. It then combines duplicate findings and assigns independent AI agents to challenge the initial results before generating a report. Findings include how untrusted input reaches affected code, an independent reviewer's assessment, and a severity score based on the Common Vulnerability Scoring System 4.0, and they follow the Security Analysis Results Interchange Format data standard.

The tool supports diff-aware reviews of commits, branches, and pull requests, and organisations can customise it with CWE-based security playbooks. CommBank Chief Security Officer Nicola Nicol said the bank built the capability to strengthen its internal defences before making it publicly available. CodeCheck is a free download from GitHub for businesses using Codex or Claude Code, though organisations remain responsible for costs tied to their AI coding agents and underlying models. The bank recommends running the tool in an isolated environment, mounting reviewed code with read-only permissions, restricting network access, and preventing AI agents from accessing credentials, warning that prompt-based restrictions are not deterministic.

CBA also notes that CodeCheck sends reviewed code to the selected model provider, making that provider's data-handling and security policies relevant, and that token consumption and processing costs rise as the codebase grows, so it recommends spending limits or timeouts for unattended reviews. Some providers restrict cybersecurity-related requests, which can interrupt authorised reviews or end responses early, and the final report might not always show when part of an assessment was interrupted. CBA has released CodeCheck as a one-time open-source project and does not plan to actively maintain, update, or provide ongoing support for the public repository. Organisations that adopt the tool will be responsible for maintaining their own versions and evaluating any modifications they make.

stories.Headline: Police find South Korean exam perfect scorer Lee Jin-woo in cardiac arrest

A 32-year-old South Korean man named Lee Jin-woo was found in a state of cardiac arrest on Thursday at an undisclosed location in Gangdong district, according to a brief police statement. Police said the finding followed a report filed that day over suicide concerns involving a man in his 30s. Lee had drawn public attention this year after scoring perfect marks on the law school admission test while studying dentistry at Seoul National University. Suspicion had swirled around him since Sunday, when the top scorer in this year's national tax accountant exam confessed to cheating using AI.

Lee denied the allegations against him and pledged to demonstrate his abilities by livestreaming himself taking the Korean language section of the college entrance exam on Thursday. He failed to show up for that livestream. Questions have also emerged over his college entrance exam scores, which rose sharply from his results in the 2010s and secured him a place at the university's dental school. Local media have also reported allegations of past assault and extortion that are unrelated to the AI cheating claims.

Police said that if Lee is pronounced dead, authorities will conduct a forensic examination and other procedures to determine the circumstances. South Korean authorities often take time to pronounce people as dead, categorising the lifeless as being in a state of cardiac arrest. The police statement referenced the report over suicide concerns without giving further details about the location or his condition. No further information was provided on his current status.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the possibility of a forensic examination if Lee is pronounced dead. stories.Headline: Court Rules Fourth Amendment Bars AI from Establishing Probable Cause
stories.Summary:
A federal court ruled that police cannot arrest someone on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match, and it denied qualified immunity to a Kentucky detective who jailed a Nebraska man on a bad-check charge, according to LavX News. Officers arrested Alain Osorio over a charge of passing a bad check at a bank in Florence, Kentucky, where detectives had only the bank's CCTV footage as a source for the suspect's image. Detective Ryan Kilmer of the Florence Police Department ran a screenshot from that footage through the department's facial recognition program, which matched the suspect to photos on Facebook belonging to a profile named "Yony Smith Npoles Charon." Kilmer concluded that "Yony" was Alain Vizcay Osorio, a man whose booking photo appeared in police files, and the court did not name the facial recognition program. The use of Facebook photos suggests Clearview AI, a company that has scraped hundreds of billions of images from the open web.

Osorio lived in Nebraska, and officers arrested him there and extradited him to Kentucky, where he posted bond on Jan. 24, 2025, the day after his arrest. A grand jury indicted him in March 2025, a court arraigned him two months later, and he pleaded not guilty, while the state attorney's office dismissed the charges after Osorio proved he was working in Nebraska when the suspect passed the bad check. Osorio does not resemble the man in the security footage or the Facebook profile, since he has a different head shape, haircut, facial features and complexion, though both men are Black with facial hair. Kilmer told the court in an affidavit that he used "investigative tools" to "match" Osorio to the suspect, but the court found he used one tool, the facial recognition program. Under Florence Police Department policy, facial recognition AI alone cannot establish probable cause, and Kilmer used it despite the policy.

The court wrote that the Fourth Amendment does not allow a detective to delegate to AI the task of assessing probable cause, and that the Constitution does not permit an arrest based on nothing more than an uncorroborated conclusion by AI that the individual committed a crime. The judge stripped Kilmer of qualified immunity, the legal doctrine that shields officers from civil liability unless they violate clearly established law, and Kilmer can appeal. A higher court could affirm the decision or reverse it, and if Kilmer loses his appeal, the ruling would apply beyond facial recognition. Police departments use AI to steer patrols through predictive policing software, officers use AI to generate reports from body camera footage, and Axon has added AI tools to its body cameras.

The article states that running a photo through an algorithm does not constitute detective work, that a match is a lead rather than a conclusion, and that departments across the country use facial recognition as an investigative shortcut. Detectives cannot treat an algorithm match as detective work, according to the piece, which cites Techdirt as its source.

stories.Headline: Senator Tillis plans to hold LoSapio's CISA nomination after he denies January 6 was an attack
stories.Summary:
Michael LoSapio, Palantir's chief information security officer and the nominee to lead the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, appeared before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on Thursday alongside six other nominees, and his nomination may now be in doubt after he said the January 6, 2021, storming of the U.S. Capitol was not an attack. When Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat, asked all the nominees whether January 6 was an attack, LoSapio first said he did not know, then said he did not believe it was an attack, adding that he was not involved in politics and knew what he saw on the news. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who is retiring in January, told reporters he plans to put a hold on LoSapio's nomination after those comments, which narrows his path to confirmation because he is unlikely to be included in any Senate nominations package before Democrats take the majority in the new year. CISA has been without a Senate-confirmed director since January 2025, and the Trump administration's previous nominee, Sean Plankey, withdrew his name this spring after his nomination sat in the Senate for 13 months. During the hearing, LoSapio declined to say whether he thinks CISA needs more staffing and resources, even as the agency hires hundreds more people after widespread departures last year.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, asked for his views on the Trump administration's proposed $385 million cut to CISA's budget for fiscal 2027 and the reduction of approximately 1,000 employees at the agency since January 2025, and LoSapio responded that he could not comment on the current state of CISA because he is not inside today, saying he comes from the private sector and can speak to his private sector experience about budgets and cuts and funding. Slotkin argued that recent outages and concerns about AI security point to the need for more CISA resources following the administration's cuts, and LoSapio responded that he does not necessarily believe more money means more security, saying he believes spending money on the right solutions in the right ways actually decreases risk. Sen. James Lankford, an Oklahoma Republican, referenced recent technology outages and asked how LoSapio would respond to similar scenarios as CISA director, and LoSapio said it is really important to understand the landscape of the systems out in the wild, the systems operated day to day, the systems relied on and the systems ancillary to the work, and to do an extensive evaluation of their vulnerabilities, whether they have been patched, how they have been architected and their defensive capabilities, both things that need to be added and things that exist today, as to how that maps to the threats being faced. LoSapio's hearing came a day after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was also pressed on CISA staffing during a hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee. Earlier this year, Mullin said CISA needs to hire 600 new staff following the loss of 1,000 employees between January 2025 and January 2026, and in September, acting CISA Director Nick Andersen said CISA was making progress on hiring, with roughly 250 new hires waiting to get through the security clearance process.

Asked by Homeland Security Committee Chairman Andrew Garbarino, a New York Republican, about the status of CISA hiring, Mullin said he would follow up about the numbers, but he said the Trump administration wants to increase CISA staffing, alluding to the clearance process and government pay scales as hiring barriers, saying the administration is able to meet those needs today but wants to grow capacity and that it takes time, and also takes a long time to get people cleared to a TS/SCI clearance and above level, that not everybody can pass those background checks, and that the government has to work with industry because its pay scale is much lower than what industry is paying. Members of the Homeland Security Committee have also introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a pilot program at CISA to help recruit AI and emerging technology experts, and Mullin backed such an effort during the hearing, calling it a very forward-leaning bipartisan bill that is needed more of and saying it gives the flexibility needed to compete with industry, bring the best into CISA and pay them competitively. CISA has some existing authorities to pay cyber experts more competitively, including under the Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity Talent Management System, or CTMS, but CISA also scaled back some cyber pay incentives earlier this year, leading to concerns that more employees could leave the agency. Rep. Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican who was the lead House sponsor on the legislation creating CISA in 2018, pushed Mullin to prioritize recruiting at the agency, saying there are 600 people to hire and urging him to get CISA full steam because the threats have not gone away and CISA needs to be in full force.

stories.Headline: Pension regulator chair Ramann urges MeitY to create a centralised AI regulatory framework
stories.Summary:
S. Ramann, the chairperson of the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority, asked the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to set up a centralised regulatory framework for artificial intelligence that regulated entities could access. She made the request while speaking at the CII-DFS Financing Summit 2026, according to a report published by The Hindu BusinessLine on November 19, 2026. In her view, the regulation should concentrate on how AI is deployed rather than trying to place guardrails around large language models themselves. She argued that any entity using AI to deliver goods and services must be required to keep sufficient guardrails within that delivery of service.

Ramann said AI-based services should carry an absolute liability clause for their providers, together with the right legal frameworks, before those services are adopted. She also demanded explainability of any AI-driven process, saying this is where the move toward explainable AI becomes necessary. She warned that poor-quality AI output in financial advice could put people's life savings at risk and further erode trust. On the sidelines of the event, she said Tamil Nadu had come on board for the National Pension System with its own pension scheme. She added that Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan have stayed outside the NPS for the past three to four years, while Punjab has exited the scheme but continues to make contributions to a funded account.

The push comes as the pension regulator seeks safeguards that make AI more explainable for the entities it oversees. Ramann framed the proposal as a way to ensure accountability, with liability resting absolutely on providers of AI-based services. The article does not say whether MeitY has responded to the request or what a central framework would contain. It also gives no timeline for any regulation, so what happens next on the AI proposal is not stated.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendments push high-risk HR system obligations to December 2027
stories.Summary:
The EU Digital Omnibus Package amended the EU AI Act and entered into force on July 27, 2026, Mary T. Costigan of Jackson Lewis P.C. wrote on November 19, 2026. The Commission presented the Digital Omnibus in November 2025 as a package to simplify EU digital law, Éric Le Quellenec of Flichy Grangé Avocats said. The package has two parts, and the first reopens the GDPR, which is still being negotiated, Le Quellenec said. The second part amends the AI Act, and that one is now law, he said. Luís Neto Galvão of SRS Legal and Le Quellenec offered five practical steps for general counsel and HR leaders at multinational businesses.

Obligations for systems listed in Annex III, including recruitment and career management, were due to apply in August of this year, Le Quellenec said. They now apply from December 2, 2027, and from August 2, 2028, for AI built into regulated products, he said. The prohibitions have applied since February 2025, the AI literacy obligations as well, and the transparency rules since August 2026, he said. High-risk systems in use before December 2, 2027, only fall under the Act if their design is significantly changed afterward, he said. Point 4 of Annex III covers recruitment, including targeting job ads, filtering applications, and evaluating candidates, and decisions on the employment relationship, including promotion, termination, task allocation based on behavior or personal traits, and monitoring and evaluating performance.

The five steps are inventory and classify AI-enabled HR tools, strengthen oversight and vendor contracts, mitigate bias, train relevant teams, and prepare recruitment practices for compliance, the article said. Neto Galvão said clients should not think they have nothing to do until 2027 and that now is the time to put a compliance plan in place. He said a year goes very quickly when you have to map your tools, renegotiate vendor contracts, and train your teams. Le Quellenec said the vendor is usually the provider and the employer is the deployer, but this can change. He said that if the employer puts its name on the tool, modifies it substantially, or changes its intended purpose so that it becomes high risk, it becomes a provider, which brings much heavier obligations.

Le Quellenec said the employer should check the conformity assessment, CE marking, EU declaration of conformity, and registration in the EU database before buying. He said the employer must use the system in line with the instructions, assign human oversight to people with the competence, training, and authority to overrule it, and make sure the input data the employer controls are relevant and representative. He said the employer must monitor the system, suspend use immediately and inform the provider if a risk appears, report serious incidents, and keep the logs for at least six months. He said the employer must inform candidates and employees who are subject to decisions and, before the tool is introduced, inform workers' representatives and the workers concerned. He said individuals have a right to an explanation of the role AI played in a decision that significantly affects them, and a rejected candidate can ask for it.

Le Quellenec said the fundamental rights impact assessment introduced by the AI Act applies to public bodies, private entities providing public services, and credit and insurance uses. He said a private employer generally does not have to do it, and for them the key assessment remains the GDPR DPIA. Neto Galvão said human oversight must be designed into the process, not added as a label, and a manager who can only confirm the system's output is not providing meaningful oversight. Le Quellenec said HR owns the use case, IT owns integration and security, the data protection officer owns data protection and privacy, and legal owns the contracts. He said the French Lawyers' Guide on Ethics and AI was adopted in March this year and draws attention to how the way you phrase a question shapes the answer.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Woman sues Los Angeles police for investigating her stillbirth under California privacy law
stories.Summary:
A woman is suing the city of Los Angeles and detectives within the Los Angeles Police Department for allegedly unlawful interrogation and investigation following a stillbirth she had in 2024. The complaint was filed late last week by If/When/How, a pregnancy-rights nonprofit, alongside law firm BraunHagey & Borden LLP. The plaintiff was granted anonymity Thursday and is referred to in the complaint as Jane Doe. This is the first known lawsuit under California's Reproductive Privacy Act, which was amended in 2022. The suit comes two years after California authorized patients to sue for being investigated due to their pregnancy outcomes.

The Reproductive Privacy Act, amended in 2022, prohibits the state from taking punitive action based on pregnancy decisions and outcomes. At least 13 states and the District of Columbia have enacted measures protecting pregnancy decisions and outcomes, including California, Colorado, Hawaii, Illinois, Michigan, Missouri, Montana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Vermont, Virginia and Washington. Among places that explicitly allow damages suits, including D.C., Colorado and Illinois, California is the only state to eliminate common legal immunities for law enforcement, Ainsworth said. In the first three years after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, more than 900 women faced criminal charges for conduct related to their pregnancies.

The vast majority of those charges were for child abuse, neglect or endangerment, most related to substance use during pregnancy. Sara Ainsworth, chief legal and policy director at If/When/How and one of the attorneys representing the plaintiff, said all the different things done to Ms. Doe are a violation of the Reproductive Privacy Act. Ainsworth said it is very important to show state actors in California that they must abide by the law, which prohibits criminalizing somebody. She said California's strong right-to-sue protections could become a legal roadmap for other states. Ainsworth said it is typically hard to hold government officials accountable for wrongful criminalization because of legal barriers.

She said the Reproductive Privacy Act explicitly allows a private right of action and eliminates some immunities, allowing government actors who normally are shielded to be held accountable. The Los Angeles Police Department declined to comment citing the pending litigation. Shantal McNeil, litigation counsel, helped Doe navigate the investigation and petitioned the city attorney not to bring charges. McNeil said reputational damage and other harms often outlast these types of arrests and investigations, even when charges are dropped or never filed.

She said police often investigate vulnerable women like the California plaintiff, who according to her attorneys is a young woman. McNeil said people mistakenly think every pregnancy ends in a healthy baby, so if you don't act the way police think you should, it's suddenly suspicious or criminal behavior. The plaintiff alleges that in November 2024 she was unhoused, living in a city shelter and menstruating irregularly due to her epilepsy medication. An emergency visit for stomach pains revealed she was pregnant, but the fetus did not have a heartbeat.

According to the complaint, Doe was initially informed she was still in the first trimester and could miscarry at home but subsequently learned she was around 29 weeks' pregnant. She passed significant blood clots in the shelter toilet, left without flushing and was taken by ambulance to the hospital and treated for significant blood loss. The complaint says Doe didn't realize she had passed the stillbirth. According to the complaint, police showed up at the hospital, shackled her to a bed and interrogated her for hours, telling her a fetus had been found outside the shelter.

The complaint said this was the first time Ms. Doe learned she had passed into the toilet and the first time she heard someone had reportedly moved the fetus from the toilet to an alley outside the shelter. The complaint alleges police continued to pursue a homicide investigation for about a year despite being told by a medical examiner that fetal demise had occurred in utero. In California, Doe alleges she had to leave the shelter after police told reporters they suspected a homicide and headlines circulated about a newborn baby dropped from a fourth-floor window. In February 2025, she contacted a legal helpline run by If/When/How and started working with McNeil.

stories.Headline: Ashwini Vaishnaw says India will issue an AI regulation consultation paper within a month
stories.Summary:
India’s government is drafting an AI law, and on 8 October Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said a consultation paper on AI regulation would come within a month and would probably form the basis of future regulation. In July, media reports said MeitY was examining the autonomy of AI agents as part of a possible new law. The article, by Manoj Chugh, was updated on 18 November 2026 and published on ETGovernment. It argues that the AI that should worry policymakers most is not the one that fakes a video but the one that approves a loan, files a return or moves money with no human pressing the final button. That is agentic AI.

The article says the government’s signals so far point to safety, a human-first approach, skilling, deepfakes and psychological harms. It says an agent is given a goal, access to systems and the authority to act, and it reads an invoice, checks it against a contract, raises a payment and emails the vendor. It proposes five principles: shared, graded accountability with a named deployer and a named executive for every agent acting with real authority; autonomy tiered by consequence, so any action that moves money above a set threshold, signs or changes a contract, or touches sensitive personal data needs human approval; tamper-evident action logs; agent incidents in the six-hour regime; and precise definitions of agents by their authority to act. It cites the 2026 amendments to the IT Rules requiring platforms to label AI-generated audio and video, CERT-In’s 2022 directions requiring cyber incidents to be reported within six hours, the RBI’s FREE-AI framework recommending board-approved AI policies for banks and other regulated entities, and the DPDP Act, whose consent manager framework comes into force this week, with penalties of up to ₹250 crore.

Dr. Pavan Duggal, a Supreme Court advocate of over 30 years, Global Chair of the AI Accountability Forum and author of more than 200 books on cyber law and AI, said on the Corridors & Boardrooms podcast that the old instinct to blame whoever built it no longer works because the builder cannot predict how an agent will behave. He proposes graded liability, looking at what each party contributed, whether model creator, integrator, deployer or user, and assigning liability accordingly. He pointed to a deeper gap: the Contract Act recognizes agency but not AI as an agent, so when an agent takes a decision on someone’s behalf, the law is silent on whether that decision is binding. Experts suggest a presumptive burden of proof, so once harm is claimed those who built, integrated and deployed the agent must show they took due care. The article says the defense that the algorithm did it is not good enough.

Dr. Gulshan Rai, whose team drafted the IT Act in 2000, said on the same podcast that the hardest problem was converting the virtual into something the law could recognize, and that at that time there was not even a digital signature in the country. His team wrote the Act in plain English because the common man would have to live with it. Section 66A, added in 2008, was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 because its language could reach ordinary online speech, and Dr. Rai believes 66A would not have been enough for generative or agentic AI anyway, adding that drafters should be very, very careful. In July 2016, hackers sent about $171 million out of Union Bank of India’s accounts through SWIFT, and working with the RBI and the government the bank recovered all of it within days; Dr. Rai, who coordinated the national response, says the lesson was that you need a single authority who can talk to regulators, banks and foreign governments at once. The article says enterprises should not mistake the absence of an AI law for the absence of law.

The article says the AI debate for two years has been about what models say, misinformation, bias and deepfakes, and that agents change the question to what AI systems do. It says content harms are about what people believe while agent harms are about what happens to their money, their data and their contracts, and that the second category needs its own chapter. It says a person harmed by an agent usually cannot prove what it did, so the courts can offer no remedy. It says the 2025 governance guidelines relied on existing laws and voluntary compliance, and that MeitY Secretary S. Krishnan has since signaled that the time for more may have come. It says the cyber security policy Dr. Rai wrote in 2013 still awaits a successor because, as he put it, somebody has to be made accountable and sit down and do it.

The article says the consultation paper is where the intent to examine AI agents must become concrete, and that the consultation paper should state plainly that the enterprise deploying an agent is the data fiduciary for what that agent does. It says boards do not need to wait for MeitY and can start by having the executive team take an inventory of every agent in production or pilot, including those inside vendor platforms, mapping each agent’s authority, what it can approve, spend, send, change or delete, and building and testing a kill switch. It says boards need to plan for resilience, and that experience shows the process fixes about half of security problems and configuration about 30%, while the role of technology is only about 15%, yet that is where most of the money goes. It says the question to ask every quarter is what the agents did that no human approved and whether it could be explained to a regulator. It says that if agents are left out of this paper, the next chance may be years away.

Articles.Title: Why India’s upcoming AI law must regulate autonomous agents, not just deepfakes

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson vetoes a city council ordinance banning artificial superintelligence
stories.Summary:
Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson announced on Thursday afternoon, Nov. 19, 2026, that she will not sign an ordinance the city council approved 7, 0 earlier that month, which would prohibit the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence within city limits. The ordinance was presented to the mayor on Nov. 9 at 5:13 p.m., according to the city clerk’s office, giving her until 5:13 p.m. Thursday to sign it or return it to the council with a veto message. Because she did neither, the ordinance is considered vetoed under Indiana law. Seven councilmembers voted for the ordinance on Nov. 4, when two members, Sydney Zulich and Kate Rosenbarger, were absent. Councilmember Dave Rollo introduced the ordinance and put forward all four amendments the council adopted before its final vote.

The ordinance would add a new chapter to Bloomington’s municipal code under Title 14, which governs peace and safety, and would prohibit distribution and deployment of ASI within the city, including through websites, software and other electronic interfaces, even when the computers hosting those systems are physically located elsewhere. It defines superintelligence in terms of agency, generality and intelligence, describing autonomous systems capable of modifying their own algorithms, executing computer code outside restricted environments and undertaking complex tasks without continuous human oversight, combined with capabilities vastly exceeding human cognitive performance. The ordinance does not establish a testing procedure or designate an independent authority to determine when a particular AI system has crossed the threshold into superintelligence. It invokes the city’s powers under Indiana’s Home Rule Act and compares superintelligence to hazardous substances and industrial processes that local governments can regulate in the interest of public safety, and it would authorize the city’s legal and police departments to seek civil penalties and court orders against violators, with enforcement discretionary rather than mandatory. One amendment explicitly excluded end-user access from the prohibition, so a Bloomington resident would not violate the ordinance merely by accessing an AI system through an electronic interface, and another removed Rollo’s original proposal to require approval from more than 95% of Bloomington’s registered voters, along with findings establishing an extremely high level of scientific certainty about the safety of superintelligence, before the ban could be lifted, retaining a scientific-safety objective in the preamble but no longer making the finding and referendum requirements for repeal.

Thomson said, “Bloomington is working hard to grow our innovation economy, and artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work,” and that “AI already contributes to advances in research, medicine, education and many other fields.” She added, “We also need to be careful about creating unnecessary barriers that discourage those very people from investing in our community.” Thomson said, “As mayor, I have a responsibility to lead the team that implements and enforces our ordinances,” and that “This ordinance leaves significant questions about how the City would identify violations, what authority we have to regulate them and what enforcement would require.” She said, “The potential need to monitor private digital activity is especially troubling given our recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance,” and that “Passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle,” adding, “We need to be confident that we can implement and enforce the laws we adopt.”

Thomson acknowledged the risks Rollo is attempting to address, saying, “I appreciate Council’s efforts to address the risks of increasingly autonomous AI systems and the national conversation this legislation has helped advance,” and that “Those risks deserve serious consideration.” Rollo told The B Square he is still optimistic about working with the mayor on a version of the ordinance she might eventually be willing to sign, because superintelligent AI is “a deadly risk for everyone,” and he added, “Obviously, we’re racing forward as the horizon is racing at us. I mean, this is madness. And there are huge consequences.” Rollo said at the start of the Wednesday night, Nov. 18, council meeting, less than 24 hours before the mayor’s deadline, that the ordinance “is emphatically not what tech businesses are using here or at IU,” and he said, “This particular AI, ASI, hasn’t yet arrived,” while contending that developing such systems is the goal of leading AI companies and that the technology could arrive soon. Rollo contrasted that goal with work at Indiana University, which he characterized as human-centered artificial intelligence emphasizing ethical deployment, human oversight and beneficial social impacts, and he said, “Local tech applications and IU are to be lauded for their approach.” Rollo rebutted Thomson’s surveillance concern, saying, “We don’t need to surveil anyone,” and suggested violations could be reported through complaints or investigated by testing whether a prohibited system was accessible from a city-operated computer.

The ordinance vetoed by Thomson represents a third effort by Rollo to persuade Bloomington’s city government to address what he and others warn is the existential danger to the human species posed by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence. In July 2023, Rollo proposed a resolution calling for a moratorium on developing artificial general intelligence until adequate safeguards could be established, and he withdrew it after officials with Indiana University raised concerns about possible implications for research funding, and sufficient support from council colleagues appeared unlikely. On June 10 of this year, the council unanimously adopted a resolution calling on governments at other levels to address the existential risks of artificial intelligence and urging a moratorium on developing advanced AI until the technology could be aligned with human values and well-being, and that resolution was nonbinding, expressing the council’s position without establishing a local prohibition. The ordinance approved by the council in early November goes further by attempting to make distribution and deployment of superintelligence a violation of Bloomington law. Rollo’s goals extend beyond Bloomington, and the ordinance is part of a strategy he envisions being replicated by hundreds of municipalities, with local prohibitions eventually generating enough pressure to prompt state, federal and international restrictions on advanced AI development.

The council could attempt to override the veto at its next regular meeting, scheduled for Wednesday, Dec. 2, at 6:30 p.m., and an override would require six votes in favor from the nine-member council. Thomson’s objections come despite several amendments the council adopted before its final vote, intended in part to narrow the ordinance’s scope, address concerns that it could affect ordinary users of AI technology, and other issues identified soon after Rollo introduced it. The amendments reduced the potential reach of the ordinance but did not resolve the underlying question of how Bloomington would identify prohibited systems or determine whether companies outside its boundaries were distributing them within the city. Whether Indiana’s Home Rule Act powers would support a prohibition extending to remotely operated digital systems is an unresolved legal question. Thomson’s surveillance concern comes just five weeks after the city council voted 7, 0 on Oct. 14 to prohibit automated license plate readers and certain surveillance camera systems that allow outside entities to access recordings and data, and the superintelligence ordinance does not itself authorize new surveillance of internet activity.

Articles.Title: Bloomington mayor vetoes AI superintelligence ban, citing research, enforcement and surveillance concerns - The B Square Bulletin

stories.Headline: Socialist MEP González Casares criticizes EU data center assessment plan as insufficient
stories.Summary:
Members of the European Parliament have on their desks the draft of the future Cloud and Artificial Intelligence Development Act, known as CADA, the Demócrata article of 19 November 2026 reports. The rapporteurs have presented their proposed report, opening the phase in which political groups will try to incorporate their positions into the initiative. The Socialist group intends that the rule coming out of its processing in the European Parliament, before negotiations begin with the member states, guarantees a “people”-centered approach. The European Commission presented the proposal on 3 June 2026 as COM(2026) 502, and it is processed through the ordinary legislative procedure. The file number is 2026/0138(COD), and as of 19 November 2026 the text is in the committee work phase of the first reading.

The text sets out four different levels of assurance at EU scale to regulate security, operational autonomy, and the location of data in computing services. The initiative aims to consolidate the continent’s technological sovereignty and reduce its dependencies on third countries. The draft links the expansion of data center capacity to compatibility with the European climate targets for 2050 and proposes that these infrastructures actively contribute to decarbonisation. Before declaring an area as an acceleration area for data centers, member states must carry out an impact assessment verifying that projected electricity demand is compatible with their Integrated National Energy and Climate Plans and with households’ supply needs. The draft adds that these areas must endeavor to cover practically 100% of their energy demand through local, zero-emission renewable sources.

The Socialist MEP and member of the Committee on Industry, Research and Energy, Nicolás González Casares, said this week during a closed-door meeting that “each law is an opportunity.” He argued that the continent “needs rules to also recover citizens’ trust” in technological development that works “not only for the digital world, but also for people.” He explained that crossing Germany, Finland, Denmark or Portugal would reveal different approaches, and argued for common requirements at the European scale with room to adapt them to each territory. He added that geographical realities must be taken into account because not all member states have the same energy mix or the same climate. He said of the proposed classification system “it is not enough,” and that “we have a very nice label, but we do not know the reality.”

González Casares is critical of some approaches being developed by the Community Executive, especially the assessment scheme for these infrastructures. He considers that the proposed classification system does not provide sufficient information to know the real impact of data centers. He regrets that the assessment includes no specific data on absolute electricity consumption in megawatt-hours or kilowatt-hours, the total volume of water used, or the amount of renewable energy consumed over the year. He pointed out that when labels are added without knowing the total energy consumption of these data centers, “we probably do not have a complete picture.” The draft also analyzes the feasibility of interconnecting smaller or geographically distributed data centers so they can train artificial intelligence models in parallel.

The European Commission’s initiative seeks to harmonize the efforts of the member states and establish a common framework for a sector considered strategically important for the Union. Regulatory fragmentation and differences in national criteria can hinder the expansion of infrastructures and Europe’s capacity to compete in a market shaped by computing and artificial intelligence model development. The legislation will have to address the impact of data centers on electricity consumption, the availability of water resources, and the needs of national networks. The draft proposes that, when direct and continuous supply is not technically feasible, the rest of the needs may be met through grid electricity, storage systems, or flexible demand management mechanisms. Interconnection could reduce electricity consumption during periods of peak demand on the grid by distributing computing tasks across different facilities.

Political groups now begin to shape their priorities and the modifications they intend to introduce in the report. The committees have not yet approved the draft report and the Plenary has not set its position, so it is not an approved regulation nor is it in force. Parliament and Council must agree on the text through the ordinary legislative procedure. The socialists see in this phase an opportunity to strengthen demands for transparency, sustainability, and control of consumption. The articles leave open how the negotiations between Parliament and the Council will conclude and what the final text will contain.

stories.Headline: South Korea activates emergency response team to stop AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
An anonymous user on the online community DC Inside claimed to have used artificial intelligence to cheat on the 2024 Suneung exam. This individual allegedly used a miniature camera disguised as a shirt button and a smartphone to obtain an average percentile score of 98.6. These claims surfaced shortly after Han Won-seok, the top scorer on this year's tax accountant qualification exam, confessed to using similar AI tools. Han admitted to using a miniature camera and generative AI during both rounds of the national exam in April and July. He scored 397.5 out of 400 points and achieved perfect scores in three of the four subjects.

The current situation requires the Education Ministry to implement strict measures to prevent the use of hidden cameras and smart glasses. YouTuber Kim Min-woo, known as Mimiminu, has urged the government to postpone the upcoming Suneung to ensure proper security. He noted that the exam was previously delayed in 2017 due to the Pohang earthquake and in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. To combat these threats, Prime Minister Han Seong-sook vowed on Tuesday to root out AI cheating by activating an interagency emergency response team. The government plans to ban smart devices and deploy additional staff at testing sites to maintain the integrity of the process.

Several education experts have expressed deep concern regarding the ability of authorities to detect modern cheating devices. Kim Min-woo explained that tiny devices hidden in bracelets or buttons can solve complex questions very quickly. Kang Sung-tae, the founder of Gongsin.com, argued that checking for thick-framed glasses is insufficient because many smart glasses from China have discreet designs. He stated that he has warned for years that AI-assisted cheating was inevitable and hoped his warnings would raise awareness. These experts believe that the current screening methods are outdated and cannot stop sophisticated technology.

The South Korean government is now racing to curb these technological breaches before the college entrance exam takes place this Thursday. Authorities are focusing on identifying a wide variety of smart glasses and other wearable electronics that students might smuggle into the rooms. The Education Ministry must now decide if the existing laws allow for a schedule change to better prepare for these threats. If the government cannot guarantee a fair environment, the pressure to delay the exam may increase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cyprus chamber and communications office hold AI and cyber summit in Limassol
stories.Summary:
The Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Office of the Commissioner of Communications will hold a Communications, Cyber and AI Summit in Limassol on December 9 and 10, the Cyprus Mail reported on November 19, 2026. The event will take place at the City of Dreams Mediterranean under the auspices of the President of the Republic of Cyprus. It will bring together public authorities, businesses and technology experts to discuss developments shaping the digital future of Cyprus and Europe. The summit aims to provide a platform for dialogue between representatives of European and national institutions, regulatory authorities, public organisations, businesses and technology specialists.

The agenda will centre on electronic communications, cybersecurity and artificial intelligence, with discussions on emerging European and national policies, regulatory requirements, digital infrastructure, business resilience and security, and the responsible use of AI. Among the legislative and regulatory developments expected to feature are the NIS2 Directive, the AI Act, the Cyber Resilience Act and the Cybersecurity Act. Other subjects will include next-generation networks, critical digital infrastructure, cyber threat management, regulatory compliance and the use of artificial intelligence in cybersecurity. The organisers said the event would give businesses an opportunity to keep up with the latest European and national legislative and regulatory developments and to gain practical insights into compliance, risk management and digital resilience.

The summit is aimed particularly at chief executives, managing directors and board members, as well as chief information officers, chief technology officers, chief information security officers, data protection officers and professionals in cybersecurity, technology, risk management and compliance. It is also relevant to businesses and organisations affected by changing digital security requirements and the transformation associated with artificial intelligence. Participation is free of charge, although advance registration is required, and the official language will be Greek with simultaneous interpretation into English. The full two-day programme, including details of speakers, thematic sessions and registration, is available on the summit's official website. The organisers encouraged businesses and their executives to attend, describing the event as an opportunity to stay informed about developments affecting their operations and competitiveness while building connections with relevant institutions, specialists and business leaders.
