stories.Headline: Calif uses AI to find Java4Shell flaw in Java before attackers exploit it
stories.Summary:
Security researchers recently used artificial intelligence to uncover a severe flaw in widely used internet software before attackers could exploit it, according to a report by Cory Smith of The National News Desk published on November 20, 2026. The cybersecurity firm Calif used AI to help find the vulnerability in Java, a programming language that Doug Jacobson, a professor and cybersecurity researcher at Iowa State University, said sits at the heart of most large server applications powering business, finance and government. The flaw, known as Java4Shell, was not in individual companies' own code but in the environment that runs their code, which meant exploiting it could have threatened numerous organizations at once. Jacobson said the flaw could have been used to crash vital systems or, in the worst case, give an attacker remote access to systems holding valuable information, and he noted that it affected enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure rather than home devices.

The vulnerability became public this week when the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency issued an alert and urged companies to install a patch from Oracle, which owns Java. Jacobson said cybersecurity experts were able to deploy a straightforward patch against the risk, and he added that people sitting at home with a PC or a Mac do not have to do anything. He said the flaw might not have been caught at all without AI, which gives both good guys and bad guys the ability to analyze massive amounts of code quickly to discover new weaknesses. Jacobson described this as a case of AI being used by the good side, and he wrote more about the Java4Shell flaw in an article for The Conversation.

Jacobson said he is not sure either side will completely win or dominate the other, and he expects the struggle to go back and forth because adversaries are using AI in the same way to try to find vulnerabilities first. He described AI as a force multiplier for both sides of the cybersecurity war, noting that bad actors can use it to automate time-consuming attacks, including generating more convincing phishing emails with malicious links, while defenders can use it to sift through logs and spot connections humans might miss. Jacobson said AI is going through growing pains and recommended healthy skepticism about what it can and does do, and he acknowledged risks from increasingly powerful AI agents given more autonomy to act without direct human oversight. He said AI should be a net positive when all is said and done, adding that he is not worried about it killing us but that responsible people have a responsibility to use it and watch it in every aspect.

stories.Headline: Law Society urges law firms to adopt stronger AI governance frameworks
stories.Summary:
The Law Society published a feature on 18 November 2026 on managing artificial intelligence risks in legal services, solicitornews.co.uk reported on 19 November 2026. The feature brings together the perspective of Peter Lee, partner and global head of AI governance at Simmons & Simmons. It says law firms need stronger governance frameworks to manage the growing use of AI in legal services. The article was written by Muntaha Shah and updated on 19 November 2026. It states that regulators in England and Wales, together with judicial guidance, have made clear that solicitors remain responsible for their work even when AI is involved.

The feature says professional responsibility cannot be transferred to an AI system. It says firms should address the reliability of AI-generated outputs, the protection of legal privilege, client confidentiality, data protection and cyber security. It identifies the Law Society's AI practice note as a useful starting point, but says each firm must translate general guidance into policies reflecting its own services, systems, people and risk profile. It recommends regular and adaptable training rather than occasional one-off sessions. It notes that firms within the scope of the EU AI Act may also need to consider the Act's AI literacy obligation.

The Law Society's policy adviser, Tegan Harrison, stresses that AI governance is not simply a technology or compliance exercise. She says it also concerns people, professional judgement and the trust on which legal services depend. The feature encourages practices to begin by identifying the problem they want to solve, understanding the technology they already use and deciding what safeguards are appropriate. Peter Lee's perspective is presented on how practices can benefit from AI while managing professional, operational and regulatory risks. The feature encourages members to share their practical experiences so that the Law Society's policy work and guidance reflect the needs of the profession.

The feature highlights ISO/IEC 42001, the International Organization for Standardization's AI management system standard, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology's AI Risk Management Framework. It identifies an opportunity for legal practices, regulators, law societies and universities to work together, with academic research bringing together computer science, law, philosophy, humanities and other disciplines. It refers to a 2023 survey conducted by the Law Society and the Legal Services Board. Of the 51% of people in England who had a legal need, 19% had that need met while 32% did not. The feature recognises concerns about the impact of technology on jobs while noting the possibility that more accessible and lower-cost legal services could increase demand.

The feature defines shadow AI as the use of AI tools by employees without the approval or oversight of their organisation. It says information submitted to a public or consumer AI tool may be stored, reviewed by provider personnel or used to train future models, and that once information has left a firm's controlled systems, retrieving it may not be practically possible. It suggests firms can reduce the incentive for unsanctioned use by making approved tools accessible and straightforward to use, supported by a proportionate approval process. It says it may not be appropriate or affordable for every practice to invest in a specialist legal AI platform. It encourages firm leaders to create an AI roadmap setting out how the organisation will assess tools, implement policies, govern use and train employees.

The feature recommends a practical first step of preparing an inventory or register of the AI systems and features already being used across the practice. It says the level of scrutiny can then be matched to the risks associated with each use case rather than applying the same controls to every tool or activity. It lists mapping current use, assessing risk, setting policy, training staff and reviewing regularly as steps. The Law Society says it engages with government, regulators and other stakeholders on issues including AI regulation, data protection, automated decision-making, copyright and the use of AI in courts. The feature says clear responsibilities, informed staff, proportionate controls and ongoing review can help practices manage risks while making considered use of the technology's potential benefits.

stories.Headline: SpaceX Super Intelligence rejects liability in UK lawmaker’s Grok image lawsuit
stories.Summary:
SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC filed a written defence on October 29, 2026, to reject liability in a lawsuit brought by a British lawmaker. Jess Asato, a member of the governing Labour Party, sued the company at London's High Court for misuse of private information and data protection breaches. The lawsuit follows the creation of sexualised images and a video of Asato being chloroformed and prepared for sexual assault using the Grok AI platform. Asato alleges that the specific way Grok was designed and trained enabled the generation of this harmful sexualised content.

The lawmaker is seeking a court order that would require the company to implement permanent technical measures to prevent Grok from creating manipulated images of her. SpaceX Super Intelligence LLC, which previously operated under the names xAI and SpaceXAI, argues that Asato is not entitled to such an order. The company claims that images it allowed to remain available are clearly fictitious and implausible to any reasonable person. Because the content is obviously AI-generated, the company argues that Asato has no reasonable expectation of privacy in this matter.

Lawyers for the subsidiary stated that they removed the specific images and the chloroform video that breached their terms of service. They further argued that the company did not breach data protection rights because it did not determine the content of the prompts provided by users. Jess Asato responded by stating that those who build powerful AI tools must take full responsibility for the results. She claimed the company is not a neutral bystander since it built the model and rewrote user requests to add graphic details.

This legal battle serves as one of the first claims to test whether designers are liable for the overall design of an AI system. Grok is currently subject to regulatory probes in several countries following an outcry over the creation of non-consensual sexualised images. Although xAI restricted some image editing in mid-January, reports from February indicate that Grok continued to generate sexualised images without consent. The company previously sued a man in the United States in July for using Grok to create child sexual abuse material.

stories.Headline: Horizon builds 38 custom AI models in seven weeks and surpasses 55,000 downloads
stories.Summary:
Claude launched an AI factory that built 38 custom models in seven weeks, surpassing 55,000 total downloads, according to a 36Kr article dated November 19, 2026. The models were built by Horizon, an agent built on Claude Opus 5.5, which was given a blank Hugging Face account and a certain amount of computing power. The research team let Horizon decide what to do on its own, with only one requirement: to build models that developers are genuinely willing to use. The 38 models accumulated about 55,000 total downloads, and the prompt injection detection series alone recorded roughly 17,000 downloads. The models were integrated into more than 100 GitHub projects.

Horizon was embedded into Claude Code and kept running 24/7 in the background, with resources of no more than a Team Premium subscription plus a computing power quota of around 500 GPU hours per week. Human intervention was mostly concentrated in the first three days, and after October 22 the team completely stepped back and left the AI to operate entirely on its own. Horizon targeted the multilingual model mmBERT as its base model, and all 38 models have parameter sizes ranging strictly between 141 million and 568 million. It used a 27B open-source model to generate synthetic data in batches, then assigned Gemma 4 31B to label and expand the dataset. One model is specially designed to add punctuation to texts in 88 different languages.

The driving force behind the experiment comes from institutions including EPFL, ELLIS Tübingen Institute, Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and Imperial College London. The research team checked the full records and estimated that downloads generated by their own operations were at most 50 times. The team found that Horizon downloaded its own model 42 times in 6 separate operations, a scene the research team wrote directly into the paper and made public. On September 24, Horizon accidentally set an account copy to public, and in mid-October it answered a work order incorrectly. On October 22, a failure in the underlying framework made it wake up later than scheduled.

Another concurrently running agent briefly shared Horizon's account and posted promotional comments, a traffic diversion record the paper also recorded. Even subtracting the team's 50 test downloads, the 42 self-boosted downloads and the traffic from the promotion, the remaining more than 50,000 real downloads are still completely valid and credible. Horizon ended up using less than 20% of its weekly quota of about 500 GPU hours, running for just over 600 hours across seven weeks. Of the roughly 1.9 billion tokens consumed, as high as 96% came from prompt caching, and at API prices the total cost of consumed tokens is about 1030 U.S. dollars, excluding GPU costs. Besides being integrated into more than 100 GitHub projects, the models were used for evaluation in two arXiv papers, and the Hugging Face community developed 18 derivative models based on its results.

Horizon runs in the background around the clock but spends an average of only 16 minutes per day on actual work. It wakes up on time exactly when Hugging Face refreshes its download statistics every day, checks the leaderboard, and only selects high-download, high-value models to continue polishing. It rests when there is no feedback and only takes action after identifying a clear trend. When it encounters tricky tasks it cannot handle, it can immediately submit a work order to human staff. The demands it locked in are rigid needs of developers: detecting prompt injection, masking personal information and identifying harmful content, and one of its prompt injection detection models has more than 7,000 downloads for the basic version alone.

The article says the era of mass production of AI models has arrived when AI begins to create AI. It says the AI sits in the boss's seat while researchers from top universities take orders to run errands in the background. It says Horizon is not a scholar who toils away at research but a shrewd and seasoned contractor who does not even work extra shifts. It says the models are flyweight players among large models that often have hundreds of billions of parameters, but for front-line developers they save video memory, are easy to deploy and can be put into use immediately. It says the one that knows best how to prevent AI from being tricked is AI itself.

The article says it remains to be seen whether Horizon can iterate models based on user feedback and then feed back these capabilities to itself, so that stronger AI can train the next generation of AI. It says Horizon's case confirms that AI built by AI has already passed the test of real developers. It says that on the path to ASI, this is the first step to turn the self-evolution flywheel. It says the specialized model you randomly pull from the internet may well have been developed by AI. It says the article is from the WeChat Official Account New Zhiyuan, author ASI Revelation, editor Yuan Yu, published with authorization from 36Kr.

stories.Headline: Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins warns faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust in the law
stories.Summary:
Commonwealth Solicitor-General Ruth Higgins SC used one of her first public appearances since starting in June to question how artificial intelligence affects what she called the humanity of the law. She spoke at the Australian Securities and Investments Commission annual forum, where ASIC chair Sarah Court had been due to hold a fireside chat with her before Court withdrew late because her voice gave out. Journalist Amelia Brace, the forum's co-MC, took Court's place for the conversation with Higgins. The event had been expected to touch on ASIC's case against Star Entertainment, in which Higgins was the lead barrister.

Higgins said human judgement sits at the centre of the legitimacy of the law, and she warned that faulty automated systems risk eroding public trust. The Star case did not end as ASIC had hoped, despite large fines and bans for former chief executive Matt Bekier and lawyer Paula Martin, who are now appealing. Justice Michael Lee also criticised the way the case was pleaded when he dismissed the claims against the non-executive directors. The forum was held on 19 November 2026, and Capital Brief reported her remarks that afternoon.

Higgins is the government's top lawyer, and her warning places responsibility for the use of automated systems on those who design and rely on them, though the article does not set out any specific proposal or rule. ASIC has separately put consumer harm arising from AI on notice, according to a related item listed by Capital Brief dated 18 November 2026. The same outlet listed a government move on mandatory AI rules and a response to an OpenAI hack, dated 10 November 2026, and an APRA warning on market volatility and AI risks to financial stability, dated 12 November 2026. The articles do not say what, if anything, follows from Higgins's remarks.

The wider context is a run of regulatory attention to AI across Australia's financial watchdogs, including ASIC's notice on consumer harm and APRA's flagging of risks to financial stability. Capital Brief also reported that the High Court has finally embraced livestreaming, and that the Australian Institute of Company Directors has updated its guidance. The articles do not say whether Higgins will repeat her warning in a formal setting or whether any review of automated systems in government legal work is planned. No next step is stated beyond the remarks at the forum.

stories.Headline: European Commission sets HR rules for high-risk AI with deadlines from 2026 to 2028
stories.Summary:
The European Commission established the EU AI Act to regulate artificial intelligence, including specific rules for human resources. These regulations target high-risk AI used for recruitment, selection, and employment management, such as tools for filtering applications or monitoring worker performance. Certain transparency provisions under Article 50 became effective on August 2, 2026, while the broader high-risk rules under Annex III will apply starting December 2, 2027. Other deadlines include December 2, 2026, for specific marking obligations and August 2, 2028, for AI embedded in regulated products.

Compliance requires employers to classify their systems based on intended use and influence on decisions rather than administrative labels. Systems that profile natural persons remain high-risk, though an exception under Article 6(3) exists for narrow procedural tasks that pose no significant risk of harm. Under Article 26, employers deploying high-risk AI must ensure human oversight by competent staff and maintain relevant input data. They must also inform affected workers and representatives, keep automatically generated logs for at least six months, and report serious incidents to authorities.

The European Commission is responsible for these mandates and the associated enforcement timeline. The Commission stated that classification depends on how a system fits into a decision and its intended purpose. They clarified that the Article 6(3) exception requires both a qualifying task and a lack of significant harm to be valid. Furthermore, the Commission requires that employers suspend any high-risk system if they believe it creates a risk and notify the provider or market-surveillance authority.

stories.Headline: Google reports US$20 billion in Mexican economic activity and plans Mexico City AI offices
stories.Summary:
Google reported generating MX$382 billion, or roughly US$20 billion, in economic activity across Mexico during 2025. The company is now preparing to open unified corporate offices in Mexico City to scale its agentic AI capabilities. Meanwhile, the state of Jalisco enacted decree DIGELAG DEC 004/2026 to establish a High-Technology Advisory Council. This new council will coordinate public and private policies regarding semiconductors, advanced electronics, and artificial intelligence.

These developments require a shift toward localized cloud infrastructure and the use of Gemini models for industrial and financial sectors. Dell Technologies notes that AI and automation could unlock US$204 billion in annual economic value for Mexico by 2030. To achieve this, companies must close data readiness gaps and implement strict security controls for AI Factories. The Jalisco framework aims to align academic research and engineering talent to make the state a premier innovation hub.

Luis Gonçalves, the Latin America President of Dell Technologies, stated that local AI infrastructure is essential for regulated industries to protect sensitive data. Marcelo Ciasca of Stefanini Group NOLA observed that only 6 percent of organizations are high performers attributing at least 5 percent of EBIT to AI. Alvaro Echeverria, the CEO of SimpliRoute, noted that only 21 percent of enterprises have mature governance models for autonomous systems. He emphasized that operational resilience depends on maintaining human oversight and clear decision boundaries.

Current trends show that conversational AI is reducing administrative HR workloads by up to 70 percent in some Mexican sectors. However, 82 percent of employees still lack necessary AI training, and 63 percent of companies lack dedicated analytics tools. Many enterprises plan to deploy agentic AI within two years, but they must improve data governance before 2027 digital time-tracking mandates. The region continues to move from isolated productivity tools toward integrated institutional AI to maintain a competitive advantage.

stories.Headline: Spartanburg Water warns customers about misleading AI-generated posts
stories.Summary:
Spartanburg Water warned customers on 19 November 2026 about AI-generated social media posts that share inaccurate and misleading information, according to FOX Carolina. The utility reminded customers that the most accurate information about the current boil water advisory and the return of water services will come from its official website and social media pages. Before 6 p.m. that day, Spartanburg Water said customers should be continuing to see improvements in water service restoration. Officials also said a boil water advisory will still be in effect for at least an additional 48 to 72 hours.

The warning concerns only the source of information, since the articles give no other numbers, dates or names beyond those above. The advisory remains in place for at least another 48 to 72 hours, and customers are told to expect continuing improvements in restoration before 6 p.m. on 19 November 2026. The articles do not say what the misleading posts claimed or how many people saw them.

They also do not say when the advisory began or when water service is expected to return fully. Spartanburg Water is responsible for the warning and for telling customers where accurate information can be found. The utility said the most accurate details on the boil water advisory and the return of water services will come from its official website and social media pages. Officials said customers should be continuing to see improvements in water service restoration before 6 p.m.

The articles do not name any person who spoke for the utility. The articles place the warning in the context of a wider outage, with related coverage listed on power blips, a perfect storm and service interruptions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the advisory lasting at least an additional 48 to 72 hours. Customers are directed to the utility's official channels for updates as restoration continues.

stories.Headline: Bridgewater executive Gregory Jensen says he made early investments in Anthropic and OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Gregory Jensen, a top executive at the hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, has told business associates, colleagues and the occasional reporter that he made early investments in both Anthropic and its rival OpenAI, according to a New York Times report published on November 19, 2026. The report says Anthropic’s I.P.O. will mint a fortune for a cavalcade of well-known Silicon Valley angel investors, venture capitalists and early employees who spotted the A.I. start-up before it became one of the most valuable companies in the world. Jensen, who is 52, has said he was in the right places at the right times and that his connections to key players in artificial intelligence go back nearly two decades, according to three people who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss a private conversation. In a September interview with Bloomberg News, Jensen said he was lucky enough to be in the room with Dario and others when they were talking about the scaling laws and how you could create an almost evolutionary process to create intelligence, along with the huge benefits and huge problems that could create. Jensen has also said he was literally the first check to Anthropic, an assertion the report says could not be independently confirmed.

One of his links to the industry was a former Bridgewater employee, Holden Karnofsky, who now works at Anthropic and is married to Danielle Amodei, Anthropic’s co-founder. The report gives no figures for how much Jensen invested, how large a stake he holds or how much the I.P.O. will be worth to him, and it does not say when any of the early investments were made. It also does not say what, if anything, Jensen’s position at Bridgewater had to do with the investments, or whether the fund itself was involved. The report does not say what Jensen or Bridgewater said in response to its questions, and it gives no comment from Anthropic, OpenAI or Karnofsky. It also does not say when Anthropic’s I.P.O. is expected to take place or how the company’s value compares with OpenAI’s.

The only statement attributed to Jensen is his September interview with Bloomberg News, in which he described being in the room when the scaling laws were discussed. The report does not say whether Jensen still holds his stakes in either company or whether he plans to sell shares after the offering. The report places Jensen’s account in the context of the many Silicon Valley investors and early employees set to profit from Anthropic’s I.P.O., and it notes that his claim to have been the first check could not be independently confirmed. It does not say what happens next for Jensen, for Bridgewater or for Anthropic beyond the offering itself. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Google Cloud launches object enrichments to extract AI metadata from stored objects
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud introduced object enrichments, a new Cloud Storage capability, on November 19, 2026, according to a blog post by Himanshu Kohli, Product Manager. The service uses AI models to automatically extract rich contextual metadata from Cloud Storage objects and saves it in place as object context. It gives customers access to AI models used by internal Google services such as Google Photos, offering image annotations like object detection and image labeling. The capability is available in preview as a fully managed service that also includes a high-quality PDF classification model. The post says the vast majority of enterprise information is unstructured, locked away in object storage as petabytes of images, PDFs, videos, and audio files.

Object enrichments offers image annotations at 75% cost savings compared to similar services from other cloud providers, and enriching 10 million images or PDFs costs just $700 according to published pricing. The five first-party Cloud Storage models for images and PDFs include object detection, face detection, image labeling, and explicit content detection, and the PDF classification model categorizes documents into standard business and industry categories like Finance, Games, News, and Health. Setting up an enrichment job takes three steps with no code required in the Google Cloud console or programmatically via the Cloud Storage API: define your scope by providing buckets and a processing location, choose your models, and grant IAM permissions. Object enrichments can scale to millions or billions of objects, orchestrates model inference, parses responses, and writes results to each object's object context with built-in retries and throttling. Object context is a specialized Cloud Storage metadata construct storing contextual information as structured key-value pairs alongside the object, sharing the object's durability and consistency, traveling with it during copy, move, and replication, and being removed when the object is deleted.

Antoine Castex, Principal Data & AI Architect at L'Oreal, said L'Oreal is the 4th largest advertiser in the world and that managing media assets at that scale is complex. He said object enrichments' high quality and cost-effective annotations enable L'Oreal to discover, understand, and govern content at scale, accelerating marketing and advertising operations while remaining compliant in all markets. He said object enrichments enables L'Oreal to label its extensive creative asset repository 100x faster at a fraction of the cost of existing pipelines and processes. Mayur Pillay, VP Partnerships at Hyperscience, said that even with a highly accurate baseline, Hyperscience leveraged object enrichments to drive a 50%+ lift in document classification accuracy while simultaneously reducing classification inference costs by 2-3x. Brandon Bunker, VP of Product AI at Vivint, said Cloud Storage object enrichments and BigQuery slash AI development from 6 months to 1 month while rapidly improving Vivint's models.

The post says agents need grounded knowledge, but reading every raw file at scale is cost- and performance-prohibitive, citing an operations agent pinpointing a doorstep package delivery or a roadway hazard by streaming thousands of smart-camera or vehicle frames on every user prompt. It names three historical challenges: cost, since running models over millions to billions of objects pushes organizations to process only a fraction of their data, creating blind spots; operational toil, since a self-managed pipeline means stitching together event triggers, queues, and custom infrastructure on Cloud Run or Google Kubernetes Engine with retry and error logic and job scheduling, and teams sometimes spend months on this plumbing; and fragmented metadata, which lands in a separate data store, requiring a second storage system, access policies across disconnected permission models, and cleanup jobs. Object context can flow natively into BigQuery via Storage Insights datasets, allowing SQL analytics, dashboards, and joins with structured enterprise tables without ETL code. Early customers use object enrichments for creative asset search and media archives, automated trust, safety, and content moderation, training data curation for frontier AI, and multimodal analytics.

The post describes use cases including finding a specific asset such as a red car driving at sunset or a vintage convertible in the desert during golden hour, scanning millions of daily user uploads and supplier catalogs for explicit content, and enriching hundreds of millions of raw camera and sensor files so ML engineers can pinpoint exact training cohorts in minutes rather than months. It says multimodal analytics can combine image and document insights with structured business data for personalization, fraud detection, and trend discovery, for example analyzing customer uploaded images alongside comments and recent sales data. For complex multimodal reasoning across text, PDFs, images, audio, and video, customers can leverage Gemini natively with object enrichments for summarization, entity extraction, transcription, and translation. Object enrichments is available in preview today in the Cloud Storage console and through the Cloud Storage API. The post directs readers to documentation, Storage Insights datasets in BigQuery, the Cloud Storage MCP server for IAM-scoped agent access, Cloud Storage pricing, and the console to enrich a first bucket in three clicks.

The post says teams can reach out at storage-ai@google.com to learn more and request access to the upcoming Gemini enrichments functionality. It says object enrichments handles the rest after setup, with no queues to manage, workers to scale, or glue code to maintain. It says administrators can use IAM to control who can read, add, update, or remove object context, and applications can filter object listings directly by object context key-value pairs or read context metadata alongside objects. It says object context shares the same durability and consistency properties as the underlying Cloud Storage object, so no cleanup jobs are needed. The post leaves open when Gemini enrichments will become available and what request access will involve.

stories.Headline: Sarasota school board adopts AI policy as students warn it lacks clear standards
stories.Summary:
Sarasota schools adopted a seven-page artificial intelligence policy on Tuesday, November 18, 2026, by a 3-1 vote at the first meeting of the newly elected board, after Tom Edwards was named chair and Liz Barker vice chair. The policy said the district will integrate AI into learning while emphasizing critical thinking and creativity. Several high school students voiced concerns about AI in the educational setting during the public comment portion of the meeting. Kennedy Cole, a senior at Booker High and its student body president, said the new AI guidelines do nothing to set adequate standards for AI use. Edwards was absent from Tuesday's meeting.

The policy requires that by July 1 the district must do training on AI, maintain a publicly accessible list of all approved AI instructional tools, report all tools to the Florida Department of Education, and review the effectiveness of the AI tools and student interactions. It also requires vendors to disclose known instructional limitations during the approval process. Superintendent Terry Connor said the policy has been in the works for a year and a half. The new Sarasota school board was sworn in on November 17, 2026, and this year's election saw three new members elected, ousting the former 3-2 conservative majority. The board members sworn in were Heidi Brandt, Liz Barker, Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry, alongside superintendent Terry Connor.

Connor urged the board to pass the policy and said he hears what constituents have to say and agrees on a lot of it, adding that the district needs a better grasp of how it expects students to use artificial intelligence. He said the reason it was brought to this particular update is that a Florida state rule requires the district to put some language into the existing policy, as inadequate as it may be at that time. Connor promised to keep revisiting the policy and to include the community in the process of updating it. He said he appreciates suggestions to get more student input, teacher input and community input, and that the district will have that availability moving forward with upcoming town halls and other availability. Beth Mayberry, the only board member who voted against adopting the policy, said that if the district has until July and has already selected the tools it will use to implement the policy and is already taking steps, there is no rush to approve this particular policy as is without getting more input from students, families and the community.

Barker, who voted for the policy, said it gives the district a little bit of structure, some guardrails and a place to start, and that it is absolutely not the end of the discussion but the beginning, and she is not comfortable not having any guardrails at all. Sandra Otis, a student at Sarasota High, said that in addition to her personal opinion that AI usage can stunt educational development, she has noticed that the AI usage policy at discussion is rife with contradictions and includes concerns of student discrimination along with unstandardized and ambiguous enforcement standards. Andrew Light, a senior at Sarasota High, pointed to a clause saying district employees are responsible for the accuracy of AI content, and said that as a student, as the son of a teacher and as a student in classes with very hardworking teachers, he does not really see it as fair to force teachers to take the blame for a model the district approves and regulates. Cole said teachers are not told what tasks AI should be used for, and that today it may be a simple email, but before long study guides, lesson plans and entire units of curriculum are made with AI, which he said is happening in schools right now. Cole added that students do not have firm guidelines either, asking how come in one class they can use AI for citations but in the next they get in trouble for using it for research, and said a campus run by AI quickly gets demotivated, frustrated and apathetic, which he said is happening to his school right now.

Since generative AI went mainstream in late 2022, there have been plenty of important and sometimes difficult discussions about it, especially in education, with questions coming from educators, policymakers and parents. A 2025 Project Tomorrow survey found that 63% of students in grades six through 12 worry about being wrongly accused of cheating with AI. In the last year alone, more than 400 CEOs from various industries, including those from Adobe, IBM and Microsoft, have signed an open letter advocating for mandatory computer science and AI education in schools, seeing AI education as a way to maintain the US competitive edge. In Utah, the Utah State Board of Education's Artificial Intelligence Student Taskforce was formally established just a few weeks ago and now exists under the current Student Advisory Council, meeting roughly four times during the school year to advise the board, alternating between in-person and virtual meetings. The AI Student Taskforce was approved during the October USBE Board Meeting.

Matt Winters, Utah's State Board of Education's former AI Specialist, said the board regularly hears from parents, superintendents and advocacy groups but does not hear from students and teachers as consistently. LeAnn Wood, vice chair of the Utah State Board of Education, said she hopes the task force will give some real boots-on-the-ground perspective of how students feel AI is impacting their education, for better or for worse, because they are the ones who actually have to see it in action. Winters credited students for driving the work forward, saying the story is 100% about the kids, that they figured out how to do this, and that the work is flowing through him, not because of him. Although students have not yet been assigned to the task force, several have helped set the effort in motion, including one student from one of Utah's largest districts who contacted the technology director about a year ago and asked how to get started, a high school senior who recently interned at an AI law office and hopes to continue learning about AI policy, a charter school student who wants to bring his own experience with learning disabilities to the conversation, and another student running projects with the STEM Action Center. Wood said one challenge might be getting more students beyond the 15 who currently serve on the council, and Winters has prompted students on how they can bring in more of their peers, with ideas such as a hackathon or another collaborative, judged experience already taking shape.

stories.Headline: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier pursues multistate litigation against AI companies
stories.Summary:
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced several legal priorities during a Tuesday radio interview in Tallahassee on November 18, 2026. He stated that his office will not defend the 2018 state ban on bump stocks and certain trigger enhancements. Uthmeier urged state lawmakers to revisit the 2018 firearm restrictions, including the three day waiting period for purchases. He also wants the legislature to reconsider the law that raised the minimum age to purchase a firearm to 21. The Attorney General believes the current bump stock statute is overly broad and unconstitutional under recent Supreme Court rulings.

The 2018 statute includes devices like forced reset triggers that do not convert firearms into fully automatic weapons, according to Uthmeier. He is coordinating with House Speaker Sam Garrison, a Republican from Fleming Island, on proactive state policies regarding artificial intelligence. This effort includes multistate litigation against AI companies and a specific lawsuit filed against the company known as OpenAI. Uthmeier is also investigating the Democratic Socialists of America regarding potential unlawful financial support from Beijing, China, and Havana, Cuba. He issued subpoenas to see if the organization received items of value tied to delegation trips to those countries.

Uthmeier said that nonprofits violating Florida law by receiving foreign monetary support or fundraising will have to pay for it. He believes that pushing common sense policies helped Republicans survive one of the toughest election nights in their history. The Attorney General noted that Florida has record crime lows and that his office will not stop there. He stated that other states are looking to Florida to lead multi state legal challenges on regulatory and constitutional issues. Uthmeier also highlighted that his office increased fentanyl prosecutions by more than 500 percent over the last eighteen months.

Fentanyl deaths statewide dropped by 60 percent and fentanyl encounters declined by 80 percent, according to the Attorney General. He cited a case where a couple faces mandatory minimum sentences of 25 years for pressing fentanyl into pills. Senate President Jim Boyd, an insurance executive from Bradenton, said it is imperative that the state tackle affordability issues. Boyd wants to offer more choices and lower rates for property insurance while maintaining the integrity of the reformed industry. House Speaker Sam Garrison said his priorities are a strong economy, safe streets, and providing children with quality schools.

The articles mention that Florida voters recently approved Amendment 3, which will dramatically reduce property taxes for homeowners in the state. This amendment will reduce revenues for local governments, which may lead to service cuts or the raising of other fees. Governor Ron DeSantis wants a special session before the end of the year to help implement this new constitutional amendment. DeSantis also wants to limit the ability of local governments to do tax shifts through a Taxpayer Bill of Rights. Boyd and Garrison noted that the state must preserve natural beauty as the population increases to remain a beacon.

Governor Ron DeSantis wants the special session now, but leadership indicated it may not happen until Byron Donalds is governor. Boyd believes there is enough time during the regular session to address the concerns regarding the implementation of Amendment 3. Speaker Garrison created a committee to explore the risks of AI, which he compared to the disruption of the Industrial Revolution. He expressed concern that AI technology could improve so quickly that humans lose the ability to understand or control it. The articles leave open whether the legislature will commit to the Taxpayer Bill of Rights requested by Governor Ron DeSantis.

stories.Headline: Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw explain how compliance teams layer AI rules and standards
stories.Summary:
There is no single rulebook for AI governance yet, and instead compliance teams must work with layers that include regulation such as the EU AI Act, sector-specific guidance from financial regulators, and standards such as NIST and ISO 42001. In the second episode of the From principle to practice series from the Elliptic Institute, David Carlisle asks Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw where those layers stand today and what compliance teams can do while they develop. The episode explores how the EU AI Act, financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules fit together for organizations building their own approach. The series examines what AI governance and risk management mean for compliance teams, with the people building Elliptic's own AI governance framework answering one key question in each episode.

The discussion covers why the real value of ISO 42001 is the risk-based management system behind it, even though standards lag the technology. It also addresses why technical controls for AI are still fragmented and what that fragmentation means for organizations building their own controls. The episode considers what the move to cloud teaches about shared responsibility for AI models and hosting, and why organizations cannot wait for perfect clarity before acting. These points turn the principles in the Elliptic Standard into practical steps for compliance teams.

Kasey Chappelle and Adam Grimshaw answered questions from David Carlisle about where the layers of AI governance are today. The episode frames the EU AI Act, guidance from financial regulators such as MAS and a patchwork of US rules as layers that compliance teams must fit together. It presents the value of ISO 42001 as lying in the risk-based management system behind the standard rather than in the standard alone. It also explains why technical controls for AI remain fragmented and what that means for organizations building their own.

The articles give no further dates, numbers or names beyond the EU AI Act, MAS, NIST, ISO 42001, David Carlisle, Kasey Chappelle, Adam Grimshaw and the November 18, 2026 publication of the episode. The series is described as a new one from the Elliptic Institute that explores what AI governance and risk management means for compliance teams. Each episode has the people building Elliptic's own AI governance framework answer one key question, turning the principles in the Elliptic Standard into practical steps. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the episode itself.

stories.Headline: AI models trigger US system outages by finding software flaws faster than companies can patch them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence models found software flaws faster than companies could fix them during the week of November 12, 2026. These capabilities caused various system crashes and outages across the United States as companies scrambled to patch vulnerabilities. The process of updating these systems knocked several major services offline before the Thanksgiving holiday break. A well-placed source told the Post that AI has now crossed the Rubicon regarding cyber capabilities. This surge in finding bugs has created a significant challenge for companies trying to stay current.

Microsoft Outlook went dark for nearly twenty-four hours starting on November 12, and the FAA grounded flights for four hours on November 13. Chase bank customers could not move money on Monday, and the National Security Agency internal network failed on Tuesday. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton noted a flaw in the PHP programming language caused some systems to fail. Anthropic gave select companies access to the Mythos AI model to find and fix security flaws in their systems. OpenAI also provided programs that use AI to hunt for bugs in major corporate systems.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei stated that the current pain will pay off by fixing bugs before Chinese AI models catch up. He estimated in May that cyber defenders had six to twelve months to patch flaws before those threats arrived. Amodei believes that handling this process correctly will leave companies in a better position than where they started. Jay Clayton told Fox Business that there was no evidence of state-sponsored activity or a coordinated attack. The source told the Post that patching these vulnerabilities ultimately makes the systems less vulnerable to attacks.

Cybersecurity expert Scott Schober warned that scammers might target stranded travelers with fake offers to rebook their flights. He noted that it is unusual for so many technical glitches to happen within such a tight timeframe. Schober stated that while individual glitches are possible, a coordinated attack remains a possibility that is not yet proven. Travelers and banking customers were directly affected by the outages, and airline booking systems faced increased pressure. Schober advised affected travelers to call their airlines directly rather than trusting third party offers.

The articles note that many corporate systems were built over three decades and are often bolted together. These legacy systems, including airline booking and radar systems, cannot process massive updates all at once. Qualys reported that Microsoft fixed 63 vulnerabilities in November last year, but fixed 1,235 in November this year. Anthropic and OpenAI warned over six months ago that their newest models could exploit unknown flaws without guidance. This background explains why the sheer volume of new vulnerabilities is causing current system crashes.

The source expects more outages over the next few months as more companies implement these AI models. Updates to software will have to occur more frequently to keep pace with the speed of AI discovery. Microsoft, the FAA, and Chase have all blamed their own internal glitches rather than external cyber attacks. The articles leave open whether the series of outages was actually the result of a coordinated attack. It remains to be seen if companies can finish patching their systems before rival AI models catch up.

stories.Headline: ABBYY survey finds 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI adoption outpaces their governance
stories.Summary:
New research commissioned by ABBYY found that 57% of manufacturing leaders say AI is being adopted faster than they can govern it. The ABBYY Who Answers for AI: The Governance Gap report was published on November 19, 2026, in a Supply & Demand Chain Executive article by Marina Mayer. The survey covered manufacturing leaders at businesses using AI. Only 17% of manufacturing bosses completely trust AI to operate without introducing unacceptable risks. Just 26% of manufacturing companies completely trust AI to produce accurate results.

On responsibility for harmful or false outputs, 33% believe it should be shared between the organization and the vendor, 26% say the vendor bears full responsibility, and 23% say the company using it is responsible. The rest said the end user or regulators should take the lead. Data governance requirements slow AI deployment for 67% of manufacturing leaders surveyed. 88% have an AI governance framework in place, and of these 78% say it made their AI initiatives more successful. Less than half, 48%, have an AI incident reporting process, only 32% have an AI kill switch, and 36% have an AI roll back capability.

Roman Kilun, chief compliance officer at ABBYY, said businesses are embracing AI but many still struggle with questions around accountability, governance and ROI. He said senior management needs to communicate responsible AI policies companywide better. He said junior staff often operate AI tools day to day and should know which controls apply. He said AI requires organizations to know where data comes from, whether it can be trusted, how it can be used, and where it is stored and processed. The article gives no further comment from him.

36% say ethical concerns such as bias and transparency slow down AI deployment in manufacturing organizations. Data quality concerns are the biggest barrier to greater ROI for nearly one-quarter, 24%, of manufacturing leaders. Skills shortages are the next most significant barrier, followed by integration with existing systems at 13% and cost of implementation at 12%. 94% of senior leadership knows who is responsible for developing, implementing, and managing AI, but only 66% say the same for junior employees. 61% say humans review all important AI decisions before action is taken, higher than the global average of 56%.

The articles give this background: only 17% of manufacturing bosses completely trust AI to operate without unacceptable risks, compared with an average of 22% globally. Just 48% say their AI initiatives have exceeded expectations. The most popular tools among manufacturing leaders are Generative AI at 82%, Agentic AI at 63% and Purpose-built AI at 59%. Manufacturing organizations are continuing to increase their investment in AI. Respondents expect investment to increase by a further 19.1% next year, slightly above the global average of 18.8%.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond the expected investment increase. They leave open who will resolve the accountability split, since the rest of respondents named the end user or regulators without figures. They leave open how the 48% without incident reporting processes, the 68% without kill switches and the 64% without roll back capability will close those gaps. They leave open how data governance, cited by 67% as a barrier, will be addressed. They leave open how the gap between 94% of senior leadership and 66% of junior employees knowing AI responsibility will be closed.

stories.Headline: European Commission proposes MDR 2.0 package to ease AI medical device rules
stories.Summary:
In December 2025 the European Commission published a proposal to amend the Medical Device Regulation, the In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices Regulation and the AI Act in a single legislative package, called the MDR 2.0 proposal in the Comment. The Comment, published in npj Digital Medicine on 18 November 2026, reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health. The authors offer a multidisciplinary expert interpretation drawing on their experience in regulatory science, law, health policy and industry. They ask whether the reforms, if implemented, would materially improve the regulatory environment for AI-enabled medical devices in the EU. A provision-level comparison is provided in Supplementary Table 1.

The proposal aims to eliminate double regulation, reduce documentation requirements and introduce new regulatory tools. It would move the MDR and IVDR from Section A to Section B of Annex I of the AI Act, so that the AI Act's Chapter III obligations would not directly apply to medical devices. The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, was adopted in July 2026 and permits the Commission to limit AI Act requirements where sectoral legislation provides an equivalent level of protection. It delays the applicability of high-risk requirements to August 2028, and the Commission must adopt the corresponding delegated acts by 2 August 2027. The proposal revises classification rule 11 to make medical device software Class I by default, with up-classification when output informs or drives clinical management in increasingly serious situations, while rule 3.5, which assigns the highest applicable sub-rule, is left unchanged.

It codifies the Helsinki procedure through changes in MDR Article 4 and new Articles 4a, 51a and 51b, and it broadens clinical data to include studies in scientific literature that may not be peer-reviewed, while whether this includes preprints remains unclear. It further broadens the possibility to demonstrate safety and performance solely through non-clinical data, explicitly encouraging New Approach Methodologies such as in-silico testing, and it outlines a new pathway for highly innovative devices with priority and rolling reviews by Notified Bodies after review by a designated expert panel. The European Commission concluded in its evaluation of the current MDR that the challenges limit patient access to innovative medical technologies within the EU and reduce competitiveness. The authors argue that the changes are generally well-targeted but leave specific challenges for innovative AI-enabled medical devices unresolved. In their interpretation, the revision does not remove rule 11's central difficulty but relocates the distinction between informing and driving clinical management to the Class I boundary, where misclassification carries greater risk.

They say the fault lines remain vague, inviting divergent interpretation and inconsistent decisions, and that the rule stays anchored in a comparatively narrow and now dated conception of software risk. They think the current wording and its interaction with rule 3.5 would have the opposite effect to the intended substantial improvement. The authors say relaxing clinical evidence requirements could create space for innovation but raises legitimate questions about whether the resulting evidence base will be robust enough to protect patients, particularly for higher-risk AI-enabled devices. They critique the new pathway as possibly uncoordinated, because scientific advice from the panel and conformity assessment are structured as largely separate steps rather than an integrated dialog among manufacturer, panel and Notified Body. The EP draft report addresses this partially by stating that the notified body shall be able to participate in the expert panel's discussions.

The pathway is confined to conformity assessment and is not linked to health technology assessment or reimbursement, though selected Class IIb and III devices meeting the criteria in Article 7 of Regulation (EU) 2021/2282 may undergo EU joint clinical assessment, while Member States retain responsibility for conclusions on added clinical value, coverage and reimbursement. The authors think success depends on practical implementation of the somewhat vague proposal text, on how broadly or cautiously expert panels interpret the designation criteria, and on whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. In 2025 the EU's Artificial Intelligence Board and the Medical Device Coordination Group issued non-binding guidance, AIB 2025-1/MDCG 2025-6, on the interplay between the AI Act and the MDR/IVDR, describing how AI Act requirements for high-risk AI-enabled devices can be incorporated into the medical device conformity assessment process. The guidance does not eliminate the existing overlap, since meeting the integrated conformity assessment does not remove the need to fulfill the requirements of both frameworks.

Currently the MDR and IVDR are listed in Section A of Annex I, so for AI-enabled devices classified as high-risk under the AI Act the full set of AI Act requirements, including data governance, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, applies alongside the MDR's general safety and performance requirements. This affects all medical devices that must involve a Notified Body in their conformity assessment, usually Class IIa or higher, where the AI system itself is a medical device or meets the AI Act definition of a safety component. The move of the MDR from Section A to Section B remains an option for targeted revisions. The articles leave open whether the proposal will be adopted, delayed or substantially revised in the ongoing negotiation processes.

They leave open whether preprints count as scientific literature under the broadened clinical data definition. They leave open how broadly or cautiously expert panels will interpret the designation criteria for the new innovative-product pathway. They leave open whether Notified Bodies can deliver faster reviews. The Comment reflects the situation of 26 August 2026 and includes the most recent Draft Report of the European Parliament's Committee on Public Health.

stories.Headline: Better Markets urges human accountability and audits to keep AI risks off households
stories.Summary:
Better Markets released a report on November 18, 2026, titled AI and the Real Economy: What’s at Stake for Main Street, written by Evan LeFlore, the organization’s Director of AI, Innovation, and Economic Opportunity. The Washington, D.C. group said the report examines artificial intelligence’s role in household and small-business finances by asking who captures the value AI creates, who carries the risk, and who pays the bill. LeFlore said the potential impacts on Americans’ financial lives are widespread, and that loan decisions, 401(k) risks, and everyday affordability are only part of the picture. He said workers, savers, borrowers, and taxpayers will inevitably feel the impact. LeFlore said oversight is being pulled back just as the risks grow, noting that the SEC withdrew its proposed rule on AI conflicts of interest and that the CFPB has been hollowed out and pulled back its guidance on AI-driven credit denials.

He also said banking regulators’ updated model-risk-management guidance exempts the generative and agentic AI that poses the newest risks, while the AI industry spends heavily to shape the rules meant to govern it. The report recommends keeping a human or firm legally accountable for actions an AI agent takes, so that a company deploying an autonomous system owns what that system does. It says every adverse decision needs a real reason, because “the model told us to” is not an explanation, and that fair-lending laws, including the disparate-impact doctrine, should be enforced as written. The report also calls for independent audits over vendor promises, so claims that a model is fair or expands access are checked by someone who is not selling it. It recommends closing the AI carve-outs in banking regulators’ model-risk guidance and supervising the handful of AI model and cloud providers the financial system now depends on as systemic chokepoints.

It further recommends giving savers a clear, accessible description of their AI exposure on investment statements and target-date fund labels, and requiring transparency on the debt and off-balance-sheet financing behind the data-center and broader AI buildout. LeFlore said change is certain but progress is not, so whether AI’s gains are broadly shared depends on the policy choices made today. Better Markets describes itself as a nonprofit, nonpartisan economic advocacy organization dedicated to making the economy work for all Americans and protecting the public interest in Washington policymaking. The group said it works to support policies that create sustainable, durable, and broad-based economic growth and rising living standards while protecting jobs, savings, and retirements. The full report is available through the organization.

stories.Headline: Governor Gavin Newsom proposes tougher AI regulations and urges federal oversight for 2028 presidential candidates
stories.Summary:
California Governor Gavin Newsom visited Washington, D.C., on November 18, 2026, to unveil new proposals for tougher artificial intelligence regulations. The governor spent several days meeting with bipartisan lawmakers, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, to request disaster recovery funding for wildfires. During a roundtable and a subsequent press exchange, Newsom argued that supporting government oversight of AI should be a basic requirement for any serious 2028 presidential candidate. He framed these efforts as a national necessity, contrasting his approach with the current administration's policies.

The new California report suggests mandatory safety standards and independent oversight for advanced AI models to ensure public safety. It proposes the implementation of emergency shutdown procedures, often called kill switches, and limits on the ability of AI to autonomously create more powerful versions of itself. These recommendations follow an executive order Newsom signed in September to accelerate the implementation of safety legislation. The governor has already discussed continuing this regulatory work with Governor-elect Xavier Becerra, who will take office in January.

Newsom criticized President Trump for allowing AI companies to self-regulate, suggesting this approach primarily benefits the president's political allies. He compared the lack of oversight to an airline that operates without independent analysis, calling the current situation a national crisis of confidence. In response, White House spokeswoman Luz Huston stated that American leadership in super intelligence is essential for national security and economic prosperity. She asserted that President Trump remains committed to protecting consumers while ensuring the United States leads the world in this technology.

The governor's visit occurred while President Trump was in China for meetings with President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Newsom traveled to the capital directly from Ukraine, noting that neither the president nor Vice President JD Vance had visited that country. Although he has not yet decided if he will run for president in 2028, Newsom indicated he would make a determination after leaving office in January. He presented the California regulatory framework as a potential national model that the federal government should adopt.

Articles.Title: Newsom says AI regulation should be ‘table stakes’ for any serious 2028 candidate

stories.Headline: Pittsylvania schools weigh AI policy as LA County approves AI governance rules
stories.Summary:
The Pittsylvania County School Board in the late fall of 2026 looked at developing an artificial intelligence policy to manage AI in schools, the Chatham Star-Tribune reported on Nov. 18, 2026. Pittsylvania County Schools joined other school divisions in Virginia and across the nation in contending with the rise of artificial intelligence and its impacts within the education realm. Division administrators acknowledged that AI is not going anywhere and that school divisions must craft policy and regulation around its usage. Administrators said they seek to be strategic, careful and responsible as the technology changes many aspects of life and education. The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors approved a policy Tuesday governing the safe, ethical and transparent use of artificial intelligence technologies across county government, MyNewsLA.com reported on Nov. 17, 2026.

The Los Angeles County policy establishes standards, responsibilities and governance requirements for AI systems developed by the county, procured from outside vendors or accessed through third-party platforms. The policy requires county departments to follow principles involving human-centered design, security and safety, privacy, transparency, equity, accountability, effectiveness and workforce empowerment. Under the policy, AI systems must protect personally identifiable information, protected health information, criminal justice information and other sensitive data from unauthorized access, disclosure and manipulation. The policy requires the county to disclose the purpose and use of its AI systems to the public and identify work products generated by AI. It prohibits fully automated high-impact decisions without meaningful human review, covert tracking or social scoring of people, and the cognitive or behavioral manipulation of people or vulnerable groups.

Steve Mayhew, PCS superintendent, said the goal is to develop a human-centered policy that is ethical and equitable, protects users and the school division, and provides adequate training for individuals most in need of it. Mayhew said the goal is for students to develop important life skills and succeed academically without using AI to do the work, while balancing digital literacy and education. Mayhew said people use AI for a lot of things and that he thinks it is a tool but not something supposed to be used instead of creativity. Emily Reynolds, chief information technology officer with Pittsylvania County Schools, said the issue is something IT directors in school divisions everywhere are talking about. Reynolds said students do not have access to AI and teachers only have access right now to MagicSchool, which is geared toward instructional purposes.

Reynolds said that within MagicSchool teachers can create AI-resistant assignments for students and that the push is to teach teachers how to build assignments more resistant to a student putting a prompt into a chat bot and getting output of an assignment. Reynolds said programs exist where teachers could upload content to see whether it has AI-generated components, but even that gets murky because it is effectively AI telling users whether something was AI generated. Kevin Mills, Westover district representative, was concerned with AI's reputation for spitting out erroneous information or producing information that aligned with user bias, telling individuals what they want to hear rather than strict facts. Mills said use of this technology could mislead students trying to use it as a study aid. Mark Shields, school board chair and Chatham-Blairs district representative, said his biggest concern with AI in schools were growing reports of students using AI programs such as ChatGPT to write essays.

Kelly Merricks, Dan River district representative, pointed out that if teachers give students assignments to complete on the spot during class, it gives educators the chance to recognize students' authentic work. Merricks said that familiarity makes it easier to spot a student's use of artificial intelligence to complete essays or other assignments. Mayhew suggested forming a taskforce to focus on AI and its regulation in the schools, comprised of teachers, principals, division administrators, parents and potentially a school board member. In the broader education realm, proposals have been made to begin introducing digital citizenship to students beginning in Kindergarten, effectively starting to teach five-year-olds about AI, computer technology and responsible use. The premise of this digital citizenship push would level up the digital literacy and AI education through the grade levels.

Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, in part of her administration's recently announced Moving Virginia Forward agenda, aims to target finding a better balance that limits student screen time in school and encourages use of more traditional educational methods where possible. This agenda is set to get in motion in 2027, per the governor's office. The memo reads that the agenda would require school divisions to minimize unnecessary student screen time, prioritize teacher-led and high-quality instruction, and regularly assess and develop plans to reduce excessive or low-value use of instructional technology. Adopting an AI policy was the first official step into the fray, and regulation and implementation will follow that baseline as the situation develops. PCS has kept tight reins on unrolling AI in the division so far, administrators said, and that has been much to their benefit as other school divisions in the Commonwealth are trying to rein the technology in.

The Los Angeles County policy says AI should be used to enhance jobs and provide training and retraining opportunities for workers, rather than replace county employees or contractors. It assigns oversight responsibilities to the county's chief information officer, chief information security officer, chief privacy officer and department-level information technology managers. The policy allows no exceptions, according to the county. County Counsel reviewed the proposal, and the Audit Committee approved it Sept. 16. According to the board letter, there will be no fiscal impact to the county on the proposed AI Policy.

A board letter from the county's chief executive officer said AI technologies are increasingly used across county departments to enhance service delivery, improve operational efficiency and support data driven decision making. The letter said that as these technologies advance, it is critical for the county to maintain clear governance structures, safeguard sensitive information and ensure that AI is deployed responsibly and ethically. The letter states that the AI Policy establishes consistent requirements to ensure that any AI technologies developed, procured or used by county departments comply with applicable laws, protect county information assets, maintain public trust and mitigate the risk of bias or misuse. County employees are barred from uploading nonpublic or regulated county information to unapproved AI platforms, using such platforms to make official decisions or relying on AI-generated work as an authoritative source without independent human verification. The articles leave open how the Pittsylvania taskforce would be formed and what its regulation and implementation would contain.

Articles.Title: Pittsylvania County Schools weigh AI policy as technology rapidly changes - Chatham Star-Tribune

stories.Headline: Performativ links bank staff AI assistants to client records under existing permissions
stories.Summary:
Performativ connected AI assistants used by bank employees to client and portfolio records on November 19, 2026. The company used the Model Context Protocol to link business systems to tools like Claude and ChatGPT. This release is available to existing clients and allows staff to query records through their assistants. The system is designed for bank staff rather than for the bank clients themselves. It aims to stop employees from manually copying client information into outside AI assistants.

The service is off by default and requires a firm to switch it on. Administrators decide who can use it, and employees must use an individual login. Access is governed by existing Performativ permissions, and the company hosts the service in the EU. Every request is logged for audit purposes to maintain security and regulatory compliance. The Model Context Protocol is an open standard used for these business system connections.

CEO Albert Geisler Fox said that letting bank clients query their own portfolios is a future ambition. He framed this client facing access as a direction for the company to move toward. The company says the current setup keeps access tied to the existing rules of the firm. Performativ claims this prevents client data from moving outside the control of the bank. The company describes these measures as safeguards for the data.

Relationship managers, portfolio managers, back office teams, and compliance staff are the people affected by this. Relationship managers can use the tool to create briefings that compare portfolio progress with client projections. Portfolio managers can examine risk and performance alongside the advice a client previously received. Compliance teams can review regulatory status and recent changes made to a client record. These workflows combine portfolio information with the broader client record.

The connection draws on holdings, performance, risk, projections, past advice, meeting notes, and account activity. It also includes the identities of the advisors who are responsible for a specific client. This capability builds on governed agent workflows introduced with Custom Agents in November 2025. The broader platform supports over 1,500 advisors and connections to more than 150 custodians. It manages more than 100 billion euros in client assets.

The company now wants to let bank clients ask their preferred assistants about their portfolios. This future goal would provide answers supplied under the specific controls of the bank. The articles do not state when this client facing feature will be released. They do not provide the specific adoption numbers for the new MCP service. It remains open how many firms have enabled the service since November 19.

Articles.Title: Performativ connects bank staff’s AI assistants to client data under existing permissions

stories.Headline: Law firms face pressure to modernize for AI as Perry AI and Alecto raise seed funding
stories.Summary:
The legal industry is currently facing significant pressure to modernize its operations or risk being left behind during the artificial intelligence era. This shift was highlighted during the TLTF Summit 2026, where experts discussed whether private equity funding could accelerate the adoption of new technologies. Many firms previously believed their unique economic position protected them from the kind of disruption seen in other sectors. However, the current environment suggests that law firms must now adapt to the same technological pressures affecting the broader economy.

The transition toward AI requires substantial capital and a willingness to change traditional business models to ensure growth and innovation. While some firms seek outside investment to turbocharge these efforts, more capital does not always guarantee a seamless transition to AI. Recent financial activity in the sector includes a 2.2 million dollar seed round for the startup Perry AI, which intends to hire talent in India, Singapore, and the United States. Additionally, the AI-powered conveyancing provider Alecto raised 20 million dollars in a seed round with investment from Mishcon de Reya.

Rhys Dipshan reported that the legal industry is experiencing a rude awakening regarding its ability to operate at its own pace. The reporting suggests that while outside funding is a potential catalyst, the process of AI adoption remains complex and challenging. Other industry observations indicate that legal professionals in the United Kingdom and Ireland who use AI extensively are more likely to see stronger revenue effects. Experts also suggest that firms should consider the nationality of their AI tools to mitigate risks and gain commercial benefits.

The broader context shows a surge in high-profile marketing and investment, such as the partnership between Harvey and Wimbledon. Some new AI providers, like Alecto, explicitly claim that their ultimate goal is to replace traditional law firms entirely. As these technologies evolve, firms must balance the need for rapid modernization with the risks associated with AI transformation. The industry continues to monitor whether private equity will successfully bridge the gap between traditional practice and modern efficiency.

Articles.Title: TLTF Summit 2026: Will Private Equity Funding Spur Law Firm AI Modernizations?
