stories.Headline: House lawmakers introduce bipartisan bill to create federal cyber and AI review board
stories.Summary:
House lawmakers introduced a bipartisan bill on Wednesday to create a federal review board. Rep. Morgan Luttrell of Texas and Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York introduced the measure. This action follows recent outages that disrupted workplace software and air travel. It also follows disruptions to operations at the National Security Agency. These events occurred over the last week of November 2026.

The ROOT CAUSE Act would establish a National Cyber and AI Investigations Board within CISA. This board would investigate major cyberattacks, technology failures, and incidents related to artificial intelligence. The executive branch could not abolish or consolidate the board without another act of Congress. Investigators could examine AI failures and configuration errors even without evidence of an attack. National security systems would remain outside the authority of this proposed board.

Rep. Morgan Luttrell stated that action is critical as adversaries become increasingly sophisticated. Rep. Matt Van Epps said AI agents on federal networks present new targets for adversaries. Rep. Andy Ogles noted that recent attacks exposed dependence on shared IT infrastructure. He stated that stronger coordination between government and industry is needed as threats grow. These lawmakers are proposing safeguards for AI agents and stronger coordination with technology providers.

Sens. Maria Cantwell and Mike Rounds urged Jay Clayton to coordinate a national response. They wrote that the digital economy cannot rely on individual companies to solve problems. The senators cited AI's role in uncovering serious flaws in PHP website software.

They noted that banks cannot always distinguish authorized AI agents from rogue actors. These threats affect the entire digital economy and civilian federal networks. The proposal comes two years after the Trump administration emptied the Cyber Safety Review Board. That previous board had faulted Microsoft for security failures involving senior U.S. officials' emails.

A recent FAA ground stop delayed over 10,000 flights on Friday. A Microsoft outage disrupted workplace tools, and maintenance slowed the NSANet network on Tuesday. A global Outlook outage also recently exposed vulnerabilities in shared IT infrastructure. The AI INSIGHT Act would direct CISA to track AI agents within one year.

The SECURE IT Act would codify DHS' responsibility for securing the information technology sector. Democrats will take control of Congress in January with Rep. Bennie Thompson leading. Sen. Maria Cantwell is in line to chair the Senate Commerce Committee. The articles leave open whether these three bipartisan bills will pass into law.

Articles.Title: Bipartisan bill would create cyber and AI review board amid series of tech outages

stories.headline_source: Bipartisan bill would create cyber and AI review board amid series of tech outages

stories.Headline: Anthropic floats on the US stock exchange, making its seven founders multi-billionaires
stories.Summary:
Anthropic is floating its business on the US stock exchange on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, to sell shares at $83 each. Seven founders who left OpenAI in 2021 created the company behind the AI platform Claude and will now become multi-billionaires. The company is worth more than a trillion dollars, and the founders will each hold shareholdings worth at least $19.3 billion. Dario Amodei is the 43 year old chief executive, while 39 year old Daniela Amodei serves as the company president. Tom Brown is 39 and the chief compute officer, and 37 year old Jack Clark is the head of public benefit.

Jared Kaplan is 42 and the chief science officer, Chris Olah is 34, and Sam McCandlish is 36 years old. Dario Amodei left OpenAI because he worried that some people within that firm were putting profit before safety. Daniela Amodei says that her brother is the person who makes the company ambitious. Tom Brown has argued that datacentres are an enormous source of prosperity. Jared Kaplan's work on scaling laws helped provide AI firms with a framework for predicting AI behaviour.

Sam McCandlish helps shape and implement the company policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. The New York Times describes Chris Olah as boyish and says he has the zeal of an evangelist. Olah has spent much of the last year convening meetings with faith leaders from across the religious spectrum. Sam McCandlish takes less of a public facing role than the other founders of the company. Each founder will own around 1.6 percent of the company after the shares go on sale.

The founders grew from an unknown start-up to a tech giant in the space of just five years. Dario Amodei studied physics at Princeton and Stanford before switching to biology and biomedical sciences. Daniela Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz and worked for representative Matt Cartwright. Jack Clark studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and worked as a journalist. Chris Olah left the University of Toronto early but secured a Thiel Fellowship of $100,000.

The founders' stakes will crystallise into hugely valuable assets as the company floats on the US stock exchange. Dario Amodei's holding is worth $19.7 billion, and Daniela Amodei's holding is worth $19.8 billion. Tom Brown's holding is worth $20 billion, while Jack Clark and Jared Kaplan each have $19.8 billion. Chris Olah and Sam McCandlish each have holdings worth $19.9 billion.

Articles.Title: The seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multi-billionaires

stories.Headline: Walmart (WMT) Ad Revenue Jumped 25% As AI And TV Deals Gain Traction
stories.Summary:
Walmart reported on November 20, 2026, that its global advertising revenue rose 25% in the latest period, while U.S. ad sales climbed 37%, according to a Simply Wall St article published on Yahoo Finance. Management tied the advertising gains to recent moves in connected TV, including acquisitions involving Vizio and Vibe.co, and the retailer also highlighted new AI powered retail media tools and conversational commerce features as part of its advertising push. The article said Walmart runs a global network of stores, clubs, websites and apps that generate vast shopper data, which gives its advertising unit a direct line to purchase behavior across consumer retailing. The piece was described as general in nature and produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St.

The article said the 25% advertising jump feeds into a broader pattern its research has tracked, and it noted that its analysis turns up one warning sign for Walmart as well. It framed the ad rise as fitting Walmart's narrative that higher margin businesses such as advertising, marketplace services and memberships gradually matter more to earnings than low margin store sales, and it said the main factor that has to go right is continued growth and profitability of those alternative profit pools. The article also said the news sharpens a key risk already flagged in that narrative, that regulators are scrutinising Walmart's use of AI and digital pricing, and that tighter rules on how Sparky or digital shelf tools work could slow the profit streams investors are now cheering. It pointed readers to a full story suggesting a $129 fair value for Walmart.

The article did not name any Walmart executive or provide direct statements from the company, attributing the advertising figures and the connected TV and AI details to management and the retailer generally. It said the advertising surge gives bulls fresh evidence that the ad unit is not just an add-on but a material earnings contributor that differs from traditional retailers such as Target or Costco. It also said that to judge what the headline really means for Walmart, readers need a clear view of where its mix of low margin retailing and higher margin services is heading over time, which it said is exactly what a narrative tries to spell out. The article stated that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that the piece does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock.

The context the article gave is Walmart's effort to build higher margin income streams alongside its store sales, with advertising, marketplace services and memberships expected to matter more to earnings over time. It said the advertising gains were supported by AI tools and connected TV deals and described the ad unit as increasingly material rather than incidental. The article did not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to add Walmart to a watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out, and it noted that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It also said the article does not take account of readers' objectives or financial situations.

Articles.Title: Walmart (WMT) Ad Revenue Jumped 25% As AI And TV Deals Gain Traction

stories.Headline: Cognizant executive says legacy systems absorb up to 80% of banks IT budgets
stories.Summary:
Ashish Bhatnagar, Head of Banking & Financial Services for Cognizant in the UK & Ireland, gave a Q&A to FinTech Magazine, published on November 20, 2026, about how banks can move beyond pilots to enterprise AI. The article was written by Maya Derrick for FinTech Magazine. Bhatnagar said legacy technology can absorb up to 80% of banks' IT budget through simple maintenance. He said many legacy systems support critical services and contain decades of business rules and institutional knowledge. He said architecture reviews, risk assessments and security approvals often cannot scale with the volume and pace of a major transformation programme.

Bhatnagar said UK banks spend an estimated £3.3bn (US$4.3bn) annually managing core legacy systems. The article states this figure is nearly a quarter of banks' IT budgets. It states core banking management and maintenance consumes an average of 24% of UK banks' IT budgets. Bhatnagar said banks carry substantial below-the-line costs from additional employees and manual processes needed to keep systems running. He said legacy environments can make banks less attractive to scarce technology talent.

Bhatnagar said governance, security and regulatory controls are indispensable in banking but can become bottlenecks. He said the answer is not to weaken oversight but to embed it into delivery from the beginning. He said security, compliance, data permissions and usage rights should be designed into the architecture and supported by repeatable, automated controls. He said an AI-ready bank has moved beyond isolated pilots and can deploy AI securely, responsibly and at enterprise scale. He said AI readiness means AI becomes part of how the organisation operates, not simply another tool.

Bhatnagar said existing systems often contain valuable assets including business rules, customer context, historical data and institutional knowledge. He said AI-driven automation, predictive DevOps, automated testing and self-healing systems can improve productivity and reduce the burden of technical debt. He said banks can modernise in controlled stages, focusing investment on the value streams that matter most. He named three priorities for banking leaders: reduce structural friction, organise delivery around value streams, and build intelligence from existing systems. He said security, compliance, permissions and responsible-AI controls must be designed in from the outset.

The article lists Cognizant's alliance with Microsoft, combining Azure, Copilot and enterprise security with Cognizant's financial-services expertise for fintechs, payments providers and credit unions. It lists Cognizant's AWS partnership supporting cloud migration, modernisation and AI-enabled transformation. It says joint work with ACI Worldwide has demonstrated high-volume card-processing performance in the cloud. It says Cognizant's expanded Google Cloud relationship focuses on accelerating enterprise AI, including Gemini and agentic AI. It says Cognizant is a certified Temenos partner delivering consulting, integration, data migration, testing, upgrades and support across Temenos platforms including T24 Transact, Infinity and Payments.

The article says Cognizant and ACI Worldwide demonstrated that ACI's BASE24-eps card-processing platform can run at scale on AWS. It says the platform processed more than 4.6 million transactions without failure in performance testing. Bhatnagar said fear of failure can create paralysis because a new system failing can affect whether people can pay bills or access their money. He said every hour and pound devoted to maintaining ageing infrastructure cannot be used to improve customer experiences, introduce new products or integrate AI. The article leaves open which banks or how many have adopted the three priorities.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Cognizant: How Banks Can Turn Legacy into AI Advantage

stories.Headline: Salt Security finds 77 percent of firms using AI see agents act outside authorized behavior
stories.Summary:
Salt Security reported on November 19 that 77 percent of organizations using or exploring AI saw agents act outside authorized behavior. This finding came from a poll conducted by Censuswide between September 10 and 18. The survey included 500 C-suite professionals from organizations with 50 or more employees. These respondents were split evenly between the United States and the United Kingdom. The report also found that 92 percent of executives would allow agents some independent action.

The poll showed 64 percent of leaders restricted, delayed, or canceled AI projects due to regulatory, governance, or security concerns. While 97 percent of AI users keep agent inventories, 19 percent admit these lists are not consistently updated. Other surveys show different results, such as a 49.8 percent rate from Salt's October 13 report of 380 professionals. EMA reported 65 percent of 202 leaders saw agents exceed scope, while a 2025 CSA survey of 445 professionals found 53 percent. Illumio and Sapio Research polled 1,100 decision-makers, finding 26 percent of agents connected without approval and 24 percent accessed unauthorized data.

Salt co-founder and chief operating officer Michael Nicosia stated that executives give agents authority over money, data, code, and customer relationships. He argued that governance cannot be a one-time approval and requires continuous visibility into agent actions and reach. Nicosia believes organizations must monitor runtime behavior and discover APIs and Model Context Protocol servers. Salt sells tools designed to govern these connections and discover agents. He suggests that static inventories are a weak foundation for governance.

The EY survey of 202 senior executives at US companies with $1 billion in revenue found a 26 percent detection gap. Many organizations are affected by the confused deputy problem, where programs are tricked into misusing their privileges. The UK National Cyber Security Centre warned in December 2025 that language models are inherently confusable deputies. Some users are affected by prompt injection, which the center says may never be totally defended. The EMA survey found only 32.7 percent of organizations provisioned agents with least privilege.

The articles note that AI agents often inherit access through existing identities, APIs, and applications. This allows agents to act within legitimate permissions while still performing actions a manager never intended. The term AI agent has no standard definition, which complicates how authorized behavior is measured. Salt Labs found that the Singapore-based agent platform Manus was vulnerable to hidden email prompts. This attack used JSFuck obfuscation to run JavaScript in the server-side runtime before notifying the owner.

Microsoft announced at Ignite 2026 that agents operate under existing Azure identity, permissions, and policy controls. Microsoft previewed Entra Agent ID controls, a firewall for MCP servers, and a lifecycle policy for agents. Salt continues to argue that single approvals are insufficient compared to continuous runtime control. The articles leave open whether control should happen when access is granted or during execution. They also leave open the exact severity of the incidents reported by the 77 percent of executives.

Articles.Title: Salt Security Poll: 77% of Firms Using AI Saw Agents Act Outside Authorization; 92% Allow Autonomy

stories.Headline: Tristan Harrison urges comms teams to ask six questions before commissioning AI video
stories.Summary:
The article is a set of six questions for PR and comms teams to ask before commissioning AI video, written by Tristan Harrison, who spent years in PR agencies before running a production company that combines AI with live action and traditional filmmaking. He says the Christmas season ended the theoretical stage of the AI advertising debate, pointing to the backlash over Dior's animated holiday short and to Very, which was upfront about combining CGI with AI-assisted animation and achieved its highest-ever pre-launch audience-testing score. He also notes that the IAB has updated its industry framework on AI transparency and disclosure and that the EU AI Act's transparency rules are already in force. His conclusion is that audiences are not necessarily against AI, since they want good creative and honesty about how it is made, and that AI video is a reputational decision for comms teams rather than only a creative or production one.

The six questions cover who is actually making the film and who is responsible for the final cut, since the software is not an acceptable answer, and where AI genuinely adds value, since it is not always quicker or cheaper and the technology should serve the idea. They also cover approval points, because a small change such as a shirt going from green to red can mean rebuilding an entire sequence, and Harrison describes getting clients to approve static AI-generated frames before animation and asking for a PPM meeting as with traditional film making. Ownership is the fourth question, covering likeness rights, consent, synthetic voices, music licensing, the tools used and ownership of the finished assets, with the warning not to assume a supplier's software licence covers the brand's intended use. Disclosure is the fifth, which he says should not be an awkward conversation after the film is finished, since not every AI-assisted production task requires a public label but nobody involved should be left guessing, and discussing it only at launch is too late. The sixth asks whether the supplier can deliver beyond the demo, with advice to see completed client projects rather than showreels and to find out how revisions are handled when AI does not deliver what was expected.

Harrison gives one example from his own experience, a brief involving precise eye movements that proved difficult to control with AI, where an actor and a camera would have been simpler. He says the best approach might be fully AI-generated, live action or a hybrid, and that suppliers should be asked why they recommend a particular route and whether they considered the alternatives. He describes comms teams as often the last line of defence for a brand's reputation and says that with AI video they should also be the first people asking the right questions. The article ends with an invitation to sign up for the publication's free twice-weekly editorial alert and to register for free analysis on techniques and campaigns in the PR sector.

stories.Headline: SimonMed's Sean Raj presents studies showing AI cuts fracture reporting time and improves chest X-ray reports
stories.Summary:
Sean Raj, MD, MBA, chief medical officer and chief innovation officer at SimonMed, will present two scientific studies at the Radiological Society of North America 2026 meeting in Chicago, the company announced on November 16, 2026. Both studies draw on data from SimonMed's nationwide outpatient network. One examines how AI-driven worklist prioritization shortens the time it takes to report fractures on musculoskeletal X-rays. The other evaluates how fine-tuning a vision-language foundation model on outpatient data affects the quality of automatically generated chest X-ray reports. The fracture research analyzed more than 510,000 musculoskeletal radiographs from over 200 centers, tracking turnaround from before the AI system was introduced in 2022 through its full integration in 2025.

Mean turnaround time fell 83.8% for exams showing a fracture, from about two days to under eight hours. Turnaround for fracture-negative studies improved as well, and the company said the gains came without penalizing routine workflow. Raj will present that paper, titled "AI Worklist Reprioritization: Measuring Fracture Detection Turnaround Time for MSK X-Rays in Nationwide Outpatient Imaging," on December 2. Earlier that day, Raj will present a poster on the vision-language model for automated chest X-ray report generation, before and after institution-specific fine-tuning. The investigational model was trained on more than 5 million chest X-ray image-report pairs, fine-tuned on more than 150,000 SimonMed adult outpatient exams, and tested on a consecutive cohort from 143 outpatient centers.

Fine-tuning improved sensitivity with a modest reduction in specificity, and the largest gain came in pulmonary nodules, where sensitivity rose from 62.6% to 80.8%. Raj said the research shows AI can reduce fracture reporting times from days to hours, and that autonomous chest X-ray report generation represents a step toward helping radiologists work more efficiently. The findings support improved generalizability through local model adaptation, and suggest fine-tuned report generation models may reduce radiologist workload while maintaining clinically acceptable performance. SimonMed said the work highlights its efforts to advance AI technology designed to interpret medical images and generate clinically relevant reports, with the potential to improve both diagnostic performance and radiologist workflows. For referring physicians, the company said, actionable results arrive within hours instead of days.

Articles.Title: SimonMed AI-Powered Fracture Detection, Radiology Reporting

stories.Headline: Rio Grande Valley coalition adopts term sheet setting community benefits for AI data center deals
stories.Summary:
In 2026 the Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition brought residents, community organizations and local governments together to explore how communities can negotiate with AI data center developers, according to an op-ed by Jordana Barton-Garcia published by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society on November 18, 2026. The result was the RGV AI Data Center Community Benefit Agreement Term Sheet, which sets out what the region expects in return from developers. Those expectations include protections for water, air and wildlife, local jobs and support for workforce programs, affordable broadband and adoption, and public accountability. The Lower Rio Grande Valley Development Council board, the local Council of Governments, adopted the term sheet on October 28, 2026, for cities and counties in the region to use in negotiations with developers. The coalition translated its priorities into five broad areas, which are environment and resources, workforce and jobs, closing the digital divide, healthcare and telehealth, and governance and accountability.

It also set principles for any agreement, including no NDAs so that all terms are public, and English and Spanish throughout. The principles call for an advisory board with resident-majority representation, and for binding commitments rather than aspirations. Any commitments should be specific, long-term and regional in scope, according to the term sheet. Barton-Garcia is identified in the article as director of the Texas Rio Grande Valley Broadband Coalition. The article says that when an AI data center developer comes to a city or county in the Rio Grande Valley, local leaders are now prepared for the conversation.

The term sheet is described as setting out what the region expects in return from developers. The article does not name any developer, city or county that has used the term sheet in negotiations. The op-ed was published on November 18, 2026, by the Benton Institute for Broadband & Society, which describes the piece as an op-ed. The article does not say what happens next beyond the term sheet being available for cities and counties to use in negotiations with developers. It also does not report any response from developers or from the council board.

stories.Headline: Judge Ehsan Amirkhani proposes a reverse-traceability test for judges to verify AI drafts against the original record
stories.Summary:
On 9 October 2026 the judiciary of England and Wales published a position statement on judicial use of AI, JURIST reported on 19 November 2026. The statement says judicial decisions remain with judges and AI cannot displace evaluation of evidence or judicial reasoning. It says every AI output used in judicial work must be reviewed, verified and approved by the responsible judicial office holder. It describes cautious testing of lower-risk applications including summarisation, chronologies and document analysis. It does not give blanket approval for AI to draft judgments.

The article poses a design question: what should a judge verify when the danger is a missing argument rather than a false quotation. It sets out a hypothetical civil claim where service of a prescribed notice is a prerequisite to possession. The claimant establishes title, the defendant puts service in issue and identifies evidence suggesting the notice never arrived. A draft correctly sets out the law of ownership, cites genuine decisions and grants possession. If service is a necessary condition of relief and remains disputed, the reasoning has bypassed a question on which the outcome may turn.

The author is Dr Ehsan Amirkhani, presiding judge of Branch 2 of the General Civil Court of Kermanshah, Iran, and an independent legal researcher writing in a personal academic capacity. He says no confidential case materials are used and all case examples are hypothetical. He proposes a short, judge-led reverse-traceability test beginning with the authorised record: the pleaded issues, material written submissions, relevant hearing record and evidence properly before the court. The judge identifies objections that, if well founded, would defeat an indispensable factual or legal step in the proposed disposition. The test then asks where the final reasons answer each such objection.

The article cites Ruiz Torija v Spain and Hiro Balani v Spain, both decided on 9 December 1994, in which the European Court of Human Rights examined failures to address arguments of potential significance. It cites the Court's Guide on Article 6, civil limb, on reasoned decisions enabling parties to understand they have been heard and to exercise a right of appeal. It says the Convention doctrine is not directly applicable to Iranian courts or a universal mandate to answer every pleading point. It says the transferable insight is that a court must make intelligible the path from the legally material disputes to its decision. It says repetitive submissions need not be restated, some objections become immaterial once a case is resolved on an independent ground, and other points can be answered by the reasoning as a whole.

The article says the judiciary's October 2025 AI guidance warns against hallucinations and disclosure of confidential material and emphasises the personal responsibility of judicial office holders for work produced in their names. It says a procurement or deployment policy should preserve traceable access to sources and that a polished interface concealing the record can make meaningful verification more difficult. It says controlled evaluations of authorised tools could assess whether reviewers identify omitted outcome-sensitive objections, whether final reasons treat them accurately, and how much time the procedure adds. It says such testing should distinguish errors caused by document extraction, summarisation and drafting and should examine false alarms. It says nothing justifies feeding parties' pleadings or non-public evidence into public AI services and that the judiciary of England and Wales confines judicial use to approved systems under its own arrangements.

The article says the same reverse-traceability check can be performed manually where no approved tool exists and that the legal safeguard should not depend on purchasing technology. It says the judge should check the losing party's strongest legally relevant case, not merely arguments fitting an early draft, and that institutional audits should ask whether the procedure consistently represents both sides. It says the proposed working aid creates no new general right of public access to judicial notes or draft deliberations. It says the next task is to make the October 2026 commitment to human oversight operational. It says that if the path from the original objection through the governing law and relevant evidence to the reason actually adopted is broken, the drafting process is not finished.

Articles.Title: The Objection an AI Draft Leaves Out: Why Judges Must Check Rulings Against the Original Record

stories.headline_source: The Objection an AI Draft Leaves Out: Why Judges Must Check Rulings Against the Original Record

stories.Headline: AXS, Visa and Mastercard connect AI agents to bill payments in Singapore
stories.Summary:
AXS, Visa and Mastercard are working together to let artificial intelligence agents pay bills on behalf of consumers in Singapore, connecting those agents to AXS's network of more than 800 billing organisations, which include hospitals, power companies, telcos, insurers, finance companies, country clubs and government agencies such as the Housing Board and the police. The service is meant to cover telco, electricity and healthcare bills as well as housing loan instalments and fines, and it removes the need for customers to manually check for outstanding bills, log into multiple apps and key in one-time passwords. AXS declined to give a roll-out timeline for consumers, but it plans a trial of bill payments with the Grab AI assistant, and it announced the tie-up around Nov 18, with The Straits Times reporting on it on Nov 19, 2026. Visa demonstrated the idea at the Singapore FinTech Festival at the Singapore Expo on Nov 18, showing a customer typing a request in a chat box for an AI agent to pay a telco bill, after which the agent confirms the amount and card and a biometric face check completes the transaction.

Existing card protections from Mastercard and Visa apply to these AI payments, and the guardrails include letting users set payment limits, specify which transactions are permitted and require their approval before a payment goes through. Visa's Asia Pacific head of innovation and growth products, Abhijeet Ramesh, said only a legitimate agent verified to pay on the customer's behalf can start a transaction, explicit customer approval with biometric verification is needed to complete it, and the card details are never shared with the agent. Instead the agent receives a random token unique to the customer's device and a separate one-time code unique to each transaction, and neither can be used for other payments, including to other billing organisations, even if stolen, while a payment of a different amount from the one approved is blocked. AXS group chief executive and executive director Jeffrey Goh said connecting partners' own AI agents to the AXS network extends its reach beyond existing channels and lets partners create new payment experiences for their customers, and Ramesh said the system-driven controls ensure an agent cannot simply do whatever it wants and that the user is always in control.

Because agentic payments are still in their infancy, Visa is working on how to help banks, which eventually disburse the funds, with more checks and balances, including updating banks on agentic transaction data so they can set rules for different types of payments to different types of organisations, such as a monthly cap on transactions to a particular biller based on billing trends. Visa will use its existing framework for resolving card payment disputes for payments made by AI agents, and a tamper-proof record of each action an agent takes can be used to settle disputes and determine whether an agent is at fault for an unintended transaction. Ramesh said Visa is continuously reviewing its dispute resolution framework and rules to see what changes are needed for agentic payments, adding that it is still early days, no changes have been made yet and the company is actively working on it. AXS, Visa and Mastercard did not say which AI agents the capability will be available for, though AXS said consumers could ask an AI assistant in their banking app or digital wallet to help with bill payments, and ChatGPT maker OpenAI said on Nov 13 that it was also working with American Express, Mastercard and Visa to let its dots AI agent make payments with those cards, initially only for US customers.

Articles.Title: AXS, Visa and Mastercard partner to let AI agents pay bills without multiple app logins

stories.Headline: Michael Burry flags Nvidia financing gap as $500 billion plan deploys no money
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry drew attention on Thursday to a financing problem for Nvidia, according to a Wall Street Journal report he shared on X. A Wall Street initiative to mobilize $500 billion for Nvidia's AI chip customers has yet to deploy any money, the report said. Talks on the first chip-backed deal are ongoing, with a closing unlikely before 2027, the Journal reported. Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang helped bring together Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR in August. The firms signed a nonbinding agreement that set a fundraising ambition of $500 billion over time.

How much risk Nvidia would take has become a sticking point in the talks. Huang said Nvidia's credit support would cover up to 25% of project costs, and lenders have sought greater protection. Nvidia has separately disclosed up to $118 billion in guarantees, including up to $105 billion tied to an Ohio data-center campus that will host Nvidia hardware under leases to OpenAI. Those guarantees take effect in stages as buildings become operational, with the first expected in fiscal 2029. Nvidia still expects about $130 billion in fiscal fourth-quarter revenue.

The financing question is whether customers with less access to capital can fund future chip purchases on schedule. The first signed deal would show how much lenders are willing to commit and how much risk Nvidia must take to secure that funding. Burry has previously called Nvidia's $500 billion AI financing push a Wall Street stunt. He has also called Nvidia AI spending fugazi and said billions in GPUs are hidden through a complex financing structure.

Articles.Title: Michael Burry Zeroes In on One AI Giant's $500 Billion Push

stories.Headline: Providence schools official says district limits generative AI to 2 of 58 student apps
stories.Summary:
A Providence Public Schools official told the School Board Policy Committee on Tuesday that the district operates under a self-imposed moratorium on artificial intelligence, and that only 2 of the 58 software programs available to students use generative AI, limited to grades 9 through 12, according to the committee's published meeting recording. The official, who said they serve on the district's AI committee alongside the district's IT director, said students reach the 58 programs through Clever, the district's single sign-on system. The official said Amira, the elementary reading and dyslexia-screening program that drew parent complaints, is not generative and is not a chatbot, and that it was misinterpreted. The remarks came the night before the full School Board's meeting, where committee members said an AI resolution was expected. The official said the district is moving deliberately and cautiously, and described Providence as a low-use, very little AI district that has been aggressive in protecting student privacy, calling it probably one of the most aggressive districts in New England.

The official said the district called every parent who reached out and met with parent groups, and said they have 5 children themselves and want to protect all kids. The official said they had written that evening offering to speak at the next night's board meeting because there is so much misinformation about Amira and AI, and had attached a summary of four major steps the district has taken since July. A speaker noted that RIDE, the Rhode Island Department of Education, has a generic AI policy for students and that the district is drafting its own internally, and said questions about adults using AI are a separate issue. One committee member said the board is not the expert on AI, calling it very much integrated into curriculum and an operational issue, and said they did not want the board prematurely slinging opinions about things it is not expert on, hoping to propose at the board meeting that the resolution be referred to committee first. Another speaker agreed the resolution could go to the Policy Committee followed by a district presentation at its next meeting, a different speaker said it really should be an administrative call, and another agreed while noting three or four parents had spoken at an earlier public comment period with strong concerns and that there should be a place for their input.

A speaker pointed to an online petition launched Nov. 13 that asks the School Board to pause student-facing generative AI in pre-kindergarten through eighth grade and to give parents notice and opt-out rights, describing it as drawing hundreds and hundreds of people. A district staff member said the district needs to know whether the board or the administration owns AI policy so the two sides do not duplicate work, and that the district's AI work had not yet gone through its internal policy process or to the superintendent's cabinet. No vote on AI was taken at the committee meeting, and members said the district's draft AI policy should come to the Policy Committee so members can really get into the weeds of it. A speaker raised the idea of a full presentation, possibly in December, on which AI tools students use and what protections are in place. Members said their next committee meeting is Tuesday the 15th at 5:30 p.m.

stories.Headline: HPE builds Lux AI supercomputer with AMD for Oak Ridge, ranking 14th on TOP500
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise was scheduled to report its next quarterly results on November 23, with traders watching backlog conversion and cash flow according to a TradingView key facts summary. The company announced its Lux AI cluster, co-built with AMD for Oak Ridge National Laboratory, which ranked No. 14 on the TOP500 list with 220.79 petaflops and supports U.S. scientific AI research. HPE said its networking solutions will be deployed for the first time at a U.S. Department of Energy national lab, powering Lux with 800G switches and data-center management tools. HPE invested $37 million in kind to advance the Genesis Mission and support research, and half of Lux's 3.5 million annual node-hours will go to the mission. Citi kept a Buy rating on HPE but cut its price target to $80 from $92, according to the summary.

Barclays cut Hewlett Packard Enterprise to Equal Weight from Overweight, citing uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. Elliott Investment Management cut its stake in Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. by 16.3% to 27.0 million shares as of September 30, 2026, compared with June 30, 2026. The summary drew on sources including BusinessWire, Invezz and Reuters, and it carried a disclaimer that it is AI-generated and may contain inaccuracies. The articles do not say what the November 23 results showed, because the summary was published on November 17, 2026, before the scheduled report.

They also do not say how the analysts' rating and target changes affected the share price or what the company said about the cuts. The only stated reason for a downgrade is Barclays' cited uncertainty about whether AI demand is accelerating hardware adoption and business performance. The summary gives no further context on the Genesis Mission beyond HPE's $37 million in-kind investment and the share of Lux node-hours reserved for it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Exa raises embedding throughput about 50% on AWS Inferentia2 chips to index billions of documents
stories.Summary:
Exa boosted embedding throughput by about 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips, the company said in a post published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said it is building one of the few true web indexes by aggregating and serving knowledge from across the web, along with private and synthetic sources. Exa said it optimizes the index for semantic search, grounding agents and humans in true, high-quality data. Exa said it uses multi-tower semantic machine learning models to embed web data and query data into the same vector space. Exa said the keystone technology behind this is an in-house vector database.

Exa said the database must ingest as much high-quality web data as possible and embed all of it. Exa said the unit economics of embedding therefore underlie everything it does. Exa said that at the scale of tens or hundreds of billions of documents, finding hardware that delivers the best performance per dollar is not a tuning detail. Exa said any per-document cost improvement compounds into a significant number. Exa said inference runs on an asynchronous pipeline that must be high-volume and fast to serve recent data quickly and shrink the time between discovery and serving.

Exa said every structured web document it ranks as high enough quality must be embedded before it can be served. Exa said raw web data moves from crawlers into an asynchronous pipeline of parse, moderate and filter, then embed, with the result served from a vector database. Exa said its experience with the Neuron hardware family began with a backfill. Exa said moving to a superior document model meant re-embedding its existing corpus, and it selected 30 billion high-priority documents for re-embedding. Exa said a migration like this temporarily doubles the embedding load, which made it exactly the right moment to re-evaluate its hardware choices.

Exa said the doubling was a clear trigger to reconsider its hardware and optimization choices. Exa said AWS Inferentia2 figures refer to performance on the smallest instance type, an Inferentia2 xlarge instance (inf2.xlarge), with one chip and two NeuronCores. Exa said its workload runs on a single NeuronCore, so it runs Kubernetes pods that pack onto larger instances without leaving any cores idle, giving container homogeneity across the embedding fleet. Exa said the same process runs on a Trainium2 NeuronCore and scales the same way through data parallelism. Exa said its initial Inferentia2 implementation was a straightforward data-parallel, FP16 representation of the model.

Exa said that from that baseline it became a march to push throughput as high as possible, using the Neuron SDK and support from the AWS Trainium team. Exa said a progressive series of optimizations ultimately delivered roughly a 1.5× throughput improvement from the naive compile. Exa said the first was weight layout optimization, which eliminates unnecessary transposes by aligning the weight layout with the scheduling and layout of the broader model. Exa said it also enabled autocast, letting the compiler downcast matrix multiplications to lower precision while preserving dynamic range. Exa said the downcast outputs met its correctness gate of 0.999 cosine similarity against the reference, so the accuracy impact was within its acceptance threshold.

Exa said the Neuron Kernel Interface library provides optimized kernels for common model layers and operations. Exa said these pre-built kernels deliver immediate gains on common features, and it used them to quickly remove the most straightforward sources of inefficiency. Exa said a drop-in attention kernel gave it the next bump in performance. Exa said profiles from the Neuron Explorer consistently showed large amounts of spill and reload from high-bandwidth memory, which kept the Tensor Engine from being fully utilized through the forward pass. Exa said it wrote a custom weight-stationary fused SwiGLU MLP kernel that eliminated the HBM stalls, using the higher-level NKI language for layout operations, loops and memory operations and dropping into the lower-level NKI ISA only for specific tensor operations.

Exa said keeping most of the kernel in the higher-level language makes it more understandable for engineers and easier to debug. Exa said per-accelerator throughput measured with the other on-chip core idle was significantly higher than what it saw with both cores running simultaneously. Exa said that gap meant its theoretical data-parallel throughput should have been well above its realized aggregate performance, which pointed to contention between the cores. Exa said profiling and experimentation showed its workload was not yet saturating the Tensor Engine, and the remaining headroom was its to claim by making the computation leaner. Exa said it rewrote the attention kernel around the exact shapes in its model to cut FLOPS spent on padding.

Exa said generic kernels are built to handle any shape, so they cannot take advantage of the specific shapes in a given architecture. Exa said it also folded attention operations into single matmuls where the generic kernel used multiple instruction steps. Exa said that cut the inner-loop operations needed to compute the same values, which reduced HBM round trips and produced the final significant speedup. Exa said its final version was a 47% improvement in performance and cost per 1 million documents embedded, against its initial baseline. Exa said agents developed all of these optimizations inside a simple three part harness that lets them verify correctness, measure performance and profile the workload to find the next direction.

Exa said that using Flyte, an ML ops workflow platform, each agent runs its own workflow. Exa said the workflow compiles a NEFF Neuron executable and checks a forward pass against a baseline dataset, which must reach 0.999 cosine similarity to the canonical model. Exa said it then profiles one forward pass and runs a 30 minute saturation benchmark on real hardware. Exa said the harness supports agents at different costs, with lightweight models handling tedious work like grid searching compiler parameters and correctness checks preventing drift. Exa said reasoning agents test complex hypotheses and find bottlenecks, while the strongest code generators write custom kernels to fix them.

Exa said matching each agent to its task keeps costs in check, and validation keeps capable agents from drifting. Exa said that because many agents do not know the latest features and syntax, neuron agentic development skills also helped. Exa said it has so far optimized Inferentia2 for the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2), but tuning one hardware family in one Region has hard limits. Exa said spot and on demand availability vary by Region, and organizations with many consumers compete with themselves. Exa said locking into one Region or instance type almost guarantees a compute shortage, and possibly degraded service.

Exa said it schedules compute across multiple Regions from one Kubernetes control plane. Exa said its scheduler compares performance per dollar across instance types and packs pods onto the cheapest nodes, rescheduling as embedding demand shifts. Exa said each hardware type it optimizes for brings it closer to the global optimum, which is why its Inferentia2 work carried over directly to Trainium2. Exa said shifting hardware profiles lets it free up nodes other teams need or absorb their unused reserved compute. Exa said that for a long lived model, optimizing across hardware pays off enormously.

Exa said that at the scale it operates, extracting maximum cost-performance from a flexible pool of hardware is what matters. Exa said adding Neuron hardware to that pool and optimizing it with NKI has proven to be a major source of long-term cost savings. Exa said the post was published on the AWS blog on November 18, 2026. Exa said the post details how it optimized its embedding infrastructure for cheaper, more flexible inference workloads on AWS Neuron hardware, AWS Inferentia2 and AWS Trainium2. Exa said an agentic development workflow drove the optimization.

Articles.Title: Exa boosts embedding throughput by 50% to index billions of documents on AWS AI chips

stories.Headline: BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warns tighter AI rules could push US into recession
stories.Summary:
Larry Fink, the chief executive officer of the asset management firm BlackRock, issued a warning on November 19, 2026. During a joint interview with TV Tokyo and Nikkei, he discussed the potential dangers of strict artificial intelligence rules. He stated that implementing tighter regulations on this technology could potentially push the United States economy into a recession. This economic downturn would likely have negative consequences for the global economy as well. The CEO believes that the United States requires a massive amount of capital to support this technological shift.

He estimates that the country needs between 7 trillion and 9 trillion dollars in related investments to succeed. These funds would be necessary to build the infrastructure and systems required for advanced artificial intelligence. Without this level of investment and a flexible regulatory environment, the economic risks increase. Larry Fink spoke about these concerns while he was visiting Tokyo, Japan, for a board meeting.

He explained that overly restrictive laws could stifle the growth and innovation needed for economic stability. The executive suggested that the balance between safety and progress is critical for the financial future of the nation. He emphasized that the global market depends heavily on the success of American technological leadership. More to follow.

Articles.Title: BlackRock CEO warns tighter AI regulations could lead to US recession

stories.headline_source: BlackRock CEO warns tighter AI regulations could lead to US recession

stories.Headline: AWS adds full fine-tuning to SageMaker AI serverless model customization
stories.Summary:
Amazon Web Services added Full Fine-Tuning to SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization on November 19, 2026. This update allows businesses to continue training pretrained large language models on their own specific data. The process helps models adapt to a particular style, task, or domain. It aims to provide better accuracy for domain-specific work than general-purpose knowledge. This method also reduces costs by using smaller specialized models instead of frontier models.

The service removes the need for GPU provisioning, cluster setup, or distributed-training configuration. Users can now choose TrainingType.FULL instead of TrainingType.LORA within the SageMaker Python SDK. Experiments used a Qwen3-4B base model and the Magicoder-Evol-Instruct-110K dataset. This dataset contains 110,000 coding instruction-response pairs split into 99,000 training, 5,500 validation, and 5,500 test records. Other supported base models include DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, Nemotron-30B, and Gemma-4-26B.

AWS stated that Full Fine-Tuning overcomes the low-rank limitations of Parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods. They explained that this method updates model parameters simultaneously to absorb complex domain-specific knowledge. The company noted that this approach avoids the localized distortions found in low-rank methods. AWS claimed it results in stronger model convergence and better activation alignment across layers. They said it allows models to capture target task distributions and pre-trained knowledge.

The company noted that LoRA hits an accuracy plateau as datasets scale beyond tens of thousands of examples. This affects users performing complex tasks where large, high-quality datasets are available. For code generation tasks with over 100,000 examples, Full Fine-Tuning achieved 90.0 percent semantic correctness. Evaluation used Amazon Nova Pro as a judge, alongside PRIMECODE and MMLU benchmarks. These tools measure semantic correctness, code generation fidelity, and general knowledge retention.

Low-Rank Adaptation previously reduced GPU requirements by updating only a small subset of model parameters. This method injected small replacement matrices into model layers while freezing the pre-trained weights. However, the low-rank nature of these updates limited the representation power of the models. This trade-off hampered the ability to capture complex patterns needed for diverse tasks. Full Fine-Tuning instead modifies the model weight matrix uniformly using full representational capacity.

Users can now sweep hyperparameters like learning rate, batch size, warmup ratio, and epoch count. Fine-tuned models are automatically registered in the SageMaker Model Registry as versioned Model Packages. The articles explain how to use the SFTTrainer to launch these serverless customization jobs. They provide guidelines for hyperparameter tuning based on controlled experiments using the serverless service. The text leaves open the specific effective hyperparameter values for different tasks.

Articles.Title: Full Fine-Tuning (FFT) on SageMaker AI Serverless Model Customization | Amazon Web Services

stories.Headline: AMD opens Lux AI factory supercomputer to scientists at Oak Ridge
stories.Summary:
AMD announced on Nov. 16, 2026 that the Lux SI + HPC supercomputer is open to scientific users at the U.S. Department of Energy's Oak Ridge National Laboratory. AMD said Lux was developed through a public-private partnership between AMD and the DOE. The system was built by HPE and brings together AMD EPYC processors, AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs, AMD Pensando networking and AMD ROCm software. Lux is ranked 14th on today's TOP500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers. Lux provides the first dedicated U.S. AI Factory for the Genesis Mission, the DOE-led initiative to advance AI-driven science.

Genesis Mission projects allocated to run on Lux span AI-assisted fusion power plant design, an AI-based foundation model factory for materials development and advanced manufacturing, and Earth system prediction to forecast water availability, streamflow and river temperature in the Tennessee Valley Authority region. Lux combines AI with high-performance modeling and simulation to expand U.S. capabilities in science, energy and national security. Lux marks the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission. Lux builds on the computing foundation established at ORNL by the Frontier supercomputer, the first supercomputer to break the exascale barrier. The upcoming Discovery supercomputer will extend this commitment with deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing.

Thomas Zacharia, senior vice president, Global Public Sector and Strategic Partnerships at AMD, said Lux shows what is possible when national laboratories, government and industry work together to advance scientific discovery. Zacharia said bringing high-performance computing and AI closer to researchers helps them explore new approaches to complex problems and make better use of simulation and experimental data. Zacharia said the partnership builds on a strong foundation at Oak Ridge and supports an open, sovereign AI stack with tools that can benefit researchers across the country. Georgia Tourassi, associate laboratory director for Computing and Computational Sciences at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, said Lux represents the first major addition to DOE's computing infrastructure in support of the Genesis Mission. Tourassi said Lux will help accelerate the integration of SI, modeling and simulation, and experimental data to advance discovery in areas critical to the nation's energy, economic competitiveness and security.

Trish Damkroger, senior vice president and general manager, HPC & AI Infrastructure Solutions at HPE, said HPE, together with Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD, has delivered breakthrough engineering innovation to advance the nation's scientific computing resources. Damkroger said HPE is proud of its continued collaboration and investment in the Genesis Mission to stand up one of its first AI systems. AMD is also working with ORNL to support DOE's American Science Cloud, a national platform designed to extend advanced AI and high-performance computing capabilities across DOE laboratories, universities and mission partners in support of the Genesis Mission. For researchers, Lux provides an opportunity to train and refine models using scientific data, to combine AI with established simulation methods, and to investigate problems that require computing beyond their home institutions. Its delivery extends the AMD and ORNL collaboration behind Frontier into dedicated capacity for AI-driven science.

At SC26 in Chicago, AMD said it now powers 202 systems on the TOP500 list, capturing over 40% total market share. AMD revealed deployment progress for next-generation supercomputers in Finland and France using Instinct MI430X and 6th Gen EPYC "Venice" processors. AMD unveiled a roadmap for next-gen Instinct MI430X GPUs and 6th Gen EPYC "Venice" processors, with native 288 TFLOPS of FP64 high-precision compute and PCIe 6.0 support, targeting the Scientific AI market including nuclear physics and climate modeling. AMD announced alliances with IBM, PsiQuantum, Cornelis Networks and Rancher Government Solutions, spanning quantum error correction, high-speed interconnects and secure container scheduling. AMD is partnering with IBM and Cornelis to build an open heterogeneous ecosystem, leveraging its exclusive Versal FPGA advantage for Quantum Error Correction hierarchical decoding while challenging NVIDIA's proprietary interconnects with standard Ethernet technology.

The SC26 conference kicked off in Chicago the week of the announcement, following NVIDIA's reveal of its Rubin HPC architecture, slated for 2028, and the 20th anniversary of CUDA. AMD is launching an "Open Heterogeneous Computing" counter-offensive in the national-level supercomputing space. AMD's press release carries forward-looking statements concerning the features, functionality, performance, availability, timing and expected benefits of AMD products, including the Lux and Discovery supercomputers. The release also covers expected benefits of the collaboration among AMD, the DOE and Oak Ridge National Laboratory, including support for the Genesis Mission and the American Science Cloud. The release states that forward-looking statements are based on current beliefs, assumptions and expectations, speak only as of the date of the press release and involve risks and uncertainties.

Researchers and organizations interested in using Lux to advance Genesis Mission research are encouraged to contact ORNL's Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility to discuss their computing needs and applicable access pathways. AMD directs readers to visit the ORNL Lux resource page to learn more about the system and connect with the OLCF team. The articles do not state when Discovery will arrive or what its capabilities will be beyond deeper integration of AI and high-performance computing. The articles do not give the timing or terms of the alliances with IBM, PsiQuantum, Cornelis Networks and Rancher Government Solutions. The articles do not state when the Finland and France systems will be deployed or their full configurations.

stories.Headline: Manipal University Jaipur adds AI and emerging technology electives to five online degree programmes from January 2027
stories.Summary:
Manipal University Jaipur announced significant curriculum enhancements for five of its online degree programmes on November 19, 2026, in Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. The university introduced these changes to meet evolving industry needs and strengthen the professional relevance of its various academic offerings. These updates include new electives in artificial intelligence, generative AI, data analytics, finance, digital business, and other emerging technologies. The university also revised existing course content and restructured selected programmes to better equip learners with specialised knowledge and skills. These curriculum changes were officially approved by the university Academic Council to ensure they align with current professional landscape demands.

The revised curricula will come into effect starting from the January 2027 admission session for the five affected online degree programmes. These programmes include the Master of Business Administration, Master of Computer Applications, Bachelor of Computer Applications, Master of Commerce, and MA Economics. The online MCom programme will reduce its total credit requirement from 100 to 80 to follow the NEP-related credit framework. The online BCA programme introduces six elective pathways, including Agentic AI and Intelligent Systems, Cyber Security, Cloud Computing, and Full Stack Software Development. The online MA Economics programme now offers three pathways: Global Economics and Finance, Economics, Data and AI, and Public Policy and Development Economics.

The university Academic Council is responsible for approving these changes to keep academic offerings responsive to emerging industry requirements. The university stated that these enhancements aim to enable learners to build relevant competencies and strengthen their overall professional capabilities. By offering flexible learning pathways, the institution intends to enhance the career readiness of its students in a technology-driven environment. The university believes that introducing specialised electives will allow learners to explore emerging interdisciplinary domains while building on foundational knowledge. These efforts represent a continued commitment to improving the quality, relevance, and flexibility of online higher education for all graduates.

Learners in the online MBA programme can now choose Artificial Intelligence for Business to gain insights into strategic decision-making and functions. These students can select one elective for super specialisation or two electives for dual specialisation to align with their aspirations. MCA students are affected by new options in Next-Generation Technologies, Business Analysis, Generative AI and Agentic Systems, and Enterprise Resource Planning. These new MCA electives complement existing options in Cloud Computing, Cyber Security, AI and Machine Learning, and AI and Data Science. MCom students are affected by three new pathways covering Accounting, Taxation, Global Financial Reporting, Financial Analytics, AI, Decision Science, and Fintech.

Manipal University Jaipur was established in 2011 as a multidisciplinary university and holds a NAAC A+ accreditation for its quality education. Its online degree programmes are UGC-entitled and are recognised as being at par with the corresponding degrees offered on campus. The university currently offers nine degree programmes in online mode to a community spanning over 85 different nationalities worldwide. These learners come from more than 7,000 towns and cities across India and attend live interactive classes with experienced faculty. The institution provides placement assistance through skill assessments, industry-readiness sessions, resume-building support, and various virtual placement drives for its students.

The university will implement these revised curricula for all new students entering the specified online degree programmes in January 2027. The MBA programme continues to offer specialisations in Finance, Human Resource Management, Project Management, International Business, and Marketing, among other fields. Other MBA specialisations include Operations Management, Supply Chain Management, BFSI, IT and FinTech, Information System Management, Retail Management, and Digital Marketing. The articles do not state when the university will review these new electives or if further credit reductions will occur. They also leave open whether other online degree programmes beyond the five mentioned will receive similar technology-driven curriculum enhancements.

stories.Headline: Sea Limited launches Sea Cloud to offer AI services to enterprise customers
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix and Micron are two of the world's largest memory chipmakers, and both stocks soared as the AI boom fueled demand for high-bandwidth memory chips. Both stocks pulled back sharply over the past two months, and Leo Sun examined why they cooled off and whether either is still worth buying as a long-term AI play. The article was published by The Motley Fool on Nov 17, 2026 at 4:45PM EST and syndicated by The Globe and Mail on 2026-11-17T06:00:00Z. SK Hynix trades on NASDAQ under SKHY and Micron trades on NASDAQ under MU. SK Hynix became the first memory chipmaker to mass-produce HBM3 chips in 2022, and Micron completely skipped the HBM3 generation.

SK Hynix, based in South Korea, is the world's second-largest producer of DRAM and NAND memory chips after Samsung, while Micron, based in the U.S., ranks third in both markets. Both companies generate most of their revenue from DRAM chips rather than NAND chips, and both rely on HBM, a specialized high-density DRAM chip that supports Nvidia's data center GPUs in AI clusters. SK Hynix started producing HBM3E chips in 2024 and HBM4 chips in early 2026, and Micron started mass-producing its first HBM3E chips in 2024 and made the leap to HBM4 chips in early 2026. SK Hynix still leads the global HBM market, while Samsung and Micron rank second and third, respectively. As both companies allocate more manufacturing capacity to HBM chips, they have less capacity for conventional DRAM and NAND chips, causing a shortage of other memory chip types.

In 2025, SK Hynix's revenue surged 47%, its gross margin expanded year over year from 48.1% to 60.3%, and its net income soared 117%. For 2026, analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to jump 275% and its net income to rise more than sixfold. In fiscal 2026, which ended in September, Micron's revenue more than tripled, its gross margin more than doubled to 80.7%, and its net income rose nearly tenfold. Analysts expect SK Hynix's revenue to rise 60% in 2027 and 17% in 2028, and they expect Micron's revenue to soar 107% in fiscal 2027, followed by just 16% growth in fiscal 2028 and nearly flat growth in fiscal 2029. SK Hynix trades at just three times this year's earnings, while Micron trades at four times this year's earnings.

Sun wrote that both chipmakers should see growth slow over the next two years, and that the current AI growth cycle will inevitably cool off as the market matures. He wrote that both stocks are still valued as cyclical chipmakers rather than high-growth AI stocks. Sun said inflation and elevated interest rates could curb AI spending and make it more difficult for smaller neocloud companies to expand. He said construction of new data centers in the U.S. could be more tightly regulated in several Tier-1 data center states, including Texas, Ohio, and Georgia, after the Democrats swept the midterm elections in early November. Sun said SK Hynix and Micron could both experience significant volatility over the next 12 months.

Sun said that if he had to pick one over the other, he would stick with SK Hynix instead of Micron for three simple reasons: it is larger, it is growing faster, and it will remain the market leader in HBM chips. He noted that the Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now, and SK Hynix wasn't one of them. He cited Netflix, which made the list on December 17, 2004, when a $1,000 investment would have grown to $327,620. He cited Nvidia, which made the list on April 15, 2005, when a $1,000 investment would have grown to $959,410. He noted Stock Advisor's total average return is 802%, compared to 205% for the S&P 500, with returns as of November 17, 2026.

Sun disclosed that he has no position in any of the stocks mentioned, and that The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Nvidia. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy, and the article contains syndicated content that the site has not reviewed, approved, or endorsed and may receive compensation for placing. Market data was provided by Barchart, with exchange delay details and data provider terms noted, and information may be delayed and is provided as is for informational purposes only. Micron was listed at $712.42, down $6.60 or 0.92%, with a market cap of $813.51B, a day's range of $666.88 to $726.99, a 52-week range of $192.59 to $1,255.00, and a dividend yield of 0.08%.

stories.Headline: Tencent reports slower revenue growth as AI demand boosts cloud unit
stories.Summary:
China's Tencent reported an eight per cent climb in third quarter revenue on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, in Beijing. This growth was weaker than expectations and results from the previous quarter because gaming business growth cooled. The company reported revenue of 207.3 billion yuan, which is equal to 31.1 billion US dollars, for September. This figure was slightly below an LSEG consensus estimate of 210.8 billion yuan, while the previous quarter grew 11 per cent. Net profit edged up 0.8 per cent to 63.61 billion yuan, beating analyst expectations of 59.46 billion yuan.

Fintech and business services, including the cloud unit, rose 9 per cent to 63.7 billion yuan due to AI demand. Value added services, including gaming, rose 3 per cent to 98.3 billion yuan, with domestic games growing 11 per cent. International games revenue slid 9 per cent, while capital expenditure in the September quarter was 81.4 billion yuan. This spending was higher than the 52.8 billion yuan spent in the June quarter for the same company. Tencent spent 84.7 billion yuan in the first half of the year, exceeding the 79 billion yuan spent in 2025.

Chief executive officer Pony Ma said cloud revenue growth increased because of WorkBuddy and more compute for GPU rental. He noted that the company allocated more compute to Model as a Service to drive the growth of cloud services. CEO Ma Huateng stated that the company is making substantial progress toward building a new, AI empowered Tencent. He mentioned this progress is happening in terms of intelligence, applications, and infrastructure for the large Chinese tech firm. These leaders are managing heavy AI spending to see if it pays off or if it is squeezing margins.

Investors are monitoring the spending, and shares in Chinese cloud service providers, including Tencent, slid on Tuesday. These investors are concerned about whether the heavy spending on artificial intelligence is starting to pay off for the firm. Other affected parties include Chinese tech giants who have struggled to obtain advanced Nvidia chips because of US export restrictions. Washington announced new rules this week that restrict remote access to advanced US AI chips through overseas data centres. These restrictions have put Chinese companies on the back foot compared to their competitors in the United States.

Tencent said a year ago that chip shortages were constraining its cloud growth as it prioritised internal AI chip use. The company prioritised using these chips internally over renting computing power to external clients during that specific time period. The articles mention that CXMT has overtaken Tencent as the most valuable Chinese firm amid a general AI frenzy. Tencent also released an AI image model to compete with other companies like ByteDance and the firm Alibaba. Reports indicate that Tencent leases 100,000 chips from Oracle to accelerate its push into the artificial intelligence field.

The company will continue to monitor if its heavy AI spending is paying off or if it is squeezing margins. It remains to be seen how enterprises will navigate power constraints and sustainability targets while using these cloud services. The articles leave open how the new Washington rules on remote chip access will impact long term growth for Tencent. It is unclear if the company can overcome the struggle to obtain advanced Nvidia chips due to US export restrictions. Future results will show if the AI image model successfully catches competitors like ByteDance and the firm Alibaba.

stories.Headline: Huawei presents financial AI scaling capabilities at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026
stories.Summary:
Huawei unveiled financial AI scaling capabilities at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on November 20, 2026. The company shared insights on advancing agentic finance with global financial institutions and industry partners. Jason Cao and Alvin Feng delivered keynotes on the Festival and Frontier stages. Huawei showcased solutions for central banks, securities, insurance, and application modernization. They also presented achievements from the 4-Win ecosystem and the RONGHAI Financial Partner Program.

The event took place from November 18 to 20, 2026, at the Singapore EXPO. GeekyAnts participated at Booth 4G34 in Hall 4, while the festival expected 70,000 participants from 142 countries. The Monetary Authority of Singapore and Global Finance & Technology Network organized the event with the Association of Banks in Singapore. MAS issued AI Risk Management Guidelines on October 7, 2026, with oversight expectations due by October 7, 2027. Lifecycle controls and organizational capability requirements must be met by October 7, 2028.

Jason Cao, CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, said scaling AI requires hybrid infrastructure and standardized engineering. He stated that financial institutions must own their data, knowledge, and business logic to remain competitive. Alvin Feng, President of Huawei International Financial BU, unveiled the Fintelligent AI Solution for security and scalability. Kunal Kumar, Chief Revenue Officer at GeekyAnts, said that regulation and compliance will be as important as innovation. He discussed the movement from digitized financial services toward intelligent operational systems during a Mumbai event.

Financial institutions are affected by new governance requirements for security, operational control, and AI risk management. A survey by EY and the Institute of International Finance found 98 percent of 65 institutions saw AI benefits. About 70 percent of those institutions reported that agentic AI is moving from development into production. These systems are being explored for risk management, payment operations, customer onboarding, and fraud detection. Policymakers and technology providers are discussing how these forces influence products for different global markets.

Huawei has served over 7,100 financial customers over 16 years, including 54 of the top 100 banks. The company uses three intelligent factories for agent development, token operations, and high quality data supply. The festival theme focused on the coming rewiring of the financial system regarding new risks and rules. Five forces reshaping finance include capital, talent, policy, geoeconomics, and technology. GeekyAnts previously attended the Global Fintech Fest 2026 in Mumbai as a Bronze Partner and exhibitor.

Huawei is exploring an architecture using two super agents and multiple specialized agents for banking capabilities. Banks must now ensure their services can be understood and invoked by these proactive AI agents. Institutions must determine where automated decisions can support workflows and where human review remains necessary. The articles leave open how specific cross border payment infrastructures will adapt to these new AI regulations. They do not state which specific top 100 banks are currently using the Fintelligent AI Solution.
