stories.Headline: Firecrawl opens its first office outside the US in downtown Toronto and hires for research, growth and engineering roles
stories.Summary:
Firecrawl, a company based in San Francisco, opened its first office outside the United States in downtown Toronto. This expansion occurred around November 2026 to support the company's growth in the artificial intelligence sector. The firm provides tools that allow AI agents to search and pull information from the web. It is currently hiring for several new roles in research, growth, and engineering. This move marks the first time the company has established a site outside of California.

The company is hiring a back end infrastructure engineer with a salary between 217,000 and 233,000 dollars. A web automation engineer role also pays between 217,000 and 233,000 dollars and requires three years of experience. The founding security engineer position pays between 208,000 and 226,000 dollars and reports to the head of core platform. These hybrid roles require employees to be on site three days per week in Toronto. The team will expand Alexandria, which offers one interface to government indexes, research development, and data providers.

CEO Caleb Peffer stated that AI is creating a new knowledge economy where people are paid for sharing knowledge. He described Alexandria as the economic model that makes this new knowledge economy possible for users. Peffer noted that Toronto has been at the heart of modern AI and is the best place to build. The company aims to support a fast growing community of developers who are building AI agents in Canada. These new hires will help bring more data providers onto the Alexandria platform for the company.

Mayor Olivia Chow said that Toronto is where much of modern AI was born and welcomed the company. She stated that companies choose Toronto because of the city's diversity, universities, and the available local talent. Chow believes this investment provides good jobs for Torontonians and helps the city grow as an innovation home. The expansion affects local developers and job seekers who can apply for the open positions online. Other tech companies like Lyft and OpenTable have also opened offices in Toronto during this year.

Firecrawl is based in San Francisco and creates infrastructure for AI agents to access the live web. Lyft opened a 90,000 square foot office at 100 King Street West in September for 500 jobs. OpenTable debuted a 24,000 square foot office at 134 Peter Street in May for its global team. These companies are joining a growing ecosystem of technology firms establishing a presence in the Canadian city. The articles highlight Toronto as a primary hub for artificial intelligence and high skilled technical talent.

The Toronto team will now work to expand the indexes of the Alexandria knowledge infrastructure for AI agents. They will focus on making Firecrawl fast and reliable against a web that constantly changes and fights back. The company will continue to hire for roles in legal, finance, and people and culture in Toronto. The articles do not state the total number of employees Firecrawl intends to hire for this office. It remains open how many data providers will eventually be integrated into the Alexandria platform.

stories.Headline: Code Effects releases Version 7 with secure AI agents and rule auditing for .NET
stories.Summary:
Code Effects Software, LLC released Code Effects Version 7 on November 18, 2026, according to an announcement dated Atlanta, Nov. 18, 2026. The release was reported by GlobeNewswire and published by The Manila Times on November 19, 2026. The company described itself as a provider of embeddable .NET business rules engine technology. Version 7 introduces AI-assisted rule authoring, secure AI agent integration, centralized rule repositories, version management, testing, production evaluation auditing, and AI-powered reporting. The platform lets organizations incorporate artificial intelligence into business rule management while preserving deterministic execution, granular permissions, and human oversight of production operations.

Version 7 includes an embeddable Model Context Protocol server that lets external AI clients and autonomous agents interact with business rules, source objects, versions, tests, and evaluation history. It supports user-delegated agents, which operate on behalf of authenticated users and inherit their permissions and access restrictions, and independent agents and services, which operate under separate identities with individually configured permissions. Both models are subject to additional, non-bypassable security restrictions enforced internally by Code Effects, even if the host application mistakenly grants permissions authorizing the operations. AI agents and independent services cannot approve rules, delete rules or source objects, publish rules to production (Go Live), or take production rules offline. AI-generated changes also require human approval before production deployment.

Users can create, modify, and investigate business rules through natural-language interactions, and an AI assistant can translate business requirements into structured rules using the fields, methods, and operators exposed by the host application. Generated rules remain readable and editable in the Code Effects visual Rule Editor and are validated against the application's source definitions. The platform follows a Bring Your Own AI approach, allowing organizations to integrate any commercial or privately hosted language models without depending on a proprietary AI provider. Through the MCP server, authorized users and agents can request rule explanations, compare versions, investigate failed tests, analyze evaluation history, and generate reports using natural language. The new Code Effects Rule Repository provides embeddable web-based interfaces for managing rules, source objects, versions, tests, approvals, and user activity.

Version 7 introduces centralized rule storage, rule and source versioning, draft management, approval workflows, and permission-controlled access. Built-in testing allows users to define input values, specify expected outcomes, execute tests against individual rule versions, and inspect detailed results, and saved tests support regression testing when business logic changes. The new Code Effects Audit component records production rule evaluations, including executed rule versions, relevant inputs, results, and execution details, and authorized users can investigate why a particular decision occurred, review historical evaluations, analyze rule behavior, and replay recorded evaluations for testing and troubleshooting. AI assistants can use this information to answer questions about rule performance, execution history, and decision outcomes, subject to the requesting identity's permissions. Audit is designed to operate asynchronously without unnecessarily delaying normal rule execution.

Version 7 also enhances the core rules engine and editor with additional operators, collection functions, string and date operations, improved nullable-value handling, inline rule execution, rule composition, and enhanced validation. The engine continues to execute approved business logic deterministically within the host application's .NET environment, without requiring an LLM for ordinary rule execution. Code Effects Version 7 remains an embeddable, self-hosted platform, and customers maintain control over their infrastructure, authentication, permissions, business rules, and evaluation data. The repository initially supports Microsoft SQL Server and PostgreSQL, with Oracle and MySQL support planned for subsequent releases. Core assemblies target .NET Standard 2.0, while the MCP server requires .NET 8 or later.

Code Effects was founded in 2009 and develops embeddable business rules engine and rule management technology. Code Effects Version 7 is available through the company's distribution and licensing channels, and product development contact Sergey Minin can be reached at [email protected]. Code Effects also plans to release the entire Version 7 platform for Java in Q1 2027, including the rules engine, visual editor, repository, audit, MCP server, and AI integration capabilities. The articles leave open the pricing of Version 7 and the timing of Oracle and MySQL support. The articles also leave open how the Java release will be delivered and licensed.

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6.2 Astra, which builds working websites from written prompts
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced GPT-6.2 Astra, a new frontier model that can build functional, interactive websites from written descriptions, the company announced on Tuesday. TechGig published its report on the model on Nov 20, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. OpenAI's own announcement of GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol is dated 2026-11-17. The model shows improved coding, visual design, and handling of complex projects that require multiple steps. A test used a single detailed prompt to build a family command center website.

The test site included a calendar, meal planner, grocery list, and chore tracker, and it was fully functional, interactive, mobile-friendly, and remembered changes. GPT-6.2 Astra is available through ChatGPT Work for eligible Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users. Users can customise prompts to build simple web applications such as vacation planners or budget dashboards. OpenAI also introduced GPT-6.2 Sol, an efficient, versatile model for everyday work, and both models deliver better results with fewer output tokens. In the API, GPT-6.2 Astra's input and output token prices are 20% lower than GPT-6 Astra's, with a 60% discount on cached input at $8 for input, $0.40 for cached input, and $40 for output, all per million tokens, while GPT-6.2 Sol keeps GPT-6.1 Sol's API token prices.

OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra sets a new quality bar for AI in complex professional work, with slides, spreadsheets, and documents that read less like AI and follow the templates and conventions of a user's field. OpenAI said the model writes cleaner code and builds frontends that look and work better, particularly for websites, gaming, and 3D design. OpenAI said it believes GPT-6.2 Astra is the best model in the world for scientists. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Sol is smarter and more efficient than GPT-6.1 Sol and lets users complete more tasks on the same paid plan. OpenAI said many of its employees use GPT-6.2 Sol as their default model for technical and non-technical tasks.

On Agents' Last Exam, GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra at less than a third of the cost and 5.5 points ahead of Claude Fable 5.2 at just 5% of the cost, with Fable 5.2's leaderboard results excluding nine tasks that used a fallback model. GPT-6.2 Astra scored 9 percentage points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Terminal-Bench-Science 0.1 at less than one-third the cost and set a new high on the Vals Science Index. In Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, GPT-6.2 Sol came within 0.5 points of GPT-6.2 Astra at about one-fifth the cost, both at max. On LifeVal, GPT-6.2 Sol outscores GPT-6 Astra at about one-seventh the cost. On Harvey LAB-AA v1.1, GPT-6.2 Astra more than doubled Claude Fable 5.2's pass rate at about one-sixth the cost, and Astra for Law scored even higher.

On the internal GDPval v2 benchmark, GPT-6.2 Astra was up 6.2 percentage points from GPT-6 Astra while using 22% fewer output tokens, and GPT-6.2 Sol improved 5.3 points from GPT-6.1 Sol. On Artificial Analysis's AA-AnalystAgent, GPT-6.2 Astra answered 62.5% of questions correctly on all five independent attempts. Marquis Wong, Principal AI Engineer at IMC, said Astra's documents were a significant step up from GPT-6 Astra. Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, said Astra used 62% fewer tokens than GPT-6.1 Sol on complex legal-agent tasks and scored higher than alternative models on 8 of 10 research tasks across tax, M&A and litigation work. Niko Grupen, Head of Applied Research at Harvey, said Astra completed more than 3x as many Legal Agent Benchmark tasks with 34.5% fewer output tokens.

Jay Hack, Head of AI at ClickUp, said GPT-6.2 Astra edged out ClickUp's production model in blind testing with about 40% fewer tokens and 30% fewer review rounds. OpenAI said Astra's more precise computer use lets it work down to individual parts and connections in CAD and simulation tools. OpenAI asked GPT-6.2 Astra to visualize chassis dynamics of a car on a mountain road, and Astra created the 3D model, wrote a Python solver to simulate dynamics between the tires and suspension, and animated the results in Blender. OpenAI's team used GPT-6.2 Astra to turn the scalloped balconies of Chicago's Marina City towers into a paper lamp, and the site generated by the model can be used to create your own paper lamp. OpenAI said GPT-6.2 Astra brings stronger visual reasoning to web design, choosing layouts and imagery that give each site a distinctive look.

stories.Headline: Ravi Menon says employers choose whether AI lifts or removes junior workers
stories.Summary:
Speakers at the Singapore FinTech Festival discussed the ongoing impact of artificial intelligence on jobs on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. Ravi Menon, the former managing director of the Monetary Authority of Singapore, participated in a panel discussion about these developments. Dr Michael Spence, a professor at Stanford University, also spoke about the current age of uncertainty regarding AI. These experts examined how automation and augmentation affect the workforce, particularly for those in entry level roles. The event highlighted the tension between increasing productivity and the displacement of workers across various economic sectors.

The panel titled Geoeconomics 2.0: Statecraft in the Age of Intelligence focused on the need for a social licence for AI. This licence depends on the balance between wages and jobs, as noted by Ravi Menon in Singapore. Another panel, The AI and Employment Equation: Balancing Productivity, Displacement, and New Jobs, explored the specific effects on workers. Dr Michael Spence divided the AI landscape into frontier work, involving infrastructure investment, and the diffusion of adoption. He noted that displacement of young people is already appearing in the financial sector and professional services.

Ravi Menon stated that AI can either lift the junior worker or remove her, and this outcome is a choice. He explained that automation tends to displace jobs, while augmentation can raise wages and create new opportunities for workers. Menon warned that AI faces the same test as globalisation, which failed to share gains and support displaced people. He noted that entry level roles feel the most pressure, though AI can also lift the least experienced workers. He believes that avoiding past mistakes is essential to prevent a populist backlash against these new technologies.

Dr Michael Spence said it is too soon to know the ultimate productivity effects of AI on the global economy. He cautioned that the coming period will be disruptive, as the scope of virtually every job will likely change. Spence argued that investment banks must invent new models to bring in talent since AI now does beginner work. He stated that firms still need young people for the long term, specifically for their needs ten years later. These changes primarily affect young professionals who traditionally started their careers with basic tasks now handled by AI.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong addressed how these shifts would play out within the small nation of Singapore. He noted that the whole world is short of AI talent, so Singapore must keep its doors open. Gan acknowledged that many Singaporeans are anxious because AI carries the risk of changing lifestyles faster than people adjust. He stated that while the government cannot protect every job, they intend to protect every single worker. This approach involves giving workers new skills to take advantage of opportunities created by the rise of AI.

The government aims to build trust between industry players and the state to strengthen the ecosystem for local talent. Gan Kim Yong believes that anxiety about the pace of change is healthy if it prevents people from being static. He warned that everyone will be in trouble if they ignore the impact of AI and treat it as business. The articles leave open exactly how the new models for training junior talent will be invented by firms. They also do not specify the exact skills workers need to acquire to remain employable in this environment.

stories.Headline: Calif researchers use GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java flaw and build a working exploit for under $200
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the cybersecurity startup Calif, with help from OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model, discovered a memory corruption bug in Java that can be used to take over computer systems, according to Engadget. On some machines, feeding Java's base64 decoder a string of 64 "A" characters followed by an equals sign triggers a memory error that usually causes a crash but can be finessed to gain full unauthorized access. Calif showed the bug could be used to hack into Keycloak, a widely used login system protecting organizations like CERN and NASA. The Record reports that CISA issued a notice on Tuesday night about CVE-2026-114938, which researchers are calling "Java4Shell," warning that attackers could crash the critical Java Virtual Machine and conduct unauthenticated remote code execution. Oracle released a patch for the bug in its November Patch Tuesday release, writing that it carries a severity score of 8.1, and credited Quang Luong and Albert Yang of Calif with discovering the vulnerability.

Java is the world's third most popular programming language and powers about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies, according to Calif, which said banking, aviation, telecommunications and nearly every critical sector runs on it, including national security systems. Calif said it took Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability and two more hours to develop the first working exploit, at a total token cost of less than $200. The company explained that there is no universal exploit and each system may require different steps to exploit, and Luong noted he found the bug while developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. Calif said it is holding back on releasing application-specific exploits and weaponized chains for individual products until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. Several other companies confirmed Calif's findings and urged organizations to patch the bug immediately.

CISA urged organizations to review their software inventories for affected Java installations, including those bundled within third-party applications, and to prioritize internet-facing systems. Calif says the bug isn't easy to weaponize, which should give defenders some breathing room, but Engadget notes that some systems will inevitably go unpatched and Calif estimates the bug could linger for five to 10 years. Calif also discovered the highly publicized vulnerabilities impacting PHP last month and used AI to find this bug, as it did with PHP2Shell. Although officials' public statements haven't linked the past week's outages at Microsoft, the FAA, banks and Apple to AI, Engadget describes the events as a picture of aging digital infrastructure unprepared for what comes next.

stories.Headline: Fujitsu Japan and partners verify AI cuts clinical trial screening work by 89 percent
stories.Summary:
Fujitsu Japan, the National Cancer Center Hospital East, and Paradigm Health conducted joint research to streamline clinical trial candidate screening. This project used a Large Language Model and the Paradigm Platform to identify potential candidates for new drug trials. The verification study took place between June and the end of October 2026 in Kawasaki and Kashiwa. The partners confirmed that this AI approach significantly improved the efficiency of the candidate identification process. This research aimed to shorten patient recruitment timelines and expand participation opportunities for domestic and international trials.

The study used data from 22,334 patients in the Department of Respiratory Medicine to simulate a trial for EGFR gene mutations. Fujitsu Japan processed electronic medical records for 3,027 lung cancer patients through anonymization and structuring using a Large Language Model. Paradigm evaluated 540 patients with EGFR gene mutations based on five specific criteria to determine their clinical trial eligibility. The AI identified 57 priority candidates, and physicians later confirmed that 51 of these individuals were promising candidates. This automated overnight processing reduced the number of patient records requiring manual review by approximately 89 percent.

Fujitsu Japan, led by CEO Izuru Kokubu, aims to commercialize a service for candidate screening and enrollment by fiscal year 2027. The company promotes the Uvance business model to create social value and streamline clinical trials through the use of AI. Toshihiko Doi directs the National Cancer Center Hospital East, which collaborated to verify the application of the Paradigm Platform. Paradigm Health, based in Columbus, Ohio, and led by CEO Kent Thoelke, provided the matching platform for the research. These partners stated that the system allows institutions to determine eligibility based on standardized criteria without relying on individual expertise.

Medical professionals, including physicians and clinical research coordinators, are affected because they previously relied on manual reviews and personal knowledge. The research shows that AI can alleviate the burden on medical staff and expedite clinical trial opportunities for patients. Patients are affected because the system helps them avoid missing opportunities to consider new treatment options for their conditions. The process ensures that final eligibility is determined by physicians based on trial requirements and the consent of the patient. These results represent candidates identified during research and do not guarantee that these individuals will actually participate in trials.

Drug loss is a pressing social challenge where new treatments available overseas are not developed or approved within Japan. Personalized medicine based on biomarkers and genetic mutations has advanced in oncology, making clinical trial participation criteria increasingly complex. Medical staff must currently review dispersed information across genomic data, test results, treatment histories, and electronic medical records. Differences in medical data formats and unstructured data in Japanese records create obstacles for the utilization of global data. This background creates an urgent need to promote clinical trials for new drugs to expand treatment opportunities for patients.

Fujitsu Japan will now proceed with commercializing a service to support the process from candidate screening to patient enrollment. The company targets a launch by the end of fiscal year 2027 to help expand clinical trial capacity. Partners will promote the adoption of this solution at medical institutions across Japan to facilitate broader access to therapies. The company intends to use Uvance to eliminate drug loss and provide higher quality healthcare to every single patient. The articles leave open whether the identified candidates will actually enroll or if other medical institutions will adopt it.

stories.Headline: Google Labs acquires Howie to build AI scheduling agents for small businesses
stories.Summary:
Google Labs acquired the Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant during the week of November 16, 2026. The experimental arm of Google announced this purchase in a post on X on Monday, November 17, 2026. This acquisition aims to build the next generation of intuitive AI tools specifically designed for small businesses. The deal brings the Howie team into the Google Labs division to continue developing their scheduling product. Terms of the purchase were not disclosed by the companies when the news was released this week.

The tool allows users to cc Howie on email threads to coordinate meeting times and add events to calendars. It follows up as needed and flags conflicts using fine-tuned language models and human scheduling experts for low confidence tasks. Customers set rules in a preferences document, such as setting pitch calls to 25 minutes and using Zoom for meetings. PitchBook data shows Howie was valued at 14 million dollars in 2024 before the acquisition by Alphabet Inc. occurred. The product was originally built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar to manage scheduling and calendar tasks for users.

Google Labs stated they are excited to welcome the team and learn from their years of calendar management experience. CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith wrote on LinkedIn that Google Labs is the perfect place to advance the product. Petersmith said that his team will continue building the tool while working within the experimental division of the company. Both Petersmith and Google Labs did not respond to requests for comment regarding the specific terms of the deal. They also did not confirm if the tool will be integrated into other Google apps and services soon.

The tool served more than 1,000 paying customers, including venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants, journalists, and various startup founders. At its peak, the AI assistant was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings every week for these diverse professional users. Google is competing with rivals like OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and xAI to build agents that complete tasks for users. These AI agents represent an advancement beyond simple question and answer chatbots by performing digital actions on behalf of users. This push for agents follows the May release of Gemini Spark, which organizes files and scans inboxes for emails.

Austin Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman, who previously co-founded a company called Assembly in 2013. The two partners prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 but decided that the market was not ready at that time. Howie launched publicly out of private beta in September 2025 after raising a 6 million dollar seed round. This funding round was led by True Ventures to help the Seattle startup grow its user base and operations. Google Labs previously acquired ProducerAI in February, a music platform using the Google DeepMind Lyria model for its generation.

The Howie team will now work within Google Labs to develop more intuitive AI tools for the small business market. Google continues to race against other tech giants to create agents that can proactively complete complex digital tasks for consumers. The company has already introduced the Gemini AI agent to handle workplace tasks and a 100 dollar monthly plan. It remains unclear if the Howie tool will be merged into existing Google Workspace services or remain a separate product. The articles leave open whether the human scheduling experts used by Howie will be retained by Google Labs.

stories.Headline: Texas provost Angela Bauer urges universities to let faculty decide where AI belongs in learning
stories.Summary:
Angela Bauer, executive vice president for academic affairs and provost at Texas Woman’s University, wrote a Texas Tribune opinion piece published November 19, 2026, arguing that higher education is gripped by an existential debate over artificial intelligence playing out nationwide at governing board meetings, in news headlines and on social media feeds. She said conversations at times devolve into a rigid binary of either banning AI to protect academic integrity or embracing it wholesale to stay relevant. She said the polarization is understandable because AI can perform tasks once viewed as uniquely human, such as reasoning through problems, constructing arguments and generating original text. She said AI is forcing higher education to rethink the nature of learning, what constitutes mastery and the evolving role of the professor. She said academic leaders have a fundamental responsibility to confront these existential questions head on rather than letting the debate polarize them.

Bauer wrote that preparing Texas students for an AI-integrated workforce requires moving beyond false choices and embracing the complexity of this moment. She said there are times when learning must occur in an explicitly AI-free space, because building cognitive muscle, developing a unique voice and mastering foundational logic require unassisted human effort. She compared a student letting a machine do the heavy lifting to a runner who cannot build endurance riding in a golf cart. She said that in business, healthcare and graphic arts, AI is rapidly altering how work gets done and AI fluency is no longer optional but fundamental. She cited a recent Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas study highlighting how generative AI is shifting the entry level job market for college graduates, automating routine tasks and raising what employers expect on day one.

Bauer said that at Texas Woman’s University, leaders have trusted their experts, namely faculty, to develop an AI roadmap for students rather than giving top-down system mandates. She said faculty within their specific disciplines determine where AI belongs and where it does not, with an English professor possibly requiring pen-and-paper drafts for a personal reflection while a nursing or business professor might integrate AI tools to analyze clinical data or develop marketing strategies. She said this nuanced approach honors academic rigor and disciplinary expertise, and that faculty have been equipped with both the autonomy and the resources to navigate these decisions because so much is at stake for students. She said a digital divide is emerging as AI reshapes the economy, with students who had prior access or experience with technology gaining AI fluency informally while first generation students risk falling behind. She said closing this literacy gap is central to the mission and that failing to teach students to use AI tools critically, ethically and strategically risks leaving them behind in the economy they are being prepared to lead.

Bauer said the issue extends far beyond the job market, because as statewide and national debates continue about policy guardrails around digital safety, data privacy and automated decision-making, society needs an educated citizenry that understands technology. She said policies alone are not enough and that voters, professionals and community leaders must understand how these models function, how to apply the technology ethically and its potential impact on human health and the environment. She said that as an academic year gets underway across Texas, the polarization should be left behind. She said AI is not going to replace the human element of higher education but is challenging people to refine it. Texas Woman’s University is described as the nation’s largest public university with a woman-focused mission.

Kate Perez of the Chicago Tribune reported that at DePaul University roughly a dozen students routinely wrestle with how much artificial intelligence should and could influence the human experience, spending hours at the Responsible AI Systems and Experiences, or RAISE, Lab on the university’s Loop campus exploring how AI affects daily life. DePaul recently released “Guiding Principles on Artificial Intelligence,” a tome calling for academic integrity, intellectual honesty, transparency and human-centered use of the technology. The principles were born out of the school’s 26-member Provost’s Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, which worked for over a year to develop them and meets monthly to discuss policy, practices and how AI is used in the classroom. Jay Cunningham, RAISE Lab creator and assistant professor of computing, said DePaul’s principles, published last month, go beyond issues of academic integrity. Cunningham, who launched the lab in 2025, said his goal is to help students understand that AI is a tool that attempts to model human behavior, human interactions and human decision-making, and that the job of humans is to wield tools in ways that serve them best.

Cunningham said that over the past half-decade he has seen more fields demand that workers understand AI, creating a need for students to learn the technology as it progresses. Professor of English John Shanahan said DePaul published a statement on AI in 2023, but in this age of rapid transition that is like 100 years ago. Shanahan, who chaired the university’s Advisory Committee on Artificial Intelligence, brought together colleagues who worried about AI’s implications for higher education and others who thrived in the new technology, creating a communal space for faculty across disciplines from acting to computer science to talk about the new programming. He said launching the committee was a chance to get a sense of what is going on in the units, provoke discussion so faculty talk about what they hear from students, and vet good ideas about what to do moving forward. Other Chicago campuses have formed committees to examine how to integrate AI into higher education, launched AI classes and majors and pushed for AI literacy among students and faculty, and several schools including the City Colleges of Chicago and Northwestern University now offer AI-related programs and degrees.

Nationwide, schools are considering how to inform students about AI use and best practices through websites, classes and training, and their approach depends on the institution. At the University of Chicago, a new master’s degree in applied AI will launch in fall 2027, while the law school prohibits note-taking on electronic devices in some classes. This fall, Northwestern University launched an undergraduate major in AI and an AI webpage of tools and resources that, according to the site, enable students, faculty and staff to use generative AI effectively and responsibly. Across the schools of City Colleges of Chicago, which serves more than 73,000 students a year through its network of multiple public community colleges, the system introduced its first AI degree program at Wilbur Wright College this fall, and students can now earn an Associate of Applied Science degree in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Development. City Colleges’ Provost and Chief Academic Officer Mark Potter told the Tribune the degree is applicable and relevant across all disciplines, from history and law to transportation and distribution, and that before the new program City Colleges created a district-wide AI steering committee that helped hone and articulate the school’s position on AI.

Potter said preparing students for an AI-enabled workforce and society is essential, that the school cannot shy away from this technology or bury its head in the sand, and that students need AI competencies including responsible and ethical use of AI, a position he said the system started with and still carries forward. Potter said he hopes people recognize City Colleges as a place where they can cultivate their AI knowledge, learn skills and build careers in the field. City Colleges’ Associate Vice Chancellor of technology sector strategy, Ayoka Noelle Mota Samuels, told the Tribune the school system is intended to be a space where people can afford to learn AI skills, adding that people can learn AI in a responsible way and know that it is not just transactional. Samuels said it is important that City Colleges be a recognizable and trusted place for people of all backgrounds to learn about AI, and that being part of the larger educational conversation around AI means more people will have access to the field than before. She said that without an education community part of being in leadership around AI, different folks do run the danger of being left out, and that City Colleges makes sure people are included at whatever level and stage of understanding and interest with AI.

Shanahan said that back at DePaul there has been a growing recognition over the last two years that AI does not necessarily have to be feared. He said the evolution of AI has brought a mix of enthusiasm, excitement, skepticism and fear, and that the advancements have benefited the institution, while acknowledging that they are at the beginning of this. He said the university is having conversations and being proactive about meeting the challenges of AI integration. He said AI is not going to go away, so there is a recognition of the need to negotiate a place with it and to ask what it means to be a creative person, a thinker and a writer with AI next to you all the time. He said there will be times when it is useful to use and times when it is better to think your own thoughts and write your own sentences, and that it is both.

stories.Headline: Mullin says DHS will convene industry call on preventing future outages
stories.Summary:
A string of technology outages struck in November 2026, including a nearly daylong Microsoft 365 outage caused by a hidden defect in the company’s cloud gateway. Saturday’s nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground-stop was caused by a telecommunications network failure linked to a router upgrade. “Routine maintenance” took down a classified communications network at the National Security Agency. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton described the outages as “several unrelated issues that have recently caused service disruptions.” During a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday, government leaders said there is no evidence the outages are part of a coordinated cyber campaign.

Clayton said the incidents are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state sponsored attack. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he is “’98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems.” Mullin said Department of Homeland Security officials are convening a call with industry to discuss the outages and how to avoid them in the future. Some of the outages have also been linked to efforts to rapidly patch software in response to artificial-intelligence driven vulnerabilities. Clayton said the rate of patching and upgrading of systems is increasing.

Mullin said it would be helpful if the industry doing an upgrade could inform customers that it is going to take place. He said patching and aging infrastructure are part of the challenge, and that “We’re not pressuring the industry to do it.” He said the aim is to have a conversation about communicating, because what happens online is a tremendous amount of fear. Clayton said that anytime such work is done, systems are taken down and brought back up. Clayton said the American people should ask these questions.

Anjana Rajan, CEO of cybersecurity firm Atalanta and a former White House cyber official, said Mullin’s call with industry comes at a crucial time, as the private sector owns and operates most U.S. critical infrastructure. Rajan said the ability to understand what systems will do under normal, abnormal, or hostile conditions is not keeping pace as critical infrastructure becomes more software defined. She said the catastrophic impact is the same regardless of the root cause, with people stuck on the tarmac, credit cards not working and email out. Lauren Zabierek, CEO and co-founder of the Software Safety Institute and a former Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency official, said the outages prove that “software doesn’t have to be hacked to cause harm.” Zabierek said national security, the economy, and public health and safety all depend on software, and too much of it is built with unsafe components and practices and shipped with unsafe defaults.

Zabierek and former CISA colleague Bob Lord recently co-founded the Software Safety Institute to tackle technology vendors shipping products with known defects and vulnerabilities. The institute’s work builds on CISA’s “Secure by Design” initiative. Lord, the institute’s chief strategy officer, said the online panic points to a lack of safety and security data about software, which he said contrasts with other critical sectors. Lord said that without enough information, people “connect the dots” on their own, and that “We don’t have transparency.” Zabierek said Mullin could use his perch at DHS to reconstitute CISA’s Cybersecurity Advisory Committee and the DHS Cyber Safety Review Board, which investigated major cyber incidents before it was disbanded last year.

Lawmakers on the homeland security committee introduced a bipartisan bill Tuesday that would reconstitute the board under a new name. Zabierek said Mullin could tell Congress that CISA needs the authority to set standards for technology manufacturers and hold them accountable. Rajan pointed to a January 2025 report co-authored by CISA and other agencies on “closing the software understanding gap,” which calls on the U.S. government to close a gap in how technical investments in new software products have outstripped investments in efforts that verify their functionality, safety, and security. Lord suggested DHS strengthen the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures program, which catalogs publicly disclosed cyber vulnerabilities using standard identifiers and whose participation is voluntary. Lord said companies continue to sell products containing years and even decades-old programming dangers, such as memory safety vulnerabilities, and asked how to reduce these recurring classes of coding error.

stories.Headline: Former Wall Street enforcement chief warns AI bubble will burst and cause recession before 2028 election
stories.Summary:
A former top Wall Street regulator said in mid November 2026 that the artificial intelligence bubble will likely burst and cause a recession by the 2028 election, according to CNN. The warning came as a survey reported by the Chosun Ilbo on November 15, 2026 found that 87% of Wall Street experts cite AI as a major risk. The two reports together frame a market that has risen sharply on AI enthusiasm while professionals increasingly flag the danger. The CNN report identifies the speaker as Wall Street's former top cop, a reference to a senior enforcement official, though the supplied text does not name the person.

The CNN account says the expected burst would be severe enough to tip the economy into recession before voters go to the polls in 2028. The Chosun Ilbo figure of 87% is the share of Wall Street experts who named AI as a major risk in the survey it reported on November 15, 2026. Both dates fall in November 2026, which places the warnings roughly two years before the 2028 election. The articles give no further numbers, no specific forecast dates beyond the election, and no named companies or individuals beyond the former official described in the CNN headline.

Responsibility for the warning rests with the former enforcement chief, who according to CNN expects the bubble to pop and drag the broader economy down with it. The Chosun Ilbo survey places the concern among a large majority of Wall Street experts, who see AI as a major risk rather than a purely positive force. The former official's view, as CNN frames it, is that the run-up resembles a bubble that cannot hold. The experts surveyed by the Chosun Ilbo did not, in the supplied text, offer a single unified prediction beyond flagging the risk.

The context is a market that has climbed on AI optimism while a growing share of professionals warn of a correction, and the CNN report ties that correction to a possible recession before 2028. What happens next depends on whether the bubble deflates gradually or bursts suddenly, and the articles do not say which outcome they expect beyond the former official's warning. The Chosun Ilbo survey suggests the concern is widespread rather than isolated to one voice. Neither article, in the text provided, gives a timeline for the burst beyond the 2028 election horizon.

stories.Headline: Scrunch launches Citation Optimisation to show brands which sources AI answers cite
stories.Summary:
Scrunch has launched Citation Optimisation, a tool that helps brands identify the third-party sources cited in AI-generated recommendations, the company announced on 18 November 2026. The feature is designed to show marketers which publishers, review sites and other external pages are used in answers generated by services including ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode and Microsoft Copilot. It also ranks those sources by influence and by how easily a brand can secure inclusion. The system lets marketers see where their brand already appears in cited material, where competitors are being referenced instead and where outreach could improve visibility. It can then help users prepare pitches based on the source involved, the opening identified and the brand's approved information.

Alongside Citation Optimisation, Scrunch introduced a separate feature called Imposter Detection, which is intended to identify suspected impostor sites that may be cited by AI systems and provide steps for brands seeking takedowns. Scrunch linked the release to findings from its study of Fortune 500 businesses, which found that 17% had an impostor website cited in AI answers across a range of major AI services. In three out of four answers citing a known impostor, the AI presented the site as the brand's official source, according to Scrunch. The company estimated that AI assistants deliver more than one million answers each year that cite websites impersonating real brands.

Scrunch said research from ScrunchLabs found that more than 40% of AI sessions involved neither an open-web search beforehand nor a click to the open web afterwards, compared with 21.5% of traditional search sessions that remained self-contained. Chris Andrew, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Scrunch, said every AI recommendation is built on a network of publishers, reviewers and other sources that most marketers have never been able to see clearly. He said Citation Optimisation makes that network actionable by showing who matters, where there is an opportunity to earn a stronger presence and how to approach them. Andrew said marketers are able for the first time to participate in the conversations that decide whether AI recommends them.

The release extends a series of recent product launches by Scrunch, which was founded in 2023 and says it has signed more than 500 customers. In the past 100 days it has also released Knowledge Studio, Site Optimisation, Agent Pages and Content Generation, products designed to help marketers monitor how AI systems describe their brands, adjust their websites to address content gaps and present information in formats intended to be easier for AI systems to interpret. Scrunch said its data also feeds into Sitecore's MarketingIQ product, linking citation insights with broader campaign and content planning across SitecoreAI, and it is working on integrations with partners including Noble, Stacker and Getfluence to automate more of the outreach and activation process tied to citation opportunities. Citation Optimisation is available now.

stories.Headline: Google makes its Tasks AI agent free with limits and renames Spark
stories.Summary:
Google renamed its Spark AI agent to Tasks and made it free for users on November 18, 2026. This change occurred just months after the initial release of the agentic tool. The company also retired Gems one day prior to this announcement. Existing Gems were converted into Skills during this transition. The rebrand reportedly began gradually in mid-October.

Tasks is free in the US, Canada, Korea, Japan, Australia, and India. US users can text or email Gemini, but calling businesses is unavailable in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska. Users have five hours of access before paying, and non-AI plan users have a 32k token context window. The tool runs on the Gemini 4 Hydrogen model. It competes with OpenAI Dots at 100 dollars monthly and Anthropic Claude Duet starting at 20 dollars.

Google stated that users can adjust task settings, disconnect apps, or delete chat history at any time. The company's new landing page suggests using the tool for personal finance and identifying recurring expenses. A new Memory summary feature allows users to edit personal information the chatbot holds. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said Muse is free for up to 100M tokens per week. He envisions AI assistants managing careers, finances, relationships, and everyday tasks.

ZDNET's David Gewirtz called Meta Muse the worst AI agent for privacy and was not blown away by Spark. Joe Thomas, a South Carolina businessman, is suing Meta for 75,000 dollars in Oconee County Court. Thomas claims Meta suspended his epoxy countertop business pages for a week, costing him 25,000 dollars. His Muse agent, Baby Mia, helped him sue Meta by contacting the FBI and the California Attorney General. Baby Mia also contacted Senator Tim Scott, the FCC, the FTC, and various journalists.

The agentic tool can handle grocery shopping, booking appointments, and analyzing heating bills. These products target a society reliant on tech for convenience and productivity. Meta's Muse platform allows agents to produce promotional material and AI-generated videos. Ziff Davis filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI regarding copyright infringement. AI agents are noted as security risks because they can autonomously place orders and review files.

Users can now toggle to Tasks from the standard Gemini Chat setting. It remains unclear if Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark besides leaving the beta phase. The lawsuit against Meta has not yet established that the company is legally responsible for losses. 404 Media raised concerns about AI agents simultaneously contacting government offices and courts. The articles leave open whether the legal claim by Joe Thomas will ultimately succeed.

stories.Headline: KPMG launches AI-native audit platform KCi across US teams
stories.Summary:
KPMG LLP, an audit, tax, and advisory firm in the United States, introduced an AI-native audit platform in the country on November 18, 2026. This new system, called KPMG Clara intelligence or KCi, is built upon the existing KPMG Clara audit platform to improve quality and insights for auditors and management teams. The platform integrates artificial intelligence, data, workflow tools, and collaboration functions into a single connected system based on the firm's audit methodology. It utilizes specialized agents within audit procedures to link client data, risk assessments, and technical information rather than functioning as separate software.

The new technology requires a shift in how auditors handle routine tasks and initial documentation through automation. This change allows teams to analyze full transaction populations and move supervisory activities earlier into the audit cycle. The firm plans to implement KCi in all private company audits starting in 2027, while a phased rollout for public company audits is currently being prepared. This deployment involves more than 125 teams within the United States and 500 teams across the globe.

Christian Peo, the vice-chair of KPMG US Audit and Assurance, is responsible for overseeing these developments. He stated that the profession is experiencing a defining moment similar to the transition from paper to digital workflows. Peo explained that while technology cannot automate auditor judgment, it helps remove the barriers between data, analysis, and action. The firm believes the platform can identify anomalies and patterns in wider datasets, which helps auditors ask questions of clients and internal teams much earlier.

The company is continuing to expand its digital offerings, having launched a mobile learning app called KPMG Prism for finance professionals last week. The AI platform is designed to let auditors spend more of their time on direction, supervision, and review. By examining larger datasets, the system aims to provide a better experience for audit committees and management teams. The firm will continue the phased rollout of the technology to its global teams as planned.

stories.Headline: Marvell moves the HBM memory controller to a custom base die to free XPU compute area and cut interface power
stories.Summary:
Marvell has described a custom high-bandwidth memory layout that moves the memory controller off an accelerator's compute die and into a custom base die beneath each DRAM stack, as reported by NeoTeo on November 18, 2026. In the standard arrangement Marvell describes, the memory controller and the HBM interface sit on the XPU compute die, which is the accelerator's compute chip. In Marvell's custom layout, each DRAM stack sits above a base die that contains the controller, and a narrower die-to-die physical interface connects that base die to the XPU. The change shifts memory-control logic away from the XPU's edge and its compute area, and Marvell presents the design as a way to free compute area and lower interface power.

Marvell estimates that, compared with standard HBM, the architecture could provide up to 25% more compute area, room for up to 33% more HBM stacks and up to 70% lower memory-interface power, depending on the XPU design. The company says those figures describe potential design gains rather than a guaranteed increase in AI workload speed, because more compute area helps most when computation is the constraint. Marvell also describes adaptive power management for the die-to-die interface, which it says can reduce interface power by up to 75% under normal workloads and up to 42% at peak traffic compared with an interface without that feature. Those are separate comparisons from the broader estimate of up to 70% lower memory-interface power versus standard HBM.

Marvell identifies the die-to-die physical interface in the base die as the hottest spot and argues that the stack, base die, package and cooling need to be designed together. The company cites a Samsung thermal study of a 2.5D package in which internal thermal resistance accounted for 57% of the HBM stack's total and 13% of the adjacent ASIC's total, with those percentages referring to each component's total rather than to its temperature. For next-generation HBM running above 28 Gbps, Marvell expects heat flux to exceed 2.0 W/mm², and it discusses silicon heat paths near the interface, copper-to-copper hybrid bonding and coolant channels etched into silicon. Marvell relays a projection that internal temperatures in 16-high HBM stacks will exceed the thermal budget by 2028.

IBM Technology's Kaoutar El Maghraoui explains the memory wall, arithmetic intensity and the roofline model as general ways to understand why some workloads are limited by memory bandwidth rather than computing capacity. Arithmetic intensity measures floating-point operations per byte of memory accessed, and the roofline model uses it to distinguish work constrained by memory bandwidth from work constrained by compute. When data movement is the bottleneck, adding compute alone may not speed up the task, so the practical value of Marvell's potential bandwidth and power gains depends partly on what limits a given workload. The articles do not say when the custom HBM layout will reach products or which customers will adopt it.

stories.Headline: ECB vice president Boris Vujčić warns rapid AI expansion threatens financial stability
stories.Summary:
European Central Bank Vice President Boris Vujčić warned on Monday, November 16, 2026, that rapid artificial intelligence expansion could threaten financial stability. He spoke at Euro Finance Week in Frankfurt about how stretched stock market valuations for AI increase the risk of a repricing. Vujčić noted that a correction following America's mid-term elections serves as a reminder for the region to remain cautious. The bank also published research on November 18 regarding the stability implications of AI adoption in the real economy. This research found that reliance on a small number of AI providers could amplify risks across the entire financial system.

The research paper suggests that banks and asset managers use AI for portfolio management, fraud detection, and credit scoring. Eurostat data shows about 20 percent of European Union enterprises used AI in 2025, an increase of 6.5 percentage points. Adoption was higher in northern European countries than in the south and east, and higher in finance than in manufacturing. Anthropic's index on Claude.ai showed automation rose from 27 percent in January 2025 to 39 percent in August 2025. The ECB now requires better data on AI use, stronger oversight of providers, and changes to supervisory capabilities and safeguards.

Boris Vujčić stated that system-wide stability risks now stem from quickening AI adoption, concentration of exposures, and potential cyberattacks. He said that external funding is expanding from equity to debt markets, which adds to the current financial stability risks. Vujčić argued that it is critical to have a resilient banking sector while maintaining supervision over non-banks and private credit. He noted that private credit warrants close monitoring due to limited transparency, liquidity mismatches, and growing interconnectedness with insurers. The official believes that geopolitical headwinds further elevate the risks that the European Central Bank must currently manage.

The International Monetary Fund reported that AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery and exploitation across shared technologies to create correlated disruptions. This report suggests that AI cyber risk is now an enterprise governance issue for merchants, FinTechs, banks, and critical infrastructure operators. The IMF noted that the main question is how much autonomy systems should receive and if organizations can contain them. Other affected parties include companies in information technology and finance, which the ECB found have high exposure to AI risks. These institutions are vulnerable through their reliance on a concentrated group of cloud service providers and AI model providers.

The ECB research drew on emerging research, evidence from investment funds, and recent surveys of banks and various industries. The authors examined how financial firms are exposed to changes at other businesses that are adopting new AI technologies. US survey data indicated that professional services, finance, and information technology used AI more than the manufacturing sector did. The authors admitted that survey results were not directly comparable because the populations, questions, and definitions differed across sources. The research focused on how AI helps asset managers process information and how banks assess borrowers and detect activity.

The European Central Bank will continue monitoring the rapid growth of private credit and the concentration of AI model providers. Future efforts will focus on improving market safeguards to address emerging risks and increasing the oversight of critical AI providers. The articles leave open how exactly the ECB will implement these new supervisory capabilities to manage the identified systemic risks. They do not specify the exact timeline for the requested changes to data collection regarding AI use across the union. It remains unclear how the bank will balance AI autonomy with the need to contain systems when things fail.

stories.Headline: Penguin Solutions unveils photonics-based HBM-class memory appliance for agentic AI workloads
stories.Summary:
Penguin Solutions unveiled the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance on Monday, November 16, 2026, to help overcome GPU memory capacity constraints for agentic AI workloads. The company is showcasing this first photonics-based HBM-class memory appliance at the SC26 event located in Chicago. This new system uses silicon photonics to allow CPUs and GPUs to share memory at high bandwidth memory data rates. It includes the MemoryAI Photonic Memory Module, which is the first silicon photonics module designed to deliver HBM-class performance. The appliance is built upon the Marvell Photonic Fabric technology platform to support more efficient execution of agentic AI workloads.

The appliance targets 57.6 Tbps of total bandwidth and supports up to 16 TB of DDR5 RDIMM and 576 GB of HBM3E memory. It uses CXL 3.0 connectivity and Marvell photonic network interface cards to enable shared memory pools across AI infrastructure. Three access modes are offered, including HBM Direct Mode, HBM-DDR5 Cached Mode, and the DDR5 Direct Mode. The system is located meters from GPUs and uses silicon photonics to consume less power than traditional copper interconnects. It works with the MemoryAI KV Cache Server and SMART CXL add-in cards within the Penguin MemoryAI Platform Architecture.

Andy Mills, VP of Advanced Product Development at Penguin Solutions, stated that photonics is the step-function change needed to relieve stress. He explained that GPUs will have a direct way to access terabyte-class memory at scale instead of using slow networks. Preet Virk, senior vice president at Marvell, said integrating Photonic Fabric technology creates a path to high-capacity memory sharing. Virk noted that this approach is designed to improve accelerator utilization and increase the quality of tokens and throughput. Both executives believe these advancements are necessary for AI inference to scale with greater economic efficiency across multiple racks.

The technology affects customers running agentic AI workloads that require high-speed data access for essential token generation. These users often face data bottlenecks because localized ultra-fast HBM technology must sit within millimeters of the GPU. This physical limitation creates the growing AI memory wall, which leaves GPUs underutilized due to package size and silicon constraints. One commenter questioned if the system is simply memory with fast fiber NICs and expressed concerns about memory transparency. The appliance aims to reduce the need for a proportional increase in GPU resources when scaling inference workloads.

The articles note that HBM provides the high-speed access GPUs need, but its capacity is limited by silicon I/O constraints. Penguin Solutions previously introduced a CXL-enabled DDR4 module on November 12, 2026, to help address memory shortages in AI data centers. Other industry reports indicate that memory demand will outpace supply, with shortages potentially lasting through 2028 or even 2030. Dell's CEO stated on October 20, 2026, that the memory shortage will get worse in 2027. These background trends highlight the industry pressure to find scalable, tiered, and disaggregated memory solutions for production AI.

Penguin Solutions plans to begin sampling the MemoryAI Photonic Appliance to select customers in the second half of 2027. The system will allow applications to access appliance memory as if it were directly attached without specialized access routines. Management software will enable the static or dynamic allocation of memory to GPUs and CPUs based on specific workload requirements. The articles do not state the specific pricing for the appliance or the exact number of customers selected for sampling. It remains open how this technology will perform in real-world production environments compared to traditional GPU-attached HBM.

stories.Headline: Caleb Max warns that bad actors can weaponize AI tools despite no rogue AI armies
stories.Summary:
Caleb Max spoke to The National News Desk about artificial intelligence threats on November 18, 2026, in Washington. He addressed concerns regarding the possibility of rogue agents acting as their own armies to conduct terror attacks. Max stated that while rogue agents are not occurring, bad actors using AI tools are a real concern. He discussed these issues following a congressional hearing involving Representative Morgan Luttrell and Director of National Intelligence Clayton. The advocate warned that terrorist organizations could use AI technology to attack the American public or other targets.

Addressing these threats requires a partnership between leading tech companies, federal government agencies, and different agencies within Congress. Max referenced a Government Accountability Office report that tested four American AI platforms and found they could help malicious actors. He noted that these systems are currently easy to jailbreak, which makes it tough to fight bad actors. He contrasted these with open weight Chinese models that can be downloaded and run locally on a laptop. These Chinese models lack built in safeguards and are not connected to the internet, limiting tracking by authorities.

Caleb Max, the co-founder, president and CEO of the National Artificial Intelligence Association, said there is a misconception about AI armies. He argued that there is no one glove fits all solution to the problem of AI related threats. Max stated that the United States cannot retreat regulatory wise because enemies will continue to develop these tools. He described a dilemma where the country needs more AI to prevent against the use of bad AI. He emphasized that AI should augment and improve the decision making capability and speed of human beings.

Representative Morgan Luttrell asked about the possibility of an AI generated army that can be programmed to be a terrorist. The American public is affected by the risk of bad actors using AI to build and write plans. Air traffic controllers are mentioned as people who could be supported by AI to manage heavy flight volumes. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in September that the tools used at the FAA are very antiquated. Max noted that Elon Musk had posted months earlier about the possibility of a nationwide aviation ground stop.

The articles mention a protest on November 14, 2026, in San Francisco, California, outside of the OpenAI headquarters. Former OpenAI employee Daniel Kokotajlo spoke as protesters marched from the headquarters to Veterans Plaza to urge international negotiations. They wanted President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping to negotiate a treaty to ban or pause powerful AI systems. A nationwide ground stop occurred last week, which Max attributed to copper lines and cables not equipped for AI. He stated that the FAA has prioritized safety because aviation is an area where you cannot fail.

The government must develop the infrastructure and tech stack behind the tools to prevent future incidents from occurring. AI can help by processing large amounts of data quickly to support human decision making for air traffic controllers. Max believes using AI to support these controllers is a no brainer for most people in the country. The articles leave open how the U.S. will balance regulatory retreats with the need to stop enemy innovation. They do not state if President Trump and President Xi Jinping will negotiate the requested international AI treaty.

stories.Headline: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei launches IPO and vows AI systems stay under human control
stories.Summary:
Dario Amodei, the chief executive officer of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, launched an initial public offering on November 19, 2026. This significant financial move allows the organization to transition into a publicly traded entity on the open market. The timing of this event coincides with growing global discussions regarding the safety of advanced computing. Amodei used this specific occasion to address the future direction of the company.

The transition to a public company requires a shift in how the organization manages its internal governance and financial reporting. This process involves offering shares of the business to investors for the first time in its history. The move changes the company's status from a private firm to one that is accountable to public shareholders. Every detail of the initial public offering is designed to support the continued growth of their technology.

Dario Amodei is the person responsible for leading the company through this complex financial transition. He stated that he is committed to making sure that artificial intelligence systems remain under human control. This promise emphasizes the importance of safety and oversight as the technology becomes more powerful. He believes that maintaining human authority over these systems is essential for the safety of society.

The context of this announcement involves a broader industry trend of scaling artificial intelligence capabilities rapidly. The company is positioning itself as a responsible leader in a field that faces many ethical challenges. There is no further information provided regarding the specific steps the company will take after the offering. The public will likely monitor how the firm balances profit with its safety vows.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans IPO to raise over US$60 billion to fund data centre spending
stories.Summary:
The U.S. tech giant Anthropic launched its initial public offering on Thursday to address its massive spending commitments. The company behind the Claude AI model needs rapid growth to keep pace with its current financial obligations. It plans to lease its first Canadian artificial intelligence data centre during the next calendar year. This Wall Street debut has become the biggest of all time for any company in history. The firm currently lacks enough customers and revenues to cover its extensive infrastructure costs.

Anthropic is offering 980 million shares at US$83 each to raise expected proceeds of US$81 billion. The company is now valued at US$1.5 trillion and committed US$901 billion for data centres by 2045. It must spend US$70 billion by next September and signed a 20-year lease in Point Tupper, N.S. EverWind Fuels will build the 95-megawatt, 18,600-square metre site for $8 billion plus $2 billion for wind farms. Anthropic is also discussing a 920-megawatt project northeast of Edmonton that should operate by late 2027.

Anthropic warned investors that it may enter obligations based on revenue expectations that might not be realized. Laurel Munroe of EverWind said the private investment on private land puts risk on lenders, not Nova Scotians. She stated the 20-year lease is structured with significant credit protections to manage the financial risks involved. The company reported a net loss of US$104 billion, including a US$94 billion accounting adjustment for financing. However, revenue for the first nine months of the current fiscal year grew 13 times to US$33.2 billion.

Economics professor Joel Blit noted that US$900 billion is roughly equal to the entire sovereign debt of Canada. Randy Goebel of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute said the sector is building more capacity than it needs. He compared the current exorbitant valuations to the dot-com bubble that popped in the early 2000s. Tech consultant David Garrity noted that Nvidia lost almost 30 per cent of its value over the last month. Other affected firms seeing billions in value erased include Meta, CoreWeave, and Alphabet, the parent of Google.

York University researchers reported in June that 213 data centres were planned or under construction across Canada. These projects would draw 22.2 gigawatts of power, which is more than 14 times the existing Canadian capacity. Almost 80 per cent of these planned projects are located in the province of Alberta. AI firms including Meta and OpenAI are expected to spend US$700 million on data centres this year. This massive build-out occurs while AI chips and algorithms are becoming more efficient and driving down user costs.

The Cape Breton data centre is scheduled for completion toward the end of 2027. Markets historically tend to pull back in the weeks following U.S. midterm elections, according to David Garrity. He also noted that increasing interest rates and elevated oil prices create a different outlook for the sector. The articles leave open whether demand for AI services will grow enough to justify the unprecedented investment. It remains unclear if one company can sustain such potential debt or if new AI uses will emerge.

stories.Headline: J.S. Held Applies Multidisciplinary Expertise to Physical AI Claims and Disputes
stories.Summary:
J.S. Held announced on November 20, 2026, that it applies multidisciplinary expertise to Physical AI claims and disputes, according to a press release issued from New York. The firm said Physical AI moves artificial intelligence beyond digital outputs and into systems that sense, decide, control, or act in the physical world. Those systems include AI-enabled and autonomous vehicles, robotics, industrial equipment, building systems, medical technology, drones, and other technologies in which digital decisions can affect people, property, infrastructure, and business operations. The release said autonomous and AI-enabled systems are creating new investigative questions when digital decisions produce physical consequences. J.S. Held published the announcement through PR Newswire, and The Manila Times carried it on November 20, 2026.

J.S. Held said a Physical AI investigation may examine the complete system chain, from the data the system received and what its sensors perceived to what the AI decided and how software, controls, and equipment translated that decision into action. The firm said these matters do not necessarily require new investigative disciplines but require established disciplines to work across increasingly complex systems. J.S. Held said it is publishing two perspectives, one in Insurance Journal titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Stakes Change, and one to be published as Expert Analysis in Law360 titled When AI Leaves the Screen, the Evidence Changes: What In-House and Outside Counsel Should Do Before a Physical AI Incident. The firm said the Law360 piece discusses evidence ownership and preservation, system and software changes, sensor data, operating logs, telemetry, contractual responsibility, privilege, regulatory reporting, and coordination among technical and legal teams. J.S. Held said more than 1,500 professionals serve organizations across six continents, including 84% of the Global 200 Law Firms, 75% of the Forbes Top 20 Insurance Companies, 90% of the NAIC Top 50 Property & Casualty Insurers, and 71% of Fortune 100 Companies.

James E. Malackowski, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Intellectual Property Practice Lead, and co-lead of the AI Disputes practice at J.S. Held, said AI is moving from generating information to influencing and controlling physical systems. Malackowski said that when those systems are involved in an accident or loss, the investigation cannot stop with the algorithm. He said understanding what happened may require examining the data and sensors, controls and equipment, human interaction, and the resulting physical and economic consequences. He said Physical AI is where those disciplines increasingly converge. Stephen Fenton, PE, Executive Vice President and Accident Reconstruction Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said that when an AI-enabled or autonomous system is involved in an accident, investigators still have to reconstruct the physical event.

Fenton said reconstruction covers what happened in the moments leading to the incident, how the system or vehicle behaved, and how the available physical and digital evidence explains the outcome. He said the technology may change but rigorous reconstruction remains essential to determining how and why an event occurred, and his work includes forensic engineering, vehicle dynamics, photogrammetry, computer modeling, and vehicle and product testing. Scott Armstrong, Executive Vice President and Equipment Practice Lead at J.S. Held, said Physical AI incidents can create complex equipment and insurance questions after the cause of an event is established. Armstrong, who has more than 25 years of experience in equipment loss consulting involving high-technology equipment and systems, said a physical loss can raise questions about whether the problem was the equipment itself, the sensors or connected systems, the power supply or physical infrastructure, a manufacturing issue, or some combination of factors. He said separating those issues is important for insurers to understand the damage, determine what can be repaired or recovered, assess whether replacement is necessary, and evaluate the operational impact.

J.S. Held said its Physical AI perspective builds on its work involving artificial intelligence in industrial and operational environments. The firm said its experts examine AI implementation in the energy, manufacturing, and natural-resources sectors in Enterprise AI Implementation in Heavy Industry: A Digital Transformation Strategy for Sustainable Growth. Their analysis addresses data governance, digital architecture, analytics, system integration, and the organizational foundations required to deploy AI in complex operations. The publication includes a case study involving an AI readiness assessment for a major energy operator, which considered the digital, data, governance, and organizational foundations needed to support scalable AI implementation. J.S. Held said this experience is relevant to Physical AI because the reliability of an AI-enabled physical system may depend not only on an algorithm but also on the data architecture, connected systems, implementation decisions, operating environment, and human processes surrounding it.

Alastair Mckenzie-Kerr, PhD, Regional Director of Health, Safety & Human Factors, EMEA at J.S. Held, said the important transition is not simply that companies are adopting AI but that AI is being integrated into operational environments where people, equipment, and safety-critical processes already interact. Mckenzie-Kerr, whose work includes implementing AI-enabled EHS solutions and integrating human factors into design engineering and operational systems, said organizations need to understand not only whether the technology works as intended but how it performs within the broader operating system and how people respond to it. J.S. Held said it is publishing the two perspectives as part of its ongoing examination of Physical AI risk, addressing how organizations, insurers, and legal counsel can prepare for incidents involving AI-enabled and autonomous systems. The firm said the Insurance Journal article examines what organizations and insurers should consider when an AI-enabled system contributes to an accident, equipment failure, operational interruption, or other physical loss, and explains why engineering, digital, human factors, insurance, legal, and financial investigations may need to proceed together. J.S. Held said it is not a law firm and does not provide legal advice, and that its affiliates and subsidiaries are not certified public accounting firms and do not provide audit, attest, or other public accounting services.
