stories.Headline: Texas senator Sarah Eckhardt urges statewide AI safeguards for schools as lawmakers convene
stories.Summary:
Last year, Texas lawmakers required public schools to restrict students' use of cell phones throughout the school day, including between classes, according to a Nov 19, 2026 Houston Chronicle opinion piece by Kris Perry. Artificial intelligence is now moving into classrooms, homework assignments, school-issued computers and the software teachers use every day, Perry wrote. When the Legislature convenes in January, Texas has an opportunity to lead the country again, she wrote. A 2026 Stanford University review examined a research repository containing over 1,600 papers on AI in K-12 education, Perry wrote. Only 52 studies met its standards for strong causal evidence, few examined long-term learning outcomes, and only five of the high-quality studies of student AI use took place in American K-12 classrooms, she wrote.

Perry called for statewide standards for AI products used by students, with providers required to demonstrate evidence of educational effectiveness and safeguards for student privacy, data security and developmental well-being before schools adopt a tool. Schools should know what information is collected, how it is used and whether students' interactions are retained or used to train AI systems, she wrote. A law should require meaningful human oversight, with teachers remaining responsible for instruction, assessment and decisions affecting students, and AI should never independently determine a child's academic progress, disciplinary consequences or access to educational opportunities, she wrote. Students should not be required to engage in unrestricted, emotionally responsive conversations with AI systems as part of their education, she wrote. The Texas Education Agency could establish an independent review process, publish approved-use guidance and maintain a transparent list of evaluated products, and schools should have the right to disable unnecessary AI features without losing access to essential educational services, she wrote.

Perry, executive director of Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development, wrote that Google has made access to search on school-managed devices contingent on accepting AI features built into the search engine. That puts schools in the position of accepting AI features they may not want simply to preserve access to a basic educational resource, she wrote. She asked who should determine how children learn: their teachers and communities, or the companies supplying their software. She wrote that a small rural district and a large urban district may have different educational needs, but children in both deserve the same basic safeguards and access to high-quality resources. She wrote that none of this requires banning every use of AI.

Perry wrote that some early studies suggest students can perform better on assignments when AI is available, but when the technology is removed, evidence of lasting learning is mixed. She wrote that evidence shows general-purpose chatbots do not support learning as well as tools designed to align with core pedagogical theory and practice, supporting learning through guided reasoning rather than supplying answers. She wrote that early research suggests AI may help teachers reduce preparation time, but schools should evaluate whether those savings preserve instructional quality. She wrote that carefully designed tutoring systems that guide students through problems rather than simply supplying answers may also prove useful, with educators directing their use and evidence determining whether they belong in classrooms.

She wrote that AI cannot solve budget shortfalls, academic struggles and shortages of individual attention, and that effective education depends on relationships with teachers, meaningful interaction with classmates and opportunities to work through difficult material with support. Perry wrote that a 2026 letter to Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick from State Sen. and Comptroller-elect Sarah Eckhardt calls for examining AI literacy, student safety and statewide guidance. She wrote that the work should become enforceable protections, not simply another set of recommendations schools are left to interpret on their own.

She wrote that parents should ask their state representatives and senators to support legislation establishing independent AI product review, strong student-data protections, meaningful teacher oversight and the ability for schools to reject unwanted AI features. She wrote that local school boards should be required to disclose which AI tools students encounter and how those tools are evaluated. She wrote that with its school phone law, Texas showed that protecting children can be a bipartisan priority. Perry wrote that the question is not whether children should learn about artificial intelligence, because they should.

She wrote that the question is whether we will allow companies to determine how children experience it before parents, teachers and researchers have established what is safe and educationally sound. She wrote that Texas still has time to make that choice. She wrote that Texas faces a harder version of the same question it answered with its phone law. She wrote that the goal should be to establish clear statewide guardrails for the use of AI in schools before a piecemeal approach becomes so widespread that meaningful oversight is difficult.

stories.Headline: Cascella and colleagues review how AI supports Mendelian randomization in oncology
stories.Summary:
A narrative review published in Infectious Agents and Cancer on November 19, 2026, examined how artificial intelligence can be integrated into Mendelian randomization workflows to strengthen causal inference across genomics, epidemiology, and oncology. The authors were Cascella, Granata, Fusco, Simonetti, Porto, Di Monaco, Natangelo, Zarrella, Esposito, Pagano, De Feo, Donnarumma, and Santoriello, and the review was structured according to the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles, known as SANRA. To synthesize methodological developments, practical implementations, and emerging analytical frameworks, the authors conducted comprehensive literature searches across PubMed, Scopus, and the Web of Science. Mendelian randomization uses genetic variants as instrumental variables to assess whether observational associations between exposures and health outcomes reflect true causal relationships, and the review examined how machine learning, deep learning, and large language models can augment this analytical process across large-scale biomedical datasets.

The authors identified three operational tiers where artificial intelligence interfaces with the Mendelian randomization pipeline, namely before, within, and around the core analysis. Upstream of the causal calculation, artificial intelligence algorithms assist in phenotype construction, exposure discovery, and biological target prioritization, while within the analytical phase they support the prioritization of biologically informed instruments and facilitate nonlinear causal estimation. When deployed around the analytical pipeline, tools facilitate workflow automation, data retrieval, reporting, and evidence synthesis without modifying causal inference itself. In oncology, the review states that these emerging frameworks offer clear opportunities for biomarker discovery and therapeutic target prioritization, with promising approaches including Deep Mendelian Randomization, foundation models, and analytical agents based on large language models.

The authors emphasized that these algorithmic tools remain entirely dependent on standard instrumental-variable assumptions and that artificial intelligence operates across distinct stages without altering the core logic of causal deduction. They concluded that algorithmic power cannot substitute for biological plausibility, instrument validity, transparent methodology, or human oversight, and that causal inference continues to depend strictly on biological plausibility, instrument validity, and transparent analytical design. The review also concluded that these innovations require rigorous methodological validation, and it stated that future progress will rely on transparent, explainable, and human-supervised artificial intelligence frameworks that strictly adhere to established Mendelian randomization principles and robust methodological design. The stated objective of the review was to critically examine the emerging integration of artificial intelligence and Mendelian randomization, highlighting current applications, methodological opportunities, limitations, and future directions.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Mendelian Randomization Frameworks for Oncology Causal Inference

stories.headline_source: Artificial Intelligence Enhances Mendelian Randomization Frameworks for Oncology Causal Inference

stories.Headline: Researchers argue AI value in finance depends on organizational readiness and governance, not just computation
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a collection of studies in Information Systems Frontiers examining how artificial intelligence is reshaping information processing, data sharing and decision-making in financial services and related data-intensive industries. Editorial authors Konstantina Spanaki, Christos Floros, Ioannis Chatziantoniou, Constantin Zopounidis and Christos Lemonakis synthesized the contributions. The collection addresses both operational capabilities and structural risks. Algorithmic architectures are increasingly deployed for predictive analytics, forecasting, reporting, fraud detection and operational optimization. The editorial appeared on bioengineer.org on November 19, 2026.

The synthesis organizes the contributions across distinct analytical domains, beginning with algorithmic intelligence, market forecasting and organizational performance. Olson and colleagues evaluated the economic viability of fifteen machine learning models applied to technical analysis data for predicting the S&P 500 index over an extended historical period. Jha and coauthors applied the Technology Acceptance Model to survey data from finance professionals. De Lange and colleagues demonstrated that spline-rule ensembles achieve competitive predictive performance while preserving interpretable rule structures for credit scoring. Ioannou and coauthors ran an experimental investigation of user adoption of automated recommendations.

The editorial authors emphasize that analytical efficiency alone cannot serve as the sole criterion for evaluating intelligent systems. They argue that technical execution must be examined alongside organizational structures, regulatory compliance and ethical oversight mechanisms. They state that artificial intelligence value creation remains contingent upon organizational readiness, leadership, user acceptance and institutional context rather than computational sophistication in isolation. They call for explainability and transparency to operate as baseline system components that reinforce institutional legitimacy across stakeholder groups including regulators, consumers and risk managers. They urge that proactive governance frameworks embed privacy controls, data minimization and audit mechanisms directly into software architectures.

Chatterjee and colleagues investigated structural and ethical factors governing generative artificial intelligence for healthcare data sharing in financial contexts using adaptive structuration theory. Lioliou and coauthors empirically analyzed risk disclosures published by publicly listed financial institutions. Oikonomidis and colleagues analyzed dynamic residential electricity pricing and proposed regulatory architectures that audit pricing algorithms and minimize sensitive consumer consumption disclosures. Fagbola and colleagues applied topic modeling and sentiment analysis to social media discussions on platform X surrounding the non-fungible token market crash. Bawack and coauthors conducted a bibliometric investigation mapping scholarship at the intersection of artificial intelligence, accounting and sustainable finance.

The editorial anchors its synthesis in established information systems scholarship, emphasizing that artificial intelligence cannot be treated as an isolated technological artifact. The authors highlight how automated decision tools depend on aligned organizational practices, technological infrastructures and institutional environments. Earlier investigations into financial technology adoption demonstrated that managerial capabilities and organizational readiness frequently determine the success or failure of digital initiatives. The scope of inquiry extends beyond conventional financial trading floors to commercial banking, managerial accounting, credit scoring, organizational risk governance, healthcare data collaboration, dynamic energy pricing and supply chain management. Methodological approaches encompass machine learning modeling, econometric analysis, multi-criteria decision-making, controlled experimental designs, survey-based modeling, bibliometric mapping and design-oriented conceptual frameworks.

The authors outline research agendas addressing accountable systems, agentic architectures and cross-organizational data ecosystems. They state that future investigations must establish how explanations translate into actionable accountability, enabling affected parties to audit or challenge automated outcomes. They urge rigorous examination of privacy-preserving methods including federated analytics and explainable access controls. They call for expanded investigation into systemic financial resilience and methodological pluralism, warning that homogeneous algorithmic models and shared financial datasets introduce potential model concentration risks. They recommend combining computational modeling with field experiments, longitudinal tracking and design science research to help practitioners and policymakers balance technological innovation against ethical responsibility and market stability.

Articles.Title: Researchers Examine Artificial Intelligence Applications and Governance Challenges Across Financial Systems

stories.Headline: Anthropic raises 81 billion dollars in record breaking Nasdaq IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic became one of the most valuable public companies in the world on Thursday. The artificial intelligence company launched a first of its kind initial public offering. This stock market debut occurred on the Nasdaq exchange on November 19, 2026. The company is the maker of the popular AI chatbot known as Claude. It completed one of the fastest trips from start up to IPO in history.

Shares began trading at an allocation price of 83 dollars each for the company. The stock price rose immediately to 111.53 dollars, taking the market value to almost 2 trillion dollars. Shares closed the day at 97.17 dollars, leaving the valuation at roughly 1.76 trillion dollars. The company raised 81 billion dollars during this record breaking debut on the Nasdaq. This event took place while President Donald Trump attended a summit in China.

President Daniela Amodei stated that the company had an AI safety team before launching its first product. She also noted that artificial intelligence carries real risks for the world. Co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei has expressed fears that future AI tools could outsmart humans. He suggested that such a scenario could potentially lead to human extinction. The company has always presented itself as one that takes technology safety very seriously.

Investors said the debut was a success because shares rose roughly 17 percent during the day. However, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3 percent on Thursday. Alphabet fell by 2.9 percent, and Amazon lost almost 3.9 percent during the same period. Strategist Neil Wilson said there is no obvious peer to compare the company to. Research leader Ben Barringer warned that the initial exuberance of investors will eventually wear off.

The company started five years ago during an era of expensive technology buildouts. Major tech companies spent more than 1 trillion dollars in the last year alone. Powerful computers now allow the processing of more data than ever before. This progress enables chatbots to simulate human speech and perform tasks like software coding. Economist Richard Whittle noted that financial bubbles usually burst later if the future becomes suspect.

The House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus formed on Thursday to work on regulation. President Trump spoke against any form of robust regulation during his summit with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. Democrats may seek to ensure AI tools have guardrails when they gain more power in 2027. Future stock prices will likely see significant swings as the company reports its first quarterly results. It remains open whether the massive investment in AI technology is actually worth the cost.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop explainable AI models to identify thrombectomy candidates before hospital arrival
stories.Summary:
A retrospective development and internal validation study published on 19 November 2026 in Scientific Reports, volume 16, article number 38698, used explainable artificial intelligence to identify endovascular thrombectomy candidates before hospital arrival. The study was based on digital real-world data from consecutive EMS-transported patients with suspected stroke in the Stroke Angel initiative in Rhön-Grabfeld, a rural region in Germany. The data covered the period from January 2015 to June 2021 and comprised 1,435 patients, among whom there were 94 EVT events, or 6.6%. The authors developed and internally validated machine learning models estimating the likelihood that a patient would undergo EVT during the acute hospital admission, using prehospital and early in-hospital real-world data. Predicted probabilities of six machine learning models were recalibrated using Platt scaling, and clinical relevance was evaluated using decision curve analysis.

The final cohort was randomly partitioned into a training set of 918 patients, a validation set of 230 and a test set of 287. Among included patients, 94, or 6.6%, underwent EVT and 356, or 24.8%, received intravenous thrombolysis. With 1,148 patients and 70 EVT events, the cohort fell short of the calculated target, increasing the risk of overfitting, so hyperparameters were tuned to constrain model flexibility toward simpler architectures. In the evaluation cohort of 287 patients with 24 EVT events, Random Forest achieved the highest AUROC of 0.85, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.78 to 0.90, sensitivity of 0.92 (0.74 to 0.99) and specificity of 0.66 (0.60 to 0.72). The 4I-SS, at a score above 2, yielded an AUROC of 0.82 (0.72 to 0.89), sensitivity of 0.87 (0.67 to 0.96) and specificity of 0.69 (0.64 to 0.74).

The study's primary objective was to develop and internally validate machine learning models estimating the likelihood of EVT during acute hospital admission from prehospital and early in-hospital real-world data. The secondary objective was to assess the calibration of predicted probabilities and to evaluate the impact of classification thresholds on prehospital triage decisions, particularly the balance between over- and undertriage. The models were embedded within an explainable artificial intelligence framework to enable interpretation of model outputs and decision logic. The study was designed as a proof of concept for data-driven prehospital EVT triage and aimed to explore the potential clinical utility of an explainable decision-support approach. SHapley Additive exPlanations values were computed to quantify individual feature contributions to model predictions.

Bootstrapped intervals overlapped across all metrics and Platt scaling probabilities, suggesting no statistically significant superiority. Precision-recall analysis yielded uniformly low AUCPR values across classifiers, consistent with the low EVT prevalence of 6.6%, and Random Forest and the neural network achieved the highest AUCPR at 0.32 and 0.34, with confidence intervals of 0.19 to 0.51 and 0.17 to 0.50. Using a predefined threshold of 0.25, ensemble models demonstrated comparatively stable sensitivity-specificity profiles across cross-validation folds, whereas simpler classifiers showed substantial fold-wise sensitivity variance. Across nested cross-validation folds, the 4I-SS showed the lowest standard deviation of 0.033, and among machine learning classifiers Random Forest and XGBoost exhibited relatively low variability, while CART, kNN, Neural Network and OneR showed higher standard deviations. Sensitivity ranged from 0.75 to 0.92 and specificity from 0.63 to 0.77, and the 4I-SS showed comparable performance with an AUROC of 0.82 (0.72 to 0.89), F1 of 0.69 and Brier score of 0.069.

The articles state that stroke ranks as the second leading cause of death worldwide and that EVT is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke with large-vessel occlusion. In many stroke systems, stroke assessment does not commence until after hospital arrival, which slows down treatment, and delays could be avoided if EMS teams recognized large-vessel occlusion and its severity on scene. Since only a minority of suspected stroke cases ultimately harbour a proximal large-vessel occlusion, routing all patients directly to a comprehensive stroke centre may not always be practical or necessary. Severity-based triage strategies commonly use a National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale threshold of 7 or more to increase the efficiency of patient selection for advanced imaging and endovascular pathways. Conventional prehospital scales have been designed to detect large-vessel occlusion yet neglect the broader determinants of EVT, and prehospital stroke scales have not achieved an optimal balance of sensitivity, specificity and predictive value.

A total of 3,628 records from Database A, the prehospital database, and 5,975 records from Database B, the hospital database, were extracted. After excluding records without valid timestamps, non-EMS missions and records outside the study period, 3,659 hospital EMS admissions remained, and of the linked candidate pairs, 2,195 records were excluded because they failed the eligibility check of a timestamp discrepancy of more than 60 minutes or an age difference of more than one year. Record linkage identified 1,464 matched records, and 29 duplicate index entries were removed, yielding 1,435 unique linked patients comprising the preprocessed data set. Transport mode and admission pathway inclusion criteria were applied prior to linkage to ensure cohort comparability. The articles state that collecting structured prehospital data and reliably linking them to hospital-based outcome measures is challenging due to heterogeneous documentation workflows and limited interoperability across emergency and hospital information systems.

The articles state that machine learning approaches integrating multimodal prehospital and hospital data have the potential to refine prehospital stroke triage, reduce transfers and increase the likelihood that patients who stand to benefit from EVT reach comprehensive stroke centres faster. They state that these predictions may support prehospital decision-making and better inform paramedics or emergency physicians, and that although real-world data has been identified as a potential source of machine learning model development, its utilisation in this field remains scarce. The articles state that hospitals without EVT capability must expeditiously transfer such patients to the nearest comprehensive stroke centre with EVT capacity, ideally while thrombolysis continues, in a drip-and-ship approach. They state that the avoidance of treatment delays necessitates formalized agreements and predefined protocols between the referring hospital, the designated EVT centre and the EMS. The articles leave open how the models would perform in prospective or external settings, and they report no statistically significant superiority of machine learning over the 4I-SS.

Articles.Title: Explainable artificial intelligence for prehospital identification of endovascular thrombectomy candidates: a retrospective real-world study

stories.Headline: Anthropic discounts new AI products to attract customers and compete with rivals
stories.Summary:
Anthropic began offering various discounts to its customers on November 19, 2026, to help the company gain ground with its newest artificial intelligence products. The company is attempting to expand its reach into new applications for its tools while facing stiff competition from established rivals. This strategic move comes as many businesses seek lower cost alternatives after experiencing a significant spike in their overall AI spending. The company is specifically trying to match the rapid growth of its Claude Code tool with several other new offerings.

These incentives include providing credits of up to 2,000 dollars per user to encourage companies to test the latest products. Anthropic has offered large customers discounts that exceed 30 percent and deals for those who prove a specific percentage of their budget goes to the firm. These efforts support the launch of Claude Cowork for non-technical users, Claude Managed Agents, and tools for cybersecurity and financial services. The company is competing against entrenched products from Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and various tools developed by OpenAI.

The report regarding these pricing strategies was published by The Information and cited several sources, some of whom remained anonymous. Anthropic did not immediately provide a comment to PYMNTS when the news about these specific customer discounts was reported. Previously, the company noted that its Claude Haiku 5.5 model cost about 75 percent less on average than the older Claude Haiku 4.5. This follows a broader trend where companies like Figma, Amazon, and Microsoft offered discounts as customers became more selective about their purchases.

Many software companies are now turning toward open source AI models, including those from China, to avoid the high costs of proprietary U.S. developers. Customers have expressed dissatisfaction with the shift toward charging for AI based on the number of tasks finished or general usage. This environment has forced developers to lower prices as model choices multiply and the cost of AI answers continues to drop. The industry is currently seeing a shift where users are more cautious about how they allocate their limited technology budgets.

Articles.Title: Anthropic Offers Discounts to Gain Ground With New Products

stories.headline_source: Anthropic Offers Discounts to Gain Ground With New Products

stories.Headline: Tesorai raises $5.3 million in seed funding to expand its AI proteomics platform
stories.Summary:
Tesorai, founded in 2024 by three former Verily colleagues, announced this week that it had raised $5.3 million in fresh seed funding, bringing its total funding to $8 million. The company's CEO is Melissa Miao, its CTO is Peter Cimermancic, PhD, and its CSO is Charlie Kim, PhD. Before founding Tesorai, Miao led business initiatives and strategic partnerships at Verily, Alphabet's life science company. Cimermancic led artificial intelligence teams at Verily, and Kim launched and led Verily's molecular science program. The announcement was reported by Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News on November 19, 2026.

Investors in the current round include Perplexity Fund, IQT, South Central Ventures, New Stack Ventures, NextGen Venture Partners, f7 Ventures, VitalStage Ventures, and ZAKA. Tesorai says it has signed contracts with both biopharmaceutical and research organizations, and its named collaborators include teams at MD Anderson Cancer Center, New York University, and the Michael J. Fox Foundation. The company plans to use the new funds to expand its work with biopharmaceutical and research customers, grow partnerships across the life sciences, and extend its platform beyond proteomics to other kinds of molecular data. Tesorai plans to take on transcriptomics data next and eventually genomics data as well. Tesorai received the first patent for its platform last year.

Miao told GEN that while at Verily the founders recognized opportunities to use advanced AI to maximize signal extraction from massive laboratory datasets, particularly in mass spectrometry-based proteomics. She said, "That's what inspired us to leave and build our own team specifically focused on building AI models to maximize the insights that you could extract from those data sets." Miao said the company sees applications across all or most drug development stages, spanning target discovery to biomarker discovery down to more development stages, and that it is currently expanding into the agrolife sciences space. She said more and more data is being generated in large part because instruments are getting more advanced, and that software wasn't keeping up, which is why the company started building its proprietary AI model. Miao said Tesorai operates a token system where customers pay for what they use, a model she described as more accessible than traditional annual licensing, and that the company is looking to be more generous with free credits for academic research teams.

Kim said that focusing on proteomics made sense given growing interest in these studies and several technological advances in recent years, and that "we can finally see the whole proteome in the way that genomics was able to 20 years ago." He said mass spectrometry data is very challenging to analyze and there are a lot of opportunities for AI to help, and that the company is excited about integrative analysis, being able to combine different layers of biological data to assemble a mechanistic understanding. Kim said Tesorai is part of an ecosystem of efforts trying to dramatically accelerate the pace of life science research, making every step bigger by getting more information out of every sample and faster through engineering, ability to process massive volumes of data quickly, and an agentic interface for executing analysis in natural language. Cimermancic noted that most tools available today only query and mine the condensed and reduced datasets available in the scientific literature, while with Trove scientists can mine raw data directly. Cimermancic explained that instead of training models on the fly, which can lead to overfitting and inaccuracies, Tesorai pre-trains its model on data from public repositories and other sources so it generalizes across experimental conditions and instrument types.

Tesorai's platform is anchored by a proprietary AI model built to analyze proteomics datasets, and its components include Tesorai Search, a deep-learning engine described in a Journal of Molecular Biology paper. According to the company, the engine reads full spectra, enabling it to find more peptides, and its model works out most of the 20 to 40 settings adopted by standard analysis tools. In the paper, the authors report that Tesorai Search consistently identifies more unique peptides compared to established search engines like MaxQuant, FragPipe (+MSBooster), PEAKS, and Proteome Discoverer, with average increases of 12 to 68%, and shows strong performance even on data not encountered during training. The platform also includes Tesorai Trove, which catalogs curated public proteomics datasets from human tissue and structures studies' metadata into searchable tables usable by humans and AI models, and Tesorai Chat, which runs quality checks, statistics, and charts using conversational prompts. On a 94-case proteomics benchmark, Tesorai Chat reached over 92% accuracy ahead of tools like Phylo and GPT-5.4, among others.

Kim pointed to a recent application of Tesorai's platform in Alzheimer's disease, where the team used it to test a newly published Alzheimer's blood panel against data from five existing brain studies. The multiprotein plasma panel, which could be a tool for distinguishing between early- and late-stage Alzheimer's, is described in a JAMA Neurology paper published this year. Details of Tesorai's work are published in a bioRxiv preprint titled "Rapid Mechanistic Bridging of an Alzheimer's Disease Plasma Protein Staging Panel Across Brain Proteomics Cohorts," posted in September. An initial read of the five datasets showed they appeared to be missing p-tau217, a well-established plasma biomarker for assessing amyloid-beta pathology in people at risk of developing Alzheimer's, and because phosphorylated tau 217 (p-tau217) and amyloid beta 1-40 (Aβ40) were not reported for any studies, raw spectra were reprocessed to quantify these proteoforms. As it turned out, p-tau217 was present in four of the five original datasets but had not been reported in the original protein summaries, and there was evidence across the cohorts that the plasma-derived biomarker panel could distinguish early from late-stage Alzheimer's disease, which was also true for other proteins analyzed in the study.

Tesorai completed the Alzheimer's analysis in three weeks without having to perform a new study, and Kim said the analysis provided a mechanistic explanation for why these proteins were changing in the blood in association with Alzheimer's disease severity. Kim said there are likely other instances where the original intent of the study authors wasn't necessarily to ask this kind of question, but the questions can be answered because the information is in the data, and that combining multiple data sets in this way can bring major accelerations in being able to validate and answer questions like this. Tesorai's AI models process raw mass spectrometry data from labs' new experiments, public repositories, and company archives. Trained models are validated in different ways, for example if models are only trained on data from one manufacturer's instruments, their performance is validated using instruments from other manufacturers, and the company's academic partners have designed ways to experimentally evaluate its models, for example using the AI to detect single gene knockouts in cell lines. Miao said the company has been able to show that it can increase the number of peptide and protein identifications as well as how the platform improves accuracy, and that because it is so scalable the company has been able to reprocess massive repositories of data.

stories.Headline: Pima County sheriff warns AI scams rise as holidays approach
stories.Summary:
Scammers are using artificial intelligence to make their schemes more convincing, and local authorities in Arizona are urging people to stay alert as the holidays approach, according to 13 News in Tucson. The Pima County Sheriff's Department says scammers use social media to find potential victims and AI to create fake identities, and voice cloning can make an impostor sound like a family member supposedly facing an emergency. Other schemes can involve fake lottery winnings, overpayments, business impersonation, romantic interests and demands to buy gold, and scammers can disguise their phone numbers to make them appear local. One of the biggest warning signs is urgency, where a caller or message pressures someone to act immediately without taking time to verify the request. According to the FBI, Arizona ranked seventh in the nation for scam complaints in 2025, with reported losses of $631 million, and the top three categories involved investments, tech support and confidence or romance scams.

Arizona ranked fourth for complaints from people over 60, and in Pima County the sheriff's department says 27.7% of victims were over 60, nearly 4 percentage points above the national rate. The department says younger people reported losing money to fraud more often than older people in 2025, but older victims may have more assets for scammers to target. Authorities say warning signs include being pressured to keep a transaction secret, drain an account or buy cryptocurrency or gold, and scammers may try to isolate a victim from people they trust. Tyler Rivas, a detective with the Pima County Sheriff's Department's fraud unit, said Southern Arizona is a hotbed for scams, especially for the older generation that comes for the weather, and that scammers know to target the increase in seasonal residents. FBI Supervisory Special Agent Gregory Clark said scammers may call and pretend to be a person's bank, claiming there are suspicious purchases on the account, then use information the person provides to carry out a scam.

The FBI advises people to take a beat before responding, and authorities recommend verifying independently by hanging up and calling the organization using a number you find yourself, such as the number on your bank card. They also suggest talking to someone you trust before sending money, screening calls, protecting personal information, monitoring accounts and being careful with checks, which the sheriff's department says can be stolen, altered or reprinted. The FBI will not demand payment or personal information through an unsolicited call, text or email, and anyone who suspects a scam can call the Pima County Sheriff's Department fraud unit at 520-351-3000 even if they are unsure whether fraud occurred. People can also contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI or through its official contact page, and authorities encourage victims to come forward even if they feel embarrassed. If you have sent money, report it promptly, because law enforcement may be able to help you try to recover lost funds, although recovery is not guaranteed and the sheriff's department says it can be harder to retrieve money sent outside the country.

Articles.Title: Local authorities warn of AI-powered scams ahead of the holidays

stories.Headline: Gold Mountain California News asks whether businesses are protected as AI enters them
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already in your business, but the question is whether your business is protected, according to an article published by Gold Mountain California News on November 19, 2026. The article asks the question directly in its headline and does not name any company, agency or person who took a specific action. It gives no date for any event beyond the publication date of the piece itself. No details are provided about what prompted the question or what incident, if any, lies behind it.

The article as published does not state what the presence of artificial intelligence in a business requires or changes. It gives no numbers, no dates beyond the publication date and no names of people or organizations involved. No rules, deadlines or requirements are described in the text. The piece offers no account of what a business must do to be protected.

The article does not identify who is responsible for protecting a business that uses artificial intelligence. It contains no statements from officials, experts or business representatives that could be paraphrased. No one is named as having said anything about the topic. The text provides no explanation of the roles of owners, regulators or technology providers.

The article gives no context about the state of artificial intelligence in business and no information about what happens next. It does not say whether further reporting, guidance or action is expected. Nothing in the text describes consequences for businesses that are not protected. The piece consists of the headline question and the surrounding page elements of the news site.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Antropics closes 17 percent above IPO price in Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Antropics, an artificial intelligence developer, made its stock market debut on Nasdaq on the 19th and closed its first day at 97.17 dollars, which was 17 percent above its initial public offering price. The listing gave the company a successful first session, and the closing bell was rung at the Nasdaq market site by Chief Commercial Officer Paul Smith, Krishna Rao and Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman together with customers. The debut came as the company faced large payment obligations, including 70.7 billion dollars due by September next year, which equals 53 percent of its current liquidity. Compute contract obligations running for three years from October next year to the end of 2030 add a further 380.9 billion dollars. Shin Seung-yoon, a researcher at Hanwha Investment & Securities, said in a report on the 20th that the listing succeeded but that conditions are not good compared with past listings of large and AI companies.

He said the initial distribution volume was small and that the release of lock-up volume is heavier than when SpaceX was listed, with 313 million strategic partner shares carrying no lock-up at all. The lock-up of general holders could be lifted early before mid-May next year, and up to 10 percent of employees' holdings will be released on the first day, so the real distribution ratio could rise from 5.4 percent to 8 percent. He also noted that Antropics' price-to-sales ratio, based on the previous 12 months' sales of 35.3 billion dollars, is 43 times, far above the peer group median of 11.2 times. Researcher Shin said sales would need to expand to between 135 billion and 176 billion dollars in 2027 for the ratio to match other big tech levels, while annual recurring sales stood at 81 billion dollars at the end of October, giving a ratio of 18.5 times. That figure is 13 times higher than NVIDIA's trailing ratio of 7.7 times and above Alphabet's 13 times, and he said the sustainability of growth and profitability to justify the corporate value has not yet been demonstrated.

He pointed to inclusion in the Nasdaq 100 as a notable event, since a company entering the top 40 by market capitalization after listing on Nasdaq is added after 15 trading days regardless of regular changes. Passive ETFs and index funds tracking the index would then be required to buy the stock mechanically, which could push the price up regardless of fundamentals. Among 16 past large and AI-themed listings, the median first-day rise over the offering price was 26.5 percent, but the gain weakened to a fall of 8.8 percent over the six-month lock-up expiration period, according to the report. Researcher Shin said Antropics carries a lower valuation burden than SpaceX but faces a disadvantageous market environment and initial sales structure. He said the company is expected to face more downward pressure from earnings and lock-up events after fluctuating from an initial surge and realizing profits immediately after its index inclusion in December.

stories.Headline: Researchers find a simple logistic regression model predicts neonatal pulmonary hemorrhage outcomes
stories.Summary:
A retrospective case, control study published in BMC Pediatrics evaluated two artificial intelligence approaches to neonatal pulmonary hemorrhage, a life-threatening complication with substantial morbidity and mortality. The investigation was conducted at a single medical center and analyzed 101 hospitalized neonates, comprising 50 infants diagnosed with pulmonary hemorrhage and 51 control subjects. Across the entire study cohort, 42 infants died during their hospitalization. The researchers selected control infants based on broad similarity in gestational age and birth weight relative to the hemorrhage cases. They did not employ formal statistical matching or predefined tolerance bands during subject selection.

The team retained an independent held-out test set of 26 neonates for an exploratory internal assessment of predictive discrimination. A prespecified, parsimonious logistic regression model incorporated pulmonary hemorrhage status, gestational age, and birth weight. This primary model achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.80, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.70 to 0.88. On the held-out test cohort of 26 patients, the model attained an area under the curve of 0.86, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.67 to 1.00, demonstrating 73 percent sensitivity and 73 percent specificity. The imaging dataset consisted of 204 chest radiographs, divided equally with 102 from the pulmonary hemorrhage group and 102 from control neonates.

The study authors emphasized key limitations and interpretive boundaries regarding their findings. They clarified that the clinical and imaging workflows remained entirely separate, as no unified model integrating clinical variables and chest radiographs was evaluated. The investigators noted that radiographic classification on retrospective pre-event scans does not establish a prospective diagnostic tool or confirmed predictive utility for clinical practice. The researchers observed no empirical evidence indicating that more complex machine-learning algorithms outperformed the parsimonious logistic regression formulation. For the hemorrhage cohort, radiographs were acquired within the 48 hours immediately preceding clinically recognized pulmonary bleeding.

Control radiographs were collected at corresponding postnatal chronological ages. An audit revealed that non-anatomical image properties alone distinguished radiograph groups with an initial area under the curve of 1.00. To mitigate this acquisition-related bias, the team implemented comprehensive image harmonization. Following harmonization, negative-control classification performance dropped to near-chance levels, exhibiting areas under the curve ranging between 0.44 and 0.59. On the harmonized pre-event radiographs, a prespecified final-analysis ensemble achieved a patient-level area under the curve of 0.78, with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.68 to 0.87.

Concurrently, the ConvNeXt-Tiny architecture attained a repeat-averaged area under the curve of 0.80, with a 95 percent confidence interval between 0.70 and 0.88, demonstrating moderate discrimination. The article was authored by Ercan, S., Okbay Güneş, A., Yağanoğlu, M., Yıldırım, İ., Kılıç, M., İşleyen, F., and Aslan, H. in 2026. The DOI is 10.1186/s12887-026-08011-x. The subject of the research was artificial intelligence models for mortality classification and pre-event chest radiograph evaluation in neonatal pulmonary hemorrhage. The news source was Harold Sullivan, writing on November 19, 2026.

Jacob Andreas, a newly tenured associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science at MIT and a member of CSAIL, develops techniques enabling AI models to communicate accurately about what they learned from training data. He said that rather than needing external tools to understand what is going on under the hood, maybe models can be trained to talk about themselves accurately. He and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. He said we used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters, but now we need mind-reading tools that can translate complicated neural computation. Andreas grew up in the San Francisco Bay Area and was a voracious reader as a child.

stories.Headline: California governor-elect Becerra says he is open to prosecuting AI companies over rogue models
stories.Summary:
Xavier Becerra, the governor-elect of California, said on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that he is open to criminally prosecuting artificial intelligence companies for the rogue activity of their models. He made the remark during a conversation with Megan Messerly at the POLITICO Pub at the New Governors Leadership Forum in Utah. Becerra said that if the incursions seen by AI agents had been done by human beings, criminal charges would have been filed against those individuals. He said that because it is a machine does not mean you should not also have the ability to prosecute when malfeasance is done. AI regulation was a key topic of discussion during the conversation.

Becerra embraced a set of stringent safeguards proposed on Wednesday by Gov. Gavin Newsom, including a proposal to give the state authority to shut down dangerous models. Becerra said on Thursday that he hoped to move swiftly when he takes office in January and downplayed the need for a dedicated special session. He said the report by the governor and his team gives a nice blueprint to work off of and then to build from there. He said he hopes there are legislators who want to move and do the right thing right away. Becerra said he is not overly concerned about the mechanics of working with a historically large caucus of 68 Democrats in the Assembly.

Becerra emphasized the importance of making partnerships and said that if you start early you will know who your partners are. He said that if you start late you will find yourself possibly working against people you thought you would be with. He said he is doubtful about big disagreements, even with Republicans, though pace could be a point of conflict among Democrats. Becerra said he does not expect so much resistance to trying to lower the cost of housing, make health care more affordable, or undo some of the Trump devastating cuts to health care. He said he is hoping California and Texas can work together, calling it a massive one-two punch.

Becerra said that as California’s attorney general, many of the cases that came against the state came from Texas, and that as secretary at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, many of the challenges to expanding health care came from Texas. He said voters have now painted Texas blue and that he is very much looking forward to forging an alliance, saying he intended to reach out to Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa. Becerra emphasized housing construction as his top affordability priority during his first 100 days in office. He said the state has more than 40,000 housing units that have the necessary permits but are lacking funding. He said the $11.25 billion affordable housing bond California voters recently approved should help move the process along.

Becerra said the state will continue to increase the ability to get things permitted faster and will work closer with local governments so that they are not standing in the way of good projects. He said the state will make sure that no community can deprive Californians of the housing they need because they may get in the way. He said housing is a California statewide issue, not just a local issue. Anthropic’s initial public offering today, the largest of all time, will only make it more of a political target, and the Dario Amodei-led AI lab is expected to disrupt and dominate the U.S. economy for the foreseeable future. Oren Cass, founder of the right-leaning populist think tank American Compass, told POLITICO on the sidelines of a Hewlett Foundation conference in Sausalito this week that the valuations we are seeing are essentially predicting broken markets and bad regulation.

Cass said in his view that Anthropic’s valuation, and that of other AI companies, reflects a belief that Congress, state policymakers and the assorted thinkers who gather at places like Hewlett will be ineffectual in offsetting technological upheaval. He said providing opportunities for the public to get a stake through the equity markets, or alternatively through public ownership, does not negate the fact that people want a measure of control over their destiny. He said there is a blaring market signal that people expect these AI labs to capture enormous rents in perpetuity. He said we should not be a country where large companies are capturing enormous rents in perpetuity. The Justice Department is dispatching Bill Essayli to Florida to work on a criminal investigation into the 2022 raid on Mar-a-Lago and special counsel Jack Smith’s inquiry into the classified documents found there, according to three people familiar with the matter.

Essayli will continue to oversee the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California as the first assistant U.S. attorney there, the officials said. A judge has ruled that the administration’s installation of Essayli as the leader of the Los Angeles-based prosecutor’s office is unlawful, but the ruling is on hold pending an appeal. The new mission for Essayli is part of a broad investigation that the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida was conducting into a so-called grand conspiracy of former officials and others who allegedly sought to undermine President Donald Trump during and after his first term in office. House Democrats filled out their leadership team today, elevating a diverse slate of lawmakers to run the caucus next term, and Reps.

Sydney Kamlager-Dove of California, Maxwell Frost of Florida and Sarah McBride of Delaware won the only contested slots to be co-chairs of the DPCC. Kamlager-Dove, Frost and McBride received 195, 238 and 180 votes respectively, leaving out a fourth candidate, Rep. Eric Sorensen of Illinois, according to a person with knowledge granted anonymity to share the private tally. Kamlager-Dove said in an interview after the vote that their messaging was united and unifying and that is what got them the majority. She said people want a continuation of that and that she is hopeful she will be able to help push for greater tools, greater access and the ability to truly connect with the American people.

Legal experts say soon-to-be House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia and others who have pledged to investigate the Trump administration should ignore letters from a federal prosecutor suggesting they could face criminal charges. The cryptocurrency industry is trying to mend fences with Democrats after their expensive midterm attacks on Ohio Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown. Five UC campuses will receive new military-grade policing equipment, some of which UCLA says is needed to prepare for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. The Oakland Coliseum is preparing to close as a sports venue after six decades in operation.

Former Sacramento City Councilmember Sean Loloee will serve 46 months in federal prison for committing financial fraud at his grocery stores. The Orange County Board of Supervisors won’t induct John Wayne into the county’s hall of fame due to racist remarks the actor made. Becerra said he hoped to move swiftly when he takes office in January, and the articles do not say what specific legislation or prosecution he would pursue. More to follow.

stories.Headline: FDA drafts policies to evaluate generative AI in healthcare as it does physicians
stories.Summary:
A USA Today article reported that the median annual price of a newly approved prescription drug now stands at more than $250,000, a sixfold increase over the past 18 years, and that the Inflation Reduction Act has had little impact on rising prices despite Medicare being empowered to negotiate them. Costs for drugs treating some conditions, such as cancer, often run much higher than that median. Dr. Benjamin Rome of Harvard Medical School said legislators need to step up with solutions, adding that the market is clearly not solving the problem. In the first week of November, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services issued a final rule under the Inflation Reduction Act that codifies the process of choosing high-dollar drugs for price negotiations into 2029 and beyond. Effective Dec. 5, the rule includes protocols for program integrity and support for small biotechnology firms, and while some pharmaceutical companies called the policy unconstitutional, legal challenges have so far stalled.

Medscape reported that primary care physicians are facing challenges as their role prescribing GLP-1 drugs for weight loss increases, with widespread drug misinformation on social media among the main concerns. Managing unrealistic patient expectations can be difficult, and research suggests clinicians spend an average of nearly nine hours a week on related administrative work, which researchers said can feed into burnout. The Wall Street Journal reported on research showing that Eli Lilly's Zepbound and Novo's Wegovy are effective for weight loss in teens and children as young as age 6, potentially widening the patient pool further, though the drugs may negatively affect a child's growth and height in some cases. Obesity medicine specialist Dr. Joey Skelton said that if clinicians can improve young patients' lifelong health outcomes through weight loss, the tradeoff may be justifiable.

TIME magazine reported that measles was gaining more of a foothold in the US as children returned to school in the fall, with noteworthy outbreaks in states such as Georgia and Pennsylvania, and the CDC said it was trying to clarify criteria for measuring measles-related deaths. Officials termed the outbreak the nation's worst in 35 years, with declining vaccination rates largely to blame. Major news outlets reported on Nov. 13 that the US had officially lost its status as a nation that had eliminated measles, after the Pan American Health Organization determined the disease had reestablished regular transmission. Epidemiologist Anne Schuchat called the reversal a very sad moment and said measles can cause unnecessary suffering, from high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications such as progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.

A Radiology Business story quoted the FDA's Dr. Rick Abramson as saying that generative AI in healthcare should be evaluated just as human physicians are, and that the agency is currently drafting policies on the subject. Abramson, a radiologist, said the policymaking effort is not just an academic paper or a thought exercise, and he called it a priority at the highest levels of government. The FDA received more than 300 responses during a public comment period on the matter, and Abramson said the submissions are currently being analyzed. He said the agency intends to read the comments and will not just run them through an AI engine.

stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched the largest initial public offering in United States history on November 19, 2026, at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York. While the company raised over 81 billion dollars and its stock closed 17 percent above the offering price, the broader artificial intelligence trade suffered a significant decline. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.25 percent and the S&P 500 dropped 2 percent to reach 7,175 during a general market pullback. This event failed to revive investor confidence after months of unstable trading and a scandal involving espionage at Nvidia.

The market is currently struggling with concerns that Washington will crack down on export controls for chips sold to Asia. A report from Hunterbrook Media alleged that firmware from AMD appeared in blacklisted companies, causing AMD stock to drop more than 7 percent. Additionally, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that a Commerce Department subagency approved the sale of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese firms. These factors, combined with a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI, have pressured risky neoclouds like CoreWeave, which closed down more than 6 percent.

Dan Niles of Niles Investment Management stated that fierce price competition between the two leading labs is hurting overall revenue and profit potential. He noted that combined revenue growth for OpenAI and Anthropic fell from 75 percent in the second quarter to 48 percent in the third quarter. During that same period, combined losses for the two companies increased from 7.9 billion dollars to approximately 8.4 billion dollars. JJ Kinahan of Cboe Global Markets added that investors can no longer blindly buy dips in the tech sector.

Market participants are now waiting for more commercial and regulatory clarity to emerge over the coming months. Trading experts believe the next few days will serve as a critical gauge for the strength of the artificial intelligence sector. A major test will occur on Monday when options for Anthropic begin trading to show if retail investors will provide a vote of confidence. Meanwhile, cybersecurity firms like CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks continue to rally as AI creates new software vulnerabilities.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's sell-off after Jensen Huang's resignation outweighs Anthropic's IPO gains and drags down the AI trade
stories.Summary:
Nvidia’s deepening sell-off, which followed a leadership shake-up announced on Nov. 12, overwhelmed the optimism around Anthropic’s stock market debut and weighed on the wider artificial intelligence trade, CNBC’s Jim Cramer argued on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. Anthropic, the maker of Claude, raised a record-breaking $81.3 billion, and its shares surged as high as $115 in their first day of trading before closing up 17% from the $83 IPO price. The excitement did little to lift the broader market, as the Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 each fell roughly 2%. Nvidia, once the center of the AI trade, dropped 3.3% for its sixth straight day of losses, a skid that began on Nov. 12, the day longtime CEO Jensen Huang’s abrupt resignation was announced amid a widening affair scandal.

Nvidia has fallen 16% since Huang’s resignation, even after reporting blockbuster earnings earlier this week, with revenue more than doubling from a year earlier and beating expectations. Cramer said Nvidia’s continued decline is dragging down other technology stocks and wiping out wealth faster than Anthropic’s blockbuster debut can create it. He argued that Huang’s desire to return could further complicate Nvidia’s search for a permanent CEO, because any successor would face the challenge of leading a company still closely associated with its founder. Nvidia’s board said it is not considering bringing Huang back.

Cramer said the continued chatter about a potential Huang return makes it so that this still-giant company is sinking like a stone, destroying the savings of millionaires and regular index investors alike. He said Nvidia is casting a pall on the market that is tainting everything, and that the bad news from Nvidia, which he called the most important knowledge generating company, is overwhelming the good news from Anthropic, which buys the knowledge and puts it to use. The damage extends well beyond Nvidia itself, because the chipmaker has helped drive investor enthusiasm for everything from semiconductor manufacturers to data center infrastructure companies. Its continued decline is now weighing on those same stocks, Cramer said, cutting against the bullish hope that Anthropic’s IPO would revive the rest of the AI trade.

ET TechGig will hold a free live online masterclass titled "Turn Conversations into Completion with AI Agents" on 30 November 2026 at 4:00 PM IST, as announced in its article published on 19 November 2026. The session features Mehar Ullipalem, Head of Solutions Engineering for India and SAARC at Zoom, and it includes a live walkthrough of how conversations can become completed work. The article says every meeting, call and chat generates information such as decisions, tasks and next steps, yet after the conversation ends the work often remains scattered across applications and documents. Teams then spend hours organising notes, tracking responsibilities and following up manually, and the session examines how connected information can bridge the gap between a conversation and completed work.

The masterclass has six modules, starting with the context gap, which explores why work slows when teams must reconstruct discussions, retrieve notes and track follow-ups after meetings or customer interactions. The second module covers making conversations actionable by bringing conversation intelligence from meetings, calls, chats and contact centre interactions together with company knowledge and connected third-party systems. The third module is a live walkthrough showing conversations becoming answers, meetings triggering workflows and projects moving towards deliverables, including natural-language interfaces that let teams describe an automation and create it without a traditional workflow builder. The fourth module explains how Model Context Protocol servers and APIs make scheduling, transcription, search, administration and contact centre actions available across AI environments, and the fifth explores AI agents that act on context, respond to external events and coordinate specialised agents, with a team lead agent consolidating their outputs into one deliverable.

The sixth module covers keeping humans in the loop, including access controls, visibility, business-specific rules and human review when agents work with enterprise information or prepare client-facing content. Ullipalem leads Solutions Engineering for India and SAARC at Zoom, with more than 20 years of experience across Unified Communications, Contact Centre and Digital Workplace domains, and the article says he translates complex business requirements into scalable enterprise solutions. The session explores Zoom's Unified Context Layer, which connects conversation history with relevant documents and business data to give people and AI agents a fuller picture of ongoing work. The article says AI needs to understand what happened, why it matters and what should happen next, because context is spread across meeting notes, calls, chats, company documents and enterprise applications.

It adds that decisions can get buried, employees manually transfer information between tools, AI assistants may lack context to answer usefully or act appropriately, and customers may repeat details when service teams cannot access previous interactions. The masterclass is designed for developers, application builders, software and platform engineers, solution and enterprise architects, AI and automation professionals, technology leaders, engineering managers, students and early-career technologists interested in enterprise integrations and AI-powered workflows. The article says the ability to provide context, integrate systems and coordinate agents is increasingly important as organisations move from AI experimentation to connecting AI with business processes. As organisations increasingly integrate AI into their operations, the article says professionals who can identify opportunities, experiment with tools and build AI-powered solutions will be better positioned to adapt to changing industry demands. stories.Headline: Anthropic lists shares on Nasdaq as Congress stalls on AI safeguards
stories.Summary:
Anthropic began trading its shares on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, 19 November 2026, as the first frontier AI developer. The company priced its initial public offering at 83 dollars per share on 18 November, raising a record 81.3 billion dollars. This debut follows a public registration statement on Form S-1 that the company filed with the SEC on 26 October 2026. The listing marks a watershed moment for a technology that may revolutionize American life while highlighting how Washington has fallen behind. This event coincides with a period of heightened scrutiny regarding the risks and rewards associated with the pioneers of artificial intelligence.

The company lists under the symbol ANT, having set an initial roadshow price range of 70 to 78 dollars on 10 November. A Long-Term Benefit Trust holds Class T stock and generally elects four of the seven directors on the company board. Anthropic must now file annual and quarterly reports with the SEC and is liable for any material misstatements in those filings. California's SB 53 law, effective 1 January 2026, requires developers with 500 million dollars in revenue to publish catastrophic risk frameworks. This law allows the Attorney General to impose civil penalties of up to 1 million dollars for each reported violation.

Anthropic stated its mission is the responsible development of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity in its official company prospectus. The company warned that its inventions are rife with catastrophic or existential danger to life and every area of human endeavor. It noted that a single catastrophic AI incident could exceed the capacity of the insurance industry if systems are misused or weaponized. President Donald Trump told reporters that the technology is almost completely good but that the bad elements must be managed carefully. Kevin Hassett, director of the National Economic Council, rejected warnings that the AI sector could face a wider financial sell-off.

Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to chief executive Dario Amodei on 27 October 2026, arguing that the listing could bring volatility to retirement accounts. She asked how the company can meet fiduciary duties under Delaware law without reducing existential risks and requested answers by 3 November. Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the American AI Sovereign Wealth Fund Act on 18 June 2026, proposing a one-time 50 percent stock tax. Senator Ted Cruz blocked the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act, which would require government safety reviews before any model release. Displaced workers and businesses are affected by a lack of federal measures to address mass job losses and the safety net.

The Trump administration and Republican majority in Congress have done little over two years to mitigate hazards like mass job losses. The Brennan Center tracker, updated 9 November 2026, shows only one of 56 bills from the 119th Congress became law. A Stanford Digital Economy Lab paper from 12 August 2026 found employment for young workers in AI-exposed jobs fell 19 percent. In Europe, the EU AI Act has allowed the AI Office to request documentation and impose fines since 2 August 2026. Anthropic published its Frontier Compliance Framework on 19 December 2025 to meet the requirements of the California Transparency in AI Act.

Governor Gavin Newsom recommended on 18 November 2026 that California extend its framework to include mandatory independent oversight and emergency shutdown authority. This proposal would require new legislation to limit recursive self-improvement and ensure that the AI developers are held to higher standards. Many federal bills intended to contain security threats or address the energy grid and tax code remain stuck in the Congress. The articles leave open whether Anthropic or Senator Warren's office will ever publish a response to the letter sent in October. It remains unclear if public shareholders can influence company changes because Anthropic is designated as a controlled company under its governance.

stories.Headline: IAM Union president Brian Bryant urges collective bargaining as the guardrail for AI at work
stories.Summary:
Brian Bryant, the president of the IAM Union, joined thought leaders from Silicon Valley and the U.S. Labor Department on a panel about how artificial intelligence can change work, according to an article published by goiam.org on November 19, 2026. The panel was convened by the College of Employment and Labor Lawyers to discuss the future of work, and Bryant used the appearance to speak out about the biggest tool workers have to make sure AI enhances their jobs rather than replaces them, which he said is their union. He explained that the IAM Union is not opposed to AI that improves vital safety protections at work or otherwise improves jobs, such as the use of AI in simulation safety trainings. At the same time, he called for increased protections against AI that would replace human work, and he said one of the best protections is a union collective bargaining agreement that lets members negotiate over how and when AI is used at work.

Bryant said that everyone is going to be impacted by AI, with some people adversely impacted and some positively impacted, and he noted that the union is already seeing the impact of AI. He said artificial intelligence was on the ballot and that what the country does with it really needs to take focus, adding that the people who voted are in fear of where this is taking the country and society and are asking whether guardrails will be up that protect workers. He said the union does see advantages of AI and looks at employers that share its perspective, so that if AI can enhance a person's job and let them produce more product quicker, safer and more efficiently, then the union is in favor of it being used. Bryant said the union has taken on the initiative to get the strongest language it can that addresses the need for an employer to sit down with the union when bringing in a new technology such as AI and to negotiate over the terms and conditions of how it impacts members. If jobs are going to transform because of AI, he said, the union wants to make sure members have a say in how that impacts their workplace.

Bryant pointed out that although corporations were present at a recent AI Summit convened by the White House, workers and their unions were conspicuously uninvited. He also cautioned that in some cases automation and AI bring neither safety nor public benefits, and in those instances he was clear that sometimes it is okay to just say no, citing Waymo as an example. The article was published alongside other IAM news items, including reports that IAM Local S6 members at Bath Iron Works ratified a historic five-year labor agreement and that IAM District 70 members in Wichita voted to pursue coverage under the IAM-Boeing Master Agreement. Other items reported that Lewis Ginter Botanical Garden workers voted to strike in an escalating fight for a fair first contract and that Arizona IAM members ratified an unprecedented Raytheon contract with 24% average wage growth. The article does not say what happens next after the panel.
