stories.Headline: Experts urge Samsung and SK Hynix to expand into advanced packaging and foundry services
stories.Summary:
Semiconductor experts from the United States and Japan met on November 18, 2026, at the Global Future Technology Forum hosted by Korea Economic TV. They warned that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix cannot maintain their market dominance by relying solely on the performance of high bandwidth memory chips. These South Korean companies must now expand their capabilities into advanced packaging and foundry services to remain competitive. The experts argued that the ability to integrate memory with logic semiconductors is now as critical as the memory itself.

Success requires securing logic and memory interface capabilities, as well as mastering 2.5D packaging to bind GPUs and memory together. Takashi Yunogami noted that TSMC currently holds a near 80 percent monopoly over the 2.5D packaging market. South Korean firms must also look beyond current memory to develop technologies like High Bandwidth Flash to support agentic AI. Meanwhile, China has increased its share of domestically supplied equipment to between 20 and 30 percent in certain segments.

Paul Triolo stated that securing advanced packaging is the top priority because next generation memory is essentially a packaging and foundry problem. He also observed that Chinese companies have already surpassed several technical benchmarks for logic and memory semiconductors. Takashi Yunogami explained that Japan's Rapidus failed to build a foundation for mass production despite receiving GAA technology from IBM. He believes it is impossible for Rapidus to mass produce 2 nanometer semiconductors because they lack experience in intermediate process generations.

The competition is shifting from selling individual memory components toward total system integration and the creation of a broad industrial ecosystem. Douglas Fuller suggested that industrial policy should prioritize dynamic efficiency and technological learning over short term costs or profitability. He noted that while lithography limits may hinder China's DRAM progress, the pursuit by YMTC in the NAND market requires more vigilance. South Korean companies must accumulate yield and mass production experience to avoid being pushed to the periphery of the AI supply chain.

stories.Headline: California agency recommends state safety standards and shutdown powers for frontier AI developers
stories.Summary:
California’s Government Operations Agency recommended on 16 November 2026 that the state require large frontier AI developers to meet state-set safety standards, accept ongoing oversight by licensed independent verifiers and face emergency shutdown orders, in a report released on 18 November 2026. Governor Gavin Newsom’s office announced the recommendations on 18 November 2026 under the title AI Safety in 2026 and Beyond, prepared by the California Government Operations Agency with the California Office of Emergency Services and an outside expert group. The 85-page report answers Executive Order N-9-26, which asked for proposals in four areas: standards, independent verification organizations, critical safety incident reporting and emergency shutdown requirements. The governor’s announcement summarises the package as baseline standards for all AI developers, mandatory ongoing third-party oversight, authority to order a shutdown in an emergency and authority to cap recursive self-improvement. The office defines recursive self-improvement as a scenario in which an AI model can design its own successor without human input, and the recommendations are not law.

The report recommends that the state set baseline safety, security and transparency standards for large frontier developers, with independent verification organizations translating them into technical tests and updating them as the science moves. It recommends that every large frontier developer submit to ongoing oversight by licensed IVOs with full access to the people and information they need, with unredacted assessments going to the state, and that developers could contest a state determination in court before it takes effect. It recommends cutting the deadline for most critical incident reports from 15 days to 48 hours, keeping 24 hours for imminent catastrophic risks, adding a near-miss channel, extending whistleblower protection to former employees and contractors, and treating models capable of catastrophic-risk actions as frontier models even if trained with fewer than 10^26 operations. It recommends that each developer maintain a Risk Containment Protocol verified by an IVO, that state officials could order an immediate shutdown on credible evidence of an imminent catastrophic risk or major loss-of-control event, and that the order would stay in force pending judicial review although a developer could seek a temporary restraining order. It recommends that developers report metrics on how much of their AI research and development is automated, including the share of compute devoted to it, and that the state get standby authority to cap recursive self-improvement if it finds a risk of catastrophic harm.

Unite.AI added that the proposals include a quarterly breakdown of how automating developers divide their compute among training, research experiments, safety work and customers, and that open-weight developers would face containment duties only for deployments under their control. The report says the state should draw on organizations outside government, including industry, civil society organizations and universities, to build AI evaluation capacity, and the SB 813 definition of an AI auditor it quotes includes an academic institution. The report says demand for chips has been pricing out talented researchers who are working on vital safety and security issues, and it recommends funding CalCompute, the public cloud cluster that SB 53 floated but which has not been funded, through a surcharge on the fees large frontier developers pay for IVO oversight, reserving capacity for independent safety and security research. The intended users would be researchers doing independent safety and security work, and the report leaves the surcharge level to the legislature. The report says it hopes to inform the legislature’s discussions as the legislature returns next month, and Unite.AI reported that the recommendations are intended to shape legislation when lawmakers return in December 2026.

Newsom said the federal government’s reckless failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American. Government Operations Agency Secretary Nick Maduros said we don’t have to choose between safety and innovation. Expert-group member Rob Reich, a Stanford professor and former senior adviser to the US AI Safety Institute, said there is more oversight of the cafeteria offering sandwiches to employees at a frontier AI developer than of the AI models they design. Gillian Hadfield, a Johns Hopkins professor, said she was pleased the report recommends requiring developers to allow in expert independent evaluators responsible to the state and rapidly building a sector of independent verification organizations. The group also included Alondra Nelson of the Institute for Advanced Study and Jason Goldman, according to the governor’s office.

The report notes that Newsom signed SB 53, the first US law governing frontier AI development, a year ago, and that SB 813 and AB 1405 this autumn created a framework for IVOs and a registry of AI auditors. The report argues that the federal government has not acted, stating that no federal law requires AI companies to follow baseline safety or security standards, undergo independent testing or verification, or shut down their models if they threaten the public. It cites loss-of-control incidents, including an OpenAI incident involving Hugging Face this summer, as evidence that the evidence base has changed. Universities with evaluation, security or AI-safety groups are potential IVO or auditor candidates if the recommendations become law, which would raise questions for research offices about independence, conflicts of interest, confidentiality duties and licensing that the report says IVOs would carry. Institutions that collaborate with frontier developers should also note the whistleblower and incident-reporting proposals, which would extend protections to former employees and contractors.

The next step is legislative: the report says the legislature returns next month, and Unite.AI reported December 2026 as the date lawmakers return. Any bill would have to set the surcharge level, the licensing rules for IVOs and the thresholds for emergency orders, which the report leaves open. The Governor’s office also called on Congress and President Trump to adopt California’s framework or use it as a floor, not a ceiling. The report leaves the surcharge level to the legislature. The recommendations are not law.

stories.Headline: Greenland starts bulk shipments of TMAH products to overseas advanced packaging supply chains
stories.Summary:
China's Greenland confirmed during earnings briefings on November 18 and 19, 2026, that its TMAH series products have entered the overseas advanced packaging supply chain. The company completed production-line testing and validation with international customers, passed system certification, and has now started bulk shipments. This expansion follows the company's successful entry into the supplier systems of various pan-semiconductor enterprises, including stable volume supply to customers located in Taiwan. These developments require Greenland to accelerate its new product expansion to meet changing market demands and build a diversified product matrix. The company has already achieved full-factory scale supply of strippers at the Yungu facility of Visionox and completed introduction at the new Hefei Guoxian high-generation OLED plant.

Additionally, Greenland serves as a strategic supplier to MetaX, providing semiconductor developers and diluents to power device makers. Meanwhile, ACM Research reported that new orders rose 147 percent year on year in the first three quarters, with orders in hand reaching 17.073 billion yuan, or approximately 2.6 billion dollars, as of September 29. Company representatives stated that they are focusing on independent research and development while remaining open to collaborations with partners who possess mature technologies. Greenland noted that its developers provide a stable base, while strippers and advanced packaging materials represent new growth directions for the business. ACM Research officials explained that Plant A at the Lingang R&D and Manufacturing Center is nearly at full capacity, and Plant B will begin production in the fourth quarter.

They believe that once both plants reach full output, they can support an annual output value of about 20 billion yuan, which is approximately 3.0 billion dollars. The growth of these companies is driven by the increasing demand for chips and new display devices fueled by artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things. Both firms are benefiting from a broader trend of domestic substitution and supply chain self-reliance within the Chinese semiconductor and display industries. ACM Research plans to ship more than 20 units of its upgraded high-temperature SPM cleaning system to multiple customers in 2026. The companies continue to navigate challenges such as long customer validation cycles and volatility in the global components market.

stories.Headline: Deloitte Canada integrates Blue J tax bots into its internal AI tools
stories.Summary:
Deloitte Canada announced on Thursday a deal to integrate its internal content database with the tax research bots of Toronto-based Blue J, which help accountants, lawyers and auditors check tax rules. The partnership will give Deloitte Canada’s 150 internal AI tools access to Blue J’s tax library. It will also let Blue J generate responses tailored to Deloitte’s standards. Blue J raised a Series E round last week, before announcing the multi-year deal with Deloitte. Deloitte would not disclose the deal’s dollar value.

Deloitte Canada calls the arrangement a “re-engineered” and “deliberate” approach to AI. Jean-Luc Ratté-Boulianne is the chief technology officer for Deloitte Canada’s tax and legal division. He said the firm is increasingly turning down many tech tools and prioritizing AI companies that can connect into its existing systems. He said that even if a product is great, the firm more and more says “OK, thanks, but no thanks” if integration is not offered as a feature. He said Deloitte has dozens of tools that practitioners need to use every day, and “what we want to do is not add more tools.”

Ratté-Boulianne said “you want authoritative data sources, which is what Blue J is doing out of the box.” He said having one-of-a-kind software that relies on Deloitte’s proprietary content and intellectual property gives Deloitte a leg up over competitors using the “vanilla” version of the technology. He said a research company like Blue J can ensure information does not go to waste at a firm with 181 years’ worth of files. He said Blue J keeps data processing in Canada at a time when Deloitte is getting more client inquiries about the issue. The companies said no client-specific information will change hands in the partnership.

Blue J CEO Benjamin Alarie said he believes custom, fact-based content is becoming the “trade secret” that sets some AI apart from the rest. He said that in the accounting industry, where attracting and retaining talent can be a struggle, he hopes the partnership makes it slightly easier for accountants to dig up the information they need without feeling they are digging “ditches by hand.” He said “a lot of tax professionals feel like they don’t see enough of their loved ones for a few months a year,” calling that a huge human cost. He said “it’s about making tax work more pleasant to do.” Deloitte’s work with Blue J comes amid a broader shift in corporate AI use, as companies fight AI fatigue among their workers.

Tech companies are once again following Apple co-founder Steve Jobs and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen’s lead by shifting more toward bundles of bots that “just work,” without requiring workers to cobble together a series of different chatbots. Thomson Reuters is building custom products for law firm Skadden, while Intuit is working with Anthropic on a similar venture. After allegations of AI hallucination flubs at several big professional services firms, including Deloitte, the firm has tightened controls around AI governance, training and accountability, Ratté-Boulianne said. As managing and training a growing stable of AI programs verges on becoming a full-time job in many workplaces, companies like Blue J are helping big firms like Deloitte change their approach to internal AI. Blue J has been a beneficiary of the search for the killer bot, on the heels of a fundraising spree that will see it do more custom work.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Blue J and Deloitte Canada expand AI tax research agreement across Canada
stories.Summary:
Blue J, a tax research and advisory platform, announced on November 19, 2026 a multi-year enterprise agreement with Deloitte Canada to deliver advanced AI-powered tax research capabilities across Canada, deepening the relationship through content and MCP integration that re-engineers the practitioner experience across Deloitte Canada's tax practice. The collaboration centers on Blue J's purpose-built AI-powered tax research solution, which is trusted by more than 6,500 organizations worldwide, and it equips Deloitte Canada's multidisciplinary team of over 1,500 Tax and Legal professionals serving governments, corporations, Indigenous communities, nonprofit and private organizations with technology that delivers faster, verifiable research support for complex tax questions. Under the expanded terms, select Deloitte Canada proprietary research and knowledge content, excluding client-specific information, will be integrated directly into Deloitte's practitioner experience available through the Blue J platform, further enhancing the precision and relevance of answers generated for its tax teams. MCP integration will also allow Blue J to connect seamlessly within Deloitte's proprietary connected practitioner experience, bringing together leading research tools, tailored agentic workflows, and over 150 Deloitte-built codified skills and sub-agents available to all Deloitte tax practitioners.

Deloitte Canada initially chose to adopt Blue J's platform because of its advanced AI capabilities and curated library of authoritative tax sources, and this expansion provides its tax teams access to Deloitte's own proprietary data and knowledge in a unified and enhanced research experience. Through the collaboration, Deloitte Canada will use Blue J's AI-powered research capabilities to enhance efficiency, elevate the consistency of quality, and enable professionals to focus on higher-value advisory work while maintaining the highest standards of accuracy and defensibility. Benjamin Alarie, CEO and Co-Founder of Blue J, said tax is complex, global and high-stakes, and professionals need clarity they can stand behind, adding that Deloitte Canada's tax practice has been a clear market leader in transforming how its practitioners and clients experience tax outcomes and has long been a great product collaborator. Stephen Lopes, Tax Technology Commercialization Leader for Deloitte Canada, said the firm is deliberate in how it adopts AI, particularly in high-stakes areas like tax where accuracy and defensibility are paramount, and that after seeing the impact on research efficiency and confidence in practice, expanding Blue J to create a more unified practitioner experience anchored on its proprietary IP was a natural next step.

The collaboration marks continued momentum for Blue J following its recent growth milestones, including a US$176 million Series E funding round in November 2026 led by JMI Equity, a leading growth equity investment firm. Annual recurring revenue grew 165% in the 15 months after Blue J's 2025 Series D, and more than 6,500 organizations now use Blue J, including Big Four firms and Fortune 100 companies. The company has doubled its team over the past year and expects to exceed 200 employees by year-end, and in October it partnered with Legora to bring its tax research into Legora's agentic operating system for legal work, which is used by more than 140,000 legal professionals. Blue J, founded in 2015, says it is trusted by more than 45,000 tax professionals at over 6,500 organizations and has answered over 15 million tax questions to date.

stories.Headline: EY deploys agentic AI across its assurance division in April 2026
stories.Summary:
EY rolled out enterprise-scale agentic AI across its Assurance division in April 2026, built with Microsoft technology and embedded in its global audit platform, which reportedly processes more than 1.4 trillion lines of journal-entry data each year. Deloitte followed on 24 June 2026 with a linked network of agents inside its Omnia platform, handling early-stage tasks such as scraping data, sifting evidence and writing first drafts. In November 2026, KPMG put more than 100 AI agents to work alongside humans on a live audit of an unnamed UK-listed company in a trial called Project Exponential, with plans to expand the approach to up to 20 larger audits. PwC US, meanwhile, is training more than 85,000 employees to interrogate AI outputs rather than simply accept them.

The firms say the agents draft and humans sign, and that algorithms do the legwork while people carry the legal liability. KPMG's trial showed the agents are not flawless, since one agent could not match regulations to the documents it was checking, which is why people stay in charge of the result. The trial ran alongside a traditional audit, with reviewers checking every conclusion, and KPMG found the bots occasionally asked more probing questions and dug deeper into tricky financial details than the humans in the room. The UK's Financial Reporting Council has warned that sharing AI-derived insights with audit clients can threaten an auditor's objectivity and independence.

PwC's response to the risk is a Critical Thinking and Judgment certificate programme for more than 85,000 US partners and employees, starting in December with a target of June 2027 and built to sharpen their ability to challenge what AI tells them. The worry behind it is over-reliance, since AI is fast, fluent and extremely sure of itself even when its output is incomplete or wrong, and an auditor who takes a confident answer at face value wears down the scepticism an opinion depends on. Junior work is changing too, with less mechanical testing and more reviewing and interpreting of whatever the agents produce. The firms say they are not trying to have AI issue audit opinions.

KPMG's plan to move to as many as 20 larger audits will test how far the draft-and-sign rule goes when the workload gets heavier. There is no evidence yet that these digital assistants are cutting client bills or thinning out audit teams, and the loud emphasis on human oversight hints the industry still does not trust algorithms to master audit evidence, independence and healthy scepticism on their own. The next round of audits will show how quickly that doubt starts to melt away.

stories.Headline: Baker Tilly's Millet says AI amplifies poor data hygiene without regular cleanup
stories.Summary:
Chris Millet, managing director of digital advisory services for the NetSuite practice of Top 10 firm Baker Tilly, spoke at the Finance and Accounting Technology Expo in New York. He said AI tools without a strong data foundation can amplify the classic garbage-in-garbage-out problem for data analysis. He said AI just reports what it is given and can technically learn bad habits if not trained appropriately. He said this includes all the errors in a dataset. Chris Gaetano reported the remarks for Accounting Today on November 19, 2026.

Millet raised the example of a vendor master record, which he said commonly has data hygiene issues. A record might contain duplicate vendors, which can lead to the wrong people being paid or the right people being paid improperly. Duplicates can also kneecap spend analysis because the AI will treat the same company as separate ones. Another common issue is inconsistent general ledger mapping, meaning the organization cannot map expenses to the right accounts, which will impede AI automation. Outdated information can lead to errors and disconnected systems that gum up workflows.

Millet said AI can amplify these problems and lead to recurring costs for the organization, and it will get worse the longer it goes on. He said it will learn patterns of inconsistent coding, so the more you use the automation the worse the problem gets. He said AI can also get you out of the mess, provided an organization approaches things deliberately and methodically and with plenty of human supervision. He recommended running datasets through an AI hygiene analysis, instructing the model to look for missing, incorrect, outdated or incomplete data. He said the user can then tell the agent to go fix the dataset if confident about the agentic AI work.

Millet said this should be done across multiple systems, ranging from AP to bank recs and anywhere else clean data is especially important. He said it should be done again and again because even clean data can get dirty over time. He equated data hygiene cleanliness checking to inventory counts, something you do not do once at the end of the year but constantly stay up on. He said it is something an organization could do every 90 days to help build and maintain a good data foundation. He said the process would first involve profiling and prioritizing what is most valuable for cleanup and assigning an owner for each dataset who is ultimately responsible for its accuracy.

Millet said the organization should then review the data in the most important set, cleaning files to get rid of duplicates or inaccuracies while filling in missing information. He said controls should then be put in place to make it easier the next time and to keep data AI-ready between cleanups. He said the controls include named ownership so each domain has an owner responsible for the dataset's accuracy, who could be a vendor, a processor, a controller or someone else. He said the controls also include consistent rules for data entry such as required fields, continuous monitoring of the dataset, and maintenance of a proper audit trail that includes not just the numbers but the context and logic behind them. He said the organization should then move on to the next set and do it again, and when finished with all the sets, prepare for the next cleanup.

Millet repeatedly stressed the importance of doing this regularly versus annually or only when things get dire. He said this is never done, that you cleanup once and automatically start again. He said that while AI can automate much of the data cleanup process, it is important to assign the proper level of automation to each step. He said an AI might fix a simple typo automatically, but for more important changes it needs to ping the human for confirmation. He said there are certain tasks, such as changing bank or remittance details, that AI should never do, and that automated processes always have to happen within an agreed-upon rule.

Articles.Title: AI needs consistent and regular data hygiene to be fully effective - Accounting Today

stories.Headline: August AI raises $12 Mn to expand its healthcare assistant in the US
stories.Summary:
AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its healthcare assistant in the US. Founder and CEO Anuruddh Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. The startup claims to have helped 10 Mn people understand their health through its AI companion. The development comes after Inc42 exclusively reported in August that the startup was in talks to raise around $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners. August AI previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding from Accel and Claypond Capital in October 2025.

The $12 Mn fundraise is from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital, the family office of Manipal Group chairman Ranjan Pai. The new capabilities are available in beta in the US, with users able to join a waitlist for access. In September, August AI launched August Care, a $39-a-month membership offering telehealth consultations, discounted laboratory tests, prescription services, and insurance guidance. Mishra said August AI spent 24,286 minutes on hold while finding in-network doctor appointments for early users over the past few weeks. This included 366 minutes for a single user, and he also claimed the platform helped another user save $1,255 on an insurance claim.

Mishra, an IIT-BHU alumnus who founded August AI in 2022, said the AI agent calls doctors' offices, checks availability, and books the earliest available appointment with the user's approval. He said it can also call nearby pharmacies to compare medicine availability and prices, review medical bills for potential errors and savings, and follow up with insurers and hospitals on denied claims. The company says licensed physicians make clinical decisions within the August Care service. Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. The startup claims to have helped 10 Mn people understand their health through its AI companion.

August AI initially built an AI-powered health companion to help users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports. The platform also offers personalised health insights, nutrition guidance, and medication reminders. It is now extending its offering to tasks patients must complete to access care, from finding a doctor covered by their insurance to locating prescribed medicines. The administrative assistant builds on the startup's existing US healthcare offering. The startup is expanding beyond answering health questions to handling administrative tasks for patients, including calling doctors' offices and following up on insurance claims.

August AI's expansion comes amid increased investor interest in startups using AI to manage healthcare workflows, both for patients and providers. In September, Bengaluru-based Prodoc AI raised a seed round to develop agentic AI solutions for hospital workflows, including patient engagement, appointment conversion and care coordination. US-based Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in an extension round led by Z47 in October to expand its AI agents for appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills and other administrative tasks. stories.Headline: Infosys invests JPY 1.59 billion for a 10.1% stake in NTT DOCOMO Playspace joint venture
stories.Summary:
Infosys said on 19 November 2026 that its Singapore subsidiary, Infosys Singapore Pte Ltd, would enter into a joint venture agreement with the Japanese telecommunications company NTT DOCOMO, and that it would invest JPY 1.59 billion, or about ₹92.75 crore, in the venture called NTT DOCOMO Playspace. Under the deal, Infosys will acquire a 10.1% stake in the joint venture and serve as its technology and AI partner, according to the company's exchange filing. The investment will also give Infosys the right to nominate one director to the board of the joint venture. The venture will focus on developing metaverse-based experiences, digital twins and virtual commerce, and it aims to build a virtual economic ecosystem in Japan that connects immersive digital experiences with businesses and real-world commerce.

Infosys would contribute its AI engineering capabilities alongside its Topaz and Metaverse Foundry capabilities to the partnership. The company did not disclose the venture's expected revenue, its commercial launch timeline or its projected financial returns. Infosys also did not specify which businesses or customers the NTT DOCOMO venture would initially target, or how it plans to generate revenue from its virtual ecosystem. The venture's virtual commerce focus comes as AI agents begin to take on more tasks in online shopping, an emerging model called agentic commerce in which AI agents handle product discovery, checkout and payments with user consent.

The investment comes as Infosys expands its AI partnerships, having partnered with OpenAI in April to deploy the latter's Codex coding agent across enterprise workflows, combining it with Infosys Topaz for software engineering, legacy system modernisation and DevOps automation. In March, Infosys expanded its collaboration with Intel to help enterprises move AI projects from pilot stages into production. Digital twins are also finding applications outside conventional enterprise software, and in February The ePlane Company announced plans to develop a digital twin of its electric air taxi using NVIDIA Omniverse to simulate flight conditions, aerodynamic interactions and aircraft systems before physical testing. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the signing of the joint venture agreement.

stories.Headline: Vectorial AI models 2.5 million users with SAPIENS to test products before launch
stories.Summary:
Vectorial AI, a startup founded in 2024 and headquartered in San Francisco with a 12-member team across the US and India, has built a model called SAPIENS that creates virtual representations of target audiences so product, design and marketing teams can test ideas before launch, and it raised $3 million in seed funding in October 2026 from SenseAI Ventures, Smilegate and investors associated with the Berkeley and Stanford ecosystems. The company says it has modelled more than 2.5 million users, including 500,000 in India, and run more than 30,000 simulations, and it reports that SAPIENS is 87% accurate in predicting behaviour and has matched previous customer research by 85 to 95% in some comparisons. The founders began exploring commercial uses in 2024, worked with design partners from mid-2025 and launched in January 2026, and SAPIENS began as a question-and-answer interface that worked like a focus group with a simulated audience before expanding to let businesses test software interfaces, physical product concepts and advertising campaigns. Its announced customers include boAt, GoodRx, Suki AI, MIDI Health and Concrete Software, and it targets healthcare, gaming and technology companies building software products and digital experiences. Co-founder and CEO Taranveer Singh, who spent the last 10 years modelling human behaviour and worked with Andrew Ng's team at Coursera while at Carnegie Mellon University before joining Berkeley AI Research as a visiting research fellow, says a traditional study can take three to 12 weeks depending on scope and that user research becomes a bottleneck as AI speeds up product development.

Singh says some companies skip research because of time or cost, which he said can waste millions of dollars on failed products, and he argues that simulations can replace conventional research for many decisions while still encouraging calibration against live participants. He says the company encourages customers to run studies with live people during the calibration phase so it can show how accurate it is, and he insists that it is not making up users but modelling real people against real behavioural data. Jasmine Kaur, the chief business officer, graduated from Stanford Graduate School of Business and worked on synthetic users for marketing at Pfizer, while Rahul Garg, the chief product officer, has worked in product leadership at Blinkit and Housing.com and on a behaviour graph for sales conversations at Zime AI. SAPIENS is built on behavioural data from partners and AI-moderated interviews with paid participants, which the company uses to profile how people behave across locations, lifestyles and income groups, and Vectorial aims to deliver feedback within hours at around one-twentieth of the cost of a conventional study, charging a base platform fee to develop an audience model and then running additional simulations. Researchers remain cautious, with a 2026 survey by User Interviews finding that 47% were sceptical and wanted more evidence and 88% cited quality and accuracy of insights as a concern, and Singh notes that it is one thing to have a model accurate sometimes for some audiences but another to have it accurate in all possible scenarios a customer can influence.

Vectorial addresses this with a broader pipeline of behavioural data and a calibration period that compares simulated responses against previous studies and interviews with real people, gathering more data where it finds gaps. Its competitors include Maze and UserTesting along with AI-moderated research companies Listen Labs and Outset AI, and Singh says AI-moderated interviews can accelerate research but are limited to about 100 people and each new question requires a new study, whereas Vectorial keeps a model of the audience that customers can query repeatedly. Vectorial will use the seed funding to develop SAPIENS 2.0, expand behavioural data partnerships and invest in product-led growth, and its tools include a Chrome Web Store beta and a Figma plugin, with an MCP server planned so compatible AI tools can interact with simulated audiences. The company adds around five customers per quarter and expects that to accelerate, with a lower-cost product for individual developers planned, and it is targeting double-digit million-dollar revenue by the end of 2027 while not having disclosed its current revenue or run rate. Singh says that when the company first pitched SenseAI Ventures, the firm clearly understood that Vectorial is a category creator and that behaviour models and simulations are going to be the new way to build and launch products.

stories.Headline: Wadhwani AI and LinkedIn launch a 12-month programme to train 2,000 Northeast India entrepreneurs in AI
stories.Summary:
Wadhwani AI and LinkedIn signed a memorandum of understanding to launch a programme called AI for Future SMEs, which will train 2,000 small and micro entrepreneurs across Northeast India in using artificial intelligence for their businesses. The partnership was announced in an article published by Analytics India Magazine on 19 November 2026, and the initiative is set to run for 12 months. The programme covers five states, namely Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Meghalaya and Manipur, and it targets businesses in sectors such as handloom, handicrafts, bamboo, food processing, tourism and agriculture-linked activities. The training is meant to help these entrepreneurs build digital skills and apply AI tools in everyday tasks including marketing, customer communication and inventory management.

The curriculum is divided into two tracks, with the first covering foundational AI and digital literacy, including machine learning, generative AI, prompt engineering and responsible AI practices, as well as privacy, misinformation and digital safety. The second track focuses on applying generative AI to small-business operations, ranging from market research to workflow automation, and the training will include practical examples of creating product catalogues, developing social media campaigns, researching competitors and engaging with customers. To reach entrepreneurs in areas with limited connectivity, the initiative will use a mobile-first learning model, open-source AI tools and offline-friendly materials, alongside classroom sessions and continued mentorship with content adapted to local business needs. Participants will present their work through a project showcase and receive joint certification, and the organisations will assess changes in digital fluency, understanding of responsible AI, confidence in using the technology and adoption of AI tools through baseline and endline evaluations.

Shekar Sivasubramanian, Head of Wadhwani AI, said in a statement that AI can become a meaningful growth enabler for small businesses when it is practical, accessible and rooted in real economic needs, and he said the partnership with LinkedIn aims to bridge the digital gap by equipping entrepreneurs with practical, business-focused AI capabilities that can be applied immediately. Kumaresh Pattabiraman, Country Manager of LinkedIn India, said the Northeast is home to a new wave of entrepreneurs building businesses rooted in the region's craft, culture and communities, and he said the partnership will help them use AI to reach new customers, run their businesses more efficiently and grow well beyond their local markets. The article does not name any other officials or give any further statements from the two organisations about the programme. It also does not say what happens after the 12-month period ends or whether the initiative will be extended to other regions.

stories.Headline: Karnataka hosts nearly half of India's AI centres of excellence, Zinnov-KDEM report finds
stories.Summary:
Karnataka hosts more than 120 artificial intelligence and machine learning Centres of Excellence across over 100 global capability centres, which amounts to nearly half of India's AI and machine learning CoE base, according to a Zinnov-KDEM report. That network is around four times the size of the next-largest hub in the country, and one in three of these centres now works on generative AI or agentic AI mandates. These centres help global capability centres develop AI products and platforms for global enterprises. The report was published on 19 November 2026.

Karnataka is home to 1,088 global capability centres, or 51% of India's total, including 320 Global 2000 centres, the report says. Between FY2021 and FY2026E the state added 90 software and internet global capability centres, accounting for 51% of India's additions. The state also has 111,000 global capability centre AI and machine learning professionals, or 43% of the national total. India's global capability centre ecosystem has 1.1 million emerging tech professionals and 259,000 AI and machine learning professionals, representing 47% and 11% of total global capability centre headcount.

In Karnataka, emerging-tech talent makes up 54% of global capability centre employees, while AI and machine learning professionals account for 13%, and the state has 451,000 emerging-tech professionals, or 41% of India's global capability centre pool. Nitika Goel, CMO and Managing Partner at Zinnov, said in the report that the industry is now in a third wave, which she called Value 2.0, where value is measured by AI itself, not by pilots and proofs of concept but by large-scale enterprise value created and deployed in production. The report identified four drivers of Karnataka's AI position: global capability centre ownership of AI architecture and platforms, specialist talent and leadership, dedicated centres of excellence, and an ecosystem of start-ups, investors, research institutions and policy support. Surveyed Karnataka global capability centres scored 1.12 times India's average in AI maturity.

Bengaluru's AI hiring intensity reached 13.6% of global capability centre job postings in 2026, against 9.8% at the same companies' offices elsewhere in India, and around 69% of surveyed Karnataka global capability centres provide role-specific AI training, compared with 53% nationally. Between 2024 and 2026, GitHub Copilot's share of AI-related postings grew 26 times, prompt engineering 8.1 times, LangChain 7.8 times, and Vertex AI six times. The centres are applying AI across software development, finance, chip design, retail, telecom, industrial maintenance, healthcare, and IT services. The report describes a cycle in which AI talent attracts global mandates, which in turn creates demand for specialist engineers and architects.

stories.Headline: IDC names Cloudinary a Leader in AI-enabled digital asset management for the second time
stories.Summary:
Cloudinary has been named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide AI-Enabled Digital Asset Management 2026, the second time it has received that ranking, according to IT Brief Australia. The assessment highlighted Cloudinary's combination of asset management, media delivery and activation, and it also cited the breadth of its API and extensibility tools, including REST APIs, SDKs, command-line tools, webhooks and user interface extensions. Digital asset management software helps companies organise, store and distribute images, video and other media across websites, apps, marketing systems and commerce platforms. Artificial intelligence has become a key focus for vendors as businesses look to manage larger volumes of content and automate more of the work around it.

IDC said Cloudinary's product was suited to organisations handling high volumes of image and video content and connecting digital asset management systems to wider business functions. Jordan Jewell, senior research director for content and digital experiences at IDC, said Cloudinary is well suited for midmarket and enterprise organizations with high volumes of image and video content that need to connect DAM directly to commerce, marketing, product content, and digital experience delivery. The report also said Cloudinary stands out for combining asset management with dynamic media delivery and activation, and it added that the company shows notable depth in API coverage and extensibility. More than 4.5 million developers and 14,000 customers use its platform, according to the company, which lists customers including Adidas, Etsy, Grubhub, Mattel, Minted, Paul Smith and Zalando.

Cloudinary also says it works with more than 300 partners, integrations and plug-ins. Rob Daynes, vice president of global new business at Cloudinary, said the company viewed the ranking as recognition of a broader shift in how businesses use digital asset management. He said Cloudinary was proud to be named a Leader by IDC MarketScape for the second time, and that he believes it reflects what DAM has become, which he described as a business-critical content operations engine. He said that when teams can manage, transform, and deliver images and video from one platform, at any scale and alongside AI agents, they create visual experiences that engage and convert across every channel.

The latest ranking comes as software suppliers across the content and marketing stack push AI-based features into their products. In digital asset management, that includes tools for tagging, searching, transforming, routing and delivering visual content, as well as support for automated workflows. Cloudinary sells software for managing and delivering image and video content, an area that sits between content operations, eCommerce and digital marketing, and businesses use these systems to maintain a central library of approved assets while adapting files for different devices, channels and customer experiences. That ecosystem matters in a market where buyers often want digital asset management software to connect with content management systems, retail platforms, product information tools and internal workflows.

stories.Headline: Pierre du Preez says human-centered design counters AI blandness by making thinking collaborative and visible
stories.Summary:
Pierre du Preez, director of Notitia, wrote in an article published by IT Brief Australia on 19 November 2026 that human-centered design is the antidote to what he called "AI blandness." He said AI works well for known solutions to known problems, where the requirement is well documented and understood. He said that as requirements become less straightforward, solutions become less defined and innovation becomes key. He defined innovation as the practical implementation of new ideas, methods or products that create measurable value, solve problems or improve efficiency. He said AI is becoming inward-looking, rehashing the same content with variation driven only by how the prompt is written.

He said this generates increasingly bland output of ever diminishing value. He said innovation begins at the discovery phase, including the context of the requirement and what is actually needed in the context of the business. He said this includes how the requirement affects the rest of the business and the practical people and process implications to deliver it. He said humans are very good at innovation and largely responsible for all innovation in recorded history, save for a few happy accidents. He said innovation comes from inspired leaps of understanding that bring loosely connected ideas and threads together to create something new.

He said discussion, exploration of ideas, challenging assumptions and arguing competing viewpoints evolve both the requirement and the solution, especially in complex, overlapping or interconnected problems. He said the most effective approach is where the requirement and solution are developed together, with time and environment allowing the best overall solution to be reached by the humans who require and use it. He said this human-centered approach can be very effective for solutions required to operate across departments, complex solutions, solutions that have failed before, solutions driven by material changes in operating environment, systems or competitive environment, and prior to a major software buy or build decision. He said a very clear understanding of future requirements at that stage reduces the risk of an expensive software project that isn't fit for purpose and ultimately fails. He said human-centered design is a collaborative approach to problem-solving that involves the people who experience, understand or are affected by a problem.

He said the process brings people together to create an agreed upon solution. He said incorporating the design of the solution into the outcome, capturing the workflow, practical real world use and look and feel, lets the result serve as a design specification, changing "Can it do X?" to "We need X to be done this way." He said human-centered design can include facilitated workshops, interviews, user persona creation, process mapping, and prototyping or iterative wireframing. He said its purpose is to make people's internal knowledge of how the business works visible, challenge assumptions, and develop a shared understanding of the problem before choosing or building a solution.

He said it confirms at a practical, day-in-the-life level what is actually required to deliver an outcome. He said the valuable part is the interaction, where people challenge assumptions, explain why something works the way it does, add context and practical experiences, make connections and reach decisions together. He said that context is often where the real insight sits and is very difficult to recover once flattened into a generic brief or fed into an AI tool without sufficient thought. He said the risk of AI is not simply that organisations will begin producing similar-looking strategies, but that we substitute pre-generated outputs for the harder process of drawing out the knowledge, experience and judgement of people. He said human-centered design is an antidote to "AI blandness" because it makes the thinking collaborative and visible and allows a better, practical solution to be developed.

He said reducing the uncertainty from the cost of developing a solution is achieved through a robust requirements confirmation process. He said mapping out requirements with human-centered design creates practical outputs that confirm in absolute detail what is required by a user or team to deliver an outcome. He said this output, in the form of mock-ups and wireframes, allows a day-in-the-life walk-through of the proposed solution, uncovering inconsistencies, missing or overlapping authority, data or other departmental or workflow dependencies. He said the approach ensures the solution meets both individual and organisational objectives and is fit for purpose in the context of the organisation. He said the output allows more informed decisions on collaboration, cost, planning of a Minimum Viable Product and additional phases, and buy-in from executives or key users.

He said clients told Notitia the design process allowed them to better "understand how other departments use our data" and how the organisation uses data for its mission. He said clients described the approach as low stress and said it allowed them time to work through the changes they needed to make to "deliver better outcomes for our customers." He said clients reported a more intuitive and effective solution that aligns with their day-to-day workflow. He said clients described the booking and appointments process as super easy and a stress-free exercise for their customers, with clear feedback and proactive status updates. He said clients described the solution as "sophisticated and elegant" and said it "nailed the brief."

He said Notitia uses human-centered design to work through complex requirements by creating a collaborative environment for discovery and innovation. He said this delivers a detailed design specification with context to allow a deliberate assessment of strategic options, build versus buy versus augmenting existing systems, as well as tactical options such as which solutions to assess if buying. He said human-centered design ensures that the human remains fundamental to the process. The article carried no further statements on what happens next.

Articles.Title: Human-centered design is the antidote to 'AI blandness' - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: Pretxt raises $5 million seed round to supervise AI agents as they act
stories.Summary:
Pretxt emerged from stealth with USD $5 million in seed funding and said it is introducing a new category of AI supervision, according to an announcement covered by IT Brief Australia. The round was backed by Deciens Capital, Howdy Partners, NSV Wolf Capital and Service Provider Capital. The company says its product is designed to supervise AI agents as they carry out tasks and to intervene before an action reaches a customer or a system. Pretxt was founded by Brian Soby and Aaron Costello, both of whom previously worked at AppOmni, and the company says its wider team has experience at Salesforce, MITRE, SAP, Deloitte, VMware, HackerOne and AppOmni.

Pretxt says its system evaluates agent behaviour in the context of a task and aims to steer agents back on course when they deviate from approved processes, which it says can happen without human review and without using a large language model to judge each step. According to the company, that approach makes the system 60 times faster than alternatives that rely on an LLM as a judge, while avoiding added latency, cost and inconsistent judgments. In testing on Zapier's AutomationBench, which Pretxt described as representing real-world support workflows, the company says it reduced agent actions that violated company policy from nearly one in five to zero, and it did not disclose customer numbers. Pretxt says businesses define expected agent behaviour in plain language and can test supervision plans against their own examples before approving changes, and it also says it analyses agent behaviour over time to suggest refinements, subject to human review. The company says the product is available through an early access programme and that it is initially targeting sectors including financial services, healthcare, insurance, pharmaceuticals and customer support.

Soby said the issue goes beyond prompt injection attacks, arguing that you do not need such an attack for an AI agent to do something it should not, and that security remains essential but the next question is whether enterprises can trust agents to carry out real work according to their standards. He said you cannot supervise a workforce of AI agents with hope, a rulebook and reviews after the fact, and that AI needs supervision while it acts, which he described as the category Pretxt is there to establish. Chris Steffen, Vice President of Research at Enterprise Management Associates, framed the issue as one of accountability, saying enterprises have invested heavily in tools that ask whether an agent is secure, compliant or observable, while far fewer can answer whether the agent is correctly doing the job it was given. He said organisations that deploy AI own their outcomes no matter who is asking, and that most tools can only report what went wrong after the fact, while Pretxt intervenes while the outcome can still change.

Nate Pacer, a Partner at NSV Wolf Capital, said the return on AI agents is limited by how much real work a company is willing to hand them, and that Pretxt expands that limit by holding every action to an organisation's own standards as it happens. Vishal Rana, a Partner at Deciens Capital, said AI agents are moving into workflows where mistakes have real consequences, and that the firm invested because it believes supervision at runtime will become a foundational layer of enterprise AI infrastructure. Pretxt argues that existing security, governance and observability tools do not fully address whether an agent is following an organisation's rules and procedures as it works, and it says these failures can happen even without an external attack. The launch reflects a broader debate over how businesses control AI systems once they move beyond drafting text and begin taking actions inside enterprise software, such as issuing refunds, verifying customer details, processing claims or making commitments on behalf of a company.

Articles.Title: Pretxt raises USD $5 million to supervise AI agents - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: An AI agent builds an Android app over 44 days while an engineer sends no messages for 22 of them

stories.Headline: Bunnings cuts 350 tech jobs, shifts work to TCS teams in India
stories.Summary:
Bunnings, Australia's largest hardware retailer, will cut 350 technology roles in Australia and transfer the work to Tata Consultancy Services teams in India and the Philippines, according to media reports. The move will affect 230 permanent technology employees and 120 contractors. The transition is expected to begin in December 2026 and continue until June 2027. Bunnings plans to retain an in-house technology workforce of approximately 500 employees in Australia. The multi-year outsourcing partnership aims to reduce costs and strengthen the company's technology capabilities.

Mike Schneider, Managing Director of Bunnings, said the change is necessary but important, and that the company needs a technology model and partner that keeps pace with its customers. He said this would let Bunnings continue to deliver the service, value and helpful advice people expect. The development highlights a growing trend among Australian businesses to move technology and corporate functions offshore, aiming to consolidate operations, access specialised capabilities and reduce operating costs. National Australia Bank is investing over AUD 300 million annually to expand its workforce in India.

Supermarket retailer Coles has signed an agreement with Accenture to move several hundred corporate positions, potentially reaching 1,000, to India. Woolworths is another retailer shifting hundreds of corporate roles overseas, impacting employees across finance, human resources and information technology. Officeworks, a Wesfarmers-owned retailer like Bunnings, is moving a significant portion of its Australian support office workforce to a new global centre in Bengaluru, India. That transition is scheduled from December 2026 to June 2027, with full implementation by July 2027.

Bunnings' restructuring aligns with its accelerated investments in artificial intelligence and digital capabilities. The company recently became the first Australian retailer to introduce an AI-powered shopping agent, using Google's Gemini platform. This outsourcing arrangement is part of a wider transformation across parent company Wesfarmers' retail businesses. The broader restructuring reflects pressure on Australian retailers to manage costs amid changing customer expectations and technology adoption.

stories.Headline: MuleSoft finds only 27 percent of 957 average applications are properly connected
stories.Summary:
Engineering leaders often understand their source code better than the technology actually running in production, relying on outdated architecture diagrams, service catalogs and CI/CD pipelines that describe intended systems rather than operational reality, according to TechGig on August 27, 2026. Temporary services become permanent, APIs remain active after migration, and manual cloud resource changes made during incidents are frequently not returned to code. This divergence is not merely an inventory issue but a fundamental engineering, architecture and software risk problem that affects delivery speed and modernisation efforts. MuleSoft's 2026 Connectivity Benchmark Report found that the average organisation uses 957 applications, with only 27 percent properly connected. Development teams often become the de facto integration layer, maintaining custom adapters and duplicated APIs.

Consolidation efforts frequently begin with declared standards rather than observed reality, and without runtime evidence new platforms can be introduced without retiring older critical dependencies, forcing teams to support both. Cyber Asset Intelligence offers a current, accurate view of what technologies are actually in use, where they run, who owns them, what depends on them and whether they still receive traffic. Technical debt is often seen as a code-centric issue, but a significant portion resides between systems as dependency debt, appearing in unsupported runtimes, abandoned APIs, outdated libraries and undocumented data flows. Its most dangerous aspect is invisibility, because without knowing which products depend on a component or how critical it is, effective prioritisation and management are impossible. Governance practices such as SBOMs and code scanning often stop at the pipeline, and a vulnerability report might identify a package in a repository without confirming whether it is deployed, reachable or part of a critical production service.

The rapid deployment of AI coding and production agents introduces new complexities, because these agents can create software, integrations and dependencies at an accelerated pace, potentially worsening duplication and architectural drift. If AI agents operate across stale service catalogs, ungoverned APIs or unclear ownership, existing architectural weaknesses can quickly escalate into automated failures. Managing this complexity requires accurate, machine-readable context about systems, dependencies, ownership and risk, connecting source, build, deployment and runtime data to identify drift and vulnerabilities proactively. Effective governance must extend into runtime, linking the software supply chain to the actual production environment to verify that controls are enforced and that production matches intended designs.

stories.Headline: Sumitomo Life moves to ChatGPT Enterprise after executives pilot the tool and help staff adopt it
stories.Summary:
Sumitomo Life, a Japanese life insurer, began using generative AI at work in 2023, when employees mainly asked questions in chat, and by 2025 about 100 to 150 people, including executives and members of planning teams, had piloted ChatGPT Business. In June 2026 the company moved to ChatGPT Enterprise, and it plans to start expanding AI use to more employees in the second half of fiscal 2026. The insurer worked with OpenAI to assess ChatGPT Enterprise against its security standards, a review that covered how Sumitomo Life could manage workspace access and feature permissions along with OpenAI's policy of excluding business data from model training by default. Sumitomo Life continues to decide how employees can use ChatGPT based on the information they handle and the systems they connect to. Planning teams use ChatGPT to review source material and organize findings when preparing proposals for senior management, and they track developments at other Japanese insurers and find examples from overseas, supplementing public sources with firsthand information and keeping material together in projects with related chats, files, and custom instructions.

Investment teams use statistical analysis to forecast returns and assess risks such as price swings, and ChatGPT helps analysts draft the code for that work, reducing the amount they need to write themselves. Accounting and finance teams also use ChatGPT for research and analysis. The company's executives and managers were among the first to use ChatGPT, and their example and the president's encouragement helped more employees try it in their own work. Kakeru Tateyama, a senior member of the planning department, said that when senior leaders do not understand a new technology it can be hard to get it off the ground, and that here executives and managers were among the first to use it and saw for themselves what it could do, which he thinks made it easier for everyone else to start. Masakazu Obi, a deputy general manager in the planning department, said that if the company takes its existing ways of working for granted it will not get the full benefit of AI, and that the question is whether it can change the processes themselves over the long term.

Kuniaki Nakagawa, manager of the AI Strategy Task Force, said the value of insurance is the peace of mind it brings to customers and society, and that there is something only people can offer, which comes from talking with customers and understanding how they feel. Sumitomo Life tracks how often employees use ChatGPT Enterprise and estimates the return on that investment, with weekly usage over 80%. Estimated ROI averaged 55% for 8 to 15 uses per month, 231% for 16 to 30, and 524% for 101 or more, and the overall average was 203%, based on employee-reported time savings. Its quarterly survey asks employees how often they use ChatGPT, which steps in their work they use it for, and whether they use it with colleagues. For each role in the wider rollout, the insurer will identify which tasks AI can handle, where employees can work alongside it, and which responsibilities people should keep, and over the longer term it is considering AI for more specialized work including underwriting and claims payments, planning to explore new technologies and services with OpenAI as it redesigns workflows with AI in mind.

stories.Headline: OpenAI builds Codex sandbox to limit filesystem and network access for agent commands
stories.Summary:
The articles are a single OpenAI engineering post dated November 18, 2026, titled Inside the Codex sandbox, which says OpenAI built the Codex sandbox so Codex can run commands on a user's computer within filesystem and network limits the user controls. OpenAI says it takes a defense in depth approach to safeguarding agents, with training and alignment plus features in its agentic harness, Codex. The post says running commands on your computer is one of the most common and potentially risky things Codex does. It describes a sandbox as limiting what a program can access while it runs. It gives a photo-organizing example where commands could read and modify files in ~/Pictures while network access is blocked to prevent uploads.

Users configure the sandbox through permission profiles, which define the filesystem and network restrictions for a Codex session, and the post covers defaults, design, configuration, enforcement on macOS, Linux and Windows, and reuse in other tools. With a Git repository as the workspace root, the built-in :workspace profile allows writes within the workspace while keeping directories such as .git and .codex read-only, so Codex can edit source code without seeking permission for every change while preventing direct changes to .codex/config.toml or Git hooks under .git/hooks. It allows broad filesystem reads subject to the user's existing OS permissions, because compilers, runtimes and build tools depend on SDKs, libraries and configuration outside the repository, and restricting reads to the workspace would break many ordinary workflows, with the tradeoff that sensitive files elsewhere, such as config files containing API keys, may remain readable. It disables network access, blocking direct uploads to external services including attempts to exfiltrate data the command can read, and also preventing legitimate operations such as downloading dependencies. The post says these restrictions prevent a large class of bad behavior but harmful actions are still possible, for example the agent could inject malicious code into a locally installed package such as node_modules/prettier, a change that might not appear in git status because node_modules is often ignored by Git, and if the user's editor runs that copy of Prettier on save, simply saving a file could execute the malicious code outside the Codex sandbox.

The post says OpenAI prefers to invest heavily in OS-specific sandboxing rather than virtual machines or containers, so Codex constrains commands running in the user's existing environment instead of moving computation to a separate environment. It says a laptop often serves as a bespoke dev environment that developers can change on a whim, reproducing it in a Docker container can take work, and some workflows still depend on tools that run on the host. It gives the example of developing an iOS app on a Mac, where Codex inside Docker could not run the iOS build toolchain of native Mac executables or launch the iPhone simulator, and a Docker-based workflow could delegate builds and simulator operations to the Mac host but those operations would execute outside the container's sandbox and would need their own restrictions. The harness exposes the OS-specific mechanisms through a common API across macOS, Windows and Linux that takes a command and a permission profile, and if the profile allows limited network access the caller must supply a network proxy to enforce those limits. The post shows a simplified spawn_command_under_sandbox function taking program_and_args, cwd, env, permission_profile and network_proxy and returning a Child handle, and says each child process inherits its parent's sandbox constraints, so restrictions apply throughout the process tree initiated by the command, even to descendants that outlive the original process.

The post says the Codex harness executes tool calls generated by the model, and for coding tasks the most commonly used tool is a shell tool that runs commands much as a user would in an interactive shell such as Bash. It examines the one-shot exec_command shell tool, showing a simplified ExecCommandToolCall class with cmd, workdir, shell, login defaulting to True and timeout_ms of 10_000, and a perform_exec_command function that builds program_and_args from the shell or the SHELL environment variable or /bin/sh with -lc or -c and the command, calls subprocess.Popen with cwd defaulting to the turn's cwd, pipes stdout and merges stderr into stdout, and collects output and exit code. To sandbox the command, the harness replaces subprocess.Popen() with spawn_command_under_sandbox(), supplying the permission profile and, when needed, the network proxy, as shown in perform_exec_command_with_sandboxing. The exec_command tool lets the model request different permissions for an individual command, with sandbox_permissions set to use_default, with_additional_permissions or require_escalated, a justification string only for require_escalated, and additional_permissions only for with_additional_permissions.

The post says the harness decides whether to grant the request, using the default sandbox config for the turn under use_default, expanded access within the sandbox under with_additional_permissions, and execution outside it under require_escalated, evaluating the request based on the user's preferences, for example prompting the user directly or routing the request to auto-review, and if execution is authorized Codex passes the appropriate permission_profile and network_proxy with the original command arguments. The post says the shell tool is the primary consumer of spawn_command_under_sandbox(), and the harness also reuses its sandboxing infrastructure for operations such as reading and modifying local files, and the codex sandbox command lets you incorporate sandboxed command execution into your own tools. A named permission profile lets you reuse the same filesystem and network restrictions across projects, defined under [permissions] in config.toml, and the post gives a profile named dev that extends the built-in :workspace profile with the description "Development with extra read-only protections." The dev profile adds write access to ~/build-cache and places additional restrictions on files in the workspace, with filesystem entries granting read-only access (read), read and write access (write) or blocking access entirely (deny), and the :workspace_roots table lets you define rules for paths relative to a project's workspace roots.

The post says profiles starting with ":" are provided by Codex, and the description is displayed when /permissions is run in the Codex CLI. The post says the Codex CLI by default uses its working directory as its workspace root. The post says the articles leave open how the remaining sections on network permissions, layering configuration and enforcing limits, the codex sandbox command example sandboxing an MCP server, the network proxy, and building on the Codex sandbox for Linux and Windows continue beyond the text provided. It refers readers to the Codex security cookbook for guidance on tailoring sandbox permissions and combining them with other protections in an enterprise environment.

It refers to Unrolling the Codex Agent Loop for how the Codex harness executes tool calls generated by the model. It says the code shown is a simplified version of the actual API and of how the exec_command tool call would be honored without sandboxing. It says the diagram showing how the pieces fit together from configuration to running a sandboxed command is explained in the sections that follow. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Tarek Ziadé runs a 180 billion parameter model on 32GB of RAM using optimized SSD streaming
stories.Summary:
Tarek Ziadé developed a method to run large Mixture of Experts models on limited hardware on November 18, 2026. He utilized a MacBook M5 with 32 GB of unified memory to execute the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next model, which contains 180 billion parameters. This specific model features 48 layers of 512 experts with 10 active experts, totaling 121 GB in FP8 format. The process involves streaming only the necessary experts from the SSD to the memory while keeping dense weights and n-gram tables resident.

The implementation requires installing a specific pull request from the Hugging Face Transformers GitHub repository to enable optimized offloading. To fit the model within the 32 GB limit, Ziadé used 3-bit quantization for the experts and a separate cache pool for different expert sizes. He implemented a system that reads the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed to increase speed. These changes allowed the system to reach a peak memory usage of 25.4 GiB, requiring other applications like web browsers to be closed.

Ziadé explained that he wanted to rely less on online models and run larger ones locally on his hardware. He noted that previous methods like the Accelerate path were too slow, and he aimed to fix offloading directly within the Transformers library. By optimizing the KV cache and using bigger chunks for prefill, he increased prefill speeds from 68 to approximately 228 tokens per second. He stated that streaming experts directly from the SSD now performs within 6 percent of the Strata framework regarding token generation.

stories.Headline: FCA launches AI Spotlight Observatory to help firms monitor AI adoption
stories.Summary:
The Financial Conduct Authority launched the AI Spotlight Observatory on November 19, 2026, to help financial services firms monitor technology adoption. This online platform provides the industry with real-world examples of how artificial intelligence is being integrated across the sector. The regulator developed the tool alongside the technology partner NayaOne and the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship. It serves as a resource for researchers, innovators, and firms to identify new growth opportunities and emerging technologies.

The platform requires no payment for basic access, although registered users can view target client details and request company demonstrations. It currently features AI use cases from more than 200 organisations and covers 150 different areas of activity. These applications include neurosymbolic AI, agentic payments, compliance, and the detection of financial crime. The regulator intends to expand the observatory over time by allowing firms to apply to showcase their own projects.

Jessica Rusu, the chief data, information and intelligence officer at the FCA, is responsible for the initiative. She stated that the agency is committed to helping firms understand how this technology is used because AI creates significant opportunities. Rusu explained that the observatory is an open resource that allows the industry to learn from developments across the sector. This launch is part of a broader programme that includes the Supercharged Sandbox, the AI Lab, and the AI Live Testing initiative.

The agency is also exploring other emerging technologies, including a new initiative launched earlier in November to study quantum computing. The Quantum Experimentation Group will connect national research laboratories and technology providers with banks to test practical applications. These efforts aim to help financial services firms better tackle fraud and money laundering through advanced computing. The regulator will continue to integrate these tools to improve visibility and support firms as they evaluate new technologies.

stories.Headline: Turing security centre publishes UK AI sovereignty roadmap urging a shared open-weight model by late 2027
stories.Summary:
The security research centre at the Alan Turing Institute, known as CETaS, published a sovereignty roadmap for British artificial intelligence on 18 November 2026. This strategic document argues that the United Kingdom should pool its data, money, expertise, and compute to create a medium-sized open-weight model. The plan targets a first build of this sovereign model by late 2027 to ensure essential services remain functional during crises. This approach focuses on resilience through optionality rather than total self-sufficiency, providing a foundation for sensitive work in security, defence, and critical infrastructure.

The roadmap requires the AI Minister to take charge of sovereignty by early 2027 through a new Cabinet sub-committee. It proposes a Strategic AI Capability label for critical firms that commit to investing in British jobs and infrastructure in exchange for faster visas and funding. For public-sector buyers, the plan suggests maintaining two separate model options from different countries to mitigate disruption risks. The government would coordinate this effort through the Prime Minister's office and the AI Taskforce, while the Turing Institute could provide central technical leadership.

Report author Sam Stockwell stated that the choices made over the next 12 to 18 months will decide if the country keeps meaningful control over these technologies. He believes these tools are fundamental to the operation of public services and the broader national economy. The proposal follows a sovereignty vision released in September and arrives as a Commons committee seeks statutory safety rules for frontier AI. While the dual-supplier recommendation is seen as an easy procurement change, the shared sovereign model remains the most ambitious goal requiring government backing.
