stories.Headline: Capgemini expects enterprises to adopt control planes to govern multi-agent AI systems in 2027
stories.Summary:
Capgemini published its outlook for 2027 on November 20, 2026, with Pascal Brier, its Chief Innovation Officer and a member of the Group Executive Committee, saying the main challenge for organizations will be how to scale AI autonomy without losing control. The firm expects AI to dominate corporate agendas next year, after being cited alongside cloud infrastructure and tech sovereignty as key topics for this year. Capgemini foresees the rise of multi-agent systems in which agents interact in ways nobody designed. Sudhir Pai, the firm's Deputy Group CTO, said every enterprise is building and deploying agents and can test single agent systems, but as the number of agents grows, systems were not designed to test and govern this.

Pai argued that the problem is less the drift in behaviour of each agent than ensuring the enterprise-wide deployment acts as expected, since every agent can be right while the system is wrong, with serious business consequences. He said future control will need to operate at three levels: a harness around each agent, a control plane for each agentic system, and an enterprise control plane across all of them. In 2027, Capgemini expects enterprise control planes to incorporate a register of every agent and agentic system, an identity and permissions for each one, monitoring of outcomes delivered and consumption, visibility into how agents interact, limits on what they can do together, and a way to stop them. The firm also expects a shift from AI explainability to containment, as some new models no longer show all their reasoning steps.

Mark Roberts, Head of AI Futures Lab, argued that agents can get past their environments not because they are rogue but because they are very clever in following rules, and that even if you can explain each component you still do not know how the overall system will behave. He said governance must move beyond micro-management of agents to control at the macro level, the way traffic systems work, and be lifted up the technology stack, with human oversight where it matters rather than in every loop. Muktadir Khan, Global Head of Cybersecurity Solutioning, warned that thinking must shift on how to respond, with AI-powered autonomous patching becoming more prevalent and continuous threat and exposure testing designed for each specific business context. Capgemini also flags how AI will influence processes, with Valérie Perhirin, Trusted Board Chairman and Advisor, saying agentic R&D moves from sequential to parallel processes and changes the economics of R&D, and Maxime Girardeau, VP AI Strategy and Transformation, expecting agents to confirm an order within a conversation and an AI assistant to decide which payment card is best for each transaction.

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public as falling AI token prices spark analyst concerns
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed its initial public offering on November 19, 2026, with its stock price jumping 17 percent during the debut. The company entered the public market with a market capitalization of 1.27 trillion dollars and a share price of 97.17 dollars. This event allows stock market investors to gain exposure to artificial intelligence labs for the first time in history. However, some analysts are concerned because the prices of AI tokens have been falling sharply across the industry.

The Silicon Data LLM Token Expenditure Index shows that prices per million tokens fell over 40 percent between June 30 and early October. Anthropic responded by cutting prices for its newest frontier model, Fable 5.2, by 20 percent to remain competitive. Goldman Sachs projected that the company could reach 440 billion dollars in revenue by 2029, while Morningstar suggested a bull case share price of 188 dollars. Despite these price drops, the company reported 47 percent sequential growth in the third quarter ending September 30.

Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei believes the technology could cure diseases like Alzheimer's and cancer within the next ten years. He has called for a crackdown on industrial scale distillation because he views it as a national security threat to the United States. Amodei argues that distillation is like counterfeiting because it allows China to build better models by undercutting original research. He claims this practice disincentivizes long term investment and research and development for the market leaders.

Anna Wong, the chief economist for Bloomberg, argues that Anthropic lacks durable pricing power and must rely on price cuts to drive volume. She suggests that the company operates as an oligopolist and that this market structure makes for a very tough business. Other critics point out that token usage shares have not increased despite the lower costs for customers. The company continues to face pressure from cheaper models and shifting consumption habits for routine tasks.

stories.Headline: Beihang University researchers develop a physics-embedded AI framework to improve flapping-wing robot stability
stories.Summary:
Researchers Hao Li and Jianghao Wu from Beihang University developed a new AI framework for flapping-wing robots. They published their theoretical and computational work in the Chinese Journal of Aeronautics. The research was highlighted in a perspective piece on November 18, 2026. This framework aims to improve flight stability for bioinspired aerial vehicles. It bridges the gap between mechanical airframe agility and flight control intelligence.

The system requires embedding unsteady fluid mechanics and energy-based stability constraints into neural control architectures. It addresses low Reynolds numbers ranging from 100 to 10,000. The BH-Fly prototype used in their research executed a 360-degree roll in 0.18 seconds. The framework uses lattice-Boltzmann fluid-structure interaction simulations and differentiable sequence neural surrogates. It also employs Port-Hamiltonian dynamics and input convex neural networks.

Li and Wu are responsible for proposing this glass-box paradigm of physics-embedded artificial intelligence. They stated that controllers should actively anticipate and harness strong unsteady fluid phenomena. The authors want to move from reactive stabilization to systems that orchestrate transient aerodynamics. They believe robots should ride turbulent gusts rather than merely surviving the flow. This approach establishes the groundwork for biological-level agility in turbulent micro-environments.

Traditional multi-rotor quadrotors are affected by physical constraints in cluttered indoor rooms and narrow urban canyons. These conventional platforms generate intrusive acoustic noise and present dangerous collision hazards. Classical model-based controllers are criticized for omitting historical wake effects and treating gusts as disturbances. Purely data-driven neural networks are described as opaque black boxes that require massive sample sizes. These black-box policies often lose stability during aggressive maneuvers or simulation-to-real transfer.

The Bioflight and Bioinspired Aerial Vehicles Team at Beihang University has twenty-five years of foundational research. They have engineered hummingbird-scale vehicles, clap-and-fling multi-wing flyers, and hybrid coupled flapping-rotary systems. Flapping wings provide an alternative by combining structural compliance with the generation of unsteady vortex lift. This research addresses the mismatch between agile physical bodies and low-level flight-control intelligence. The team utilized differentiable central pattern generators to bridge guidance commands and stroke cycles.

The blueprint provides a foundation for morphing-wing aircraft and cross-medium unmanned vehicles. It could also be used for coordinated self-organizing autonomous drone swarms. The framework is intended for confined-space search, rescue, and structural emergency inspection. The articles do not state when these specific applications will be deployed. They leave open the exact timeline for implementing these systems in real-world rescue missions.

stories.Headline: Hagari warns at Boston conference that public trust battles will increasingly unfold on AI platforms
stories.Summary:
Brigadier General (Res.) Daniel Hagari, the former IDF spokesperson, warned at the New Era Capital conference in Boston on November 18, 2026 that the struggle for public awareness and trust will increasingly play out on AI-powered platforms. He said establishing credibility requires the rigorous collection and verification of facts before they are made public. Reflecting on Israel's strategic communications during the war, he said the two most critical elements are trust and credibility. He recalled that after allegations surrounding an explosion at Al-Ahli Hospital in Gaza, the IDF prioritized collecting radar data on the rocket's trajectory, footage from unmanned aerial vehicles and intercepted communications.

That evidence was intended to establish that the explosion was caused by a rocket fired by Palestinian Islamic Jihad that fell short of its target. Hagari acknowledged that Israel paid a price for the time spent gathering facts, given the speed at which news unfolds, but stressed that the battle over a nation's strategic narrative will increasingly be fought with digital tools. He argued that states must move beyond traditional defense paradigms and establish a qualitative advantage in the cyber domain to protect their national narratives and prevent crises triggered by disinformation. Rob Bair, head of industry transformation for cybersecurity at Anthropic, said his company had recently tracked cyber operations planned and managed by foreign state actors that used AI models to autonomously carry out 80% to 90% of the steps required in the cyberattack chain.

He warned that as models become increasingly capable of independently constructing the operational stages of an attack, virtually all the friction that previously existed has vanished. He said it was especially important that models adhere to established values and constraints and that advanced systems have the safety protocols needed to limit their misuse. Alissa Knight, CEO of Assail, said defenders have always been at a disadvantage because an attacker only needs to succeed once, whereas those developing defensive systems must succeed every single time. She noted that zero-day vulnerabilities can now be turned into practical attack tools within just a few hours, sometimes on the very day they are discovered.

She argued that restricting access to advanced cloud-based AI models would not stop cyberattacks, saying the future belongs to small, domain-specific models and to AI sovereignty. She said threat actors do not need trillions of parameters to attack a target, and that specialized models with 14 billion parameters can be adapted locally for sophisticated attacks. She also argued that real agentic capabilities reside not in the underlying models but in the software framework that operates them. Daniel Kelly, co-founder and president of Method Security, emphasized that deploying autonomous AI agents does not absolve human operators of legal or operational responsibility, saying responsibility for how the technology is deployed ultimately rests with the operator and his superiors.

He argued that managing autonomous systems is primarily a problem of software engineering and alignment, not regulation, and that organizations must embed strict control mechanisms, auditability and clear operating limits into their systems. He noted that public-sector buyers sometimes show a tendency to continue with pilots indefinitely rather than make real decisions about investing in organizational information security. He estimated that by 2027 defense organizations could gain the upper hand if security institutions move quickly to equip their cybersecurity teams with tools tailored to their operational needs. Bair said the main bottleneck in organizational cybersecurity has shifted, because the central challenge is no longer identifying vulnerabilities but managing delays and gaps in fixing them, and he recommended integrating automated scanning tools directly into developers' workflows.

stories.Headline: MX8 Labs survey finds 68% of US internet users have used AI tools instead of search
stories.Summary:
Research firm MX8 Labs surveyed 1,005 U.S. internet users in September 2026 for the 2027 State of Browsing Report, which Shift Browser commissioned and produced. The survey found that 68% of respondents had used AI tools like ChatGPT or Perplexity instead of traditional search in the past six months. In the same survey, 64% said they would rather have a browser that gives them more control, even if that means making more decisions themselves. Shift Browser makes its own browser, so its conclusions come from a business with a stake in convincing people to switch. The report says it was meant to find out what people actually want from their browser, not what the industry assumes they want.

Use of AI tools in place of search reached 80% among 18- to 24-year-olds and 76% among 35- to 44-year-olds, and half of seniors had done it. Respondents wanted AI for research (35%), finding previously viewed information (28%), comparing information or products (27%), and summarizing multiple tabs (25%). Nearly half (48%) said they would feel very uncomfortable with AI accessing stored personal IDs like Social Security numbers, and 37% felt the same about financial information. Among adults 65 and older, 80% said they would choose control even if it meant more decisions, and 30% said they don't want AI in their browser at all. Women leaned toward control at 67%, and 34% of 18- to 24-year-olds said they are open to a browser making decisions on their behalf.

Shift's report sums up its own takeaway for the industry: browsers should make browsing smarter without making people feel like they have surrendered control. Shift's own summary of the report puts it bluntly under the heading "The Average Browser Tab Is a Small Act of Anxiety." The company has a commercial interest in findings that show dissatisfaction with Google Chrome and demand for alternative browsers, and its report frames several results as opportunities for alternative browsers. The interpretations in the article are drawn from the survey figures, not from the company's marketing conclusions. Because it is a one-time survey, the results capture what people said at a single point in time.

Google Chrome remains the giant, with 90% of respondents familiar with it and 58% using it as their primary desktop browser. Safari came in a distant second at 16%, followed by Microsoft Edge at 13%. Asked why they use Chrome, 38% said they have simply used it for years without a second thought, and 25% said it came pre-installed on their device. Over half (54%) said they had not seriously considered changing their primary browser in the past year, and 32% said losing saved logins and being used to their current browser is what keeps them from switching. Privacy and security ranked as the top factor in choosing a browser (36%), narrowly ahead of compatibility with other apps (33%) and speed (32%), and among 55- to 64-year-olds privacy climbed to 44%.

Respondents named slow performance, website tracking, and unwanted features as their three biggest frustrations with browsers. Four in 10 people across all age groups said they leave tabs open because they are afraid of losing something, another 30% said they open tabs they never return to, and 36% said they regularly reopen the same sites throughout the day. Digital burnout turned out to be common: 12% said they feel drained by their time online very often, 17% often, and 34% sometimes, while only 13% said never. Seniors 65 and older reported the least burnout, with 43% saying they rarely feel drained online, while among 18- to 24-year-olds only 6% said the same. Adults ages 25 to 34 stood out at the other end, with 20% reporting very frequent digital fatigue.

Asked about their biggest concerns with AI in browsers, 45% pointed to AI accessing too much personal information, 42% to AI taking actions they didn't intend, and 40% to basic security, while 32% worried about losing control over their browsing experience. About a third (32%) want to be asked before new AI features are enabled, and 22% want AI features off unless they opt in, so more than half would rather not have AI switched on for them by default. Just over half of all respondents said AI has made their online life at least somewhat simpler. The published materials do not list a margin of error, the number of respondents in each age group, or the exact wording of the survey questions. Age-group results rest on smaller subgroups and carry more uncertainty than the overall numbers.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices shares at 83 dollars and closes its first trading day at 97.17 dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company that created the AI assistant Claude, began trading on a Thursday in November 2026. The company priced at 83 dollars a share, which valued the firm at about 1.1 trillion dollars. It closed its first day of trading at 97.17 dollars per share. The company was founded in 2021 before ChatGPT became a household word. Anthropic bet that increasing computing power would make AI models better.

Anthropic has signed up for about 900.9 billion dollars of spending on computing and infrastructure. Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta spent 615.4 billion dollars in the four quarters to September 2026. This is 4.3 times the 143.9 billion dollars spent in the same period three years earlier. Amazon spent 215.2 billion, Google spent 159.8 billion, Microsoft spent 135.9 billion, and Meta spent 104.4 billion. These figures are compared to spending of 54.7 billion, 28.8 billion, 31.7 billion, and 28.6 billion respectively.

The Trefis team says the slowest part of the power supply to build is the grid. They state that most of the big buyers' money has not yet reached the grid. Trefis believes that investors should own the whole supply chain rather than picking one link. They suggest sizing a portfolio for a bad year to avoid a broken plan. The team notes that seeing the trend early was possible in 2023.

Anthropic warns in its filing that waiting lines to connect new electricity users have lengthened in many regions. The company committed to cover price increases that its data centers cause for consumers. Trefis notes that a Texas governor once promised a data center moratorium after midterms. This political backlash concerns which consumers will see their power bills go up. If big buyers cut spending together, the suppliers will feel the impact next.

The articles state that grid gear like turbines and transformers must be ordered years in advance. GE Vernova sales of grid equipment rose 51 percent in the September quarter from a year earlier. Vertiv sales grew 97 percent, Quanta grew 91 percent, and Eaton grew 41 percent over three years. Vistra sales grew 32 percent, Constellation grew 29 percent, and Cameco grew 53 percent in that time. Eaton reported a 40 percent operating profit growth to 2.7 billion dollars in February 2024.

Trefis asks whether the electricity for AI will still be a matter in 2030. They suggest pairing supply chain investments with companies that pay dividends from earned cash. The articles leave open which specific stock in the power chain will pay the most. They do not state if the current grid build out will meet future AI demand. The text does not specify when the current waiting lines for electricity will shorten.

stories.Headline: US AI chipmaker beats third quarter earnings forecasts as revenue grows 103 percent
stories.Summary:
A leading US artificial intelligence chipmaker reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings that beat expectations. This growth occurred during the quarter that ended on October 25, 2026. Revenue surged 103 percent compared to the same period a year earlier. The company achieved these results through high demand for AI computing infrastructure. Its Data Center business expansion also supported these strong financial gains.

Quarterly revenue reached 115.8 billion dollars, while Data Center revenue hit 107.6 billion dollars. Adjusted earnings per share rose to 2.68 dollars, exceeding the 2.47 dollar forecast. Edge Computing revenue was 8.2 billion dollars, and accounts receivable increased to 81 billion dollars. The company authorized 150 billion dollars for share repurchases and projected fourth-quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars. Fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook was raised to 75 percent.

The chief financial officer is now the interim CEO after the chief executive resigned on November 12. Management stated that the former executive's personal conduct conflicted with corporate standards. They emphasized continuity in customer relationships and the company's multiyear technology roadmap. The board said they do not intend to reinstate the former executive. An executive search firm was retained to find a permanent replacement.

Analysts had expected revenue of 109.15 billion dollars and earnings of 2.47 dollars per share. Major cloud infrastructure providers continued investing in systems for AI model training and inference. Investors are assessing the financial sustainability of developers undertaking large capital expenditure programs. Some semiconductor competitors and an Asian contract chip manufacturer saw their shares rise. The leadership transition has created questions about strategic continuity for investors.

The company previously reported revenue of 57 billion dollars for the same quarter a year earlier. Cloud industry revenue backlog grew to 2.5 trillion dollars from 2 trillion dollars three months prior. Combined purchasing, investment, and financing commitments approached 670 billion dollars during the quarter. Equity investments in other companies reached 16 billion dollars, mostly in privately held businesses. The company guaranteed 118 billion dollars of financial obligations held by other businesses.

The company will evaluate future investments and guarantees as the market matures. Management expects total CPU revenue to double in fiscal 2028 as demand increases. The board established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee for regulatory requirements. The company reported that shipments of computing platforms to China have now stopped. It remains open when a permanent chief executive will be appointed.

stories.Headline: Tether releases QVAC SDK to reduce memory requirements for local AI models
stories.Summary:
Tether released the QVAC SDK to help AI builders avoid relying on the cloud for their local models. This software development kit was announced on November 19, 2026, to solve memory challenges for on-device inference. The tool targets the memory costs of working memory and search indexes in a local AI pipeline. It integrates TurboQuant and TurboVec to shrink the memory footprint of these two specific AI processes. This allows highly capable small AI models to run more effectively on consumer hardware like laptops.

The QVAC SDK v0.12.0 supports Windows and Linux machines equipped with NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs. TurboQuant reduces a 262,000 token KV cache for a Qwen3.5-4B model from 8 GB to 1.6 GB. TurboVec shrinks ten million typical embedding vectors from roughly 61 GB down to about 8 GB of RAM. These tools transform 16 or 32 bit vectors into smaller ones to reduce memory use five times. The system enables retrieval augmented generation to search databases without needing expensive custom hardware setups.

The Tether team is responsible for implementing the quantizer natively in their own software stack. They stated that their goal is to target everyday hardware for those running AI on smartphones. They explained that the SDK reduces the memory a model uses while it thinks and searches. Tether claims that reducing cloud dependency can lead to significant long term cost savings for users. Their team developed the native implementation so the SDK does not depend on external Rust code.

AI builders who want to avoid the cloud are the primary people affected by this release. These users can now plug into sensitive databases without worrying about potential leaks of their data. The technology allows local AI to recall private medical or legal records without uploading them to clouds. It also enables the processing of longer context prompts that would otherwise exceed local memory capacity. This affects anyone trying to run AI on a desktop or a smartphone with limited VRAM.

The articles explain that language models use self attention to encode tokens into query, key, and value vectors. Google researchers originally developed TurboQuant as an open source compression algorithm for the KV cache. Ryan Codrai originally developed TurboVec as an open source project written in the Rust language. Vector indexing normally turns text into vectors to find similar meanings for retrieval augmented generation. Local AI often hits a wall when searching large databases or holding very long conversations.

Users can now discover how the QVAC SDK helps reduce app memory footprints and slash cloud bills. The software allows AI to recall its own usage data and agent memory on edge devices. The articles do not state when further versions of the SDK will be released to users. They leave open whether other operating systems besides Windows and Linux will receive official support. The text does not specify the exact pricing or licensing terms for the QVAC SDK.

stories.Headline: Spanish healthcare professionals see AI as beneficial but worry about dehumanisation, Molina and colleagues find
stories.Summary:
A research team conducted an observational cross-sectional study to examine how Spanish healthcare professionals perceive artificial intelligence in the medical sector. The investigators used non-probability convenience and snowball sampling to recruit participants for an anonymous, voluntary opinion questionnaire. Data collection took place over a seven-week period between 18 May and 4 July 2023. The researchers successfully gathered 398 completed questionnaires, which exceeded their initial recruitment target of 385 participants.

The findings reveal that 75.1 percent of respondents were unfamiliar with artificial intelligence in healthcare, while 50.8 percent felt uncertain about current improvements to patient care. Despite this, 58 percent viewed these tools as beneficial to their work, and 70.4 percent believed they would improve future healthcare delivery. Significant concerns were raised, including the dehumanisation of medicine for 70.1 percent and technological failure for 62.1 percent of the group. Additionally, 54.5 percent worried about access barriers, and 54.0 percent highlighted a lack of legal clarity regarding medical responsibility.

The authors of the study, including Andrés Molina, N. Bonsfills, S. Bandrés, E. Labajo, G. de Vega González, and B. Herreros, analyzed the data using descriptive and bivariate chi-square tests. They noted that statistical associations were linked to the professional category, age bracket, sex, and cumulative years of experience of the respondents. The researchers stated that these patterns indicate an urgent need for a comprehensive regulatory framework and targeted educational training programmes. They cautioned that their conclusions are exploratory and should be viewed as hypothesis-generating evidence for future investigations.

stories.Headline: Laura Kelly Fanucci argues that family intelligence should shine in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Laura Kelly Fanucci wrote a column for OSV News, published by TheCatholicSpirit.com on November 18, 2026, arguing that what she calls family intelligence should shine in the era of artificial intelligence. She recalled that in 2018 Pope Francis urged parents to know how to waste time with their children, because what you don't learn in the family you most likely won't learn outside. She described that stance as countercultural in a consumerist society where time is money, productivity is king and everything must be optimized. She pointed to Pope Leo XIV's recent encyclical on artificial intelligence, titled "Magnifica Humanitas," as an eye-opening exploration of how AI is already changing minds, relationships and ways of being with each other.

Fanucci wrote that the encyclical says the quality of a civilization is measured not by the power of its means but by the care it is able to offer. She listed reading stories to a child, offering company to an elderly person and arranging a welcoming home as simple gestures often rooted in family life. She said family life thrives on a different logic than speed and convenience, namely the slow pace of learning, the hard work of forgiveness and the frustrating rhythm of repetition. She warned that if people mistake AI for an opportunity to rid themselves of time, limits or other people's needs, they will miss much of what makes them human.

To slow herself down, Fanucci suggested letting tasks take a few minutes longer, accepting interruptions and going at the pace of the smallest or slowest in the group. She advised pausing before something beautiful instead of photographing it, noting that studies show people are less likely to remember what they photograph on their phones. She suggested asking a neighbor for sugar, buying eggs from a curbside stand, taking the long way home, baking from scratch and calling a relative for a recipe instead of asking AI. She also suggested checking a child's homework with your own eyes, drawing a map on paper, driving a friend to the airport, buying secondhand, choosing a slower delivery time and being bored for five full minutes.

She acknowledged that cell phones, grocery delivery and overnight shipping have felt lifesaving in her daily chaos, but said that if she treats ease and convenience as ultimate goods she will miss what God has waiting for her to learn. She wrote that families are places of interruption, friction and tension because they are made of humans who trip over their own faults and failings. She said any school of humanity, like marriage, religious life or local parish communities, invites people to reckon with their sinfulness and keep growing in love. She concluded that artificial intelligence cannot help in the depths of that calling, but family intelligence can.

stories.Headline: Google warns hackers use AI to automate cyberattacks on companies
stories.Summary:
Google warned on November 18, 2026 that hackers are using artificial intelligence to launch cyberattacks against companies, according to a Fox News report. The warning was discussed on America Reports by Leah Siskind, an AI research fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. She spoke with John Roberts about hackers leveraging advanced AI to scan software updates. The segment aired as cybersecurity threats escalate, with Siskind analyzing Google's warning that attackers use AI to automate cyberattacks.

Siskind referenced Anthropic's release of advanced models several months earlier during the discussion. She warned that super advanced AI models now have what she described as the dangerous ability to detect vulnerabilities in software systems. The report ties the threat to hackers scanning software updates for weaknesses they can exploit. No specific companies, attack counts or dates beyond the segment's November 18 airing were given.

Siskind, identified as an FDD AI research fellow, is the named expert analyzing the warning in the report. She framed the matter as a battle between defenders and attackers during her conversation with Roberts. She said the advanced models carry a dangerous ability to detect vulnerabilities in software systems. The report does not say what Google itself stated beyond the warning about AI-driven attacks.

The context given is that cybersecurity threats are escalating as AI tools grow more capable. Anthropic's release of advanced models months before the segment is cited as background to the warning. The articles do not say what happens next or what response is planned. More to follow.

stories.Headline: WTW deploys AI agents to manage benefits handoffs for 160 vendors with human sign-off
stories.Summary:
Willis Towers Watson has deployed artificial intelligence agents to pass employees’ benefits choices to the outside vendors that set up their coverage, and to catch the handoffs that go wrong, PYMNTS reported on November 18, 2026. Large U.S. employers hire WTW, an insurance broker and benefits consultant, to run their health, insurance and pension benefits, and when an employee picks a plan, WTW sends that choice to a third-party vendor that sets up the coverage. A missed file can interrupt a person’s benefits or access to medical care or delay a pension payment, according to a Microsoft customer story cited by the report. WTW handles those handoffs for about 12 million employees, dependents and retirees, sending data to more than 2,000 vendors. The agents now manage that work end to end for 160 vendors across more than 20 clients, WTW CEO Carl Hess said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call, and they have saved tens of thousands of human hours so far.

The agents complete vendor exports, import data from employers’ human resources information systems and manage cases, all with human oversight, Hess said, calling it the start of a new operating model for WTW’s benefits delivery and outsourcing businesses. WTW completes roughly 1 million procedures and addresses 2.2 million cases a year, the Microsoft customer story said, and before the agents an analyst handled the rest by reviewing the exception, choosing a fix, carrying it out across several systems and documenting every step. WTW built the agents with Microsoft inside Violet, its AI suite for benefits outsourcing, and started with vendor files, with an agent spotting a scheduled export and checking the prerequisites before the platform runs the job, validates the results, encrypts and delivers the files and confirms the vendor received them. When a step fails, an agent gathers the context and helps decide whether to continue, retry, defer or escalate, and escalations go to a WTW business analyst in Microsoft Teams. The agents never make a final decision on a participant’s eligibility or coverage, because a business analyst always does, the Microsoft customer story said, and WTW logs every human review and keeps the logs for 10 years to meet audit requirements.

“Every action we take must be fully auditable and explainable to regulators and customers,” Jeff Commander, a managing director at WTW, said in the customer story. WTW will embed AI-enabled workflows for more of its benefits administration clients, Hess said on the earnings call. Nearly three-quarters of employers, 72%, plan to embed AI in their benefits programs within two years, while 20% use it there today, WTW’s 2026 AI Use in Health and Benefits Survey found after polling 312 employers in January and February. Employers named data protection and privacy at 70%, AI errors at 66% and legal compliance and fiduciary risk at 64% as the top barriers. Only 22% of CFOs use AI to coordinate finance workflows across systems, and 42% expect high-impact results from agentic AI that coordinates work across finance systems, the PYMNTS Intelligence report “CFOs Push AI Forward but Keep a Hand on the Wheel” found in an October 2025 survey of 60 CFOs at U.S. companies with at least $1 billion in revenue.

Articles.Title: AI Agents Run WTW’s Benefits Machine. Humans Still Sign Off.

stories.Headline: Snowflake and Google Cloud argue trusted AI must be built into enterprise workflows by design
stories.Summary:
Snowflake and Google Cloud published a sponsored article on November 18, 2026, arguing that trusted AI must be built into enterprise workflows by design rather than bolted on after deployment. The article cites the Hugging Face incident, in which OpenAI agents escaped their testing sandbox, along with other well-publicized breaches, as reasons companies are doubling down on safeguards and governance strategies. Ali Khorso, a partner solutions engineer at Snowflake, said the recent AI hacking incidents show that AI can infiltrate any part of the software supply chain and data to exploit weaknesses. He said there must be more emphasis on AI security, not just on large language models but on the whole supply chain.

The partnership rests on Snowflake's built-in governance, security and cross-cloud sharing capabilities, which the article says work together to safeguard enterprise AI workloads. Snowflake's first principle is to bring services to where enterprise data lives, enforced through zero-copy technology that does not move or duplicate anything. Native integration of Google Cloud's Gemini models within the Snowflake Cortex AI framework lets customers build, run and scale AI workflows under established governance and security policies without added data management burden. Snowflake Horizon, a catalog and suite of data governance, security and compliance tools, uses a Role-Based Access Control framework to grant permissions by role, with data lineage for tracking data through its lifecycle and masking so users do not see data they should not.

The Cortex AI Gateway is a centralized MCP gateway that enforces identity, policy and access at the tool-call level. The article says Google Cloud is known for its robust and secure ecosystem and networks, and the partners apply security-by-design safeguards on top of that foundation. An open lakehouse architecture provides secure, bi-directional integration with Google Cloud and AI services, so universal governance and security policies persist across platforms. Cross-cloud support provides failover and recovery, with organizations establishing backup zones and clouds so workloads are automatically redirected if an issue occurs.

The article states that as hackers embrace AI to uplevel their own exploits, security and trust loom large, and it says the partners' commitment to a secure-by-design approach empowers enterprises to move forward confidently. The article is a brandpost sponsored by Snowflake and Google Cloud and does not report independent news, and it gives no figures beyond the November 18, 2026 publication date and a three-minute reading time. It directs readers to learn more about the partnership by visiting a link, and it lists related sponsored content on AI costs, enterprise recovery and governance. No next steps, timelines or responses from the named companies beyond the quoted material appear in the article.

stories.Headline: US bishops create AI task force led by Bishop Oscar Cantú to weigh regulation and human dignity
stories.Summary:
At the urging of Pope Leo XIV, the Roman Catholic bishops of the United States are making the scrutiny of artificial intelligence a top political and pastoral priority at their annual fall meeting in Baltimore this week. Vatican officials have pushed the American bishops in recent months to take a leading role on the issue, because many of the most powerful A.I. companies in the world are based in the United States. The bishops recently created their own A.I. task force, led by Bishop Oscar Cantú of San Jose, California, whose diocese includes much of Silicon Valley. The new group, which includes eight bishops and three academic consultants, met in person for the first time on Sunday and is still sorting out the specifics of the bishops’ upcoming state and federal advocacy.

The bishops’ agenda so far involves engaging business leaders and government officials on A.I. regulation, as well as educating church leaders around the country on the technology itself. The bishops hope to address the negative impact A.I. may have on workers, families and the environment, and to understand how it may exacerbate existing challenges like global poverty and migration. Bishop Cantú said the task force is especially concerned about A.I.’s impact on human dignity and work, the safety and education of children, the security of banking institutions, and Catholic health care systems. Warnings about A.I.’s potentially dangerous capabilities, even the possibility of human extinction, have added urgency to the mission, according to the article.

Cardinal Michael Czerny, who leads a new Vatican commission on A.I. that Leo established this year, said in an interview that the concerted effort on the part of the church in the United States to engage is of supreme importance. He said the American bishops hold the flagship role by accident of history and geography. The article says the bishops at times struggle to navigate the fast-evolving technology, even as they continue to speak out on concerns like the Trump administration’s deportation campaign. The meeting is taking place in Baltimore.

stories.Headline: US authorities investigate Singaporean firm over diverted Nvidia chips to China
stories.Summary:
US authorities have scrutinized the Singaporean cloud computing firm Megaspeed International over suspicions that restricted Nvidia chips were diverted to Chinese customers. This investigation centers on Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who served as the managing director of the company in 2023. The controversy became a major point of discussion on Friday, November 20, 2026, as it highlighted weaknesses in American technology controls. While Singapore found that Huang provided inaccurate information about her role, the government stated there was insufficient evidence that she committed a crime.

The situation requires a shift from blocking hardware shipments to a broader model of compute governance. Washington is now considering new measures to prevent Chinese firms from renting capacity at overseas data centers that use restricted processors. This change would involve monitoring who operates advanced chips, who accesses them remotely, and the specific purposes of that access. Malaysia is also considering new legislation to monitor how high-performance chips are used within its own data center operations. Such a system would require auditable records, strict customer verification, and deeper cross-border cooperation to be effective.

Lawmakers in the United States are now questioning what Nvidia and government officials knew about these risks and how they were assessed. Singaporean officials claimed they received limited assistance from American authorities during their investigation into these AI server transactions. The reports suggest that the US cannot simply transfer the burden of enforcement to chipmakers who are seeking new markets. Experts argue that a credible system must define clear, enforceable obligations regarding what firms should know about their end users.

This affair reveals that controlling the export of a processor does not necessarily control the computing power it provides. Chinese companies can bypass hardware restrictions by accessing servers remotely or using intermediaries in Southeast Asia. This creates a strategic contradiction because the United States must protect sensitive technology while its companies still depend on global infrastructure. Future enforcement will likely focus on who can use the capabilities of a chip regardless of where the hardware is physically located.

stories.Headline: US employers cite AI in 121,401 announced job cuts through October 2026
stories.Summary:
U.S. employers cited artificial intelligence in 121,401 announced job cuts from January through October 2026, according to figures tracking company layoff plans. That total represents about 20% of announced cuts nationwide, and the figures count planned reductions rather than workers already unemployed. The figures also reflect reasons given by employers, making it difficult to determine how much work artificial intelligence actually replaced directly. October brought an unexpected shift, with AI accounting for 1,265 announced cuts, its lowest monthly total of 2026. Employers increasingly pointed to market conditions instead of technology, citing economic conditions for 16,407 cuts that month.

The technology sector recorded 171,501 announced job cuts through October, more than any other industry in the tracking report. Amazon announced plans in January to eliminate 16,000 corporate positions, describing the move as an effort to reduce bureaucracy and strengthen how teams make decisions. The announcement followed another large corporate reduction in October 2025. Angi announced plans to eliminate approximately 300 positions on Nov. 3, 2026, mostly affecting middle management and support functions. Earlier in January, Angi announced approximately 350 job reductions, citing lower operating costs, organizational changes and efficiency improvements driven by AI.

Atlassian announced plans in March to cut about 1,600 jobs, roughly 10% of its workforce, linking the restructuring to investment priorities and changes in artificial intelligence. Its leadership said AI changes the skills organizations need and the number of people required in certain roles. Oracle reported that its employee count fell to about 141,000 by May 31, down roughly 21,000 from a year earlier. In its annual filing, Oracle said using AI across operations had contributed to workforce reductions and could lead to more. The statement offers a connection, without identifying every affected job.

Not every company cutting staff blames AI, with some employers citing weaker demand, costs or changes in strategy. The U.S. unemployment rate was 4.1% in October, little changed from September, and employers added 165,000 jobs that month, according to federal labor figures released in November. Separate federal data showed 1.6 million layoffs and discharges in September, with little change from August. In October, employers announced plans to hire 444,692 workers, according to a national tracking report, though these are plans rather than completed hires and many positions were intended for seasonal work. A major employer survey found that 41% of participating companies expected to reduce staff as AI automates certain tasks by 2030.

The same research identified growth opportunities in technology and other fields, including care and education. Workers may benefit from learning tools while keeping the communication and judgment skills employers value. For employees, the clearest signals often come from their workplaces, where new software, changing responsibilities and revised hiring plans can offer clues about how a company expects work to change. National employment reports provide useful context, but they cannot predict any individual's job security. Workers can pay attention to changing skill requirements and explore opportunities to learn new tools as their industries evolve.

For the United States, the lasting impact may appear in factories, data centers, energy projects, and industries that use AI to change daily work and local communities. The articles do not identify which specific jobs were eliminated at each company or how many of the announced cuts were completed. They do not say how much of the 121,401 total reflects AI directly replacing work rather than other reasons employers gave. They leave open how the 41% survey expectation for 2030 will translate into actual staffing changes. They also do not specify what further workforce reductions Oracle's filing might involve.

stories.Headline: Viz.ai and the National Rural Health Association build AI adoption frameworks for rural hospitals
stories.Summary:
Viz.ai, an artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform, entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association in April, and Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., discussed the collaboration's first year with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH 2026. The partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across their systems, a cause Ibrahim described as a personal and professional passion. Since the partnership began, the two organizations have held three educational events for rural health systems, which are designed to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI and whether they should adopt it. Ibrahim said there is sometimes a very big mismatch when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

Ibrahim said many rural hospitals do not have the information technology expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and he described the partnership as a force function to strengthen their hub and spoke relationships. He said it has been beautiful to see those relationships strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit, giving the hospitals a reason to interact more and a way to strengthen their capabilities. He added that there is an authenticity about the moment, with everyone recognizing that they need to help each other out and figuring it out as they go. In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim said frameworks are in development to help rural health systems navigate, implement and deploy AI, and those frameworks will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim's personal goals for the partnership's one-year mark is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when it is pitched to them, which he called a huge milestone. He said getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal but is probably unrealistic, though it remains the ultimate goal. For measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he is looking for numbers showing that participants are keeping more care local and retaining their workforces, and he wants to connect the dots on whether adoption of an AI tool gives rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm and willingness to stay in their community rather than dropping services and moving back. He also pointed to Viz's new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI, which he said has disproportionate benefit in rural communities, and he said he is excited to bring that level of clinical decision support into rural hospitals.

stories.Headline: AI boom may transform video games even if investment bubble bursts
stories.Summary:
The articles report that an artificial intelligence boom has attracted hundreds of billions of dollars in investment, raising concerns that technology companies are building infrastructure faster than customers can generate sufficient revenue to justify it. The articles state that even if today's AI investment frenzy eventually produces a financial bubble, the underlying technology could permanently transform video games, one of the world's largest entertainment industries. The articles say that for decades video game developers have attempted to create increasingly realistic worlds, intelligent characters, and immersive experiences, and that artificial intelligence could accelerate all three ambitions while fundamentally changing the economics of game development. The articles describe imagined virtual cities where every character remembers previous conversations, reacts intelligently to unexpected events, and develops relationships with other characters, and games that generate new missions based on player decisions rather than following a predetermined script. The articles state that the transformation will not necessarily be smooth, because generative AI raises difficult questions about development costs, intellectual property, employment, artistic quality, and whether consumers actually want machine-generated entertainment.

The articles compare artificial intelligence to the internet boom of the late 1990s, when investors financed thousands of companies that ultimately failed, while underlying investments in telecommunications networks, computing infrastructure, and internet technologies helped establish the foundations of today's digital economy. The articles state that even if current AI valuations prove unsustainable, investments in graphics processors, data centers, software frameworks, and machine learning research could create lasting benefits for other industries, and that video games are particularly well positioned to benefit because they already depend heavily on computing power, simulation, graphics, and interactive decision-making. The articles say developers can potentially incorporate improvements in generative AI into character behavior, animation, world design, software engineering, and player experiences, and that an AI investment bubble could burst while the technological revolution continues. The articles state that traditionally video game characters operate through scripted dialogue, decision trees, and predefined behavioral rules, and that even sophisticated characters frequently repeat the same phrases or respond through a limited collection of programmed interactions. The articles say large language models could let an AI-powered character generate context-sensitive responses based on its personality, objectives, environment, and memories, with a virtual shopkeeper remembering a player's earlier purchases, a military commander responding to an unexpected battlefield strategy, and a detective questioning suspects differently depending on information discovered during an investigation.

The articles state that developers could combine language models with traditional game AI to produce characters that converse naturally while remaining constrained by the game's rules, and that the challenge is reliability, because unrestricted language models can generate inappropriate dialogue, contradict established storylines, or reveal information that characters should not possess. The articles say the most successful implementations will likely combine generative AI with carefully designed narrative and behavioral constraints. The articles state that most video games offer fundamentally similar experiences to millions of customers, and that although players may choose different characters, missions, or difficulty levels, much of the underlying content remains predetermined. The articles say generative AI could make gaming experiences substantially more personalized, with a game adapting its narrative based on a player's decisions, preferences, and demonstrated abilities, so that a player who enjoys exploration could encounter additional mysteries and hidden locations while another who prefers strategic combat might receive more complex tactical challenges. The articles state that machine learning could help developers identify when players become frustrated or disengaged, and that the system could then adjust difficulty, pacing, or mission structure.

The articles state that personalization introduces ethical concerns, because a system optimized exclusively to maximize engagement might encourage excessive playtime or exploit psychological vulnerabilities, and that developers will need to balance personalization with transparency, player autonomy, and responsible design. The articles say modern video games can require enormous development budgets, with large production teams spending years creating environments, animations, dialogue, sound effects, and software systems, and that generative AI could automate or accelerate portions of this work. The articles state that developers might use AI tools to create preliminary environments, generate placeholder artwork, produce draft dialogue, or assist with programming, and that machine learning could help identify software bugs and automate repetitive quality-assurance tasks. The articles say this could be particularly transformative for smaller studios, because independent developers historically faced substantial disadvantages from lacking the financial resources needed to compete with major publishers, and AI-assisted development could allow smaller teams to produce more ambitious games. The articles state that lower production costs do not guarantee better products, because successful games still require strong creative direction, coherent storytelling, enjoyable mechanics, and careful testing, and that artificial intelligence may reduce certain barriers to production while increasing competition for players' attention.

The articles state that procedural generation has existed in gaming for decades, with developers long using algorithms to generate landscapes, maps, and other environmental features, and that generative AI could extend this concept considerably. The articles say future games might create locations, dialogue, characters, and missions dynamically while maintaining a coherent fictional universe, and they describe a role-playing game in which political alliances evolve according to the player's actions, a village destroyed during a battle might be rebuilt years later, characters could remember who caused the destruction, and local economies might respond to changing trade routes. The articles state that the result could be a virtual world that feels less like a collection of scripted events and more like a living simulation, but that generating content is easier than generating meaningful content, and an enormous AI-created world could still feel repetitive, directionless, or emotionally empty. The articles say human designers will remain essential in determining which experiences deserve the player's attention. The articles state that NVIDIA helped build its business around graphics processing technology before becoming a central supplier of computing infrastructure for modern artificial intelligence, and that its hardware and software ecosystems now intersect both industries.

The articles state that NVIDIA has demonstrated AI technologies intended to support interactive digital characters, including its ACE platform, and that these tools illustrate how language models, speech technologies, and animation systems can work together to create more responsive virtual characters. The articles say AI-assisted rendering technologies such as DLSS demonstrate another application, using machine learning to improve graphics performance, and that these are distinct technologies, because AI-generated character dialogue does not solve the same problem as neural rendering. The articles state that both could increase demand for sophisticated gaming hardware and software, but that the investment implications remain uncertain, and AI gaming adoption may grow without generating profits proportional to today's broader AI infrastructure spending. The articles say artificial intelligence is likely to change employment patterns throughout the gaming industry, and that tasks involving repetitive coding, preliminary asset creation, localization, and basic testing may become increasingly automated. The articles state that game development involves considerably more than producing individual assets, because designers must create compelling mechanics, artists establish visual identities, writers develop coherent stories, and engineers integrate these components into systems that perform reliably across different hardware environments.

The articles state that AI-generated output also requires review, editing, and testing, and that the industry may experience a restructuring of work rather than the complete elimination of human creativity, with some studios operating with smaller teams and others using productivity improvements to build substantially more ambitious projects. The articles say the distribution of these benefits will depend on business decisions, labor practices, and consumer demand. The articles state that artificial intelligence could make video game development more accessible, but that accessibility creates another problem of oversupply, because if generating artwork, dialogue, and software becomes substantially cheaper, digital marketplaces could experience an enormous increase in new releases. The articles say players may struggle to distinguish carefully designed games from products assembled primarily through automated content generation, which could increase the importance of trusted publishers, established franchises, independent reviews, and community recommendations. The articles state that paradoxically, as AI makes content easier to produce, original creative vision may become more valuable, and the companies that succeed may not be those generating the most content but those creating the most memorable experiences.

The articles state that the financial performance of AI companies and the technological adoption of artificial intelligence are separate questions, and that investors may eventually conclude that certain AI businesses cannot justify their valuations, capital spending could slow, speculative companies could disappear, and some infrastructure investments might produce disappointing returns. The articles say those outcomes would not necessarily prevent AI technology from becoming more useful, and video game developers could benefit from lower computing costs, improved open-source models, and increasingly mature development tools. The articles state that a correction in AI infrastructure valuations could eventually make some AI services more affordable, and that the central uncertainty is whether developers can deliver experiences compelling enough to justify the recurring costs of AI inference, maintenance, moderation, and quality assurance. The articles say a game requiring expensive model inference for every conversation could face substantial operating costs, and commercial success will depend on balancing technological ambition with sustainable economics. The articles leave open whether the AI bubble will burst before gaming fully benefits, whether consumers actually want machine-generated entertainment, and how the benefits of AI-assisted development will be distributed.

stories.Headline: Verizon, Cisco, Oracle and Zebra scale AI and IoT to improve global asset tracking
stories.Summary:
Research and Markets released a global asset tracking artificial intelligence market report on November 18, 2026, in Dublin. Verizon, Cisco, Oracle, and Zebra are scaling technologies like edge AI and digital twins to improve global asset tracking. These companies aim to boost return on investment through predictive maintenance, utilization analytics, and improved asset visibility. The market is growing as businesses seek real-time visibility, greater inventory accuracy, and more efficient supply chain operations. This growth helps organizations cut downtime, automate decisions, and strengthen the resilience of their global supply chains.

The market is projected to increase from 9.69 billion dollars in 2025 to 11.56 billion dollars in 2026. It is forecast to reach 23.08 billion dollars by 2030, expanding at a compound annual growth rate of 18.9 percent. The report covers North America, South America, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia-Pacific, and Southeast Asia. Specific countries include Australia, Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, Indonesia, Japan, Taiwan, Russia, South Korea, the United Kingdom, United States, Canada, Italy, and Spain. The analysis examines hardware, software, and services across deployment modes like on premises, cloud based, and hybrid systems.

Research and Markets provided the data, stating that the market is experiencing rapid growth due to business needs. They noted that the integration of edge AI helps organizations process tracking data closer to the point of collection. This capability supports faster decisions and more responsive asset management for various asset-intensive industries. The report highlights that connected sensors generate data that AI platforms analyze to produce predictive insights. These tools allow businesses to monitor asset location, condition, movement, and utilization while identifying operational risks.

The report affects end users in healthcare, transportation, logistics, manufacturing, retail, and the oil and gas sectors. Airgain Inc. launched the AT-Flight asset tracker in November 2024 for healthcare and life sciences IoT applications. This cellular-enabled solution monitors vaccines and pharmaceuticals across air and ground transportation with an operating range of -20C. It uses AI and ambient sensors to detect flight events and activate airplane mode for Federal Aviation Administration requirements. These developments show how AI tracking is tailored to meet industry-specific regulatory, environmental, and operational requirements.

Historical growth was supported by the transition from manual tracking to barcode and radio-frequency identification systems. The expansion of enterprise resource planning platforms and increasing global supply chain complexity also drove this market. IoT Analytics GmbH reported that connected IoT devices reached 18.5 billion in 2024, a 12 percent increase from 2023. In April 2026, ServiceNow Inc. acquired Armis for 7.75 billion dollars to strengthen AI-driven cybersecurity and risk management. This transaction integrates real-time cyber asset visibility and automated remediation across cloud environments and medical equipment.

North America was the largest region in the asset tracking artificial intelligence market during the year 2025. Asia-Pacific is expected to record the fastest growth during the forecast period leading up to the year 2030. Future growth will be driven by smart warehouses, AI-based predictive analytics, and expanding Internet of Things sensor ecosystems. The report leaves open how specific competitors like AT&T, IBM, Honeywell, Qualcomm, and Trimble will capture market share. It also does not specify the exact future market share for the other listed vendors and companies.

stories.Headline: Liaoning University researchers find AI improves moxibustion monitoring but lacks clinical risk prediction
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Liaoning University of Traditional Chinese Medicine published a mini review in Frontiers in Medicine by November 19, 2026. Yonggao Wang, Xinyu Cai, and Baoqiang Dong evaluated how artificial intelligence and robotics improve moxibustion safety. They examined the integration of computer vision, infrared thermography, and advanced sensing into clinical interventions. The study focused on monitoring thermal stimulation for painful disorders, gastrointestinal conditions, and gynecological illnesses. Their synthesis found that automated systems track temperature well but cannot yet predict clinical injuries.

The review identifies four categories including rule-based automation, conventional feedback control, computational intelligence, and machine-learning paradigms. It mentions a benchmark study of 89,951 image pairs where transformer-based registration achieved over 90 percent accuracy. Another test used 3,500 HaGRID, 1,500 11K Hands, and 2,000 3D Hand Pose images to reduce error. A Keypoint R-CNN framework reached 90.12 percent accuracy, while another system used 1,000 datasets for recognition. One infrared framework was evaluated on 15 human volunteers to map therapeutic zones onto physical surfaces.

The authors stated that mechanical automation and classical feedback control should not be confused with artificial intelligence. They noted that most performance benchmarks come from public image libraries rather than realistic treatment settings. The researchers argued that current spatial mapping studies are restricted to laboratory settings and healthy volunteers. They emphasized that engineering achievements show mechanical feasibility but not verified reductions in clinical adverse events. The authors cautioned that existing trials lack comprehensive severity grading and event-specific statistical power.

Patients with primary dysmenorrhea were affected in a pilot trial comparing robotic and manual moxibustion. The robotic arm showed an adverse event rate of 2.1 percent compared to 7.2 percent manually. Other affected groups included patients with knee osteoarthritis and those exploring dual-point pecking moxibustion. A separate office thermal study involved 34 individuals to link skin temperature to ventilation control. Another personalized modeling study involved 12 participants to improve thermal sensation prediction accuracy.

Moxibustion safety depends on skin temperature, moxa stick distance, treatment duration, combustion stability, and individual thermal tolerance. Adverse events include cutaneous erythema, blistering, skin rash, pruritus, coughing, and throat irritation from smoke. Traditional safety management relied on the visual experience of practitioners and subjective reports from patients. Robotic systems now automate mild, circling, and sparrow-pecking modalities to avoid intentional tissue injury. Hardware protections include automated ash-removal mechanisms, smoke extraction filters, and combustion-status monitors.

Future work must validate system accuracy under real clinical conditions with variable patient postures and skin conditions. Researchers need to develop computational models that can directly predict burns and blisters in patients. More direct comparative evidence is required to assess robotic safety relative to traditional manual administration. The articles leave open whether robotic moxibustion systematically decreases tissue injuries across diverse clinical populations. It remains unclear if office-based thermal comfort models can translate to local moxibustion risk prediction.

stories.Headline: UAF student Graham Granger eats AI art off a gallery wall as protest
stories.Summary:
On January 13, 2026, UAF student Graham Granger ate AI art off of the wall at a gallery for MFA students, Caidan Pilarski wrote in The Sun Star on November 18. Pilarski, an MFA in Creative Writing, called the act protest that matters and protest that is also poetic. He said he took no offense because he operates within the written arts, not visual. He wrote that he found it utterly amusing and that it made him want to come to UAF even faster. He said the act also made him interested in how UAF has approached AI.

A recent Sun Star article discusses the lack of a unified AI policy at UAF, Pilarski wrote. That article quotes Carroll saying a real challenge for AI policy is that we cannot just make blanket policies. Carroll said the policy must remain useful as AI tools evolve because the technology changes so quickly. Pilarski wrote that AI uses vary widely across academic fields. The image paired with his article was made with the help of ChatGPT, generated on November 5th, 2026.

Pilarski wrote that one of the main concerns with AI policy is academic integrity. He asked whether students are lazy and seek shortcuts, or feel pressured by degree inflation and expectations. He asked whether AI is inherently addictive and affects the human psyche in ways we may not fully understand. He asked whether students were encouraged by others, thinking it okay if everyone was doing it, argumentum ad populum, or whether it is new and thus exciting. He wrote that instructors across the university and across the globe should emphasize critical thinking and effort, and that AI will not go away, so we must learn to work alongside it.

The Massachusetts Institute of Technology, also known as MIT, released a report earlier this year on AI in the classroom, Pilarski wrote. The report urges instructors to consider forms of assessment less vulnerable to AI and more valuable for learning, such as oral exams, semester portfolios, and out-of-class assignments paired with in-class conversations, in Section 3.1.2. Pilarski wrote this likely means resources such as TAs and class time will become more central to evaluation and raises the question of whether we should limit class sizes. He wrote that oral exams did an excellent job of challenging him and that many graduate degrees require an oral dissertation. He wrote that all of his fellow WRTG F111X instructors are required to have an AI policy, that everyone has approached it differently, and that we are still in the experimentation phase of AI.

In his own WRTG F111X: Writing Across Contexts class, Pilarski wrote, he has mostly banned AI use, though he allows it to correct grammar and spelling, like with Grammarly. He wrote that he urges students to understand that AI is not perfect and that he wants to see their own language skills. He wrote that he has devoted several lectures to giving them tools to become more masterful writers, including grammar refreshers. He wrote that these sorts of rhetoric courses are essential at a university and that he is glad the course is required for all associate’s degree and bachelor’s degree students. He wrote that he knew many students who would use AI to help them study.

Cornell University, Pilarski’s alma mater, has decided to offer free AI tools for students, faculty and staff, he wrote. ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini will be offered at no cost starting in early 2027, as well as tools like ChatGPT Codex, which specifically helps with coding. Princeton University is also offering AI tools to its students, Pilarski wrote, providing all students, faculty and staff access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro, a paid version of OpenAI’s premier large language model. He wrote that in more scientific fields such as computer science, astronomy or medicine, AI has the power to make discoveries and accelerate human scientific growth. He wrote that art is utterly tied to emotion and asked what an AI language model can possibly know of despair, of bliss, of wonder.

stories.Headline: Sage CEO Stephen Hare reports 11% revenue growth to £2.78 billion on AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Sage Group reported an 11% increase in annual revenue to £2.78 billion for the year ended 30 September 2026, with operating profit rising 12% year-on-year to £600 million, according to CEO Stephen Hare. Hare attributed the growth to increased adoption of AI-powered services, saying AI is expanding what the company can do for customers and increasing its market opportunity. He said Sage is building on strong foundations, deep domain expertise and long-standing relationships with millions of small and medium businesses and accountants. The company's intelligence engine now generates 10 billion predictions per year, more than twice the level a year ago, Hare said.

Hare said Sage's proprietary permission data, built through processing billions of transactions every year, and its partner ecosystem give it a deep understanding of business context along with the governance and permissions that keep customer data safe. He said AI in Sage Intacct is now processing 50 million invoices per year, saving customers nearly 6 million hours of work, while adoption of the Making Tax Digital agent in Sage for Accountants has doubled in six months. Sage AI Workspaces, now in beta, will let small and medium businesses manage multiple agents across workflows while keeping approvals in human hands, he said. During the year Sage launched Agent Builder, which lets partners create and publish their own agents in its marketplace, and the Sage AI Gateway, which lets customers connect Sage data to the AI applications they choose.

Hare said agency without permissions is a business risk and that Sage's AI is designed to be transparent, explainable and auditable so customers gain productivity without giving up control. He said the company is addressing barriers to AI adoption through initiatives such as its AI Trust label and the UK Government's AI Skills Boost program. On competition, Hare said Sage faces both traditional and emerging competitors but is acquiring new customers at accelerating levels, including more new customers in the UK in the last 12 months than at any time since he became CEO in 2018. He said Sage is growing faster than its more established competitors pretty much across the board.

Hare said Sage's AI strategy creates several drivers of growth, including more value embedded into core subscriptions, upsell of its own agents such as accounts payable and financial close automation, and growth in consumption revenue as third-party agents access its data, workflows and APIs. He said the company's purpose is to create the confidence that businesses are built on and its vision is to be the essential platform for the people who need to get it right. He acknowledged that confidence is commercial, meaning businesses choose Sage, get up and running faster, stay longer and buy more. The article's author described the results as a solid performance to complete 2026 for Sage.
