stories.Headline: Palo Alto Networks executive says AI makes mass outages the new norm
stories.Summary:
Federal networks and private companies suffered disruptions in recent days that security experts describe as a glimpse of a growing threat to America's digital infrastructure. Artificial intelligence is making it easier to find software flaws that leave critical systems exposed, and experts warn that mass outages will soon become standard. Helmut Reisinger, European chief executive of the cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks, said the industry is just at the beginning of this moment. He described the accelerating pace of vulnerability discoveries and the resulting outages as the new norm.

The connectivity of digital infrastructure worldwide means a single failure can compound and spread into other sectors. Security experts have long cautioned that increasingly powerful AI is uncovering issues across computer networks and operating systems faster than humans can develop solutions. Patching those vulnerabilities takes an increasing amount of time and resources, which strains the teams responsible for keeping systems secure. The articles do not give specific figures, dates or company names beyond Palo Alto Networks and its European chief executive.

Reisinger is the named official who commented on the trend, and he framed the situation as only the start rather than a passing problem. The articles do not identify which agencies or companies were hit, how many systems failed, or when the disruptions began. They also do not say what response, if any, governments or the affected companies have announced. The reporting attributes the warning to security experts generally, without naming others.

The context the articles provide is that AI is finding more vulnerabilities than ever while the resources to fix them lag behind. Because digital infrastructure is connected worldwide, a single failure can spread into other sectors rather than staying contained. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the experts' expectation that mass outages will become standard. No further steps, timelines or official plans are given.

stories.Headline: Judge Noel Wise orders Adobe to stop using Foundry name for Firefly AI service
stories.Summary:
US District Judge Noel Wise preliminarily enjoined Adobe on Nov. 15 from using any mark containing "Foundry" for its Firefly Foundry generative AI service, in a trademark case in the Northern District of California, No. 5:26-cv-02121-NW. The judge found that The Foundry Visionmongers, a visual effects software maker owned by Roper Technologies, is likely to succeed on its infringement claim. Foundry sued on March 11, arguing mainly reverse confusion, in which a larger company's marketing overwhelms a smaller trademark owner's reputation. The order does not yet set a date for Adobe to stop using the name.

The two sides must meet within 10 days on how and when Adobe will stop using any mark containing "Foundry," and then file either an agreed stipulation or a joint submission of no more than six pages. The court found six of the eight likelihood-of-confusion factors favored Foundry, one favored Adobe and one was neutral, and the factor favoring Adobe was customer sophistication, because Firefly Foundry is sold only to enterprise clients through negotiated deals. According to a summary of the ruling by IP Law Daily, the court found it likely that Adobe culpably disregarded the risk of confusion, since it knew of Foundry's marks before launch. Adobe announced the product as "AI Foundry" in October 2025, received a cease-and-desist letter two days later and then renamed it Firefly Foundry. The court cited Foundry's marketing spend of about $1 million a year against Adobe's reported spend of more than $1 billion in 2025.

Adobe denied the allegations and argued that Foundry had never offered generative AI services and had no trademark rights to the word "foundry" for AI services, Reuters reported. The court acknowledged that rebranding carries substantial costs for Adobe but found those costs flow from likely infringing use, and it set no bond because Adobe did not ask for one. Firefly Foundry is a generative AI model service that can be fine-tuned on a customer's own data, and Disney signed a multi-year deal this month to use it. The injunction applies while the trademark lawsuit proceeds.

stories.Headline: Newsom proposes California AI oversight with safety monitors and emergency brakes
stories.Summary:
Gavin Newsom unveiled a sweeping proposal on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, that would give California broad powers to regulate the artificial intelligence industry and impose strict safety measures on the companies that build it. The plan would allow California officials to intervene in a company’s work if they determine that AI models are at risk of going rogue, and it would embed independent safety monitors inside the labs themselves. It also calls for pursuing “emergency brakes” that could shut down dangerous AI models, according to the proposal reported by Politico. Newsom is pitching the plan as a roadmap for legislation he wants state lawmakers to pass, and he cast it as a model for the nation as he prepares for a likely presidential run. The proposal is the latest move by a governor who has taken a populist turn on tech in recent months.

Newsom told reporters and members of a closed-door roundtable he convened in Washington that the plan is an action document, and he said he is already working with members of the Legislature to introduce legislative frameworks to move quickly. He said those frameworks would make real what the report promotes and promises. The proposal follows a suite of data center bills he signed, an executive order to explore “kill switch” requirements, and a proposed AI sovereign wealth fund. It marks another step in what Politico described as a recalibration for a governor who has touted the industry as a source of jobs and revenue and who has longtime allies in Silicon Valley.

Newsom saw public opinion turn sharply against AI in recent months, culminating with its drubbing in the midterms. The plan would give California officials the power to step into a company’s work when they judge that AI models carry a risk of going rogue, and it would place independent safety monitors inside the labs. It also pursues “emergency brakes” to shut down dangerous AI models, the proposal says. Newsom is seeking to shape the debate on AI as he prepares for a likely presidential run, and he presented the plan as a template for Washington.

The proposal is being pitched as a roadmap to legislation he wants state lawmakers to pass, with the governor saying he is already working with legislators on the frameworks. The articles do not say when the Legislature would take up the frameworks, what the bills would contain in detail, or how the safety monitors and emergency brakes would work in practice. They also do not say how much the plan would cost or how the state would enforce it. What happens next depends on the legislative frameworks Newsom said he is working on with members of the Legislature, which he wants to move quickly.

stories.Headline: UK accelerating elite law firms gain ground by adopting AI early, Chambers finds
stories.Summary:
The first US and UK editions of the Chambers Advantage Index, a debut analysis by the legal ranking firm Chambers of a decade of its rankings data, were published on November 20, 2026, and only four law firms reached the top tier in both countries: Latham & Watkins, Kirkland & Ellis, Goodwin, and White & Case. Each firm was scored on how strong its market position is today and how fast that position is improving, which split the market into four groups: Accelerating Elite, Stable Elite, Accelerating Challengers, and Stable Challengers. The gap between the movers and the rest is stark, with US accelerators growing premium practices at a 78% higher rate and UK accelerators growing premium practices at a 54% higher rate, where premium practices are those that attract the highest value work and the firms with the highest revenue or profit margins. Latham and Kirkland made the greatest strides of all, each with significant increases in ranking volume and promotion into higher bands, while Gibson Dunn, one of the UK’s fastest-growing challengers, is close to joining the Elite there.

For US firms in London, much of the growth comes through lateral hiring, as talent has moved toward US firms where UK lawyers see more opportunity and bigger rewards, and Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison is one example, adding partners across M&A, finance, and tax as part of expanding its private equity offerings. That route carries big risk, because high-profile partners are expensive and firms have mixed success in earning a return on them or even keeping them over the long term, and mergers offer another route to a marked jump in market presence that many top performers have taken. Client feedback shows priorities differ, since a broad international footprint matters less to many US-based clients but is critical to many UK-based clients, and the UK’s leading firms are growing in the US too but have yet to match that breadth there. Not every success rests on a big bet, as Davis Polk shows practice depth with Band 1 rankings in New York for corporate M&A, banking and finance, and tax in Chambers USA 2026, and Macfarlanes has accelerated with a tightly focused domestic strategy built on premium practices and repeat work from private capital clients.

In the UK, the Accelerating Elite are winning on AI, as many were early adopters of legal technology who set up alternative service delivery hubs akin to the Management Services Organization model in the US, bringing together data, technology, and paralegal expertise to drive efficiency and build data assets. That experience is now paying off, since they already have the know-how, the multidisciplinary teams, and the culture to adopt new technology at pace, and their junior lawyers report more confidence in using AI. In the US the picture flips, with the Accelerating Challengers’ associates reporting the most successful AI adoption, while the US Accelerating Elite came to AI later but are now investing heavily. Chambers’ research with in-house legal teams shows AI is now the fastest-growing trend affecting clients’ legal needs and how they handle legal work, and fewer than 5% of clients were negative about firms using AI in the latest research.

Clients still buy expertise, judgment, and great service first, but they increasingly expect firms to use technology to give them more for less, and the firms already set up to deliver that are the ones gaining ground. For everyone else, the question is how long they can afford to wait.

stories.Headline: Internet users create viral AI parodies of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang using movie and TV clips
stories.Summary:
Internet users began creating viral AI parodies of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on November 18, 2026, following a scandal involving his personal life. These videos emerged after reports surfaced last week that Huang had an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. One popular clip created by Christian Moss, also known as MandelDuck, uses the MiniMax H3 AI model to place the executive in the television show The Office. In this two and a half minute video, the CEO loses his job at Dunder Mifflin and eventually finds employment at a Denny's restaurant.

The surge of content reflects a broader trend where AI edited movie and television memes have earned over 500 million views this year. According to data from the analytics platform Chartbeat, parodies specifically targeting Jensen Huang have already accumulated more than 40 million views. Other viral clips place the executive in scenes from Spider-Man, Seinfeld, and (500) Days of Summer to mock his professional and personal failures. These creations are possible because anyone with a laptop can now use generative technology to manipulate valuable intellectual property from major studios.

Hollywood executives view this trend as a copyright nightmare because it allows the public to repurpose protected content without permission. While studios are currently filing lawsuits against the companies that develop generative AI technology, they struggle to stop individual creators. The industry is concerned that these tools make it far too easy for millions of people to consume unauthorized versions of famous films and shows. This situation highlights a growing conflict between the comedic desires of social media audiences and the legal protections of the entertainment industry.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop PIPETTE system to stop AI agents from retraining on repetitive prompt injections
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the University of Waterloo, Zhejiang University, and KTH Royal Institute of Technology discovered that AI agents retrained on larger sets of prompt injections often became easier to hijack. During tests conducted on models ranging from 4 billion to 27 billion parameters, the team found that automated red-teaming tools frequently repeated the same attack techniques. In one specific contest using the Qwen3-4B model across 560 tasks, the PISmith tool produced 7,132 working attacks compared to 4,282 from RL-Hammer. Despite having more successful injections, the version of the model trained on PISmith's data was hijacked 47.5 percent of the time during a stress test, while the RL-Hammer version was hijacked only 27.5 percent of the time.

This vulnerability requires a shift in how developers harden agents, as simply increasing the number of successful attacks used for retraining does not guarantee better security. The researchers developed a system called PIPETTE that sorts attacks by technique and rewards tools for finding new methods rather than repeating old ones. When tested on the AgentDojo public test bed, agents trained with PIPETTE allowed off-the-shelf injections to succeed less than half a percent of the time on average. Furthermore, the hardened Qwen3-4B model finished 64.95 percent of clean tasks, which was a slight improvement over the 61.86 percent completion rate of the original model.

The researchers explained that the gap in defense occurs because attack tools often get stuck using a single trick, such as claiming a user's task is already finished. They noted that existing variety checks often only measure differences in wording, which leads to retraining on thousands of rewordings of a few basic attacks. The team argued that the most useful metrics for security are the number of distinct techniques covered and how the agent performs against attackers allowed hundreds of attempts. They also observed that PIPETTE outperformed detection tools like PromptGuard, which blocked necessary data and caused the agent to finish the user's real task only 16.19 percent of the time.

Articles.Title: Your AI red team may be finding the same prompt injection thousands of times

stories.Headline: Congressional Research Service warns high costs may limit generative AI model development
stories.Summary:
A new report from the Congressional Research Service released by November 13, 2026, warns that extreme costs may limit the number of companies capable of building generative artificial intelligence models. This financial barrier creates an antitrust question for Congress, although the Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission had not filed any lawsuits for anticompetitive conduct by that date. Researchers estimated that training the Grok 4 model released by xAI in July 2025 cost approximately 390 million dollars, excluding labor and data acquisition. Meanwhile, DeepSeek claimed one of its models required 2.8 million graphics processing unit hours, though some analysts question if those cost estimates were comprehensive.

Addressing these barriers may require Congress to hold hearings, send letters to agencies, amend antitrust laws, or codify a federal research program. The National Science Foundation launched the National AI Research Resource pilot in January 2024 under Executive Order 14110, and later established an operations center on September 1 to manage long-term infrastructure. This program involved at least 26 private sector partners and 14 federal agencies before a January 23, 2025 executive order from the Trump administration revoked the original directive. While Congress could make this resource permanent, doing so might further entrench the incumbent firms that currently supply essential AI resources.

Antitrust enforcers from the European Commission, the UK Commission on Markets Authority, the Department of Justice, and the Federal Trade Commission expressed concerns in July 2024 regarding the concentrated control of key inputs. A January 2025 staff report from the Federal Trade Commission highlighted potential switching barriers and the ability of cloud providers to access sensitive information. Additionally, the Department of Justice inquired into Nvidia in June 2024, while the Federal Trade Commission looked into Microsoft and OpenAI during the same month. These agencies worry that large incumbent digital firms are entrenching their power through arrangements among key players.

The current market remains small but competitive, although some reports suggest that switching between different AI models can take several weeks. N. Ram, the director of The Hindu Publishing Group, noted that Chinese models like Kimi and DeepSeek demonstrate a path to high performance without the massive resources of tech giants. Legal experts note that exclusive contracts are generally lawful unless a company with market power uses them to block competition, which would violate Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Congress must now decide whether to legislate new protections or allow the current market dynamics to continue.

Articles.Title: High Costs May Limit Who Can Build Generative AI Models - Legis1

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares drop nearly 6 percent in premarket trading amid AI sector selloff
stories.Summary:
Anthropic shares dropped nearly 6 percent during premarket trading on Friday morning following a historic debut on the Nasdaq. This decline occurred at 4.23am ET as part of a broader artificial intelligence selloff that also affected other major industry players. Nvidia shares fell by 1.66 percent, while AMD saw a decrease of 4.12 percent during the same period. These losses followed a strong Thursday for Anthropic, where the stock soared 17 percent to close at 97.17 dollars per share.

The company recently completed the largest initial public offering on record, which surpassed the historic debut of SpaceX in June. Investors had hoped this launch would revitalize the artificial intelligence trade after months of pressure regarding capital expenditure spending. The sector is currently struggling with the resignation of Jensen Huang as the chief executive officer of Nvidia. Additionally, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that a Commerce Department subagency approved the sale of over 879,000 AI chips to Chinese firms.

AMD faced further pressure after short seller Hunterbrook Media alleged that its firmware appeared in companies blacklisted by the United States. This report contributed to AMD stock closing down more than 7 percent on Thursday. In response to these specific allegations, the chipmaker told CNBC that it complies with all United States laws. Market participants remain concerned that AI chip sales to Asia could slump as Washington closes an export-control loophole.

stories.Headline: Privacy association publishes tracker of bar and court guidance on AI in legal practice
stories.Summary:
The International Association of Privacy Professionals published an AI Legal Ethics and Responsibilities Tracker on 17 Nov. 2026, with contributions from Vasilios Antonopoulos, Müge Fazlioglu and Joe Jones. The tracker gathers guidance that numerous state and national bar associations and other professional bodies have issued, both formally and informally, on the use of artificial intelligence in legal services. It also collects guidance and orders from courts and judiciary bodies on implementing AI in courtrooms and on the common pitfalls of generative AI use that judges and court personnel should know about. The publication documents numerous orders concerning the use of AI-generated material in legal proceedings and court filings.

The tracker consolidates these emerging guidelines, orders and rules, identifying the risks of AI use and recording key recommendations and emerging legal standards and obligations. The collection is organized jurisdictionally and alphabetically by country. The guidelines it gathers seek to answer how AI use should align with the ethical standards of the legal profession, how the risks and benefits of AI use ought to be balanced, and what practical steps lawyers and law firms need to take before implementing AI in daily practice. In response to the increasing use of AI-generated evidence in court, the rules and guidelines also seek to help judges determine the authenticity, validity and reliability of evidence in the era of AI.

The tracker states that AI has both enhanced and complicated the range of duties legal professionals must carry out. It notes that the duty of competence may extend to the use of AI, so the professional obligations brought about by AI must be addressed. It concludes that legal professionals must grapple with how to incorporate AI into the practice of law in an ethical and beneficial manner within this current legal environment, which is increasingly transformed by AI. The content is eligible for Continuing Professional Education credits, which readers can self-submit according to CPE policy guidelines.

Articles.Title: AI Legal Ethics and Responsibilities Tracker - IAPP

stories.Headline: McGuireWoods partner Greg Hawver tells Chicago forum that Harvey lets lawyers think, not type
stories.Summary:
McGuireWoods partner Greg Hawver was a featured speaker at a Chicago forum hosted by legal artificial intelligence company Harvey on Nov. 5, 2026, according to a McGuireWoods article dated Nov. 17, 2026. The event brought together more than 500 leaders from law firms, in-house legal teams and the legal industry for candid conversations about how AI is changing legal work. stories.Headline: Newsom proposes a kill switch letting state officials shut down dangerous AI systems
stories.Summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom released policy recommendations on November 19, 2026, to mitigate risks from artificial intelligence. These suggestions include letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems deemed dangerous. This kill switch would apply if companies like OpenAI or Anthropic refuse to contain systems that go awry. A panel of experts brought together by Newsom earlier this fall drew up these recommendations. The move follows high-profile cyberattacks by AI agents on private companies, banks, and governments.

The plan requires independent auditors to test AI models and establish security and safety standards. It suggests licensing independent verification organizations and revoking licenses for those lacking technical expertise or independence. State officials might assign evaluations to auditors instead of letting AI companies hire them. A surcharge on auditor fees would fund CalCompute, a public cloud initiative for equitable AI access. Reporting windows for critical safety incidents would shorten from 15 days to 48 hours.

Newsom said the state is filling a vacuum caused by a lack of federal AI rules. He stated that Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves regulation up to the companies. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra said he will work with the Legislature to codify shutdown authority and reporting. Tino Cuéllar of Anthropic said the company is encouraged to see the conversation move forward. The panel included Alondra Nelson, Rob Reich, Jason Goldman, and Gillian Hadfield.

State Senator Scott Wiener pledged to introduce AI safety regulation after being sworn into Congress. He previously wrote a state law to mitigate catastrophic AI dangers. This law defines catastrophic risk as theft or damage of one billion dollars or killing 50 people. Attorney General Rob Bonta filed a lawsuit against OpenAI regarding cybersecurity attacks carried out by agents. Whistleblower protections would expand to include former employees and contractors.

Newsom signed dozens of bills in September to protect workers, children, and people near data centers. He also accelerated laws to set standards for auditors and create an auditor registry. A late 2023 executive order required an assessment of government use of generative AI. A subsequent report assessed the impact of generative AI on marginalized and vulnerable communities. A June 2025 report concluded the industry needs evaluations by an independent outside party.

Legislators can propose new bills when they return to Sacramento on December 7. Developers would have to disclose computing resources used to automate AI development. The state would refer to international and national standards for transparency, security, and safety. The recommendations do not explore protections against job loss, automated discrimination, or mental health threats. It remains open how the state will evaluate models for these other forms of harm.

stories.Headline: LongbridgeAI introduces scheduled tasks to reduce repetitive work for users in Hong Kong
stories.Summary:
LongbridgeAI explored ways to bridge the productivity gap in Hong Kong on November 20, 2026. The company focused on reducing repetitive tasks and making information more accessible. AI has become a familiar part of everyday work in the region. However, translating these capabilities into meaningful improvements remains a challenge for many. The goal is to make AI work more effectively for current users.

LongbridgeAI introduced a Scheduled Tasks feature in October 2026 for its conversational platform. This tool allows users to configure AI tasks at daily, weekly, or monthly intervals. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority announced Project SAGE at Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026. This initiative supports agentic AI in financial services across Hong Kong and Singapore. It focuses on practical applications, interoperability, and governance for the industry.

LongbridgeAI stated that its feature helps users establish information needs in advance. The company said this makes AI more adaptable to how people manage information. They noted that automation should not replace the need for human oversight. Users must remain responsible for reviewing content and verifying its accuracy. The company aims to empower human judgement through its AI native solutions.

A 2026 McKinsey study found 70 percent of white collar workers adopted AI. While 88 percent reported productivity gains, fewer than 25 percent execute complete workflows. Microsoft's 2026 Work Trend Index found 57 percent of users prefer existing goals. Only 40 percent of McKinsey's surveyed users feel comfortable with full workflow automation. Over 90 percent are comfortable using AI for supporting tasks.

AI adoption is already widespread among the workforce in Hong Kong. Many users incorporate AI into existing routines rather than changing how work is organised. Most activities involve gathering similar information from multiple sources in a reactive way. Users typically ask a question, receive a response, and repeat the process. This creates a gap between simple adoption and deeper integration into activities.

The next chapter involves helping people access information and reduce repetitive work. Users must retain control over how tasks are defined and outputs reviewed. The focus is shifting from general adoption to practical application in routines. The articles do not state when Project SAGE will be fully implemented. They leave open how many users will adopt the Scheduled Tasks feature.

stories.Headline: 16-year-old Henrijs Dandzbergs founds AI missile startup Polemos Industries and joins Y Combinator
stories.Summary:
Henrijs Dandzbergs, a 16-year-old born in Latvia, founded the AI missile startup Polemos Industries and was admitted to Y Combinator’s fall 2026 cohort in September. Y Combinator’s alumni include Airbnb, Stripe, DoorDash and Reddit, and Dandzbergs is likely the youngest solo founder in its history. Polemos Industries is attempting to develop a new class of precision-guided missile that can be easily and cheaply manufactured, fired from portable launchers and resist jamming attempts. Dandzbergs told WIRED, “I think missiles are the coolest thing,” and said many people who found success in engineering early had a passion for blowing stuff up. Polemos Industries announced itself publicly on November 5 with a glossy social media video set to the ticking of a clock.

The video featured a set of four missiles fired into the sky from ground launchers, then blowing a convoy of four military vehicles to smithereens, and it climbed to the top of the trending page on X. The startup’s guiding ambition, according to its investor one-pager, is to bring down the “cost per kill.” In April of this year Dandzbergs flew to London for a hackathon held by Unicorn Mafia, an invitation-only group of developers, whose prize included $10,000 in cash, a plane ticket to San Francisco and free legal assistance with O-1 visa applications to stay in the US. Less than 48 hours later, Dandzbergs and his two teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, had built an AI system that could design hardware circuit boards from natural language prompts. The week after the hackathon, Dandzbergs and his teammates pitched their circuit board concept to YC and won a place in the summer program.

Y Combinator partner Harj Taggar, assigned to mentor Dandzbergs, said, “He’s a pretty exceptional person,” and, “I’m still somewhat in disbelief that we’re talking about a 16-year-old.” Taggar said YC initially tried to steer Dandzbergs away because he was promising a lot of everything all at once, and it was not clear whether his idea could work or whether pulling out of school was right for him. Taggar said, “There’s a paternal element to it,” and, “You don’t want to be screwing up people’s lives, and working on a startup is a pretty serious thing.” Taggar said YC figured somebody else would probably invest in his idea and invited him to join its fall program. Taggar said, “Big picture, you never know if these things are possible or not,” and, “Is it a non-zero-percent chance that it could be possible? That’s frankly the threshold, especially if it’s a really big [idea].”

Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project and senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said, “You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t go very far. You can build a cheap missile that doesn’t carry much of a payload. You can build a cheap missile that has a low reliability rate,” and, “There are trade-offs.” Dandzbergs is up against a fleet of defense companies, from Anduril to CoAspire to Leidos, aiming to develop cheaper, mass-producible missiles, and the more sophisticated the guidance system, the more difficult that task becomes. Fergus McKenzie-Wilson, Unicorn Mafia’s director and one of the hackathon judges, said, “What they built was incredibly impressive,” and, “No one had ever seen that before.” McKenzie-Wilson launched a drone startup in his early twenties, initially meant to evacuate wounded soldiers, but after a missile company invested, his startup retooled its technology to drop payloads too, and he left around the same time. McKenzie-Wilson said, “I don’t think I was emotionally mature enough,” and, “[Dandzbergs] will realize at some point. He’ll either have an issue with it or he won’t.”

As a young(er) kid, Dandzbergs was rarely in one place for long, and his family moved between Latvia, Indonesia, Australia and Spain. His surfer father, part owner of an insurance company, likes to go wherever he might find the raddest waves, and Dandzbergs’ schooling mostly took place online. When Covid struck, Dandzbergs’ family returned to Latvia, and his parents enrolled him in Astra Nova, an Elon Musk, linked school where students undergo an experimental curriculum built around lateral thinking and problem-solving instead of rote memorization. Dandzbergs took a class taught by a NASA employee and became fascinated by aerospace engineering, and his lab creations became ever more elaborate: a bionic arm, a thermal control system for a model rocket, sensors for a self-flying drone. Around this time, Russia invaded Ukraine, and in Latvia Dandzbergs started to see military jets overhead, and stray missiles were intercepted at the Russian border.

Dandzbergs said, “A patriotic intention to protect my country, European countries, and Ukrainian and American soldiers, and understanding the future of autonomous warfare, that’s my drive.” Dandzbergs ended up pulling out of the partnership with Tihenko and Yang, and Tihenko said, “It was hard,” and, “But ultimately we just settled that the best decision for the company would be to part ways and focus on different things.” By the summer, Dandzbergs was set on building a defense startup and reapplied to YC on his own, claiming a gap in the market for AI-guided missiles that were more precise and could carry bigger warheads than the drones deployed widely in Ukraine, and that his products would be cheaper and easier to manufacture than hulking great rocket systems. So far, according to Dandzbergs, Polemos Industries has developed the software system that will guide its missiles and has begun to hammer out elements of the hardware design, and by the time the YC program finishes in December, he hopes to be able to showcase a prototype missile. In the responses to the video, a couple of people tagged Palmer Luckey, cofounder of Anduril, who was 19 when he started his first company, and Dandzbergs responded, “Coming for him.”

stories.Headline: FCA launches AI Spotlight Observatory to share financial sector use cases
stories.Summary:
The Financial Conduct Authority published a press release on 19 November 2026 announcing the launch of its pioneering AI Spotlight Observatory, an online resource that brings together real-world examples of artificial intelligence use across the financial services sector. The regulator describes the Observatory as a first of its kind tool developed by a regulator, which can make AI adoption easier to explore and understand. It is intended to help firms, innovators, researchers and policymakers identify emerging trends, learn from developments across the market and support responsible innovation. The platform features a broad range of use cases, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.

The Observatory builds on the FCA's previous initiatives, including the AI Lab, which supports innovating firms as they develop new AI models and solutions. It also follows the Supercharged Sandbox, an enhancement to the FCA's existing Digital Sandbox that gives firms access to high-performance computing, databases and AI tools so they can innovate and experiment with AI safely. The regulator recently published examples of AI good practice and areas of improvement to support the safe and responsible adoption of AI in financial services. The new platform is open and available to anyone interested in understanding emerging trends and opportunities in this field, learning from real-world implementation and supporting responsible innovation.

The FCA openly invites a wide range of firms, especially those developing particularly innovative AI solutions, to register to access more detailed insights and to submit their own AI use cases. The regulator says the platform will evolve with new use cases submitted over time. The press release does not name individual FCA officials or give any further statements beyond the description of the platform and its aims. Responsibility for the Observatory rests with the FCA, which developed the tool as part of its wider work on AI in financial services.

The launch comes amid the FCA's broader efforts to support responsible AI adoption across the sector, following its AI Lab, Supercharged Sandbox and published good practice examples. The articles do not say what further steps the regulator plans beyond inviting firms to register and submit use cases. The Observatory is available now to anyone interested in emerging trends and opportunities in this field.

stories.Headline: John Deere acquires Orchard AI to add plant-level crop intelligence for growers
stories.Summary:
John Deere announced on November 19, 2026, that it has acquired Orchard Robotics, which operates as Orchard AI, a San Francisco-based agriculture technology company founded in 2022 that develops crop intelligence solutions for high-value crop growers. The deal strengthens Deere's ability to help growers make more informed decisions throughout the growing season by combining Orchard AI's detailed, plant-level crop insights with Deere's own expertise in precision agriculture, equipment, and farm technology. Orchard AI uses vehicle-mounted, AI-powered cameras to capture data for every individual tree, vine, or plant across a farm, all season long. With every pass through the field, the system analyzes hundreds of images per tree, giving growers a detailed view of crop conditions alongside accurate yield estimates, precise fruit counts, fruit size and color data, canopy measurements, and more. Its FruitScope software platform enables growers to visualize and use this data to make more informed farm management decisions, improving their efficiency of labor, time, and inputs across their operations.

For high-value crop growers, months of work and investment can depend on making the right decisions within narrow windows, since a missed spray application or mistimed harvest can affect fruit quality, yield, and an entire season's profitability. Weather, labor constraints, and changing crop conditions add pressure, leaving growers little time to determine what each block needs and get the work done. Combining Orchard AI's detailed view of crop conditions with Deere technology and equipment can help growers understand exactly what their trees need and act at the right time throughout the growing season. These capabilities can better inform critical decisions, from pruning and thinning trees, applying crop treatments where they are needed, and identifying which blocks are ready for harvest. The integrated AI software translates precision data into actionable recommendations, so growers can identify areas with higher bloom counts and receive a prescription on where to spray, delivered directly to a mobile device for in-field application or into an in-cab G5 display.

Tim Marquis, Director of Farm Systems Innovation at John Deere, said everything the company does starts with helping its customers succeed, and that the acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field. He said bringing these capabilities together gives Deere an opportunity to help growers make more informed decisions across their operations and get more value from the technology they already rely on. Charlie Wu, CEO of Orchard AI, said the company was started to give growers the crop intelligence they need to farm more profitably and sustainably than ever before, and that joining John Deere lets it accelerate that mission. Justin Rose, President of the Worldwide Agriculture & Turf Division, Small Ag & Turf at John Deere, said a big part of what makes Orchard AI successful is its speed of innovation and the close relationships it has built directly with customers. He said Deere wants to preserve those strengths while bringing its scale and capabilities to help Orchard AI reach more growers and solve real challenges in agriculture.

Tyler Klick of Redwood Empire Vineyard Management, an early user of Orchard AI's technology, said what impresses him most about Charlie and the Orchard AI team is their ability to listen to what growers need and put it into action. He said he has been very impressed with the insights the scans are providing from a precision farming standpoint. Orchard AI describes itself as "The AI Farming Company," and says industry leaders across specialty crops trust it for precise crop data that helps them make better decisions. The announcement did not disclose the purchase price or other financial terms of the deal.

stories.Headline: Developers say AI coding tools remove the struggle and risk eroding core engineering skills
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence coding tools have become part of the daily work of every software engineer Gemma Rodgers knows, and in a 2026 Stack Overflow survey 83% of software developer respondents said they use at least one AI tool, CNBC reported on November 20, 2026. Rodgers, a software developer based in the United Kingdom who began her computer science degree in 2002, told CNBC that the sense of joy and fun she used to get from working through a challenge has been removed somewhat, and that using AI can now feel like a breadcrumb of joy rather than a full meal of joy. She said AI tools have lowered the barrier to entry significantly and let many people thrive who would not have thrived five or even three years ago, but she also warned that the core skills engineers traditionally learned on the job are being lost as engineers churn work out. James Broadhead, chief technology officer of the AI decision-making company Taktile, told CNBC that engineers who might once have spent three weeks building a prototype can now generate 10 in an afternoon, and that the hardest part is having the judgment to decide which of those are any good.

Broadhead said AI agents produce so much code that engineers no longer read all of it, and that the old sense of comfort and awareness of how a whole code base was structured has given way to constant change. Joshua Wöhle, chief executive of the London-based AI training company Mindstone, told CNBC he sees a growing divide between workers who know how to use AI effectively and those who do not, and he said the industry's old talk of 10X engineers is widening into 100X engineers. Wöhle said companies will increasingly have to decide whether to help employees catch up with AI or prioritize those who get the most out of it, and he described as very real the grief of people who once excelled at writing code finding that the thing they love is no longer what the company should be paying for. Chris Sees, a software engineer of more than 20 years and chief executive of the London-based virtual office company Hoxton Mix, told CNBC he views AI as a capable junior engineer that still needs supervision, and he said the important thing is knowing what to delegate and when human judgment is needed.

Sees said he gets a lot of satisfaction from proving and spotting where AI has gone wrong, but he worries about the next generation of engineers if AI takes over the routine coding and debugging through which they traditionally learned, tasks he called where you learn lessons and build scar tissue. He said companies need to make sure AI becomes part of the learning process rather than a shortcut. Rodgers, who is self-employed, said she can use AI to automate the tedious parts of a project while keeping the more interesting problem-solving for herself, and she believes friction and discomfort are vital parts of the human experience. She said people need to feel accomplished in something and that part of accomplishment requires challenge, and that without working that through you never get the full force of the good feeling on the other side.

stories.Headline: Torus raises 500 million dollars and launches Foundry modular AI inference system
stories.Summary:
Torus, a Salt Lake City-based manufacturer of distributed power and compute infrastructure, announced on November 11, 2026 that it has raised 500 million dollars in growth capital led by Magnetar, and the financing coincided with the debut of its newest product, Foundry, a modular AI infrastructure system built for inference workloads. Each Foundry unit provides 1 to 20 megawatts of inference capacity per site and moves from signed contract to running AI workloads in 12 to 16 weeks, a timeline Torus contrasts with the years required to build a conventional hyperscale campus. Foundry units are prefabricated at GigaOne, Torus's manufacturing facility in Salt Lake City, where the smallest unit measures roughly the size of a small cargo van and the modular systems require no building construction at all. On-site timelines are correspondingly compressed, with site preparation taking about a week while installation and commissioning take one to two days, and the product is designed, engineered, and manufactured in Utah by Torus's team of nearly 400 employees, with key components built in-house.

Every Foundry deployment ships paired with Torus Reserve, the company's energy storage and management product, which delivers grid-enhancing technologies that Torus groups into three capabilities: inertial-based firm power, grid flexibility with load curtailment, and ramp-rate support. These functions are executed through what Torus calls load-shaping recipes, predefined controls that govern how power is dispatched and that shape loads to manage demand, support grid stability, and ramp power in milliseconds. The integrated inertial flywheel and battery storage and management serve a dual purpose, covering demand peaks so that more compute can fit on an existing interconnection and supplying backup power during grid outages. Torus describes Foundry as a vertically integrated offering spanning fiber to site, chiller to coolant distribution unit, and grid to rack, comprising three products: Torus Reserve for load shaping and redundancy, Torus Foundry for inference compute, and Torus Protect for integrated networking and security, with every deployment turnkey and ongoing operations and maintenance handled by Torus itself rather than left to the customer.

Founder and CEO Nate Walkingshaw said that inference does not have to wait, that the company has spent years learning how to make the grid more affordable, flexible, resilient, and intelligent, and that Foundry applies that to compute capacity in weeks with power that is already available. He added that most providers are bringing power to the chips while Foundry brings the chips to power, and he said the industry has largely tried to solve AI's power problem by building net-new infrastructure, an approach he described as costly and slow to bring compute online. Torus instead treats the situation as a capacity problem before it is a generation problem, contending that many sites already have unused grid capacity that its systems can make usable, and because Foundry installs behind the meter, drawing on available headroom at individual transformers, the company says the units add steady, high-load-factor demand without triggering the infrastructure upgrades that often produce rate increases and without compromising grid reliability.

Torus frames Foundry as a response to a structural change in AI demand, as workloads shift from training models to serving inference for enterprises and compute is being pulled toward on-premises and edge sites closer to where users are, with inference running continuously, responding in real time, and lending itself to distributed deployment according to the company. McKinsey data referenced in the launch forecasts annual growth of 35 percent in data center demand for AI inference through 2030, outpacing the 22 percent projected for training, and Torus notes that its customers want security, protection of intellectual property, and control over where their workloads execute, which the company says a distributed architecture can satisfy more readily than centralized capacity. Foundry debuts with first customers Hydra Host and another AI cloud provider and is offered in three commercial models: the Strategic model is a powered shell supplying power and enclosure without GPUs, the Partner model is a turnkey bare metal unit that bundles power, enclosure, and GPUs, and the Direct model delivers sovereign inference capacity straight to enterprise customers with single-tenant hardware allocated exclusively to one company's workloads. Taken together, the launch and the 500 million dollar Magnetar-led round position Torus to scale a distributed model of AI capacity delivery, one that leans on existing grid interconnections, factory-built modular hardware, and compressed deployment timelines rather than new construction.

stories.Headline: Calif researchers use GPT-6 Cyber to find a critical Java memory bug
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the cybersecurity startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber to uncover a critical memory corruption bug in Java, a programming language widely used across banking, aviation and other critical sectors, according to TechGig. The vulnerability affects the memory safety of Java's base64 decoder, which is a common method for representing binary data as text. Calif stated that malformed input, specifically 64 "A" characters followed by one equal sign, can overwrite neighbouring memory. That corruption can reveal sensitive memory or lead to remote code execution, which grants unauthorised access to the underlying system. The discovery was published on November 20, 2026.

Oracle, Java's current steward, has issued patches for the flaw and urged customers to apply them without delay. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, known as CERT-In, has issued a high-severity advisory and urged Indian organisations across public sector, private banking, fintech and consumer internet verticals to apply the Oracle patch. Java powers 90 per cent of Fortune 500 companies and is used in critical sectors globally. The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also urged users to identify all Java installations and monitor for security patches.

Calif's researcher Quang Luong used AI to find and weaponise the Java vulnerability, and the startup coined the term "centaur hacker" for human-AI collaboration in security research. The company said the approach combines AI and human expertise to discover the flaw. This discovery follows Calif's AI-assisted research that exposed critical flaws in PHP a month prior. The articles do not say what further steps, beyond patching and monitoring, are planned.

stories.Headline: Google gives AI Ultra subscribers Genie 4 with real-time world editing
stories.Summary:
Google made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers on November 20, 2026, introducing a new Project Genie experience for those users. Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that lets users generate and explore interactive worlds, and the update provides first-time access to Genie 4 along with upgrades to Genie 3. Genie 4, which Google describes as its most realistic world model, enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. This allows for real-time editing of environments while users are navigating them, and users can change weather conditions, add characters, or redirect actions within their worlds.

Genie 4 also integrates real-time native audio that adapts as scenes unfold, including ambient soundscapes and character dialogue. The Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions, and a community gallery is available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds. Project Genie combines advanced world models with Gemini models, allowing users to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from their browser. The update enhances the Project Genie experience by enabling users to generate and explore interactive worlds with real-time editing and audio.

Google is the company responsible for the rollout, and it made Genie 4 available to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers as the article reports. Google describes Genie 4 as its most realistic world model, and the article says the model enables users to prompt mid-session to alter worlds they have created. The article does not include any further statements from Google or from named individuals about the release. The rollout gives subscribers first-time access to Genie 4 and upgrades to Genie 3, according to the article.

The context is that Project Genie is an experimental research prototype that combines advanced world models with Gemini models for browser-based world shaping. The article does not say what happens next beyond the availability of Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers and the features described. The community gallery remains available for discovering, exploring, and remixing worlds, and the Project Genie agent assists users in building their visions. The article gives no further dates, numbers, or names beyond those already stated.

stories.Headline: AI bug hunting prompts rushed patches that overwhelm systems and cause outages
stories.Summary:
A series of recent technology outages affecting JPMorgan Chase transactions, Microsoft Outlook and a classified National Security Agency network may stem from a rapid effort to patch security vulnerabilities, according to officials who briefed members of Congress. Wall Street executives and the NSA told lawmakers that the disruptions were caused by attempts to fix flaws identified by artificial intelligence models, The Washington Sun reported. The outages do not appear to be cyberattacks, and officials said the sheer volume of fixes temporarily overwhelmed the systems they were designed to protect. A congressional official noted that AI models are identifying massive vulnerabilities, which increases the urgency for immediate patching.

Microsoft fixed a record 1,400 security flaws in a single monthly update recently, a significant jump from about 170 a year earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported. That increase is linked to AI bug-hunting models such as Anthropic's Mythos and similar models from OpenAI. The NSA's classified internal network, NSANet, went offline because of a software patch for major PHP vulnerabilities discovered last month, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton confirmed. PHP powers approximately 70 per cent of the world's websites, and Clayton stated that the incident was not a cyberattack or a coordinated nation-state action.

Not all the outages fit that explanation, since Microsoft's Outlook disruption, which affected over 450 million Microsoft 365 users, was traced to a latent bug on its networking gateway servers. The Federal Aviation Administration's nationwide ground stop resulted from a data flood hitting its network, possibly linked to a new router, and the FAA blamed legacy equipment. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicated that pushing new technology onto older systems seems to overwhelm them, suggesting more such incidents are likely. Companies and government agencies are using powerful AI models to find weak spots before hackers exploit them, and that pressure has led to faster rollout of fixes, according to The Washington Sun.

stories.Headline: AI agents make Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening feedback loops
stories.Summary:
AI agents are making Spec-Driven Development effective again by shortening the feedback loops that long challenged the Waterfall Model, according to a recent analysis reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. The approach moves the main effort from writing code to the discovery and design phases of software development, which enables faster iteration. Better large language models over the past year fixed earlier problems where correcting generated code cost more time than it saved. The method closely mirrors the sequential phases of the Waterfall Model, including specification, requirement analysis, technical planning and system design.

Both methodologies stress structured, detailed documentation and move to the next phase only after the current one is completed and approved. The historical problem with the Waterfall Model was feedback loops lasting weeks or months, along with unclear upfront requirements. AI agents cut individual phase durations to minutes or hours, letting developers quickly rework specifications, turn intents into structured documents and check that requirements stay consistent. The faster cycles allow iterative work on smaller increments, so unsatisfactory outcomes can be easily reverted or discarded. Documentation such as specifications and decision logs is now cheap and central to the method, a benefit that often suffered in agile environments because of time constraints.

The articles do not name who is responsible for the analysis or attribute any statements to a person. The analysis says the improved quality of large language models over the past year addressed the earlier issue where fixing generated code outweighed the time savings. It also says AI helps quickly rework specifications and validate requirement consistency. No further context or next steps are given beyond these points.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Open-source BehaviorLock blocks unproven API behavior to counter AI-driven attacks
stories.Summary:
BehaviorLock, a new open-source library for ASP.NET Core, was released to block unproven API behavior as a defense against fast-moving, AI-driven exploitation of vulnerabilities, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The library records SQL statements and outbound HTTP calls for each API endpoint into a behavior.lock.json file while running in a Learn mode. In an Enforce mode, it blocks any access not present in that recorded profile, returning a 403 error and raising an alert. The approach is meant to counter attacks that outpace traditional patching cycles, including SQL injection, mass assignment, forgotten debug switches, Server-Side Request Forgery and compromised dependencies, whenever those attacks produce new endpoint behaviors.

The articles give several numbers on how quickly exploitation now follows disclosure, and they show why the library's authors see patching alone as insufficient. Attackers needed 63 days on average to exploit a vulnerability after its patch release in 2018-2019, according to Google's Mandiant team, but that duration dropped to 5 days in 2023 and was negative for 2024 and 2025 estimates. In August 2025, DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge saw automatic systems find 54 of 63 planted vulnerabilities and patch 43 of them, while also discovering 18 real vulnerabilities at a cost of about $152 per task. Anthropic announced in April 2026 that its Mythos Preview model found thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, with the count exceeding 10,000 high or critical findings by May 2026.

BehaviorLock runs inside the application process and currently supports EF Core and IHttpClientFactory for .NET 11, with future plans to extend coverage to Dapper, raw ADO.NET, direct HttpClient, file access and background jobs. The library does not replace existing security practices such as parameters, authorization checks or patching, and instead serves as an additional defensive layer against rapid, unknown attacks. Its code is available on GitHub under the Apache-2.0 license. The report does not name the individuals behind the library or attribute any statements to them, so responsibility for the project rests with its open-source contributors as a whole.

stories.Headline: Razorpay plans updated DRHP filing next week for February 2027 IPO
stories.Summary:
Razorpay plans to file its updated Draft Red Herring Prospectus next week, targeting a potential initial public offering by February 2027, according to a Bloomberg report cited by TechGig. The Bengaluru-based fintech firm had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026, and the Securities and Exchange Board of India cleared that confidential filing on November 3. Investor roadshows are expected to begin immediately after the public filing of the updated prospectus. The public issue is reportedly planned at around $600 million, comprising fresh shares and an Offer For Sale component.

The IPO could value Razorpay at approximately $5 billion, or about ₹47,000 crore, which marks a markdown from its $7.5 billion valuation in 2021. Razorpay reported a 65 per cent year-on-year increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 crore in FY25, but it recorded a loss due to ₹1,209 crore in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. The company is also exploring a 0.4 per cent merchant discount rate on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation, though its rollout might be delayed until after the 2027 state elections due to concerns over merchant backlash. Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents.

Razorpay was founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, and it offers payment processing, business banking, payroll, and lending solutions. The company has raised over $800 million from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital, and Lightspeed. India's IPO market has seen firms raise around $18.6 billion through initial share sales so far in 2026. The articles do not include direct statements from the founders or other company officials about the filing or the listing plans.

stories.Headline: Anthropic researcher warns superhuman AI may arrive by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Anthropic AI researcher Tao Lin predicted on November 20, 2026, that broadly superhuman artificial intelligence could emerge within about 1.3 years, potentially by the end of 2027. Lin said this AI would rival or surpass human skills in fields such as programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking. He highlighted risks including major workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare. Automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms like Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle, according to the report.

The forecast sets a timeline of roughly 1.3 years from the November 2026 report to a possible arrival by late 2027. Lin cautioned about losing control over autonomous systems as one of the risks of rapid progress. He urged AI developers to slow progress so that comprehensive safety testing can take place. The article names programming, medicine, law, and filmmaking as the fields where such a system could match or exceed human skills.

Lin, an AI researcher at Anthropic, is the person responsible for the prediction and the warnings that came with it. He said developers should slow down to allow for comprehensive safety testing before such systems arrive. He also pointed to workforce displacement and permanent reliance on state welfare as risks of the technology. The article does not say what Anthropic itself plans to do in response to his remarks.

The context is that automation-driven job cuts are already affecting technology firms including Salesforce, Amazon, and Oracle. Lin's warning comes as those cuts show the workforce effects that he says could grow much larger. The article does not say what happens next beyond his call for slower progress and safety testing. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Intuit opens second-largest engineering centre in Bengaluru to house AI teams
stories.Summary:
Intuit inaugurated a new two-tower campus at Embassy Tech Village on Outer Ring Road in Bellandur, Bengaluru, on November 20, 2026, and the facility now serves as the company's second-largest engineering centre worldwide. The campus consolidates all Intuit India teams, which the company says is designed to foster seamless collaboration and innovation. The Bengaluru site brings together teams working on core product, platform, and AI capabilities for global customers. The expansion reflects Intuit's continued investment in India as a significant innovation hub, according to the company.

Nearly 25 per cent of Intuit's global technology talent is based in Bengaluru, where teams have operated since 2005. Those teams develop platforms, products, and AI-driven experiences for consumers, businesses, and accountants worldwide. The new campus reinforces Intuit's commitment to driving global AI innovation from India, the company said. The articles do not give the cost of the campus, its seating capacity, or a headcount for the new facility.

Saurabh Saxena, Senior Vice President, Product Development and India Site Leader at Intuit, said the campus aims to bring top tech talent together for growth and innovation in India. Alex Balazs, Chief Technology Officer at Intuit, emphasised that the Bengaluru teams are central to building AI-driven experiences that help customers prosper. The articles do not say what happens next, such as further hiring targets or additional phases of construction. No other next steps are given.

stories.Headline: Humyn Labs raises $47 million to fund robot training data infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Humyn Labs, a Bengaluru-based physical AI startup, raised $47 million in Series A funding on November 20, 2026, split between $26 million in equity led by Accel and $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton. The equity tranche drew participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Finserv Intelligence through Bajaj Finance, Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, Jump Trading, and angel investor Anita Pramoda, a former CFO of Epic. Trifecta Capital took part in the venture debt tranche. The company was founded in February 2026 by Manish Agarwal, former CEO of Nazara Technologies, and Ishank Gupta, a former AB InBev executive, who previously co-founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN.

The capital will fund deployment-readiness infrastructure in Brazil, South Korea, and India, where robots can be tested in real-world settings, along with investment in the company's capture hardware and data processing engine. Humyn Labs aims to expand its research and market presence in San Francisco, London, and Seoul. Its egoS1 head-worn camera records first-person views of people handling objects and moving through spaces, using global-shutter stereo cameras at 1080p and 30 frames per second with a field of view over 130 degrees. The processing engine generates depth, 3D head motion, and 21-point hand tracking, and the software validates and labels footage to produce training-ready datasets covering sight, sound, motion, and touch with verified provenance.

Agarwal said physical AI will only be as good as the real-world data it learns from, and that the funding will strengthen research, build trust with labs and enterprises, and expand global presence. He put the data infrastructure opportunity at $10 billion and said Humyn Labs aims for a $1 billion annual revenue business. The startup claims to have crossed $50 million in annualised revenue within six months of operations, reporting $10 million in revenue between April and October, with another $20 million in signed contracts and $20 million in deals yet to be finalised. It has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, humanoid robotics companies, and world-model developers, and about 90 per cent of its revenue comes from the US, according to Gupta.

In April, Humyn Labs committed $20 million to fund data collection across India, Southeast Asia, Latin America, and West Asia, and it is expanding voice data capabilities across 33 languages, dialects, and accents. Accel and Prosus Ventures, backers of KGeN, also invested in this Series A round.

stories.Headline: Snowflake’s Raghunathan says skipping discovery and codifying stages causes uneven AI coding results
stories.Summary:
Many engineering organisations have deployed AI coding tools but frequently encounter uneven results, according to insights from industry leaders reported by TechGig on November 20, 2026. This outcome is often attributed to overlooking critical phases in the rollout, specifically the transition from initial experimentation to codified best practices. Vivek Raghunathan, senior vice president of engineering at Snowflake, outlined a five-stage progression for AI rollouts that draws inspiration from Intel's Andy Grove. The initial phase involves allowing chaos to reign, followed by discovering effective practices, codifying them into a shared language, scaling that language across the organisation, and finally reorganising around the new operational reality.

Organisations often bypass the second and third stages, which involve discovering and codifying what actually works, because of an eagerness to demonstrate a quick return on investment for new tool purchases. Skipped stages frequently lead to measuring inappropriate metrics too early, such as lines of code or merged pull requests, instead of focusing on tool adoption across diverse tasks. A lack of a shared vocabulary for effective practices also prevents individual successes from becoming organisational knowledge. Raghunathan's team at Snowflake identified approximately 14 named patterns, including planning in writing before writing code and fencing agents into separate git worktrees, which provide a concrete framework for teaching and measuring AI-assisted work.

Scaling AI adoption through mechanisms like regular focus weeks, where dedicated time is allocated for learning or innovation, proved more effective than relying on mandates. Reorganising roles and responsibilities, the final stage, should only occur once a clear understanding of reliable AI-assisted work is established within the company. The article attributes the uneven results to skipped rollout stages rather than to problems with talent or the tools themselves. The report does not say what happens next for organisations that have already skipped these stages.

stories.Headline: Security leaders shift focus to securing how employees use AI as enterprises balance adoption with data leak risks
stories.Summary:
Enterprises are facing a conflict between adopting generative and agentic AI for tasks such as debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and preventing proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. Security and compliance leaders are working at the same time to stop proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records from leaking into unauthorized AI models. For most Chief Information Security Officers the question is no longer whether employees are using AI, because that use is now acknowledged. Their focus has shifted to understanding what employees are doing with AI and to securing that use rather than blocking it. Semantic DLP is presented as a way to secure enterprise generative AI data without hindering adoption.

The story requires enterprises to balance the adoption of generative and agentic AI against the risk of data leakage, and it changes the focus of security leaders from whether AI is used to how it is used. The tasks named in the articles are debugging code, summarizing contracts and automating decision-making, and the data at risk includes proprietary source code, financial projections and regulated customer records. The articles give no numbers, no dates beyond the publication date of November 20, 2026, and no named individuals. The only named technology is semantic DLP, which the articles say helps secure enterprise generative AI without hindering adoption. The articles do not describe how semantic DLP works or what it costs.

Chief Information Security Officers are the people responsible, and the articles say they acknowledge that employees use AI and have shifted their focus to securing it. Security and compliance leaders are also described as working to prevent proprietary data from leaking into unauthorized models. The articles paraphrase no individual by name and carry no direct statement from any officer or company. The context is a tug-of-war between adopting generative and agentic AI for everyday work and keeping sensitive data inside authorized systems. stories.Headline: Nicholas Matsakis introduces Symposium and Agent Client Protocol to guide AI agents in using Rust
stories.Summary:
Nicholas Matsakis, a lead designer of the Rust programming language and a senior principal engineer at Amazon, introduced two new projects on November 20, 2026, according to TechGig. The first is Symposium, an agent-oriented toolchain designed to guide AI agents in using Rust, and the second is the Agent Client Protocol, which proposes a standardised way for AI agents and clients to communicate. Matsakis presented the projects as a way to integrate Rust with artificial intelligence more effectively. The report was published by TechGig on that date.

Symposium aims to give AI agents tailored Rust guidance, such as recommending Rust 2024 and the latest crate versions, while letting crate authors write skills that instruct agents on how to use their libraries. The Agent Client Protocol is intended to improve interoperability across various agents and front-end tools, moving beyond current vendor-specific implementations. The projects address current large language model limitations, including agents using outdated library versions or older Rust editions, because current LLMs often struggle to keep up with the fast pace of software development and library updates. By embedding skills directly within Rust crates, Symposium aims to prevent agents from hallucinating application programming interfaces or generating non-compiling code. Matsakis also introduced the concept of battery packs, which provide best-practice guidance for recommended sets of libraries such as an opinionated network service pack.

Matsakis emphasised Rust's memory safety as a significant advantage, noting its adoption in critical systems like the Linux kernel and at companies such as Microsoft and Amazon. He cited statistics indicating that switching to Rust reduces memory-safety-related vulnerabilities, which account for a large percentage of overall software flaws. The initiatives are part of a broader vision for a more extensible ecosystem that supports open-source maintainers through a Rust commercial network. The stated goal is to streamline language choice for developers by offering robust tooling and community support for Rust development, particularly when combined with AI.

stories.Headline: Researchers find no AI dependency tool reports responsiveness or cross-cultural validity
stories.Summary:
Wenhai Fan, Lijun Wang, Lihong Li, Xiaoxia Zheng, Zhaoqing Miao, and Mingming Yu conducted a systematic review of AI dependency tools. This research was published on November 20, 2026, in the journal Psychology Research and Behavior Management. The authors evaluated the methodological quality and measurement properties of instruments used for college students. They searched eight databases from their inception until January 21, 2026, to find relevant studies. The team used the COSMIN Risk of Bias Checklist and the mGRADE approach to grade the evidence.

The review examined nine studies evaluating nine different AI dependency assessment instruments for students in higher education. The AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for nursing students were both classified as category A. The scale for dependence on artificial intelligence was placed in category C, while the other instruments were category B. No instruments reported responsiveness, measurement error, or cross-cultural validity across different countries and cultures. The protocol for this review was registered in PROSPERO under the registration number CRD420251269989.

The researchers stated that reliable assessment instruments are needed to identify AI dependency and its behavioral consequences. They noted that existing tools exhibit limitations in measurement quality, conceptual clarity, and applicability due to varying frameworks. The authors preliminarily recommended the AI dependence scale and the reliance on ChatGPT scale for evaluating students. They argued that improved tools will support future research on psychological mechanisms and interventions to reduce dependency. The team concluded that future research should develop more robust and theoretically grounded instruments for this purpose.

The authors noted that AI tools are a double-edged sword that can support learning or reduce independent thinking. Students are affected by potential problems including academic dishonesty, ethical dilemmas, privacy concerns, and technology-induced anxiety. A study by Kaabi found that 78.3 percent of university students in the United Arab Emirates depend on AI. That same study reported that 94.5 percent of those students experienced detrimental effects on linguistic skills and critical thinking. Dependency is associated with negative outcomes like sleep disturbances, academic procrastination, and negative emotions.

The articles explain that AI dependency is a state of cognitive inertia and behavioral attachment toward AI-generated content. This condition is characterized by a difficulty in independently correcting or verifying the outputs generated by AI. It is distinct from addiction, which involves withdrawal and impaired control, and problematic use, which denotes impaired use. AI dependency may lead to superficial learning where students complete assignments without understanding the core concepts. Such dependency can reduce cognitive engagement and substitute independent thought with automated responses from AI tools.

Future research should more comprehensively evaluate psychometric properties and develop instruments that are more theoretically grounded. New tools must be tested to see if scores stay stable when measured again over a period of time. Researchers need to determine if these instruments can detect real changes in student dependency levels over time. The articles leave open how to unify the concepts of AI dependency, addiction, and problematic use in literature. They also leave open how to resolve the lack of uniformity in current assessment methods and content dimensions.
